Department of Health and Human Services
Administration for Children and Families
45 CFR Part 96
RIN 0970-AD49
AGENCY:
Office of Community Services (OCS), Administration for Children and Families (ACF), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
ACF proposes to amend its block grant regulations to modernize requirements, reduce administrative burden on States and Tribal grantees, and improve the clarity and efficiency of program administration. The current regulations include outdated provisions and procedural requirements that no longer reflect statutory authority or agency practice. The proposed revisions are intended to streamline grantee obligations, eliminate unnecessary requirements, and align the regulations with current law and policy.
DATES:
In order to be considered, written comments on this proposed rule must be received on or before November 30, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit written comments, identified by docket number ACF-2026-0628 and/or RIN number 0970-AD49, by one of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
https://www.regulations.gov
. Follow the instructions for submitting comments.
Email:
Deregulation@acf.hhs.gov
. Include the docket number ACF-2026-0628 and/or RIN number 0970-AD49 in the subject line of the message.
Instructions:
All submissions received must include the agency name and docket number or RIN number for this rulemaking. All comments received are a part of the public record and will be posted for public viewing on
www.regulations.gov
,
without change. Please be advised that the substance of the comments and the identity of individuals or entities submitting the comments will be subject to public disclosure.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Adam N. Jones, Deputy Chief of Staff, Immediate Office of the Assistant Secretary, Administration for Children and Families, Department of Health and Human Services, Washington, DC 202-417-0115 or
Deregulation@acf.hhs.gov
. The docket on
https://www.regulations.gov
will include a plain language summary of the proposed rulemaking.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Statutory Authority
This proposed regulation is being issued under the authority granted to the Secretary of Health and Human Services by Title XX of the Social Security Act, as amended (
42 U.S.C. 1397
et seq.
), the Community Services Block Grant Act (
42 U.S.C. 9901
et seq.
), and the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Act of 1981 (
42 U.S.C. 8621
et seq.
)., and the Department's general administrative authority under
5 U.S.C. 301
.
II. Background
45 CFR part 96
, “Block Grants” is a comprehensive regulatory framework established under the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981 (Pub. L. 97-35) that governs the administration of multiple federal block grant programs administered by HHS. Originally published on July 6, 1982, this regulation applies to seven major block grant programs: Community Services Block Grant (CSBG), Preventive Health and Health Services, Community Mental Health Services (MHBG), Substance Use Prevention, Treatment, and Recovery Services (SUBG), Maternal and Child Health Services, Social Services Block Grant (SSBG), and Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP).
Part 96 establishes uniform procedures for grant applications, awards, payments, financial management, audit requirements, and enforcement mechanisms across these programs. It includes specific provisions for financial management requirements (Subpart C), direct funding of Indian tribes and tribal organizations (Subpart D), and enforcement procedures including complaint resolution and hearing processes (Subparts E and F). The regulation also contains program-specific requirements for each block grant, such as the SSBG annual reporting requirements using uniform service definitions (Subpart G) and LIHEAP weatherization waivers (Subpart H).
Since its initial promulgation, Part 96 has continuously been amended to reflect statutory changes to the underlying block grant programs. Significant amendments include revisions reflecting the LIHEAP amendments enacted in 1984, 1990 and 1994; revisions reflecting the SSBG reporting changes enacted in 1988; and periodic updates to the program-specific subparts to reflect reauthorizations and conforming amendments to the underlying statutes.
III. Executive Summary
This notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) proposes to remove multiple regulations that are either unnecessary or wholly obsolete. The regulations contained in this NPRM to be removed and reserved can be categorized into three groups: those that have obsolete language, those that are duplicative of another Federal regulations or statute, and those that are better suited as a different type of sub-regulatory format.
Several provisions across Part 96 contain transitional language tethered to fiscal years that have long passed. ACF proposes to remove these transitional clauses. The fiscal-year triggers they reference are decades in the past, and the provisions they once activated are now either fully effective by their own terms or entirely inoperative. Retaining this language clutters the Code of Federal Regulations with text that no longer governs any current conduct, creates confusion for grantees attempting to identify their present obligations, and burdens agency staff
(
printed page 68098)
who must explain why time-bound language remains on the books.
The duplicative regulations in the Code of Federal Regulations, carry no impact as the authority and requirements stated in the regulations exist or are stated elsewhere, such as in statute. This renders the language found in the regulations to be either duplicative or otherwise unnecessary. ACF proposes to remove these provisions. They add no operative requirement beyond what Congress has already enacted, and their continued presence in part 96 creates a risk that subsequent amendments to the underlying statutes will produce a mismatch between the statutory text and the regulatory paraphrase. Removing these provisions simplifies the regulations without eliminating any substantive obligation, because the statutory provisions remain directly enforceable.
The regulations that are better suited to a different format,
i.e.
, as a sub-regulatory document, are those that generally read like a Frequently Asked Questions document or are overly prescriptive and carry technical details that belong in programmatic instruction. These documents are being proposed to be removed from part 96 and published in the more appropriate format.
Severability
The provisions of this NPRM, once it becomes final, are intended to be severable, such that, in the event a court were to invalidate any particular provision or deem it to be unenforceable, the remaining provisions would continue to be valid. The changes address a variety of issues relevant to Block Grants. None of the provisions contained herein are central to an overall intent of the proposed rule, nor are any provisions dependent on the validity of other, separate provisions.
IV. Discussion of Proposed Changes
45 CFR Part 96
Block Grants
Subpart B—Grant Procedures
§ 96.10 Prerequisites To Obtain Block Grant Funds
Section 96.10 sets forth prerequisites that States must satisfy to obtain block grant funds, including submission requirements and certifications. Some of these prerequisites track directly to statutory requirements in the individual block grant statutes, while others reflect administrative conditions ACF layered on top of those statutory requirements. In Section 96.10, two clauses indicate that these prerequisites to obtaining block grant funds begin with Fiscal Year (FY) 2001. The proposed rewrite removes the specific time bounds.
§ 96.14 Time Period for Obligation and Expenditure of Grant Funds
Section 96.14 addresses the treatment of expenditures across program years, including rules governing when obligations incurred in one program year may be charged against another. This proposed rewrite removes Section 96.14(a)(2) as this language that also exists in other areas of this part.
See
45 CFR 96.81(b)(1)
. Furthermore, this subsection references specific dates such as “fiscal year 1982” which is now obsolete. The proposed edits to paragraph (b) remove the reference to the community services block grant as having a statutory limit on the time for expenditure of block grant funds. This restricting language is no longer accurate following a congressional change to the statute removing said cap. The regulations have never been updated to reflect this change, but is proposed to be done through this NPRM. Finally, the proposed edits to paragraph (b) add community mental health services, substance use prevention, treatment, and recovery services (the SAMHSA block grants) because the authorizing statute for these block grants imposes a two-year time limit for obligation and expenditure of allotments. These are proposed to be added as they align with statutes that have been passed since the last time this section was updated.
§ 96.15 Waivers
Section 96.15 establishes a regulatory framework for the issuance of waivers under the block grant statutes, including LIHEAP under
42 U.S.C. 8624(k)
. The proposed change removes reference to the dated FY1986 start to a Secretarial waiver authority.
Subpart D—Direct Funding of Indian Tribes and Tribal Organizations
§ 96.43 Procedures During FY 1982
Section 96.43 establishes procedures for LIHEAP funds exclusively for FY1982. This section is no longer relevant as all of the dates and processes described therein have been long since passed and are therefore obsolete.
§ 96.49 Due Date for Receipt of All Information Required for Completion of Tribal Applications for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Block Grants
Section 96.49 establishes recordkeeping requirements applicable to LIHEAP. The proposed amendment to this section removes the specific dated language that announces the implementation of the regulation will begin in FY2001.
Subpart G—Social Services Block Grants
§ 96.71 Definitions
Section 96.71 further constricts definitions beyond statutory language for both the term “integral but subordinate” and for “employees.” The term “integral but subordinate” is used in
42 U.S.C. 1397d(a)(2)
to restrict the use of funds by a grantee for “the provision of cash payments for costs of subsistence or for the provision of room and board (other than the costs of subsistence during rehabilitation, room and board provided for short term as an integral but subordinate part of a social service, or temporary emergency shelter provided as a protective service).” Thus, Congress intended for funds to be allowed to be used for temporary emergency shelter, including room and board, for children in a protective service.
However, Section 96.71 unnecessarily restricts this Congressional definition by stating that, “room and board provided for a short term shall not be considered an integral but subordinate part of a social service when it is provided to an individual in a foster family home.” This was not a condition of Congressionally approved language, but rather an extension of statutory interpretation by agency regulators that does not align with Congressional action. Therefore, the removal of this added provision will return the enforcement of this block grant's allowable uses to what was intended by the lawmakers. It will not necessarily lead to any changes in how states spend funds but will allow states to leverage the full statutory authority. This will not result in increased costs as this is a capped program but will restore state flexibility to the use of funds.
Additionally, the term “employees” is defined in Section 96.71 as “staff, contractors, or other individuals whose activities are under the professional direction or supervision of the institution.” This is beyond what the plain text definition in the original Act which made no mention of additional supervision or direction. By removing this added regulatory burden, the operation of the program will return to the original Congressional definition. For these reasons, this proposed rule removes this Section.
§ 96.74 Annual Reporting Requirements
Section 96.74 implements the SSBG annual report requirement under 42
(
printed page 68099)
U.S.C. 1397e. The proposed changes remove Section 96.74(b)(1), which references uniform definitions of services in Appendix A, which is proposed for removal, and paragraph (c) which discuss outdated terminology and technology such as encouraging the use of “computer diskettes.” References to Appendix A is also removed from Section 96.74(b)(4).
Subpart H—Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program
§ 96.83 Increase in Maximum Amount That May Be Used for Weatherization and Other Energy-Related Home Repair
Section 96.83 establishes a detailed procedural framework for grantees seeking waivers to increase the percentage of LIHEAP funds used for weatherization activities from 15 percent to up to 25 percent.
ACF proposes to remove the elements of this procedural framework that extends beyond statutory requirements. The underlying statutory waiver authority (
42 U.S.C. 8624(k)
) is preserved, but the regulatory framework layered on top of that authority represents an agency-created set of procedural prerequisites and substantive criteria that go beyond the best reading of the statute.
Removing the framework restores the Secretary's statutory discretion to evaluate waiver requests on their merits and reduces administrative burden on grantees with limited deregulatory cost, because the statutory standard for granting a waiver continues to govern the substantive decision. Thus, this Section is proposed to be reduced to remove any requirement that is not mandated by statute.
Subpart I—Community Services Block Grants
§ 96.90 Scope
Section 96.90 briefly introduces that Subpart I applies to CSBG. As the title of the subpart is stated as “Community Services Block Grants” this Section does not provide any additional information or regulatory requirements, and is therefore proposed to be removed.
§ 96.91 Audit Requirement
Section 96.91 discusses the requirements of section 1745(b) of the Reconciliation Act (
31 U.S.C. 1243 note
) regarding audit requirements, which has been repealed. The CSBG Act sets forth audit requirements at section 678D(a)(2) (
42 U.S.C. 9916(a)(2)
). Section 96.91 is superseded by the statutory audit requirements and is therefore proposed to be removed.
Appendix A to Part 96
Uniform Definitions of Services
Appendix A to Part 96 identifies the 29 categories of services and provides a brief definition of each service. This Appendix is proposed for removal as it identifies items that HHS believes belong in sub-regulatory guidance as it is merely providing the list of allowable expenditures for a specific grant fund. As grantees are required to follow a grant's terms and conditions, the removal of this Appendix is not intended or expected to impact the operations of the program.
V. Regulatory Process Matters
Paperwork Reduction Act
Under the Paperwork Reduction Act (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
) (PRA), all Departments are required to submit to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval any reporting or recordkeeping requirements inherent in a proposed or final rule. This NPRM does not contain any information collections requiring OMB approval under the PRA and, therefore, will not create any new paperwork burdens or modify existing burdens subject to OMB review.
Executive Order 13132
Executive Order 13132
requires federal agencies to consult with State and local government officials if they develop regulatory policies with federalism implications. Federalism is rooted in the belief that issues that are not national in scope or significance are most appropriately addressed by the level of government close to the people. This proposed rule would not have substantial direct impact on the States, on the relationship between the federal government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. This NPRM would not pre-empt State law. The changes proposed in the NPRM are removing unnecessary and obsolete regulations from Block Grant rules. Therefore, in accordance with Section 6 of
Executive Order 13132
, it is determined that this action does not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant the preparation of a federalism summary impact statement.
Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families Section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act of 1999 (
Pub. L. 105-277
) requires federal agencies to determine whether a policy or regulation may negatively affect family well-being. If the agency determines a policy or regulation negatively affects family well-being, then the agency must prepare an impact assessment addressing seven criteria specified in the law. HHS believes it is not necessary to prepare a family policymaking assessment because the actions proposed in this NPRM will not have any impact on the autonomy or integrity of the family as an institution.
VI. Regulatory Impact Analysis
We have examined the impacts of the proposed rule under
Executive Order 12866
,
Executive Order 13563
,
Executive Order 14192
, the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601-612
), and the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
Pub. L. 104-4
).
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct us to assess all benefits and costs of available regulatory alternatives and, when regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits. Rules are “significant” under
Executive Order 12866
Section 3(f)(1) if they “have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more; or adversely affect in a material way the economy, a sector of the economy, productivity, competition, jobs, the environment, public health or safety, or State, local or tribal governments or communities.”
Executive Order 14192
requires that any new incremental costs associated with significant new regulations “shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least ten prior regulations.” The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) has determined that this proposed rule is a significant action under
Executive Order 12866
Section 3(f).
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) requires agencies to consider the impact of their regulatory proposals on small entities. Because this is simply repealing obsolete and unnecessary language, we propose to certify that the proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) generally requires that each agency conduct a cost-benefit analysis; identify and consider a reasonable number of regulatory alternatives; and select the least costly, most cost effective, or least burdensome alternative that achieves the objectives of the rule before promulgating any proposed or final rule that includes a Federal mandate that may result in expenditures of more than $100 million (adjusted for inflation) in at least one
(
printed page 68100)
year by State, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector. Each agency issuing a rule with relevant effects over that threshold must also seek input from State, local, and tribal governments. The current threshold after adjustment for inflation is $193 million, using the most current (2025) Implicit Price Deflator for the Gross Domestic Product. This proposed rule would not result in an expenditure in any year that meets or exceeds this amount.
VII. Tribal Consultation Statement
Executive Order 13175
, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, requires agencies to consult with Indian Tribes when regulations have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes.
Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments,
65 FR 67249
. Similarly, ACF's Tribal Consultation Policy says that consultation is triggered for a new rule adoption that significantly affects tribes, meaning the new rule adoption has substantial direct effects on one on more Indian tribes, on the amount or duration of ACF program funding, on the delivery of ACF programs or services to one or more Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes. Given the nature and purpose of this rulemaking, it does not significantly impact Tribes and as such we are not engaging in Tribal Consultation at this time. For Tribes who have comments, we encourage you to submit them through the comment process.
List of Subjects in
45 CFR Part 96

AGENCY:
Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Proposed revisions to mandatory guidelines.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Health and Human Services (“HHS” or “Department”) is proposing to revise the Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs using Urine (UrMG), published in the
Federal Register
on October 12, 2023).
DATES:
Submit comments on or before December 28, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
In commenting, please refer to docket number SAMHSA-2026-0002. Because of staff and resource limitations, SAMHSA cannot accept comments by facsimile (fax) transmission.
You may submit comments in one of four ways (please choose only one of the ways listed):
Electronically.
You may submit electronic comments on this regulation to
http://www.regulations.gov
. Follow “Submit a comment” instructions.
By regular mail.
You may mail written comments to the following address: SAMHSA, Center for Substance Abuse Prevention (CSAP), Division of Workplace Programs (DWP), 5600 Fishers Lane, Room 16N02, Rockville, MD 20857. Please allow sufficient time for mailed comments to be received before the close of the comment period.
By express or overnight mail.
You may send written comments to the following address: SAMHSA, CSAP, DWP, 5600 Fishers Lane, Room 16N02, Rockville, MD 20857.
By hand or courier.
You may deliver your written comments by hand or courier to the following address prior to the close of the comment period: SAMHSA, CSAP, DWP, 5600 Fishers Lane, Room 16N02, Rockville, MD 20857. If you intend to deliver your comments to the Rockville address, please call (240) 276-2600 in advance to schedule your arrival with one of our staff members. Because access to the SAMHSA building is secure, persons without federal government identification are encouraged to schedule their delivery or to leave comments with the security guard at the front desk located in the main lobby of the building.
All comments received before the close of the comment period will be available for viewing by the public. Please note that all comments are posted in their entirety, including personal or confidential business information that is included in the comment. SAMHSA will post all comments before the close of the comment period on the following website:
https://www.regulations.gov
. Use the website's search function to view the associated comments.
Comments received before the close of the comment period will also be available for public inspection as they are received, generally beginning approximately 3 weeks after publication of a document, at SAMHSA, CSAP, DWP, 5600 Fishers Lane, Rockville, MD 20857, Monday through Friday of each week, excluding federal holidays, from 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. To schedule an appointment to view public comments, please call (240) 276-2600.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Eugene D. Hayes, Ph.D., MBA, SAMHSA, CSAP, DWP; 5600 Fishers Lane, Room 16N02, Rockville, MD 20857, by telephone (240) 276-1459 or by email at
Eugene.Hayes@samhsa.hhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Executive Summary
This notice of proposed revisions to the Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs using UrMG includes revisions that will: clarify the types of laboratories that may be certified to conduct testing for federal agency workplace drug testing programs, change invalid specimen criteria (
i.e.
, raise cutoff from pH 9.0 to 9.5), reflect the Department's decision to publish the Authorized Drug Testing Panels only when revised rather than each year, revise the initial test batch quality control requirements for laboratories and instrumented initial test facilities (IITFs), allow a Medical Review Officer (MRO) to authorize use of a biomarker test for a specimen with an invalid result based on creatinine and specific gravity, and allow a split testing laboratory to test for any HHS-authorized biomarker to reconfirm substitution based on a biomarker test (
i.e.
, may test for a different biomarker). In addition, some wording changes have been made for clarity and for consistency with the Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs using Oral Fluid (OFMG) or to apply to any authorized specimen type and to clarify direct observed collection procedures.
The Department is concurrently publishing a separate
Federal Register
Notice proposing revisions to the Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs using OFMG, including the same or similar revisions proposed for the UrMG, where appropriate.
The current authorized drug testing panel and report nomenclature table for urine and for oral fluid were published on January 16, 2025 (
90 FR 4662
).
Background
Pursuant to its authority under Section 503 of Public Law 100-71,
5 U.S.C. 7301
, and
Executive Order No. 12564
, HHS establishes the scientific and technical guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs and establishes standards for certification of laboratories engaged in drug testing for federal agencies. Using data obtained from the Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs and HHS-certified laboratories, the Department estimates that 275,000 urine specimens are tested annually by federal agencies.
As required, HHS originally published the Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs (Guidelines) in the
Federal Register
(FR) on April 11, 1988 (
53 FR 11979
). SAMHSA subsequently revised the Guidelines on June 9, 1994 (
59 FR 29908
), September 30, 1997 (
62 FR 51118
), November 13, 1998 (
63 FR 63483
), April 13, 2004 (
69 FR 19644
), and November 25, 2008 (
73 FR 71858
). SAMHSA published the renamed Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs using UrMG on January 23, 2017 (
82 FR 7920
), and the first Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs using OFMG on October 25, 2019 (
84 FR 57754

Proposed Revisions to the Guidelines
This preamble describes the proposed revisions to the Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs using UrMG, and the rationale for the changes.
Subpart A—Applicability
Section 1.5 defines terms used in the UrMG. The Department has added terms and revised definitions in this section in accordance with proposed changes to these Guidelines.
The Department has deleted “Gender Identity” (
i.e.
, term and definition) to
(
printed page 68399)
enhance the clarity of direct observed collection procedures.
The Department updated the definition of “Laboratory” clarifying that, in addition to certifying laboratories to conduct all required testing of primary (A) and split (B) specimens, the Department may certify laboratories that test split (B) specimens only and/or conduct additional drug or specimen validity tests for primary and split specimens in accordance with these Mandatory Guidelines.
The Department edited the definition of “Negative Result” for clarity.
The Department edited the definition of “Substituted Specimen” to refer to a test for an HHS-authorized biomarker rather than specifically referring to the Biomarker Testing Panel, to reflect the Department's review and approval process for an HHS-certified test facility to implement testing for a biomarker for use in Federal workplace drug testing programs.
Section 1.7 describes the circumstances that constitute a refusal to test. The Department provided additional examples for clarity.
Subpart B—Urine Specimens
Section 2.2 describes the circumstances under which a urine specimen may be collected. The Department reviewed and revised Section 2.2(a) and other wording in the current UrMG to clarify that pre-employment tests are performed for all individuals applying for a testing designated position, including federal agency employees.
Subpart C—Urine Specimen Tests
Section 3.1 describes the tests that are conducted on a urine specimen. The Department revised Section 3.2 to address when a specimen may be tested for drugs other than those in the drug testing panel and inserted a new Section 3.3 to describe the process for an HHS-certified laboratory or IITF to obtain HHS approval to test for a biomarker other than those in the biomarker testing panel. The Department renumbered subsequent items in Section 3 accordingly.
Section 3.5 describes the publication of drug and biomarker testing panels with analytes and cutoffs for urine. The Department removed the drug testing panel from the UrMG and deleted the requirement to publish the Authorized Drug Testing Panels annually. HHS will publish a FR Notice when drug and/or biomarker testing panels are changed.
Subpart D—Collectors
Section 4.4 describes requirements for an observer for a direct observed collection. The Department revised item b to refer to the sex of the observer and donor to enhance the clarity of direct observed collection procedures.
Subpart H—Urine Specimen Collection Procedure
Section 8.1 describes privacy requirements for urine collection. The Department revised item b to refer to the sex of the observer and donor to enhance the clarity of direct observed collection procedures.
The Department reworded item c in Section 8.8 for clarity and to use the same wording in the UrMG and OFMG.
The Department revised the language in item 8.9(a)(2) to remove the word “medical,” because there may be a legitimate non-medical explanation for an invalid result.
Section 8.10 describes how a direct observed collection is conducted and Section 8.12 describes how a monitored collection is conducted. The Department revised wording in both sections to refer to the sex of the observer and donor to clarify direct observation collection procedures.
Subpart I—HHS Certification of Laboratories and IITFs
The Department revised the language in item 9.5(a)(1) to refer to the drug testing panel rather than “drug classes listed in the drug testing panel.”
Section 9.6 describes National Laboratory Certification Program (NLCP) performance testing (PT) requirements for an applicant urine laboratory and Section 9.7 describes PT requirements for an HHS-certified urine laboratory. The Department reworded item a.3 in both sections to clarify that PT criteria for initial drug test results are for applicant laboratories that will conduct initial drug tests.
Subpart K—Laboratory
Section 11.12 describes the initial drug test batch quality control requirements for a urine laboratory. The Department revised item b to apply to the controls in each initial drug test batch rather than to calibrators and controls and reduced the required percentage of controls from 10 percent to 4 percent of the total controls and specimens in the batch. (The same changes were made for IITFs in Section 12.)
Section 11.18 describes the requirements for urine laboratory specimen validity tests. The Department added wording to this section for clarity as follows: (1) added an introductory sentence referencing the required urine specimen validity tests in Section 3.1(c) and optional specimen validity tests in Sections 3.1(d) and 3.6; (2) added an item a with the requirement for an invalid, adulterated, or substituted result to be based on an initial specimen validity test on one aliquot and a confirmatory specimen validity test on a second aliquot, (3) added an item b with the current requirement for controls to be analyzed concurrently with specimens, and (4) added an item h with quality control requirements for specimen validity tests other than those specified in preceding items. Other items were renamed or renumbered accordingly.
Item 11.18(e)(4)(v) was edited to reflect the invalid cutoff change from pH 9.0 to 9.5. As described below, the Department based this change on a thorough review of current information.
Currently, specimens with pH ≥9.0 must undergo laboratory confirmatory testing for pH and those with reported pH results ≥9.0 and ≤9.5 must undergo MRO review for possible explanations for the elevated pH. Specimens without a legitimate explanation and specimens requiring a valid negative result (
i.e.
, pre-employment, return-to-duty, or follow-up test) must be recollected. The additional testing, review, and recollections are a significant burden to HHS-certified laboratories, MROs, and federal agencies that does not result in identifying additional adulterated specimens.
Research on time and temperature changes in urine specimens and effects of pH on drug concentrations in urine were presented at the December 2024 meeting of SAMHSA's Drug Testing Advisory Board. The data presented was sourced from HHS-certified laboratories' invalid pH demographics, peer reviewed literature, and NLCP applied studies presented at scientific meetings after peer review of the abstracts. These data show that: (1) extended time at high temperature after collection can cause urine pH in the acceptable range to rise to 9.1 to 9.3; (2) there is a cyclical nature to the incidence of specimens in the pH range of 9.0 to 9.5 corresponding to summer months; (3) the incidence of specimens in pH range 9.0 to 9.5 is ~0.2 percent (
e.g.
, approximately 15,000 specimens/year); and (4) pH >9.5 does not occur due to elevated temperature and increased shipping time.
Regarding the effect of elevated pH on positive drug concentrations, three analytes (
i.e.
, benzoylecgonine, phencyclidine, and 6-acetylmorphine) were identified as susceptible to changes in concentration due to elevated pH. Drug loss over a typical shipping time (
i.e.
, 1 to 3 days) ranged from 13 percent for benzoylecgonine to 58 percent for 6-acetylmorphine. There
(
printed page 68400)
was no difference in the loss of drug at pH 9.0 to 9.5 and pH of 9.5 to 10.0 for benzoylecgonine and phencyclidine; however, significant losses of 6-acetylmorphine occurred at pH as low as 8.0. The Department also reviewed information on primary (A) and split (B) specimens with inconsistent concentrations of these three analytes. None of these specimens had a pH ≥9.0.
Section 11.19 describes requirements for an HHS-certified laboratory to report a test result. The Department revised item 11.19(h)(1) to state that an MRO may authorize a specimen with an invalid result based on creatinine and specific gravity to be tested for an HHS-authorized biomarker to determine substitution. The Department revised item 11.19(g) to require the laboratory to contact the MRO for authorization before conducting testing for the additional biomarker or sending the specimen to another certified laboratory for the additional test.
Subpart L—IITF
Section 12.11 describes the initial drug test batch quality control requirements for an IITF. The Department revised item b to apply to the controls in each initial drug test batch rather than to calibrators and controls and reduced the required percentage of controls from 10 percent to 4 percent of the total controls and specimen in the batch. (The same changes were made for laboratories in Section 11.)
Section 12.14 describes the requirements for IITF specimen validity tests.
The Department added wording to this section for clarity as follows: (1) added an introductory sentence referencing the required IITF specimen validity tests in Section 3.1(c) and optional specimen validity tests in Sections 3.1(d); and (2) added an item a with the current requirement for controls to be analyzed concurrently with specimens. Other items were renamed accordingly.
The Department edited item 12.14(d)(1) and (2) consistent with the revised invalid specimen criteria (
i.e.
, cutoff change from pH 9.0 to 9.5).
The Department edited wording in item 12.21 regarding IITF records available to a Federal applicant or employee to be the same as section 11.24 regarding laboratory records.
Subpart M—MRO
Section 13.5 describes MRO actions when reviewing a urine specimen's test results.
The Department revised item f to delete MRO action for invalid results based on a pH of 9.0 to 9.5, consistent with the revised invalid specimen criteria (
i.e.
, cutoff change from pH 9.0 to 9.5). The Department also edited wording in this section to address different MRO actions to be taken for invalid specimens depending on the reason for the test.
Section 13.6 describes MRO action when the collector reports that the donor did not provide a sufficient amount of urine for a drug test. The Department has reviewed and revised the previous wording in Section 13.6(b) to clarify different MRO actions to be taken for invalid specimens depending on the reason for the test.
Subpart N—Split Specimen Tests
Section 14.1 describes when a split (B) urine specimen may be tested. The Department has revised item 14.1(c) to clarify MRO action when a split specimen cannot be tested by a second laboratory because (1) there is no split specimen or the specimen has insufficient volume for testing), (2) the primary specimen was reported as adulterated and there is no second HHS-certified laboratory to test the split specimen for the same adulterant; or (3) the primary specimen was reported as substituted based on a biomarker, and there is no second HHS-certified laboratory to test the split specimen (
i.e.
, using the same or a different biomarker test).
Section 14.4 describes how an HHS-certified laboratory tests a split (B) urine specimen when the primary (A) specimen was reported substituted. The Department has renamed and renumbered items in this section. Item 14.4(b) addresses testing of a split specimen when the primary specimen was reported substituted based on biomarker testing. The Department has revised this section to allow the split testing laboratory to test for any HHS-authorized biomarker. It is not necessary to test the split specimen for the same biomarker to reconfirm the primary (A) specimen's substituted result.
Section 14.6 describes action an MRO takes after receiving the split (B) urine specimen result from the split testing laboratory. The Department has edited and reorganized this section for clarity and to describe these revised requirements:
When the split laboratory has failed to reconfirm a single or all drug positive results and reported the specimen as adulterated and the primary laboratory cannot perform the test for that adulterant: the MRO directs testing at another HHS-certified laboratory.
When the split laboratory has failed to reconfirm a single or all drug positive results and reported the specimen as substituted and the primary laboratory cannot perform a biomarker test: the MRO directs testing at another HHS-certified laboratory. It is not necessary to test the primary specimen for the same biomarker to reconfirm the split specimen's substituted result.
The Department also removed the requirement for the MRO to contact the HHS office responsible for coordination of the drug-free workplace program regarding the test results throughout this section.
General Revisions
In addition to the proposed changes described by subpart and section above, the Department has edited the UrMG to address proposed changes and has reworded some items for clarity (
e.g.
, referring to “donors” rather than “employees” or “applicants”) and/or for consistency with the OFMG or to apply to any authorized specimen type.
Impact of These Guidelines on Government Regulated Industries
The proposed revised Guidelines may impact the Department of Transportation and Nuclear Regulatory Commission regulated industries depending on these agencies' decisions to incorporate the final UrMG revisions into their programs under their own authority.
Costs and Benefits
Costs
The proposed UrMG revisions are not expected to increase current stakeholder costs. There will be some administrative costs for HHS-certified laboratories and MROs associated with the change in invalid specimen criteria (
i.e.
, pH cutoff raised from 9.0 to 9.5; see Sections 11.18 and 12.14). However, the time and labor savings from this change are expected to greatly exceed these one-time costs.
Benefits
As noted above, laboratories and MROs will incur some initial costs for changing the pH invalid test cutoff; however, this change will benefit laboratories, MROs, and Federal agencies. Currently, a large number of specimens are reported as invalid based on pH between 9.0 and 9.5, especially in summer months. The reduction in invalid specimens due to the cutoff change will reduce the numbers of required confirmatory pH tests, MRO interviews and investigations, and specimen recollections.
The proposed revision to quality control requirements for initial drug test batches in Section 11.11(b) will reduce laboratory burden and expense while
(
printed page 68401)
maintaining quality. The Department has lowered the percentage of controls in each initial drug test batch from 10 percent to 4 percent of the total controls and specimens in the batch. This will reduce time, labor, and material costs (
e.g.
, purchasing, initial verification, batch review, monitoring control results). Initial drug testing is used to report specimens as negative; specimens with a positive initial drug test are reflexed to confirmatory testing. The Department has maintained the 10 percent control requirement for confirmatory test batches.
Other UrMG revisions that will reduce stakeholder burden include those related to biomarker testing which are expected to lead to definitive results and reduce the need for specimen recollection. These include changes allowing an MRO to authorize testing for a biomarker for a specimen with an invalid result based on creatinine and specific gravity (Section 11.19) and allowing a split testing laboratory to use any HHS-authorized biomarker test to reconfirm substitution based on a biomarker test, rather than requiring the same biomarker test used for the primary specimen (Section 14.1). These revisions also strengthen the federal government's ability to identify illicit drug use and donor attempts to subvert drug tests.

Title:
The Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs using Urine
Information Collection/Record Keeping Requirements
The information collection requirements (
i.e.
, reporting and recordkeeping) in the current Guidelines, which establish the scientific and technical guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs and establish standards for certification of laboratories engaged in urine drug testing for federal agencies under authority of
5 U.S.C. 7301
and
Executive Order 12564
, are approved by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) under control number 0930-0158. The Federal Drug Testing Custody and Control Form (Federal CCF) used to document the collection and chain of custody of urine and oral fluid specimens at the collection site, for laboratories to report results, and for Medical Review Officers to make a determination; the National Laboratory Certification Program (NLCP) application; the NLCP Laboratory Information Checklist; and recordkeeping requirements in the current Guidelines, as approved under control number 0930-0158, will remain in effect.
In support of the Government Paperwork Reduction Act, the Department revised the Federal CCF to enable its use as an electronic form (
78 FR 42091
, July 15, 2013) and developed requirements and oversight procedures to ensure that HHS-certified test facilities and other service providers (
e.g.
, collection sites, MROs) using an electronic version of the Federal CCF (ECCF) maintain the accuracy, security, and confidentiality of electronic drug test information. Before a Federal ECCF can be used for Federal agency specimens, HHS-certified test facilities must submit detailed information and proposed standard operating procedures (SOPs) to the NLCP for SAMHSA review and approval and undergo an NLCP inspection focused on the proposed ECCF.
Since 2013, SAMHSA has encouraged the use of Federal ECCFs and other electronic processes in HHS-certified test facilities, when practicable, for federally regulated testing operations. In accordance with Section 8108(a) of the SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Act, SAMHSA has set a deadline of August 31, 2026, for all HHS-certified laboratories to submit a request for approval of an electronic (digital) Federal CCF. To assist all HHS-certified laboratories, SAMHSA has implemented an ECCF Recognition Program to recognize ECCF systems that meet program requirements and can be used by any HHS-certified laboratory or IITF. This program is expected to facilitate the process for HHS-certified test facilities seeking SAMHSA approval to use an ECCF and enable all HHS-certified test facilities (regardless of size) to meet the August 31, 2026, deadline for a digital ECCF submission.

The proposed Guidelines contain several recordkeeping requirements that SAMHSA considers not to be an additional recordkeeping burden. In subpart D, a trainer is required to document the training of an individual to be a collector (Section 4.3(a)(3)) and the documentation must be maintained in the collector's training file (Section 4.3(c)). SAMHSA believes this training documentation is common practice and is not considered an additional burden. In subpart F, if a collector uses an incorrect form to collect a federal agency specimen, the collector is required to provide a statement (Section 6.2(b)) explaining why an incorrect form was used to document collecting the specimen. SAMHSA believes this is an extremely infrequent occurrence and does not create a significant additional recordkeeping burden. Subpart H (Sections 8.4(c), 8.5(d)(2), 8.5 (e)(1) and (2)) requires collectors to enter any information on the Federal CCF of any unusual findings during the urine specimen collection procedure. These recordkeeping requirements are an integral part of the collection procedure and are essential to documenting the chain of custody for the specimens collected. The burden for these entries is included in the recordkeeping burden estimated to complete the Federal CCF and is, therefore, not considered an additional recordkeeping burden. Subpart K describes a number of recordkeeping requirements for laboratories associated with their testing procedures, maintaining chain of custody, and keeping records (
i.e.,
Sections 11.1(a) and (d); 11.2(b), (c), and (d); 11.6(b); 11.7(c); 11.8; 11.11(a); 11.14(a); 11.17; 11.21(a), (b), and (c); 11.22; 11.23(a) and 11.24). These recordkeeping requirements are necessary for any laboratory to conduct forensic drug testing and to ensure the scientific supportability of the test results. Therefore, they are considered to be standard business practice and are not considered a burden for this analysis.
