This update adds three entities to section 2(d)(2)(B)(ii) list of the UFLPA, which identifies entities working with the government of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region to recruit, transport, transfer, harbor or receive forced labor or Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, or members of other persecuted groups out of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region:
BGI Genomics Co., Ltd. (also known as BGI Genomics)
MGI Tech Co., Ltd. (also known as MGI)
Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd. (also known as BGI Group; and BGI Holdings)
BGI Genomics Co., Ltd. (also known as BGI Genomics) is located in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China. Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd., also included on the UFLPA Entity List, is the company's controlling shareholder. BGI Genomics' main business includes providing research services, comprehensive solutions for precision medicine testing, and health management services through gene testing, mass spectrometry, bioinformatics analysis, and multimodal intelligent analysis models. The United States Government has reasonable cause to believe, based on specific and articulable information, that BGI Genomics conducts genetic testing in the XUAR alongside the government of the XUAR and as a part of its government initiatives. Such genetic testing is utilized to facilitate the recruitment, transport, transfer, harboring or receiving of forced labor or Uyghurs Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, or members of other persecuted groups out of Xinjiang. The FLETF therefore determined the activities of BGI Genomics satisfy the criterion for addition to the UFLPA Entity List described in section 2(d)(2)(B)(ii).
MGI Tech Co., Ltd. (also known as MGI) is located in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China. MGI is under the control of the same ultimate controlling shareholder as Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd., also included on the UFLPA Entity List. MGI's business activities focus on the research and development, manufacturing, and sales of instruments, reagents, and related products in the field of life science and biotechnology. The United States Government has reasonable cause to believe, based on specific and articulable information, that MGI has provisioned genetic testing capacity to the XUAR government to conduct genetic testing in the XUAR including as a part of its government initiatives. Such genetic testing is utilized to facilitate the recruitment, transport, transfer, harboring or receiving of forced labor or Uyghurs Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, or members of other persecuted groups out of Xinjiang. The FLETF therefore determined the activities of MGI satisfy the criterion for addition to the UFLPA Entity List described in section 2(d)(2)(B)(ii).
Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd. (also known as BGI Group; and BGI Holdings) is a company located in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China. BGI Group is a genomics and biotechnology company that develops and applies genetic sequencing technologies for research, healthcare, and commercial use. It provides DNA, RNA, and metabolomics sequencing technology and can provide services, as well as equipment, technical support, and precision medicine and health solutions. The company also built and manages the China National GeneBank, a national-level biological data and sample repository. The United States Government has reasonable cause to believe, based on specific and articulable information, that BGI Group conduct genetic testing in the XUAR alongside the XUAR government and as a part of its government initiatives. Such genetic testing is utilized to facilitate the recruitment, transport, transfer, harboring or receiving of forced labor or Uyghurs Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, or members of other persecuted groups out of Xinjiang. The FLETF therefore determined the activities of BGI Group satisfy the criterion for addition to the UFLPA Entity List described in section 2(d)(2)(B)(ii).

BGI Genomics Co., Ltd. (also known as BGI Genomics) is located in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China. Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd., also included on the UFLPA Entity List, is the company's controlling shareholder. BGI Genomics' main business includes providing research services, comprehensive solutions for precision medicine testing, and health management services through gene testing, mass spectrometry, bioinformatics analysis, and multimodal intelligent analysis models. The United States Government has reasonable cause to believe, based on specific and articulable information, that BGI Genomics conducts genetic testing, including on genetic material of plants, animals, and bacterial diseases sourced from the XUAR. The FLETF therefore determined the activities of BGI Genomics satisfy the criterion for addition to the UFLPA Entity List described in section 2(d)(2)(B)(v).
Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd. (also known as BGI Group; and BGI Holdings) is a company located in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China. BGI Group is a genomics and biotechnology company that develops and applies genetic sequencing technologies for research, healthcare, and commercial use. It provides DNA, RNA, and metabolomics sequencing technology and can provide services, as well as equipment, technical support, and precision medicine and health solutions. The company also built and manages the China National GeneBank, a national-level biological data and sample repository. The United States Government has reasonable cause to believe, based on specific and articulable information, that BGI Group conduct genetic testing, including on genetic material of human beings sourced from the XUAR, as well as planning on testing genetic materials of plants and animals. title: Personnel Management in Agencies: Strategic Human Capital Management
abstract: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a final rule to modernize the framework governing personnel management and strategic human capital management in Federal agencies. This rule amends the regulatory framework for personnel management in Federal agencies to streamline human capital planning and reporting requirements, strengthen the authority of agency Chief Human Capital Officers (CHCOs), update employee survey requirements, and align the regulatory framework with Executive branch priorities for a high- performing Federal workforce. OPM carefully considered all public comments received on the proposed rule and has made targeted revisions in response.
dates: Effective November 30, 2026.

SUMMARY:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a final rule to modernize the framework governing personnel management and strategic human capital management in Federal agencies. This rule amends the regulatory framework for personnel management in Federal agencies to streamline human capital planning and reporting requirements, strengthen the authority of agency Chief Human Capital Officers (CHCOs), update employee survey requirements, and align the regulatory framework with Executive branch priorities for a high-performing Federal workforce. OPM carefully considered all public comments received on the proposed rule and has made targeted revisions in response.
DATES:
Effective November 30, 2026.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA) of 1978 established the foundational framework for merit-based personnel management in the Federal Government. Pursuant to the CSRA and subsequent statutory authority, OPM is responsible for promulgating Governmentwide regulations governing Federal human capital management, including the systems and standards by which agencies plan, implement, and evaluate their human capital strategies.
Part 250 of title 5 of the Code of Federal Regulations
establishes the regulatory framework for personnel management in Federal agencies. Subpart A sets standards for agency personnel actions and delegation agreements. Subpart B—Strategic Human Capital Management-defines the systems, standards, and metrics agencies must use to manage human capital, currently organized around the Human Capital Framework (HCF) and the Human Capital Operating Plan (HCOP), Human Capital Reviews (HCR), and HRStat quarterly reviews. Subpart C—Employee Surveys—governs the administration and public disclosure of annual Federal employee surveys and establishes a core set of 16 required survey questions.
On July 2, 2026, OPM published a proposed rule (
91 FR 40435
) to amend
5 CFR part 250
to modernize strategic human capital management across the Federal Government. The proposed rule proposed to: (1) consolidate and streamline human capital planning requirements by replacing the HCOP, HCR, and HRStat framework with Annual Staffing Plans (ASPs) and associated review processes; (2) strengthen CHCO authority and visibility; (3) require each agency to establish a Strategic Hiring Committee to oversee hiring within the agency; (4) revise the employee survey framework under subpart C, including changes to the Governmentwide core question set and survey administration; and (5) remove references to workforce diversity from the regulatory text.
In response to public comments, OPM has made targeted revisions to the proposed rule. Key changes from the proposed rule include: (1) clarifying the terminology distinguishing strategic human capital planning from operational staffing planning and tying Annual Staffing Plan development to the budget formulation cycle under the annual Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular A-11, Preparation, Submission, and Execution of the Budget, Part 6 (OMB, Circular No. A-11, Preparation, Submission, and Execution of the Budget (Aug. 29, 2025),
https://www.whitehouse.gov/​wp-content/​uploads/​2025/​08/​a11.pdf
); (2) adding an annual agency-head-certification requirement to ensure CHCO visibility, oversight, and control; and (3) permitting agencies to integrate Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Reviews into existing performance review processes. Each of these changes is discussed in detail in the comment-response section below.
In response to comments, OPM also clarifies several matters that do not change the regulatory text, including the effect of the removal of nonstatutory references to a “diverse” workforce and the scope of the Strategic Hiring Committee's role; those clarifications are addressed in the same section.

These responses came from a range of sources: individual citizens; nonprofit and professional organizations; and a former Federal employee writing in a private capacity. All nine comments are substantive and have been considered in full. All comments were posted and made available to the public in the docket. The comments are summarized below, together with OPM's responses, including where OPM has adopted, partially adopted, or declined commenter suggestions, along with OPM's reasoning. The comments are organized by issue category.
General Comments
Comment 0010 expressed general support for the proposed rule, noting it “will strengthen accountability, improve hiring practices, and enhance morale and recruitment across the federal workforce.” Comment 0010 offered additional recommendations to strengthen protections against political-to-career conversions (“burrowing in”), discussed further below.
Comments 0002 and 0005 expressed broad opposition to the rule. Comment 0002 argued the rule lacks the required cost-benefit analysis and would negatively affect employee retention and hiring quality. Comment 0005 urged
(
printed page 68014)
OPM to abandon the rule, citing concerns about administrative burden, potential for politicization of the civil service, and anticipated harm to scientific, diversity, equity, and inclusion-related roles, to include harmful impacts to sexual and gender orientation focused roles.
Comment 0002 argued that the proposed rule “does not seem to be in compliance with various regulatory requirements” because it lacks a cost-benefit analysis. OPM disagrees. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs designated this rulemaking a significant regulatory action under section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
, Regulatory Planning and Review,
58 FR 51735
(Oct. 4, 1993), and OPM has assessed its costs and benefits accordingly. A full regulatory impact analysis is required only for an action with an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more, or one that otherwise materially and adversely affects the economy or a sector of it. This rule governs the internal planning, review, and survey processes agencies use to manage their own workforces; it does not regulate the public or the private sector, and its estimated Governmentwide implementation cost, set out in the Costs section of this preamble, falls well below that threshold.
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess costs and benefits in proportion to the significance of the action, and OPM has done so: the Expected Impact section of this preamble states the need for the rule, quantifies first-year and ongoing implementation costs, describes the rule's anticipated benefits, and discusses regulatory alternatives, including retaining the existing framework. The comment's premise that no cost-benefit analysis exists is therefore mistaken. As to the comment's prediction that the rule will increase costs by harming employee retention and candidate quality, OPM addresses workforce recruitment, retention, and morale in a dedicated section of this preamble and concludes, for the reasons stated there, that the rule is more likely to strengthen than to weaken the Government's competitive position for talent.
Comment 0005 further asserted that the rule would harm scientific positions and positions focused on sexual and gender orientation. OPM disagrees. This rule does not create, abolish, classify, or reclassify any position, and it directs no agency to eliminate any occupation or occupational category. Subparts A and B govern how agencies plan, document, and review their human capital management, and subpart C governs the annual employee survey. Decisions about which positions an agency establishes and fills remain the agency's, made under the authorities governing position management and staffing and subject to applicable law. The requirement that an Annual Staffing Plan direct hiring to an agency's highest-needed positions is a planning requirement; it does not prescribe which occupations an agency must treat as high-need.
Nor does the removal of nonstatutory references to a “diverse” workforce, discussed below, alter any agency's obligations under the merit system principles at
5 U.S.C. 2301
, the prohibited personnel practices at
5 U.S.C. 2302
, or the equal employment opportunity requirements applicable to Federal employment under
42 U.S.C. 2000e-16
. To the extent the comment addresses agency staffing decisions taken outside this rulemaking, those decisions are beyond the scope of this rule.
OPM appreciates all comments received. As discussed throughout this preamble, OPM has carefully considered concerns about administrative burden and the integrity of the merit system and has made targeted revisions in response. OPM is committed to a nonpartisan, merit-based civil service and believes the final rule, as modified, reflects that commitment.
Workforce Planning Framework
Comments 0006 and 0003 raised concerns about the proposed replacement of the Human Capital Operating Plan (HCOP) framework with Annual Staffing Plans. Comment 0006 expressed support for the rule's emphasis on forward-looking workforce planning but cautioned that designating the primary planning document as a “staffing plan” may create unintended confusion between two distinct activities: (1) strategic human capital planning, which accounts for alignment with administration priorities, budget, organizational performance, and long-term talent needs; and (2) operational staffing planning, which addresses specific FTE needs, skills needs, and near-term staffing challenges within bureaus and program offices.
Comment 0006 recommended that the final rule delineate between these two types of planning and revise terminology to avoid conflation. Comment 0006 further recommended that agency staffing plans be led by the CHCO in coordination with the Chief Financial Officer (CFO), Chief Operating Officer (COO), and senior leadership to ensure that all offices have the people and skills needed to execute their missions.
OPM agrees that clear terminology is important and that strategic human capital planning should be distinguished from operational staffing planning. In response to these comments, OPM has revised the final rule to clarify the relationship between the consolidated Annual Staffing Plan and the agency's broader strategic human capital management obligations, as reflected in the definition of Annual Staffing Plan at § 250.202. The final rule makes clear that Annual Staffing Plans are the operational implementation mechanism for the agency's strategic human capital strategy and are not a substitute for aligning human capital to the agency's strategic plan, Annual Performance Plan, and administration priorities. OPM agrees that the CHCO should coordinate the Annual Staffing Plan with the CFO, COO, and senior leadership, and has added language to § 250.205 to reflect this expectation.
Succession Planning
Comment 0003 objected more broadly, arguing that replacing the HCOP with Annual Staffing Plans forces a short-term mentality onto Federal agencies designed for long-term national stability. Comment 0003 stated that managing human capital on a strict year-to-year basis makes it impossible to build and retain specialized talent pipelines and will trigger severe retention crises and skill gaps. Likewise, comment 0009 expressed concern that consolidating the planning and review framework could dilute attention to leadership succession planning. The commenter stated that multi-year investment in developing a bench of qualified career executives is “different in kind from annual hiring and staffing metrics, and it can be crowded out” if not explicitly addressed in the rule. The commenter recommended that the final rule includes explicit multi-year succession planning language to ensure succession planning is not subordinated to short-term staffing metrics.
OPM does not agree that the consolidated planning framework imposes an inappropriately short-term mentality on Federal agencies. Under the final rule, § 250.205(b)(2) specifically includes language that says the Annual Staffing Plan “must . . . enable succession planning” and the Annual Staffing Plan must support the four Human Capital Framework systems, of which Talent Management is one of the four systems and encompasses succession management. The final rule's systems and standards under § 250.203(b) (Talent Management)
(
printed page 68015)
obliges agencies to engage in designing and implementing strategies that will “attract, acquire, develop, promote, and retain quality talent.” Developing, promoting, and retaining talent are all implicitly long-term goals for any human capital management system.
In addition, succession planning for leadership and management is also covered by
5 CFR part 412, subpart B
. Further, § 250.204(a)(4) and (5) specifically mention these are responsibilities for the agencies in addition to § 250.204(a)(6) requiring a “knowledge management process to ensure continuity in knowledge sharing.” As noted in
Executive Order 14356
,
Ensuring Continued Accountability in Federal Hiring
,
90 FR 48387
(Oct. 20, 2025), the Annual Staffing Plan is intended as a dynamic implementation document that is reviewed and updated on an ongoing basis, not a rigid annual snapshot. The final rule also clarifies that the Annual Staffing Plan must be developed on a timeline consistent with the agency's strategic planning and budget formulation cycle under the OMB Circular A-11, Part 6, so that workforce planning, resource allocation, and performance planning decisions are coordinated rather than sequenced.
Administrative Burden of Quarterly Reviews
Comments 0003, 0005, and 0002 raised concerns about the administrative burden created by the proposed Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Reviews. Comment 0003 argued that forcing human resources staff into quarterly review cycles diverts resources from substantive recruiting and onboarding. Comment 0005 stated that, given recent reductions in Federal agency capacity, agencies do not have the capacity to absorb additional compliance requirements. Comment 0002 argued the rule lacks a cost-benefit analysis demonstrating that the benefits of additional oversight requirements outweigh the costs.
OPM acknowledges these concerns but does not agree that the final rule adds a review requirement. Agencies are already required to conduct quarterly human capital reviews. Current § 250.207 requires HRStat quarterly data-driven reviews of human capital performance, led by the Chief Human Capital Officer in coordination with the agency Performance Improvement Officer. This rule does not create a new review cycle; it modifies the existing one, reorienting the quarterly review from HRStat reporting to implementation of the agency's Annual Staffing Plan.
The Expected Impact section of this preamble addresses the cost-benefit analysis. The quarterly cadence is a necessary component of effective human capital oversight and is consistent with the Government Performance and Results Act Modernization Act of 2010 performance review framework, which agencies already administer on a quarterly basis through their Performance Improvement Officers. By consolidating the Human Capital Operating Plan, Human Capital Review, and HRStat quarterly review into a single framework, the final rule reduces required reporting rather than adding to it.
The existing HRStat process has been used to monitor, evaluate, and align agency strategic planning and evaluation systems as part of the Human Capital Framework. OPM intends for the Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Reviews to build upon existing agency review processes rather than create duplicative burdens, and OPM will issue guidance to minimize compliance overhead. The agency Performance Improvement Officer supports the quarterly priority progress reviews that
31 U.S.C. 1121(c)
requires of the agency head and Chief Operating Officer, and current § 250.207 already requires the Chief Human Capital Officer to conduct the quarterly human capital review in coordination with that same Performance Improvement Officer. The two processes therefore already share a participant and a quarterly cadence. The final rule accordingly makes clear that agencies may integrate the Staffing Plan Performance Review into their existing quarterly reviews where practicable, rather than convening a separate meeting.
Comment 0009 supported that integration but recommended that OPM specify a minimum standing agenda allocation for workforce metrics so that workforce issues are not crowded out by competing agenda items. OPM acknowledges the concern and may address these matters in implementation guidance.
Workforce Recruitment, Retention, and Morale
Comments 0002, 0003, and 0005 asserted that the rule will harm workforce recruitment, retention, and employee morale. Comment 0002 argued that the changes would negatively affect employee retention and hiring efforts, resulting in higher costs and lower-quality candidates. Comment 0003 predicted that year-to-year staffing planning would trigger “severe retention crises and skill gaps” and warned that a workforce that feels silenced and ignored will suffer from low morale, driving talented civil servants out of public service. Comment 0006 likewise emphasized that workload and morale measures should inform staffing plans, observing that persistent, widespread unreasonable workloads can lead to errors and mishaps, including in high-stakes environments such as emergency response.
OPM has considered these comments carefully and does not agree that the rule will impair the Government's ability to recruit and retain a high-quality workforce; OPM expects the opposite effect. The final rule requires each agency to direct its hiring to its highest-need positions, to address skills gaps, and to enable succession planning (§ 250.205(b)(2)), and it synchronizes workforce planning with the budget formulation cycle so that agencies can commit to hiring decisions when resources are known rather than after opportunities have passed.
Slow, diffuse, and poorly prioritized hiring—not disciplined planning—is what costs agencies top candidates: applicants who wait months for a certificate or a final offer frequently accept employment elsewhere. A staffing plan that concentrates hiring capacity on the positions agencies need most and is reviewed quarterly for progress should shorten that cycle and improve both the speed and the quality of Federal hiring. OPM's recently issued Guidance on Annual Staffing Plans implements this approach for the FY 2027 cycle, directing agencies to conduct bottom-up workforce planning that reserves billets and budget for mission-critical, technology, and early-career hires; to recruit through pooled hiring actions and shared certificates; and to assess every external hire using a validated technical or alternative assessment rather than a self-assessment questionnaire alone—measures aimed squarely at improving the speed and quality of Federal recruitment. OPM,
Guidance on Annual Staffing Plans
(July 30, 2026),
https://www.opm.gov/​chcoc/​latest-memos/​guidance-on-annual-staffing-plans.pdf
.
The commenters' contrary predictions that the rule will hurt recruitment rest largely on the premise that the rule adds administrative burden. But, as explained above, the rule consolidates three overlapping requirements into a single framework and permits integration with existing quarterly reviews.
Nor does the rule diminish the Government's attention to morale. The final rule retains a Governmentwide requirement that every agency survey its
(
printed page 68016)
employees annually, and the prescribed items measure conditions closely tied to morale and engagement—whether employees feel empowered, whether coworkers cooperate, whether meaningful distinctions in performance are recognized, whether supervisors provide career-development feedback, and whether employees can disclose suspected wrongdoing without fear of reprisal, a core measure of employee voice. Agencies remain free, and are encouraged, to field additional engagement, satisfaction, workload, and morale items tailored to their workforces (and to conduct additional “pulse” surveys throughout the year), and OPM's Employee Survey Playbook
[
1
]
provides model content and methodological support. The rule does not silence employee feedback; it places responsibility for gathering and acting on that feedback with the agency leaders best positioned to respond to it.
Finally, OPM notes that Annual Staffing Plans must include metrics for evaluating current and future workforce and staffing needs (§ 250.205(b)(1)), and that OPM and OMB will review implementation annually through the Annual Staffing Review. In response to comment 0009's recommendation that OPM maintain a stable set of core human capital metrics that persists across administrations, OPM notes that its Guidance on Annual Staffing Plans specifies the core hiring and workforce measures agencies must address in preparing their FY 2027 Annual Staffing Plans. OPM,
Guidance on Annual Staffing Plans
(July 30, 2026),
https://www.opm.gov/​chcoc/​latest-memos/​guidance-on-annual-staffing-plans.pdf
. That guidance directs agencies to identify mission-critical occupations and skills gaps, together with plans for closing them, and to include in each plan a detailed hiring forecast projecting—by quarter and by mission area or component—total hires, external hires versus internal placements, mission-critical occupation hires, technology hires, and early-career hires, measured against standing Governmentwide targets. Agencies must report performance against each target in their quarterly updates and must justify, and set a corrective trajectory for, any projected variance; OPM and OMB will track progress through the Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Review and Annual Staffing Review processes. This guidance illustrates how the planning cadence reflected in this rule can support multi-year workforce planning efforts based on core human capital metrics.
CHCO Visibility, Oversight, and Control
Comment 0009 expressed strong support for the proposed requirement at § 250.204(e) that agencies ensure their internal delegations, organizational structure, policies, and technological systems give the CHCO sufficient visibility, oversight, and control to carry out statutory functions under
5 U.S.C. 1401
and
1402
. The commenter noted this has been a persistent, longstanding problem, as confirmed by Government Accountability Office (GAO) reporting. The commenter expressed concern, however, that the provision as drafted “states an obligation without a mechanism for verifying compliance” and recommended that the final rule direct OPM to require an annual, agency-head-certified attestation confirming that the CHCO has the required visibility, oversight, and control, with any gaps identified and a remediation timeline attached.
Comment 0006 similarly recommended that the final rule require CHCO coordination with the CFO, COO, and senior leadership to ensure the CHCO has the organizational standing to perform the functions contemplated by the rule.
Comment 0003 raised a concern in the opposite direction, arguing that giving the CHCO top-down singular control over all human capital functions risks creating an environment detached from individual component needs and stripping sub-agencies of the operational flexibility needed to address local staffing challenges.
OPM agrees with Comment 0009 that the CHCO visibility requirement requires a compliance verification mechanism to be effective. OPM has added a requirement to § 250.206 that, as part of each Annual Staffing Review, agencies submit an agency head certification confirming that the CHCO has the visibility, oversight, and control required under § 250.204(e), and that any identified gaps are documented with a remediation timeline. This addition provides the accountability mechanism the commenter identified while preserving agency flexibility in how CHCO authority is structured internally.
OPM does not agree that strengthening CHCO authority necessarily undermines sub-agency operational flexibility. The final rule preserves the agency's ability to delegate authorities consistent with the CHCO's oversight responsibilities and does not prohibit sub-agencies from maintaining operational human capital functions appropriate to their missions.
Political-to-Career Conversion Safeguards (“Burrowing In”)
Comment 0010 expressed general support for the proposed rule and offered targeted recommendations to address political-to-career conversions. The commenter recommended that: (1) § 250.203 be amended to require agency human capital management systems to include screening for political-to-career conversions, with OPM pre-approval required before such actions are finalized; (2) § 250.204 be amended to require agencies to certify that no political influence occurred and that OPM requirements for political-to-career conversions were followed, including for reassignments and details; (3) § 250.205 be amended to require agencies to review hiring actions involving political appointees and assess whether details, transfers, and reassignments were consented to and properly justified; (4) § 250.206 be amended to require documentation of any attempts to support political-to-career conversions; and (5) a new § 250.210 be added to require written employee consent for details over 60 days, justification for involuntary details, and CHCO approval for directed reassignments.
OPM appreciates the comment's detailed recommendations and shares the concern that improper political-to-career conversions undermine merit system principles. The safeguards the commenter describes, however, are already in place and are administered by OPM outside this part.
Agencies must obtain OPM's approval before appointing a current or recent political appointee to a permanent competitive service, non-political excepted service, or career Senior Executive Service position, including time-limited appointments that would permit later noncompetitive conversion. For this purpose, a recent political appointee is an individual who held a covered political appointment within the preceding five years. OPM administers this pre-appointment review; agencies submit a pre-appointment checklist, and OPM examines the action for compliance with merit system principles and applicable civil service law before the appointment may be made. This review operates against the background requirements of
5 U.S.C. 2301
(merit system principles),
5 U.S.C. 2302
(prohibited personnel practices),
5 U.S.C. 3317
and
3318
(certification and selection in the competitive service), Civil Service Rules 4.2 and 7.1 (5 CFR
(
printed page 68017)
4.2, 7.1),
5 CFR part 317
(career SES appointment procedures), and OPM's memorandum to Chief Human Capital Officers, Political Appointees and Career Civil Service Positions (Dec. 30, 2022),
https://www.opm.gov/​chcoc/​transmittals/​2022/​Political%20Appointees%20and%20Career%20Civil%20Service%20Positions_​508.pdf
. OPM also conducts ongoing oversight of completed conversions under
5 U.S.C. 1104
and
5 CFR 5.2
.
Recommendations (1) through (4) would restate these existing obligations within part 250's human capital planning and evaluation provisions. OPM declines to do so. The pre-appointment review is already mandatory and Governmentwide: no agency may appoint a current or recent political appointee to a covered career position without OPM's advance approval, and OPM examines each proposed action for evidence of political influence before it may proceed. Layering a duplicative planning-stage approval or certification on top of that review would add process without adding protection. OPM also notes that the Annual Staffing Review and Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Review framework adopted in this final rule will give OPM and OMB regular, structured visibility into agency hiring patterns, complementing the conversion-specific review described above. Agencies remain fully bound by the pre-appointment review described above, and OPM will continue to enforce it.
Recommendation (5) is outside the scope of this rulemaking. It would establish new requirements governing employee consent to details, justification for involuntary details, and approval of directed reassignments. The proposed rule did not propose to regulate details or reassignments; those matters are governed by
5 U.S.C. 3341
and
5 CFR parts 300
and
335
, and the public was not on notice that this rulemaking might address them. OPM therefore does not adopt recommendation (5) in this final rule.
Strategic Hiring Committee and Merit System Principles
Comments 0005 and 0007 raised legal and policy objections to the proposed Strategic Hiring Committee. The comments argued that centralizing career hiring decisions in political appointees under the proposed Strategic Hiring Committee violates
5 U.S.C. 2301(b)(2)
,
2301(b)(8)(A)
,
2302(b)(1)(E)
, and
2302(b)(3)
, which prohibit consideration of political affiliation in competitive and excepted service hiring. The commenters further objected that undefined hiring criteria such as “patriotism” provide insufficient guardrails against partisan favoritism. Comment 0005 further characterized the Strategic Hiring Committee as political interference in career agency operations.
Comment 0006 did not specifically address the Strategic Hiring Committee but emphasized broadly that modernization of strategic human capital management must reinforce, not erode, the merit system principles that have long guided the Federal civil service. Comment 0009 supported the requirement that the CHCO serve on the Committee alongside the Deputy Secretary or equivalent and recommended that the final rule also require the Committee to solicit written input from the relevant career senior executive with programmatic responsibility before acting on a position within that executive's chain of command.
OPM takes seriously its obligation to administer the merit system in compliance with applicable statutes and disagrees that the Strategic Hiring Committee is inconsistent with those obligations. The Committee is not a creation of this rule.
Executive Order 14356
directs each agency to maintain a Strategic Hiring Committee through which agency leadership reviews and approves the creation of positions and hiring actions; this rule incorporates that requirement into part 250 so that it operates alongside, rather than apart from, the agency's other human capital planning obligations. The Committee's function is accordingly to oversee the agency's hiring program—to ensure that the agency's hiring is directed to its highest-need positions and is consistent with its mission needs and its Annual Staffing Plan.
This rule confers no examining authority on the Committee. Rating, ranking, and certification of eligibles are governed by
5 U.S.C. 3317
and
3318
and
5 CFR part 332
and are carried out under the agency's examining authority, and this rule makes no change to those authorities or to the requirement that an appointing official select from among the eligibles properly certified under them. That an individual official may separately take part in an assessment process under those existing authorities—for example, as a subject-matter expert—is a function of that official's role in the examining process, not of Committee membership, and this rule neither creates nor enlarges any such role. The commenters' central premise—that the rule centralizes career hiring decisions in a manner that displaces competitive examination—is therefore incorrect.
That senior agency officials participate in and are accountable for the agency's hiring decisions is neither novel nor unlawful. Nothing in the merit system requires that appointment decisions be insulated from agency leadership. To the contrary, sustained involvement by senior leadership is a hallmark of effective human capital management. GAO has long reported that the personal commitment and accountability of an agency's top leaders is among the most consistent predictors of progress in strategic human capital management—and that its absence is a central reason the area has remained on the High-Risk List since 2001.
See
GAO,
A Model of Strategic Human Capital Management
, GAO-02-373SP (Mar. 15, 2002) (identifying the “sustained commitment by agency leaders” as the first cornerstone of strategic human capital management),
https://www.gao.gov/​products/​gao-02-373sp
;
GAO, High-Risk Series: Substantial Efforts Needed to Achieve Greater Progress on High-Risk Areas, GAO-19-157SP (Mar. 6, 2019) (leadership commitment is the first of the five criteria GAO uses to assess progress toward removal from the High-Risk List),
https://www.gao.gov/​products/​gao-19-157sp
;
GAO-25-107743,
https://files.gao.gov/​reports/​GAO-25-107743/​index.html
.
The Chief Human Capital Officers Act likewise places workforce strategy with a senior official answerable to agency leadership precisely because staffing decisions are inseparable from decisions about mission, budget, and organizational design.
See
5 U.S.C. 1401
(the head of each agency shall appoint or designate a Chief Human Capital Officer to “advise and assist the head of the agency and other agency officials” in workforce management).
Executive Order 14356
and OPM's Guidance on Annual Staffing Plans carry that principle forward: workforce planning is built from the bottom up by the managers closest to the work and then validated by the Strategic Hiring Committee and the CHCO, so that the officials accountable for the agency's mission and resources are also accountable for the staffing decisions that determine whether the mission can be met. Hiring executed without leadership engagement produces the very pathologies commenters elsewhere decry—diffuse priorities, unfilled mission-critical positions, and hiring disconnected from budget reality.
An applicant or employee who believes a Committee member has discriminated on the basis of political
(
printed page 68018)
affiliation, or who has granted a preference or advantage not authorized by law, may seek corrective action through the Office of Special Counsel under
5 U.S.C. 1214
, and the Merit Systems Protection Board may discipline officials who commit prohibited personnel practices under
5 U.S.C. 1215
. Civil Service Rule IV (
5 CFR 4.2
) independently prohibits inquiry into the political affiliation of applicants and eligibles and any discrimination on that basis.
As to the concern regarding undefined criteria such as “patriotism,” this rule prescribes no qualification, suitability, or selection criteria for individual hiring actions. Qualification requirements continue to be governed by
5 CFR part 300, subpart A
, and
the
qualification standards OPM issues thereunder, and suitability and fitness determinations continue to be governed by
5 CFR part 731
. This rule confers on the Strategic Hiring Committee no authority to establish or alter either.
Comment 0007 also pointed to materials outside this rulemaking—including OPM's Merit Hiring Plan, related guidance on application essay questions, and pending litigation concerning one such question—as evidence that the Committee structure will facilitate politicized hiring. OPM affirms that no hiring criterion, however labeled, may be applied to prefer or exclude a candidate on the basis of political affiliation, and an official who does so commits a prohibited personnel practice under
5 U.S.C. 2302
regardless of the organizational setting—a hiring committee or otherwise—in which the violation occurs. The Committee exists to ensure that hiring is directed to mission needs and that agency leadership is involved in and accountable for the agency's workforce planning. OPM disagrees that this structure will facilitate politicized hiring. If anything, a standing committee whose decisions are documented against a published Annual Staffing Plan and reviewed by OPM and OMB through the Annual Staffing Review makes improper influence easier to detect, not harder: structured, recorded decisions tied to pre-established mission criteria leave a trail, while diffuse and undocumented hiring processes offer far more cover for favoritism. This rule alters none of the prohibitions, or the remedies for their violation, discussed above.
Finally, OPM does not agree that agencywide oversight of hiring is in tension with the merit system. Directing scarce hiring capacity to an agency's highest-need positions is a core management responsibility, and
5 U.S.C. 1401
and
1402
contemplate that the Chief Human Capital Officer will exercise that kind of oversight. The Committee's required composition—the Deputy Secretary or equivalent and the chief of staff to the agency head, together with the Chief Human Capital Officer—follows from
Executive Order 14356
, which requires that the deputy agency head participate, and from the human capital leadership responsibilities the Chief Human Capital Officers Act assigns to the CHCO. OPM notes that it proposed to add the regulatory provisions related to the Strategic Hiring Committee to implement
E.O. 14356
, which states: “The Strategic Hiring Committee shall include the deputy agency head and the chief of staff to the agency head, along with such other senior officials as the agency head may designate.” The final regulatory text corrects the composition of the Strategic Hiring Committee to include the chief of staff to the agency head in accordance with
E.O. 14356
. OPM acknowledges that the proposed regulatory text did not list the chief of staff to the agency head as a required Committee member. This revision does not create a new substantive obligation; it conforms the regulation to the Committee composition that
E.O. 14356
already requires and under which agencies are already operating. Because the change makes no operative legal change and simply allows the regulation to reflect existing requirements, OPM finds, pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)

Annual Employee Surveys
The single most frequently raised theme across the comments concerns OPM's proposed changes to the annual employee survey, addressed in subpart C (§§ 250.302 and 250.303), and the discontinuation of the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey. Six of the nine comments address this subject in some form (comments 0003, 0004, 0006, 0007, 0008, 0009), reflecting its evident importance to stakeholders.
The Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS) is often conflated with the annual employee survey (AES) requirement set in section 1128 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2004,
Public Law 108-136
, div. A, tit. XI (
5 U.S.C. 7101 note
), which requires each agency to conduct an annual survey covering two content areas. That statute directs OPM to prescribe survey questions by regulation, and this final rule modifies those prescribed questions. The FEVS was part of a larger effort by OPM to assess a variety of human capital topics, and OPM incentivized agencies to participate in the FEVS by including the required AES items. By participating in the FEVS, agencies would meet their required survey obligation.
In 2026, after serious consideration, OPM decided to discontinue the Governmentwide administration of FEVS, as it was felt the survey had become a check-the-box activity and did not yield actionable insights sufficient to justify the cost and burden it imposed. (OPM paused the survey for 2025 to allow agencies to focus on other workforce priorities;
see

https://www.opm.gov/​chcoc/​transmittals/​2025/​Memo%20on%20FEVS%20ReportsFINAL.pdf
(delaying the 2025 survey); OPM, Cancellation of 2025 OPM Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (Aug. 15, 2025),
https://content.govdelivery.com/​accounts/​USOPM/​bulletins/​3ede04d
).
FEVS did not provide enough meaningful assessment as a general purpose, one-size-fits-all instrument, nor did it have enough actionable feedback or make a real impact for employees to be worthwhile. OPM's reasoning is set out more fully in its survey guidance and public statements. OPM,
Annual Employee Survey Administration Requirements—2026 and Beyond
(July 9, 2026),
https://www.opm.gov/​chcoc/​latest-memos/​annual-employee-survey-administration-requirements-2026-and-beyond.pdf
;
OPM,
Measure What Matters
, Secrets of OPM (July 1, 2026),
https://usopm.substack.com/​p/​measure-what-matters
.
As OPM has explained, it believes strongly in well-designed employee engagement surveys—surveys that help managers understand whether the organization is aligned around the right objectives, whether employees understand how their work contributes to those objectives, whether managers hold team members accountable, reward excellence, and develop top performers, and whether employees can report wrongdoing without fear of reprisal. But a single, centrally administered annual instrument is poorly suited to those ends: objectives and priorities shift during the year, a “one and done” survey becomes a checkbox exercise, and organizations as large and managerially distributed as Federal agencies are not served equally well by one Governmentwide ritual. Survey data are actionable only when collected at the right level of detail, reviewed by the managers closest to the work, and used to diagnose and correct real problems—which requires agencies to own their surveys. The prescribed common questions preserve OPM's visibility into Governmentwide trends so that systemic challenges can still be identified centrally.
Core Survey Question Set
Several organizational comments (0006, 0007, 0008, 0009), along with comment 0003, objected to reducing the number of items from sixteen questions to ten, and several—most pointedly comment 0007 and comment 0008—argued this violates the statutory mandate that the survey address specific topics, including work environment, rewards and recognition, and professional development.
It is OPM's position that the statute underlying the annual employee survey requires OPM to prescribe common questions “to allow comparison across agencies” and requires that results be made public. It does not require that OPM itself administer every agency's survey instrument, dictate a single Governmentwide field period, or otherwise control agency-level survey logistics. The final rule preserves the statutorily required mechanism for comparability—a common core of required questions appearing on every agency's survey—while returning survey administration to the agencies that are closest to their own workforce populations and best positioned to tailor supplemental content to their missions. This is consistent with, not contrary to, the statutory design.
For additional context, the items required in regulation have changed before; in December 2016 the regulation was modified to change the number from 45 to 16 items. This reduction in the number of required items allowed the larger FEVS to adapt and meet new needs. The survey, either the FEVS or the AES items, was never meant to be permanent, but allowed to change as the workforce and workplace needed. While OPM acknowledges there are benefits to being able to trend results over time, there are also benefits to refreshing the content to meet the current needs.
Commenters contended that the proposed survey items do not meet the requirements of the statute regarding content areas that must be addressed (comments 0006, 0007) and that some of the items have some technical faults in their design like unclear wording or response choices (comments 0004, 0007, 0008). OPM respectfully disagrees.
Section 1128(a) requires each agency to conduct an annual survey of its employees—expressly “including survey questions unique to the agency and questions prescribed under subsection (b)”—to assess (1) leadership
(
printed page 68020)
and management practices that contribute to agency performance and (2) employee satisfaction with leadership policies and practices; the work environment; rewards and recognition for professional accomplishment and personal contributions to achieving organizational mission; opportunity for professional development and growth; and opportunity to contribute to achieving organizational mission.
The content areas Congress enumerated therefore attach to the agency's survey as a whole, which the statute defines to include the agency's own questions, and not solely to the subset of items OPM prescribes by regulation. Subsection (b) directs OPM to prescribe questions that should appear on all agency surveys “in order to allow a comparison across agencies.” It does not direct OPM to prescribe a separate item for each content area, to prescribe any particular number of items, or to require that an item use the word “satisfaction” or a satisfaction response scale. Section 250.302(a)(1) preserves each agency's ability to include questions unique to the agency, and the prescribed items accordingly operate as a floor rather than a ceiling.
The prescribed items nonetheless reach each of the statutory content areas. Leadership and management practices that contribute to agency performance are addressed by items (i), (v), (ix), and (x); leadership policies and practices by items (i), (iv), and (v); the work environment by items (ii) and (viii); rewards and recognition for professional accomplishment and personal contributions to achieving organizational mission by item (iii); opportunity for professional development and growth by item (iv); and opportunity to contribute to achieving organizational mission by items (vi) and (vii). Assessing these conditions through agreement-scaled items is an accepted measurement practice and is consistent with the approach used for the Annual Employee Survey items as administered through the FEVS. An employee's reported agreement that differences in performance are recognized in a meaningful way, or that a supervisor provides ongoing feedback to help the employee succeed and progress in a career, is a direct measure of that employee's assessment of the agency in the corresponding content area. OPM does not read the statute to require that a content area be assessed only by an item that recites the statutory phrasing.
As to the technical concerns about item wording and response options, OPM has considered each of them and concludes that they reflect differences in professional judgment about survey design and item construction rather than defects that would prevent the items from assessing the statutory content areas. Agencies retain discretion to supplement the prescribed items where they determine that additional or differently constructed items would better serve their workforce, and OPM will continue to support agencies through guidance such as the Employee Survey Playbook (OPM,
Employee Survey Playbook: A Guide for Federal Agencies
(July 2026),
https://www.opm.gov/​chcoc/​latest-memos/​employee-survey-playbook.pdf
) and OPM's annual survey administration requirements. OPM,
Annual Employee Survey Administration Requirements—2026 and Beyond
(July 9, 2026),
https://www.opm.gov/​chcoc/​latest-memos/​annual-employee-survey-administration-requirements-2026-and-beyond.pdf
.
OPM is making no changes to the proposed survey items in this final rule.
Survey Methodology, Timing, and Public Disclosure
Some comments claim that a smaller survey or distributed survey effort would be detrimental, or would lack control and standardization (comments 0003, 0006, 0008). As mentioned, part of the reason the FEVS was discontinued was because its one-size-fits-all approach makes it difficult for agencies to assess their own needs without also doing their own survey in addition to participating in the FEVS.
In fact, it was this need for customization that led three large agencies to discontinue participating in the FEVS altogether in years prior to 2025—National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and the Securities and Exchange Commission all decided to do their own surveys as the FEVS could not meet their needs. While the FEVS did allow agencies to add their own agency-specific survey items, the number of those items was limited and had to be asked to the entirety of the agency, which may not be appropriate if only a portion of the agency needed to be addressed.
By returning the responsibility of surveying their employees to the agency and decreasing the total number of survey items required, plus giving options for the methodologies that best suits them, agencies will be able to craft survey items and whole surveys that better serve their specific needs. Using these flexibilities, agencies can continue or even expand on content that the FEVS promoted, such as assessing employee engagement. OPM will continue to assist agencies by providing guidance and expert advice to meet their obligations, such as the Employee Survey Playbook which provides information and considerations for administering a proper survey.
Comment 0008 objected that revised § 250.303(a) removes the current regulation's enumerated categories of required public disclosure and permits each agency to determine the specific content of its public release, which the commenter argued could allow selective or incomplete reporting. OPM does not intend, and the final rule does not permit, disclosure that misrepresents survey results. The governing statute requires that the results of the annual survey be made available to the public, and § 250.303(a) carries that command forward: each agency must make the results of its annual survey available to the public and post them on its website, subject only to the narrow national security exception stated in the rule.
OPM will address the content of public releases—including publication of the survey instrument, response rates, and item-level results for the prescribed questions—in implementation guidance, and agencies must submit complete results to OPM and OMB under § 250.303(c), which preserves centralized oversight and enables OPM to publish Governmentwide comparisons. OPM has concluded that this combination of a statutory disclosure floor, annual administration requirements, and centralized reporting better accommodates variation in agency size and structure than a single enumerated list, and OPM therefore declines to retain the prior list in regulatory text.
Comment 0008 also expressed concern that agency-by-agency administration could weaken respondent confidentiality and, with it, employee trust and candor, particularly at small components. OPM agrees that confidentiality is essential to reliable measurement. The Employee Survey Playbook addresses anonymity, confidentiality, minimum reporting thresholds, and data-handling practices, and OPM's annual administration requirements will continue to set confidentiality expectations for agency surveys. Agencies also remain bound by the Privacy Act of 1974,
5 U.S.C. 552a
, in collecting and maintaining survey records. OPM will monitor response rates across agencies and will revisit these safeguards in future administration requirements if participation data indicate an erosion of employee trust.

B. Impact
The final rule consolidates duplicative human capital planning and
(
printed page 68022)
review requirements, reducing compliance burden on agency HR staff. The consolidation of the HCOP, HCR, and HRStat quarterly review into the Annual Staffing Plan, Annual Staffing Review, and Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Review framework is intended to free CHCO offices to focus on substantive workforce management rather than compliance paperwork, as the Senior Executives Association recommended.
The strengthening of CHCO authority, including the new certification requirement, is expected to improve the visibility and effectiveness of agency human capital leadership—addressing a persistent gap documented by GAO.
C. Costs
This final rule affects Federal agencies subject to
5 CFR part 250
. The consolidation of planning and review requirements is expected to reduce, not increase, ongoing administrative costs relative to the current framework by eliminating duplicative HCOP, HCR, and HRStat reporting. Implementation costs are expected to be modest and largely one-time, consisting of the work required to review and update agency delegations, policies, and procedures to align with the new framework. This rule affects over 80 Federal agencies, ranging from cabinet-level departments to small independent agencies. For purposes of this analysis, OPM assumes that the work will be performed by employees at the GS-14, step 5 level under the 2026 Washington, DC, locality pay table ($163,104 annual locality rate; $78.15 hourly locality rate), and that the total dollar value of labor, including wages, benefits, and overhead, equals 200 percent of the wage rate, for an assumed labor cost of $156.30 per hour. OPM estimates that, in the first year following publication of this final rule, implementation will require an average of 100 hours per agency, resulting in estimated first-year costs of approximately $15,630 per agency and approximately $1,250,400 Governmentwide.
Comment 0009 stated that this estimate likely understates the resources agencies will need, particularly because agencies are implementing this rule during the same period as the Strategic Hiring Committee and Annual Staffing Plan requirements of
Executive Order 14356
and the Merit Hiring Plan, and recommended a phased implementation with a transition year and dedicated training resources. OPM has considered that comment and retains its estimate as a reasonable central estimate while acknowledging uncertainty in both directions. Even if first-year implementation burden were triple OPM's estimate—300 hours per agency—first-year costs of approximately $46,890 per agency and $3.8 million Governmentwide would remain modest and far below the threshold for a regulatory impact analysis.
OPM has also estimated ongoing costs. Preparing the Annual Staffing Plan, participating in the Annual Staffing Review, and conducting Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Reviews are estimated to require approximately 120 hours per agency per year, or approximately $18,756 per agency and $1,500,480 Governmentwide under the same labor-cost assumptions. Those activities replace, rather than supplement, the Human Capital Operating Plan, Human Capital Review, and HRStat processes they consolidate, which OPM estimates required at least as many staff hours annually; the net ongoing effect is accordingly expected to be a modest reduction in administrative cost. Agencies will also assume responsibility for administering their own annual employee surveys. Those costs will vary with the administration approach each agency selects, are mitigated by OPM-provided guidance, templates, and the Employee Survey Playbook, and are offset by the discontinuation of agency-side coordination of the Governmentwide FEVS and of the centralized administration costs OPM previously incurred.
OPM does not anticipate that the final rule will impose significant new costs on agencies. The primary regulatory burden—Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Reviews—builds on existing quarterly performance review obligations under the GPRA Modernization Act and is expected to reduce duplicative reporting.
D. Benefits
The final rule is expected to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of Federal human capital management by: (1) consolidating and streamlining planning and review requirements and synchronizing them with OMB Circular A-11 budget and performance planning timelines, freeing CHCO offices for substantive workforce management and eliminating duplication across planning, budgeting, and performance management activities; (2) strengthening CHCO institutional authority and accountability with a verifiable compliance mechanism; (3) better positioning agencies through a decentralized survey process to design and administer surveys because they understand their own missions, structures, workforces, and management challenges, while a common set of required questions preserves the ability to track Governmentwide trends; and (4) aligning Federal human capital planning with Executive branch priorities while preserving the statutory obligations and merit system protections that govern Federal hiring.
These benefits are difficult to quantify with precision, but their potential scale is large relative to the rule's costs: Federal civilian personnel costs exceed $300 billion annually, so even fractional improvements in time-to-hire, hiring quality, or retention of high performers in mission-critical occupations would yield benefits many times the implementation costs estimated above. The rule's expected recruitment and morale effects, and OPM's response to comments predicting harm in those areas, are discussed in the Workforce Recruitment, Retention, and Morale section of this preamble.
E. Regulatory Alternatives
An alternative to this rulemaking is to retain the current HCOP, HCR, and HRStat framework without consolidation. OPM considered this alternative but determined that the existing framework creates duplicative reporting that diverts CHCO office resources from substantive work. Retaining the current framework would also leave workforce planning unsynchronized with the strategic planning and budget formulation cycle under OMB Circular A-11 and with the Annual Staffing Plan process established by
Executive Order 14356
, forcing agencies to maintain two parallel planning vocabularies and documentation streams for the same activity. Nor has the status quo produced results: strategic human capital management has remained on GAO's High-Risk List for a quarter century under the existing regulatory architecture. OPM also considered a narrower variation—retaining the Human Capital Operating Plan while adjusting its timing and content requirements—and rejected it for the same reasons: incremental adjustment would preserve the duplication that is the central defect of the current framework.
Another alternative is to continue a centralized survey administration. OPM considered this alternative but determined that a decentralized administration positions agencies better by giving them the flexibility and customizability of administering their own surveys while incorporating the items OPM issues in regulation to ensure comparability across agencies. In
(
printed page 68023)
evaluating this alternative, OPM also considered the variant urged by several commenters: retaining centralized administration while shortening the instrument and expanding agency-specific supplements. That approach would preserve the cost of central administration and a single Governmentwide field period while still denying agencies control over timing, methodology, and level of reporting detail—the limitations that led the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and the Securities and Exchange Commission to leave the FEVS even before 2025. The final rule instead secures comparability through the common prescribed items and the centralized submission of complete results to OPM and OMB under § 250.303(c), while leaving administration with the agencies where the results must be acted upon.
Finally, OPM considered delaying the effective date or phasing the new framework in over multiple years, as comment 0009 recommended. However, OPM determined that a delayed effective date would postpone the benefits of consolidation without materially reducing transition costs, because agencies are already required to prepare Annual Staffing Plans under
Executive Order 14356
regardless of when this rule takes effect.

AGENCY:
Federal Communications Commission.
ACTION:
Notice and request for comments.
SUMMARY:
As part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork burdens, and as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC or Commission) invites the general public and other Federal agencies to take this opportunity to comment on the following information collections. Comments are requested concerning: whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Commission, including whether the information shall have practical utility; the accuracy of the Commission's burden estimate; ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information collected; ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on the respondents, including the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology; and ways to further reduce the information collection burden on small business concerns with fewer than 25 employees.
The FCC may not conduct or sponsor a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget (OMB) control number. No person shall be subject to any penalty for failing to comply with a collection of information subject to the PRA that does not display a valid OMB control number.
DATES:
Written PRA comments should be submitted on or before December 28, 2026. If you anticipate that you will be submitting comments but find it difficult to do so within the period of time allowed by this notice, you should advise the contact listed below as soon as possible.
ADDRESSES:
Direct all PRA comments to Cathy Williams, FCC, via email
PRA@fcc.gov
and to
Cathy.Williams@fcc.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For additional information about the information collection, contact Cathy Williams at (202) 418-2918.

Section 105 of the Twenty-First Century Communications and Video Accessibility Act of 2010 (CVAA) added section 719 to the Communications Act of 1934, as amended (the Act).
Public Law 111-260
, 124 Stat. 2751 (2010);

, 124 Stat. 2795 (2010) (making technical corrections);
47 U.S.C. 620
. Section 719 of the Act requires the Commission to establish rules that define as eligible for up to $10,000,000 of support annually from the Interstate Telecommunications Relay Service Fund (TRS Fund) those programs that are approved by the Commission for the distribution of specialized customer premises equipment designed to make telecommunications service, internet access service, and advanced communications, including interexchange services and advanced telecommunications and information services, accessible by low-income individuals who are deafblind.
47 U.S.C. 620(a)
, (c). Accordingly, on August 5, 2016, the Commission released a Report and Order, document FCC 16-101, published at
81 FR 65948
, September 26, 2016, adopting rules to establish the NDBEDP, also known as “iCanConnect,” as a permanent program.
See
47 CFR 64.6201
through
64.6219
.
In document FCC 16-101, the Commission adopted rules requiring the following:
(a) Entities must apply to the Commission for certification to receive reimbursement from the TRS Fund for NDBEDP activities. The FCC's Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau certified 56 programs—one for each state, the District of Columbia, American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands—for a period of five years. Incumbent programs must apply to renew their certifications, if desired, and potential new entrants must also apply for certification.
(b) A program wishing to relinquish its certification before its certification expires must provide written notice of its intent to do so.
(c) Certified programs must disclose to the Commission actual or potential conflicts of interest.
(d) Certified programs must notify the Commission of any substantive change that bears directly on its ability to meet the qualifications necessary for certification.
(e) A certified entity may present written arguments and any relevant documentation as to why suspension or revocation of certification is not warranted.
(f) When a new entity is certified as a state's program, the previously certified entity must take certain actions to complete the transition to the new entity.
(g) Certified programs must require an applicant to provide verification that the applicant is deafblind.
(h) Certified programs must require an applicant to provide verification that the applicant meets the income eligibility requirement.
(i) Certified programs must re-verify the income and disability eligibility of an equipment recipient under certain circumstances.
(j) Certified programs must permit the transfer of an equipment recipient's account when the recipient relocates to another state.
(
printed page 68150)
(k) Certified programs must include an attestation on consumer application forms.
(l) Certified programs must conduct annual audits and submit to Commission-directed audits.
(m) Certified programs must document compliance with NDBEDP requirements, provide such documentation to the Commission upon request, and retain such records for at least five years.
(n) Certified programs must submit reimbursement claims as instructed by the TRS Fund Administrator, and supplemental information and documentation as requested. In addition, the entity selected to conduct national outreach will submit claims for reimbursement on a quarterly basis.
(o) Certified programs must submit reports every six months as instructed by the NDBEDP Administrator. In addition, the entity selected to conduct national outreach will submit an annual report.
(p) Informal and formal complaints may be filed against NEDBEDP certified programs, and the Commission may conduct such inquiries and hold such proceedings as it may deem necessary.
(q) Certified programs must include the NDBEDP whistleblower protections in appropriate publications. In March 2026, the Commission adopted the
Suspension and Debarment Report and Order,
FCC 26-18, published at
91 FR 18134
, April 9, 2026, which applies the government-wide non-procurement suspension and debarment framework to the NDBEDP. These rules amend
47 CFR 64.6207
and
64.6215
to require NDBEDP certified programs to submit the disclosures required under
2 CFR 180.335
when applying for certification or recertification, to update such disclosures annually, and to provide updated disclosures upon any substantive change affecting their qualifications. Certified programs must also obtain and maintain disclosures from lower-tier participants—such as contractors, subcontractors, consultants, and suppliers—that play a material role in NDBEDP transactions. These new requirements introduce additional reporting and recordkeeping obligations that are accounted for in the burden estimates in this Supporting Statement.

AGENCY:
National Labor Relations Board.
ACTION:
Notice of administrative change in status of the Memphis, Tennessee Office (Subregion 26) of the National Labor Relations Board, which will be closed and the area will be served by agents working primarily from the New Orleans, Louisiana Regional Office (Region 15) and other locations.
SUMMARY:
The National Labor Relations Board is closing its Memphis, Tennessee Subregional Office because it has determined that closing the office and serving the area with agents working at other locations will result in significant savings while continuing to effectively serve the area currently served by this office.
DATES:
Effective Date:
The closure of the Memphis office is effective immediately.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Roxanne L. Rothschild, Executive Secretary, National Labor Relations Board, 1015 Half St. SE, Washington, DC 20570-0001, (202) 273-1940 (this is not a toll-free number) or 1-844-762-NLRB (6572) (this is a toll-free number). Hearing impaired callers who wish to speak to an NLRB representative should contact T-Mobile Relay Conference Captioning by visiting its website at
https://www.tmobileaccess.com/​federal
,
and submitting a form asking its Communications Assistant to call our toll-free number at 1-844-762-NLRB (6572).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The National Labor Relations Board has decided to close its Memphis, Tennessee Subregional Office. This change is prompted by an examination of the staffing, caseloads, and rental and operating costs for the Memphis office, which has had no personnel since 2023 due to attrition. Employees from the Agency's New Orleans and Little Rock, Arkansas offices have been, and will continue to, provide service to the area formerly covered by the Memphis Subregional office. The Board expects no adverse impact on the quality of case-handling as a result of the office closure.
Region 15, which handles cases arising in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Tennessee, is headed by a Regional Director, who works in the New Orleans, Louisiana Regional office and has full authority for the processing of both unfair labor practice and representation cases in that area. Currently, the other employees in this Region work in Little Rock, Arkansas. Under this proposal, all offices except the Memphis office will continue to be open. The geographical area covered by the Region will not be changed.
In 2024, the NLRB solicited and received feedback on the proposed closure of the Memphis office. The decision to close this office in the manner set forth here was informed by comments from stakeholders. Because this is a general notice that is related to the organization of the NLRB, it is not a regulation or rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking or
Executive Order 12866
.
