[Docket No. FD 36932]
On May 12, 2026, Channel Pacific Railroad (CHPR), a noncarrier, filed a verified notice of exemption under
49 CFR 1150.31
to operate approximately 2,132 feet of track (the Line) located in a terminal facility (the Facility) in West Sacramento, Yolo County, Cal. Notice of CHPR's exemption was served and published in the
Federal Register
on May 28, 2026 (
91 FR 31318
) (
May 28 Notice
), and the notice became effective on June 11, 2026.
On July 31, 2026, the City of West Sacramento, Cal., and the Sacramento-Yolo Port District (together, the Sacramento-area Government Entities or SGEs) filed a petition to reject the verified notice, revoke the exemption, or declare the exemption void ab initio (the Petition).
[
1
]
CHPR filed a reply to the Petition on August 20, 2026 (Reply). For the reasons discussed below, the Board will decline to institute a revocation proceeding and deny the Petition. Pursuant to
49 U.S.C. 10502(d)
, the Board's decision will be published in the
Federal Register
.
Background
The Line consists of two tracks that begin at a point of connection with a rail line owned by Union Pacific Railroad Company (UP) at the northern boundary of the Facility, immediately south of Channel Drive, and extends southward to ending points immediately north of the Sacramento River Deep Water Ship Channel.
[
2
]
(Verified Notice 3;
see id.,
Ex. A (map).) The Line has no mileposts and is owned by CHPR's noncarrier corporate affiliate, Greencycle Properties, LLC (Greencycle).
[
3
]
(Verified Notice 1.)
According to the verified notice, CHPR and Greencycle have agreed that CHPR would “acquire the right to conduct railroad common carrier service over” the Line and that CHPR would “assume responsibility for the provision of associated commodity-handling and transloading services within” the Facility. (
Id.
at 2.) CHPR asserts that it is leasing the Line and Facility from Greencycle under a lease effective July 1, 2026. (Reply 26-27.) CHPR states that it will deliver “comprehensive, railroad-oriented transportation services within” the Facility, “including, among other things, the inbound and outbound transportation of railroad-borne shipments.” (Verified Notice 2-3;
see
Reply 11-12 (describing its intended services package to involve “comprehensive transload and logistics services,” including “[t]he offloading, temporary storage, and reloading of bulk commodities into motor carriers for local distribution”).) CHPR further asserts that it has “communicated its short line operations plans with UP” and that UP has indicated willingness “to coordinate with CHPR on its common carrier implementation and subsequent operating plans.” (Verified Notice 4;
see
Reply 13 (noting that CHPR and UP executed a formal interchange agreement, effective July 14, 2026).)
The
May 28 Notice
provided that petitions for stay were due by June 4, 2026; no stay requests were filed. By decision served June 10, 2026 (
June 10 Decision
), the Board waived the 60-day advance notice requirement under
49 CFR 1150.32(e)
and established that CHPR's exemption would become effective on June 11, 2026.
On July 31, 2026, the SGEs filed the Petition, arguing that the Board should reject the verified notice, revoke the exemption, or declare the exemption void ab initio. On August 20, 2026, CHPR replied to the petition.
Preliminary Matter
On September 8, 2026, the SGEs filed a request for leave to file a rebuttal to CHPR's reply. In the filing, the SGEs assert, among other things, that the reply contains factual inaccuracies and is misleading. On September 23, 2026, CHPR filed an opposition to the SGEs' request for leave. The Board's rules do not permit a reply to a reply,
see
49 CFR 1104.13(c)
,
[
4
]
and the SGEs' filing, which they characterize as a “limited rebuttal,” largely repeats or expands on arguments and information presented in the Petition. Accordingly, the SGEs' request for leave to file a rebuttal will be denied.
Discussion and Conclusions
As noted above, CHPR's notice of exemption has already become effective, with no party having sought a stay of the effective date. Because the exemption is already in effect, the Petition—which seeks rejection and revocation—will be treated as a petition to revoke.
See Middletown & N.J. R.R.—Lease & Operation Exemption—Norfolk S. Ry.,
FD 35412, slip op. at 2 n.1 (STB served Dec. 23, 2010). Pursuant to
49 U.S.C. 10502(d)
, “an already-effective exemption may be revoked, in whole or in part, if regulation is necessary to carry out the [Rail Transportation Policy (RTP)] of
49 U.S.C. 10101
.”
Mid-Atl. Gateway LLC—Lease & Operation Exemption—Certain Rail Line Assets of J.P. Rail, Inc.,
FD 36644, slip op. at 2 (STB served Feb. 15, 2023).
(
printed page 68222)
Furthermore, “[t]he Board shall, within 90 days after receipt of a request for revocation . . . determine whether to begin an appropriate proceeding.”
49 U.S.C. 10502(d)
. If it “decides not to begin a proceeding,” the Board must publish “the reasons for the decision” in the
Federal Register
.
Id.
“A party seeking revocation or rejection of a notice of exemption has the burden of demonstrating that the notice contains false or misleading information, or that regulation is necessary to carry out the” RTP.
TGS Cedar Port R.R.—Operation Exemption—in Chambers Cnty., Tex.,
FD 36627, slip op. at 3 (STB served Apr. 1, 2024) (quoting
Gen. Ry.—Exemption for Acquis. of R.R. Line—in Osceola & Dickinson Cntys., Iowa,
FD 34867, slip op. at 4 (STB served June 15, 2007)) (denying petition to revoke);
see
49 U.S.C. 10502(d)
. An exemption under
49 CFR part 1150 subpart D
is void ab initio if the verified notice of exemption contains false or misleading information that is material to the authorization process.
TGS Cedar Port R.R.,
FD 36627, slip op. at 3 (citing
49 CFR 1150.32(c)
;
Berkshire Scenic Ry. Museum, Inc.
v.
ICC,
52 F.3d 378, 381 (1st Cir. 1995)). The “[f]ailure to disclose material information can render a notice misleading by omission.”
Ohio River Partners LLC—Acquis. & Operation Exemption—Hannibal Dev., LLC,
FD 35984, slip op. at 3 (STB served Apr. 1, 2016) (citing
U S Rail Corp.—Lease & Operation Exemption—Shannon G., a N.J. LLC,
FD 35042 (STB served Oct. 8, 2008)). Information is material if the transaction would not otherwise have qualified for an exemption.
TGS Cedar Port R.R.,
FD 36627, slip op. at 3 (citing
Berkshire,
52 F.3d at 381). Additionally, in considering whether a statement is misleading, “the relevant question is whether the Board itself has been materially misled.”
Id.
(citing
Snohomish Cnty., Wash.
v.
STB,
954 F.3d 290, 303 (D.C. Cir. 2020)).
As discussed below, the SGEs argue that the exemption should be declared void ab initio or revoked because the verified notice is misleading, CHPR is not prepared to operate as a common carrier, and the circumstances are too complicated for the class exemption process. The Board addresses these arguments in turn below.
Request To Declare Exemption Void Ab Initio
Alleged omissions and misstatements.
According to the SGEs, CHPR omits material information from the verified notice and presents other material information in a misleading manner, “which appear to have been intended to mask the full scope of the owners' activities,” rendering the verified notice void ab initio. (Pet. 3.) The SGEs assert that the verified notice refers to the Facility as a railroad-served “terminal complex” but fails to discuss how “one of the primary activities at the site would be transfer of petroleum product from ships to storage tanks” and then from storage tanks to trucks. (
Id.
at 5;
see also id.
at 9-10 (arguing that the verified notice omitted details about plans for receiving asphaltic oil via maritime shipments, making related infrastructure developments, and negotiating a dock lease).) The SGEs further criticize CHPR's filing for not discussing plans to repurpose the Facility's existing chemical storage tanks to accommodate asphaltic oil storage (
see, e.g., id.
at 3), and claim that CHPR's intended operations are not “a typical rail to truck transload operation” because the “loading of trucks activity will physically occur over 300 feet from the rail spur,” (
id.
at 12). The Petition also describes interactions between the SGEs and Teichert personnel since August 2025 concerning anticipated operations at the Facility (including rail) and attaches correspondence related to such plans and related permitting issues. (
See, e.g., id.
at 2-4, 6-8, 10-11;
id.,
Exs. B, E.)
The SGEs further assert that the verified notice should have explained that Greencycle is the only entity with “physical access to the rail lines,” which, according to the SGEs, makes Greencycle the only possible shipper (
id.
at 5
[
5
]
), but that CHPR instead uses terminology that “might invoke images of a multi-tenant rail park or a logistics park,” (
id.
at 11). According to the SGEs, Greencycle “is merely a rail served customer of” UP (
id.
at 6), and CHPR's activities will occur “behind the gate” (or fence) at the Facility (
id.
at 4;
see id.
at 6, 12, 13, 14).
[
6
]
The SGEs also take issue with the verified notice's description of the track as “2,132 linear feet” without clarifying, in text, that the total embraces three segments of track (one 985-foot track, one 897-foot track, and a 250-foot connector track). (
Id.
at 5.) Additionally, the SGEs suggest that CHPR's projection of $5 million in annual operating revenues “refers to revenues from sales of asphalt,” not rail transportation. (
Id.
at 14.)
In response, CHPR argues that its verified notice provides what is required under the regulations: an accurate description of “the lines of railroad that would become the subject to the proceeding.” (Reply 9 (emphasis omitted) (citing
49 CFR 1150.33(e)(3)-(4)
).) CHPR asserts that “an exhaustive, granular inventory of . . . ancillary transportation infrastructure” is not required by the regulations. (
Id.
at 9.) CHPR also argues that its negotiations for a river dock lease and the repurposing of storage tanks have “no bearing on” the exemption criteria here, which focus on “the relevant transaction elements—specifically, the acquisition of operating rights over the track and the commitment to provide common carrier service over them.” (
Id.
at 10.) CHPR further argues that the Board should reject the SGEs' suggestion that the filing falsely “
implied
direct, side-by-side rail-to-truck transloading” despite the 300-foot distance between the truck bay and the rail spur. (
Id.
at 14 (citing Pet. 12).) According to CHPR, the verified notice made no such representations, such details would not have affected the validity of the exemption, and CHPR's plans regarding transfer of commodities are standard for multimodal logistics providers. (
Id.
)
CHPR further states that its description of the site as a “terminal complex” was accurate because the Facility will function as “a multimodal transload terminal,” with CHPR “receiving asphaltic oil via multiple modes (rail and ship), storing it in tanks, and transferring it to tanker trucks for distribution to off-site asphalt plants.” (
Id.
at 9-10;
see
Verified Notice 2, 3.) CHPR avows that the Facility “can and will be made available to other customers” beyond Greencycle and that CHPR is fully aware of—and “steadfast[ly] commit[ted]” to fulfilling—its common carrier obligation. (Reply 12;
see id.
at 23-24.) CHPR further asserts that it is standard practice for rail customers to use terminal facilities for transloading “using available ground space” without any need for an on-site real estate footprint or intermediate storage. (
Id.
at 27, 28.
[
7
]
) Additionally, CHPR states that
(
printed page 68223)
the verified notice accurately describes the length of the Line (
id.
at 14-15), and that its projection of annual operating revenues exceeding $5 million is “a good-faith estimate of the revenues to be generated from the comprehensive railroad services package CHPR will provide,” (
id.
at 11;
see id.
at 12 (stating that the estimate reflects the “comprehensive scope of projected common carrier logistics services”)). CHPR represents that the figure did not account for the sale of the commodity as “CHPR will merely transport and handle asphaltic oil for a charge; it will not be the beneficial owner of it.” (
Id.
)
The information that the SGEs claim is either misleading or omitted from the verified notice is not material because it does not bear on the exemption criteria. (
See, e.g.,
Reply 9-10.) The Board's regulations require a notice of exemption to include “[a] brief summary of the proposed transaction.”
49 CFR 1150.33
. CHPR's verified notice met this requirement. The information about CHPR's operations that the SGEs argue was omitted or misleading—such as CHPR's plans to facilitate maritime shipments (in addition to rail) or repurpose storage tanks and the distance between the rail spur and truck loading—are not required by the regulation. Additionally, the verified notice's description of the Facility as a “terminal complex” (or “railroad-served terminal facility”) was not misleading, as it appears to reflect CHPR's plans for rail service. (Verified Notice 2, 3.) Furthermore, as discussed below, CHPR has verified that it has prospective third-party customers. (
See
Reply 28-29.) The Board also does not take issue with CHPR's description of the track as 2,132 linear feet, particularly in light of the verified notice's map depicting the segments of track (
see
Verified Notice 3;
id.,
Ex. A (map depicting a “track 1” and a “track 2” as 897 and 985 feet, respectively, with a 250-foot “connector track,” and a “track 3 spur track” as 709 feet)), and the SGEs have provided no basis for the Board to find that CHPR's “good-faith estimate” of anticipated revenues was false or misleading.
Alleged lack of readiness or intention to commence common carrier operations.
The SGEs contend that CHPR is not a legitimate rail carrier and that it is seeking operating authority “to take advantage of the preemptive authority of the Board's jurisdiction . . . and avoid certain state and local land use regulations.” (Pet. 4; see
id.
at 3, 4-5.) The SGEs also claim that a lack of preparation for common carrier operations by CHPR indicates that it does not intend to provide common carrier service. The SGEs assert that “[i]nstead of . . . an interchange agreement with Union Pacific, as one would expect from a short line railroad, [CHPR] apparently has only an industry track agreement with Union Pacific, which is what one would expect of a typical rail served customer.” (
Id.
at 6 (citing
id.,
Ex. B at 5 (August 2025 letter from Teichert's attorney to City of West Sacramento noting that Teichert had “entered into a track licensing agreement with [UP] for ongoing rail service” at the Facility)).) The SGEs also question CHPR's intentions by asserting that there are no discernable locomotives or rail equipment in place yet at the Facility (
id.
at 12-13), CHPR is not listed on UP's website as a short line that it connects with (
id.
at 8, 13), and CHPR does not yet have an official Standard Carrier Alpha Code (SCAC) identifier (
id.
at 8, 13).
In its reply, CHPR acknowledges that it sought common carrier authority in part to address “the community's attempts to `regulate' away the Terminal's historic access to the interstate network.” (Reply 23.) CHPR argues, however, that it is not problematic for it to consider preemption in invoking the Board's common carrier authorization processes (
id.
at 23), and that it is “a lawful prerogative, provided the entity assumes the actual, objective obligations of a common carr[ier], as CHPR pledges to do,” (
id.
at 24). CHPR also responds with a detailed description of its preparations to provide common carrier service. (
Id.
at 12-14, 25, 26, 28-29.)
The Board's regulations and precedent do not require CHPR to have all operating assets and administrative arrangements in place prior to seeking common carrier operating authority.
See Townline Rail Terminal, LLC—Constr. & Operation Exemption—in Suffolk Cnty., N.Y.,
FD 36575 (STB served Nov. 15, 2023) (denying motion to dismiss petition for exemption and rejecting argument that the exemption filer's “failure to provide evidence that it ha[d] entered into an interchange agreement with [railroad] indicates [filer] would not be a rail carrier”);
Mid-Atl. Gateway LLC,
FD 36644, slip op. at 2 (“The grant of the exemption here does not require the parties to complete the transaction, and revoking the exemption is not necessary simply because the parties have not reached a final agreement to go forward.”). The verified notice states that CHPR was in communication with UP about its intended short line operations (
see
Verified Notice 4), and CHPR explains that it and UP now have executed a formal interchange agreement and have continued discussions regarding interline service (Reply 13 (stating that the parties “are forging ahead with other interline service arrangements consistent with UP's acceptance of CHPR's intended common carrier status”);
id.
at 26 (referring to “active, ongoing commercial discussions regarding the handling of traffic in interline service” and asserting that “UP has been highly receptive here”)).
Further, CHPR has pledged that it “will acquire the administrative identifiers and operational assets in the ordinary course of business as it acts upon its permissive authority,” (Reply 13-14), and indicates that it has been making progress on those efforts since the exemption took effect (
id.
at 25 (asserting that it is in the process of obtaining SCAC registration, developing common carrier tariffs, and coordinating with the Railroad Retirement Board));
see Riverview Trenton R.R.—Pet. for Exemption from
49 U.S.C. 10901
to Acquire & Operate a Rail Line in Wayne Cnty., Mich.,
FD 34040, slip op. at 3-4 (STB served Nov. 30, 2007) (carrier's delay in beginning operations was not a basis to revoke the exemption where it was taking “steps . . . to restore rail service” and appeared to “remain[ ] committed to instituting the proposed rail service”). Moreover, CHPR has repeatedly affirmed that it “fully understands its statutory obligations to hold itself out to the public as a common carrier” and that it “stands ready” to provide its services and Facility access to third parties upon reasonable demand. (Reply 12;
see id.
at 3, 23-24, 26);
Townline Rail Terminal, LLC,
FD 36575, slip op. at 4-5 (STB served Nov. 15, 2023) (referring to exemption filer's repeated statements “that it would offer common carrier rail service to the public for compensation”). CHPR has also represented that after it announced its plans to commence common carrier service, prospective third-party customers “promptly came forward seeking opportunities to transload additional, non-asphalt commodities,” which it states demonstrates “a plausible local need” for its intended services. (Reply 28-29.) The SGEs have not provided the Board with any basis to discredit these sworn statements.
[
8
]
Finally, to support their argument that CHPR is not a rail carrier, the SGEs primarily rely on the Board's decision in
(
printed page 68224)
Hi Tech Trans, LLC—Petition for Declaratory Order—Newark, N.J.,
FD 34192 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 5 (STB served Aug. 14, 2003) (transloading activities not within the Board's jurisdiction where, among other things, activities were “not performed by a rail carrier or under the auspices of a rail carrier holding itself out as providing those services”). However,
Hi Tech
is not applicable. Unlike the third-party transloader there, which operated a transloading facility located on a rail carrier's property and was not itself a rail carrier, CHPR has stated that it will hold itself out to the public as a rail carrier and has sought operating authority to do so.
[
9
]
Therefore, the Board finds that CHPR did not materially mislead the Board or omit material information and will deny the SGEs' request to declare the exemption void ab initio.
Request To Revoke Exemption
The SGEs claim that even if the Board does not conclude that the verified notice was deliberately false or misleading, the Petition shows that “the Board did not fully understand the situation on the ground when it issued its decision” and that this is “not a simple or straightforward transaction.” (Pet. 15;
see id.
at 19 (stating that the “circumstances concerning these so-called new railroad operations are too complicated to be handled in a notice of exemption”).) Accordingly, they claim that “it would be proper for the Board to . . . revoke the exemption.” (
Id.
at 15.) CHPR responds that the SGEs have failed to demonstrate that regulating CHPR would advance or support the RTP objectives. (Reply 15.)
However, the SGEs have not demonstrated that regulation is necessary to carry out the RTP.
See
49 U.S.C. 10502(d)
;
49 CFR 1121.4(f)
(“[t]he person seeking revocation has the burden of showing that the revocation criteria of
49 U.S.C. 10502(d)
have been met”). As CHPR points out, the SGEs have not asserted that regulation is necessary to carry out the RTP or otherwise tried to show that CHPR's operations will harm the national rail network, threaten competitive service, or harm shippers. (Reply 15.) Accordingly, the Board will decline to revoke the exemption on the basis that regulation is necessary to carry out the RTP.
For the reasons set forth above, the Petition will be denied, and accordingly, the Board will not institute a proceeding under
49 U.S.C. 10502(d)
.
It is ordered:
1. The Board declines to institute a proceeding under
49 U.S.C. 10502(d)
.
2. The Petition is denied.
3. The SGEs' request for leave to file a rebuttal is denied.
4. This decision will be published in the
Federal Register
.
5. This decision is effective on its date of service.
Decided: October 27, 2026.
By the Board, Board Members Fuchs, Hedlund, Kloster, and Schultz.
Zantori Dickerson,
Clearance Clerk.

,” (

49 CFR 1104.13(c)
.
Kan. & Okla. R.R.—Lease & Operation Exemption with Interchange Commitment—Union Pac. R.R.,
FD 36849, slip op. at 7 (STB served Mar. 20, 2026) (citing
Sunflower State Indus. Ry.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,

                         According to the SGEs, a closed gate and/or fence runs across the tracks at the Facility. (
                        See 
                         Pet. 12 (citing Pet., Ex. F (photos dated July 17, 2026)).) The SGEs similarly describe the Facility's prior owner as “a behind the fence shipper facility that was rail served by” UP. (
Id.
at 13.)
Back to Citation

                         CHPR asserts that if any customers require intermediate storage, it is possible to provide that “without triggering California subdivision laws,” as the SGEs appear to suggest. (Reply 28;
see
Pet. 12.) According to CHPR, “customers can contract for the throughput of asphaltic oil via” the existing storage tanks, or they could “execute simple facility lease agreements for the large on-site warehouse or individual storage tanks to accommodate 
                        
                        completely different rail-borne products.” (Reply 28.) CHPR states that it is “in preliminary discussions with third-party construction companies to provide exactly these services.” (
Id.
)
Back to Citation

9.
    
                         The Board has revoked exemptions where there was specific evidence indicating that a transaction was merely a sham to preempt state or local condemnation actions and the record raised significant doubt as to whether the exemption-holder ever intended to initiate rail service.
See, e.g., Milwaukee Ind. Trade Ctr., LLC—Acquis. & Operation Exemption—Line Owned by Milwaukee Ind. Trade Ctr., LLC,
FD 35133, slip op. at 7-8 (STB served June 16, 2010);
Jefferson Terminal R.R.—Acquis. & Operation Exemption—Crown Enters., Inc.,
5 ST.B. 461, 465 (2001). Here, that is not the case. Even though CHPR may have “sought common carrier status in part” to obtain preemption, there is no specific evidence on the record that its efforts to serve as a common carrier are not legitimate and thus there is no basis here for the Board to find that the verified notice was void ab initio or to revoke the exemption. Accordingly, while CHPR's failure to disclose the existence of its dispute with the SGEs was not materially misleading, earlier disclosure could have allowed the Board to address this concern more expeditiously.

Department of Homeland Security
U.S. Customs and Border Protection
19 CFR Part 4
[CBP Dec. 26-18]
RIN 1651-AB68
AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection; the Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This document amends U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) regulations by adding the Republic of Malta (Malta) to the list of countries whose pleasure vessels may be issued U.S. cruising licenses. The U.S. Department of State has notified CBP that yachts used and employed exclusively as pleasure vessels and belonging to any resident of the United States are allowed to arrive at and depart from Maltese ports, and to cruise in Maltese waters without complying with formal entry and clearance procedures. Therefore, CBP is extending reciprocal cruising privileges to Maltese-flagged pleasure vessels.
DATES:
This amendment is effective October 29, 2026. These reciprocal privileges became applicable for Malta as of June 10, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
W. Richmond Beevers, Chief, Cargo
(
printed page 68029)
Security, Carriers and Restricted Merchandise Branch, Regulations and Rulings, Office of Trade, (202) 325-0084,
ccrbranchcomments@cbp.dhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Under
46 U.S.C. 60504
, the Secretary of Homeland Security (Secretary) may allow foreign-flagged yachts used only for pleasure to arrive at and depart from U.S. ports and cruise in U.S. waters without paying any duties or fees, provided that the President is satisfied that the foreign country allows yachts owned by U.S. residents and used only for pleasure to arrive at and depart from its ports and cruise in its waters without entering, clearing, or paying any duties or fees. The statute also provides the Secretary discretion to require foreign yachts to obtain cruising licenses and to prescribe the form and conditions of those licenses.
See
46 U.S.C. 60504
;
Public Law 109-304
, 9(b), 120 Stat. 1485, 1680-81 (2006).
The Secretary has delegated to the Commissioner of CBP the authority to prescribe and approve cruising licenses for foreign countries under section 4.94(b) of
title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR).
See
DHS Delegation No. 07010.3, Revision 03.2. Accordingly, CBP has promulgated regulations governing cruising privileges for U.S. and foreign pleasure vessels. Section 4.94(a) of
title 19 of the CFR
provides that U.S.-documented vessels with a recreational endorsement, used exclusively for pleasure, not engaged in any trade, and not violating the customs or navigation laws of the United States, may proceed from port to port in the United States or to foreign ports without clearing, and is not subject to entry upon its arrival in the United States, as long as they have not visited hovering vessels, received merchandise while in the customs waters beyond the territorial sea, or received merchandise while on the high seas. When returning from a foreign port or place, such pleasure vessels are required to report their arrival pursuant to
19 CFR 4.2
.
Generally, foreign-flagged yachts entering the United States are required to comply with the laws applicable to foreign vessels arriving at, departing from, and proceeding between ports of the United States.
See
section 433 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (
19 U.S.C. 1433
). However, CBP may issue cruising licenses to pleasure vessels from certain countries if it is found that yachts of the United States are exempt from formal entry and clearance procedures (
e.g.,
filing manifests, obtaining permits to proceed, and paying entry and clearance fees) in those countries.
See
19 CFR 4.94(b)
.
To obtain a cruising license, the owner of a foreign-flagged yacht must file an application with a port director.
19 CFR 4.94(c)
. If CBP issues a foreign-flagged yacht a cruising license, the yacht may arrive at and depart from the United States and cruise in specified waters of the United States without entering and clearing, without filing manifests and obtaining or delivering permits to proceed, and without the payment of certain fees.
Id.
Such fees include entrance and clearance fees, fees for receiving manifests and granting permits to proceed, duty on tonnage, tonnage tax, or light money.
Id.
A port director may issue a cruising license for a period not to exceed one year.
Id.
Upon arrival at each port in the United States, the master of a foreign-flagged yacht with a cruising license must report the fact of arrival to the appropriate CBP office.
Id.
Section 4.94(b) sets forth the list of countries whose yachts are eligible for cruising licenses.
By diplomatic note dated February 4, 2026, the Embassy of the Republic of Malta, in Washington, DC, informed the Department of State that Malta allows yachts from the United States, used exclusively as pleasure vessels and belonging to any resident of the United States, to arrive at and depart from Maltese ports, and to cruise in the waters of Malta without entering and clearing Maltese Customs and without the payment of any related charges for entry or clearance, dues, duty per ton, tonnage, taxes, or charges for a cruising license. By letter dated June 10, 2026, the Department of State advised the Chief, Cargo Security, Carriers and Restricted Merchandise Branch, CBP, that the Maltese treatment of U.S. pleasure vessels in Maltese waters appears to satisfy the conditions for reciprocal privileges and therefore recommended that Malta be added to the list of countries under the provisions of
19 CFR 4.94(b)
.
The Chief, Cargo Security, Carriers and Restricted Merchandise Branch, has determined that satisfactory evidence has been furnished to grant the reciprocal privileges allowed under
19 CFR 4.94(b)
, effective June 10, 2026. Accordingly, under the authority of
46 U.S.C. 60504
, Maltese-flagged yachts used only for pleasure may proceed from port to port in the United States or to foreign ports without clearing and are not subject to entry upon arrival at a U.S. port, including the payment of any duties or fees. This final rule revises the list of countries in
19 CFR 4.94(b)
to include Malta for the above reasons.
Administrative Procedure Act
CBP has initiated this rulemaking pursuant to an exchange of diplomatic notes between the U.S. Department of State and the Embassy of the Republic of Malta. This rule implements the reciprocal cruising privileges established through that diplomatic exchange. Therefore, this amendment involves a foreign affairs function of the United States and is being made without notice or public procedure under
5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1)
. For the same reason, the 30-day delayed effective date does not apply under
5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1)
.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.

AGENCY:
Postal Regulatory Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Commission is noticing a recent Postal Service filing for the Commission's consideration concerning a negotiated service agreement. This notice informs the public of the filing, invites public comment, and takes other administrative steps.
DATES:
Comments are due:
November 3, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Submit comments electronically via the Commission's Filing Online system at
https://www.prc.gov
.
Those who cannot submit comments electronically should contact the person identified in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section by telephone for advice on filing alternatives.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
David A. Trissell, General Counsel, at 202-789-6820.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Table of Contents
I. Introduction
II. Public Proceeding(s)
III. Summary Proceeding(s)
I. Introduction
Pursuant to
39 CFR 3041.405
, the Commission gives notice that the Postal Service filed request(s) for the Commission to consider matters related to Competitive negotiated service agreement(s). The request(s) may propose the addition of a negotiated service agreement from the Competitive product list or the modification of an existing product currently appearing on the Competitive product list.
The public portions of the Postal Service's request(s) can be accessed via the Commission's website (
http://www.prc.gov
). Non-public portions of the Postal Service's request(s), if any, can be accessed through compliance with the requirements of
39 CFR 3011.301
.
[
1
]
Section II identifies the docket number(s) associated with each Postal Service request, if any, that will be reviewed in a public proceeding as defined by
39 CFR 3010.101(p)
, the title of each such request, the request's acceptance date, and the authority cited by the Postal Service for each request. For each such request, the Commission appoints an officer of the Commission to represent the interests of the general public in the proceeding, pursuant to
39 U.S.C. 505
and
39 CFR 3000.114
(Public Representative). The Public Representative does not represent any individual person, entity or particular point of view, and, when Commission attorneys are appointed, no attorney-client relationship is established. Section II also establishes comment deadline(s) pertaining to each such request.
The Commission invites comments on whether the Postal Service's request(s) identified in Section II, if any, are consistent with the policies of title 39. Applicable statutory and regulatory requirements include
39 U.S.C. 3632
,
39 U.S.C. 3633
,
39 U.S.C. 3642
,
39 CFR part 3035
, and
39 CFR part 3041
. Comment deadline(s) for each such request, if any, appear in Section II.
Section III identifies the docket number(s) associated with each Postal Service request, if any, to add a standardized distinct product to the Competitive product list or to amend a standardized distinct product, the title of each such request, the request's acceptance date, and the authority cited by the Postal Service for each request. Standardized distinct products are negotiated service agreements that are variations of one or more Competitive products, and for which financial models, minimum rates, and classification criteria have undergone advance Commission review.
See
39 CFR 3041.110(n)
;
39 CFR 3041.205(a)
. Such requests are reviewed in summary proceedings pursuant to
39 CFR 3041.325(c)(2)
and
39 CFR 3041.505(f)(1)
. Pursuant to
39 CFR 3041.405(c)-(d)
, the Commission does not appoint a Public Representative or request public comment in proceedings to review such requests.

title: Alaska Underground Injection Control (UIC) Program; Class VI Primacy
abstract: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or the Agency) has received a complete Underground Injection Control (UIC) application from the State of Alaska, requesting primary enforcement responsibility (primacy) for Class VI injection wells under Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) section 1422. The EPA's approval of the State's UIC program primacy application would allow the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission (AOGCC) to issue and enforce compliance with UIC Class VI permits for injection wells used for geologic carbon sequestration. In this action, the EPA proposes to approve Alaska's application to implement the UIC program for Class VI injection wells located within the State, except those located within Indian country and those located within areas of exclusive Federal jurisdiction.

Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Proposed rule; notice of public hearing.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or the Agency) has received a complete Underground Injection Control (UIC) application from the State of Alaska, requesting primary enforcement responsibility (primacy) for Class VI injection wells under Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) section 1422. The EPA's approval of the State's UIC program primacy application would allow the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission (AOGCC) to issue and enforce compliance with UIC Class VI permits for injection wells used for geologic carbon sequestration. In this action, the EPA proposes to approve Alaska's application to implement the UIC program for Class VI injection wells located within the State, except those located within Indian country and those located within areas of exclusive Federal jurisdiction.

II. Introduction
A. Federal UIC Program and Primary Enforcement Authority (Primacy)
The SDWA protects public health by regulating the nation's public drinking water supply, including both surface and groundwater sources. The SDWA requires the EPA to develop minimum requirements for effective State and Tribal UIC programs to prevent underground injection of fluids (such as water, wastewater, brines from oil and gas production, and carbon dioxide) from endangering underground sources of drinking water (USDWs). In general, USDWs are aquifers or parts of aquifers that supply a public water system or contain enough groundwater to supply a public water system. See
40 CFR 144.3
(defining USDW).
The EPA's UIC program regulates various aspects of an injection well project throughout the lifetime of the project. These regulated aspects include technical elements such as site characterization, construction, operation, and testing and monitoring through site closure. The UIC program also includes well permitting, site inspections, and reporting to ensure well owners and operators comply with UIC permits and regulations.
The SDWA section 1421 directs the EPA to establish requirements that States, territories, and federally recognized Tribes (hereafter referred to as applicants) must meet to be granted primary enforcement responsibility or “primacy” for implementing a UIC program, including a Class VI program.
42 U.S.C. 300h
. An applicant seeking primacy under SDWA section 1422 for a Class VI program must demonstrate to the EPA that the applicant's proposed Class VI program meets the Federal requirements for protecting USDWs promulgated by the EPA pursuant to SDWA section 1421.
42 U.S.C. 300h—300h-1
. An applicant must demonstrate, among other things, that it has jurisdiction over underground injection and that it possesses the administrative, civil, and criminal enforcement authorities required by the EPA's implementing regulations. See
40 CFR part 145, subpart B
. After the EPA approves UIC primacy for a State, the State's UIC program may later be revised with EPA approval. See
40 CFR 145.32
.
The EPA comprehensively evaluates each primacy application in accordance with SDWA section 1422 and the EPA's implementing regulations to determine whether the applicant (in this instance, the State of Alaska) has satisfactorily demonstrated that it has adopted and will implement a UIC program that meets applicable regulatory requirements in
40 CFR parts 144
,
145
, and
146
.
B. Class VI Wells Under the UIC Program
Class VI wells are used to inject carbon dioxide into deep rock formations for long-term underground storage, also known as geologic sequestration. The geologic sequestration of carbon dioxide in UIC Class VI wells is used as part of carbon capture and storage for carbon dioxide emissions from industrial sources. Class VI injection wells are regulated under a SDWA permitting framework that provides multiple safeguards that work together to protect USDWs.
Owners or operators that seek to inject carbon dioxide underground for the purpose of geologic sequestration must demonstrate to the permitting authority that their proposed injection well and injection activities will meet all regulatory requirements and obtain a Class VI permit for each well. The UIC Class VI program requires applicants to meet technical, financial, and managerial requirements to obtain a Class VI permit, including:
Site characterization to ensure the geology in the project area will contain the carbon dioxide within the zone where it is authorized to be injected.
Modeling to delineate the predicted area influenced by injection activities through the lifetime of the project.
Evaluation of the delineated area to ensure all potential pathways for fluid movement outside the authorized injection zone have been identified and addressed through corrective action.
Well construction requirements that ensure the Class VI injection well will not leak carbon dioxide.
Testing and monitoring throughout the life of the project, including after carbon dioxide injection has ended. Requirements include, for example, testing to ensure physical integrity of the well, monitoring for seismic activity near the injection site, monitoring of injection pressure and flow, chemical analysis of the carbon dioxide stream that is being injected, and monitoring the extent of the injected carbon dioxide plume and the surrounding area (
e.g.,
ground water) to ensure the carbon dioxide is contained as predicted.
Operating requirements (
e.g.,
injection pressure limitations) to ensure the injection activity will not endanger USDWs.
Financial assurance mechanisms sufficient to cover the costs for all phases of the geologic sequestration project including the post-injection site care period and until site closure has been approved by the permitting authority.
An emergency and remedial response plan to protect USDWs.
Reporting of all testing and monitoring results to the permitting authority to ensure the well is operating in compliance with all permit requirements.
The permitting authority ensures that these protective requirements are included in each Class VI permit. A draft of each Class VI permit is made available to the public for comment before the permitting authority decides whether to issue a final permit.

III. Legal Authorities
SDWA section 1421 requires the EPA to promulgate Federal requirements for effective State UIC programs to prevent underground injection activities that endanger USDWs.
42 U.S.C. 300h(b)(1)
. SDWA section 1422 requires that a State seeking primacy demonstrate to the EPA that it has adopted (after notice and public hearing) and will implement a UIC program that meets the requirements that the EPA promulgated under SDWA section 1421.
42 U.S.C. 300h-1(b)(1)(A)(i)
. The statutory authority for this proposed rule approving Alaska's UIC Class VI primacy program is SDWA sections 1422 and 1450,
42 U.S.C. 300h-1
and
300j-9
.
As directed by the SDWA, the EPA has promulgated regulations setting forth the applicable procedures and substantive requirements for applicants seeking primacy for UIC programs under SDWA section 1422. The regulations in
40 CFR part 144
outline general program requirements that each State must meet to obtain primacy. The regulations in
40 CFR part 145
specify the procedures the EPA will follow in approving, reviewing, and withdrawing State UIC programs, and outlines the elements and provisions that a State must include in its application for primacy. The EPA regulation at
40 CFR part 145
also includes requirements for State UIC permitting procedures (by reference to certain provisions of
40 CFR parts 124
and
144
), compliance evaluation programs, and enforcement authority, as well as requirements for sharing information between the EPA and the State. The regulations in 40 CFR part

IV. Alaska's Application for UIC Class VI Primacy
A. Background
On May 22, 2026, Alaska submitted a complete application for primary enforcement responsibility for Class VI wells under the authority of SDWA section 1422. Alaska's UIC primacy application includes a description of the State's proposed UIC Class VI program, copies of all State legal authorities and forms, applicable statutes and regulations, statement of legal authority from Alaska's Attorney General, a summary of Alaska's public participation activities, and a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) between Alaska and the EPA's Region 10 Administrator. The EPA reviewed the application for completeness and performed a technical and legal evaluation of the application materials to assess and confirm that Alaska's proposed UIC Class VI program meets Federal requirements.
B. Public Participation Activities Conducted by Alaska
In August 2024, AOGCC published notice on its intent to apply for Class VI primacy. In the AOGCC notice, AOGCC also shared that it was considering revising its regulations as a result of House Bill 50 (signed by the Governor on July 31, 2024). House Bill 50 directed AOGCC to regulate carbon storage facilities, including associated wells, within the state. In that notice, AOGCC asked subsurface landowners, industry, and any other interested or affected stakeholders for their ideas and suggestions related to providing an efficient, consistent, cost-effective, and reasonable regulatory framework that incorporates both House Bill 50 and EPA Class VI requirements, before AOGCC began drafting any specific proposed regulations. AOGCC hosted a public hearing on November 7, 2024, in Anchorage, Alaska with the option to participate remotely. No comments were received during the hearing, but six written comments were received. AOGCC responded to each comment and publicly posted its responses. On behalf of AOGCC, the University of Alaska Fairbanks hosted Carbon Storage Townhalls on November 19, 2024, in Fairbanks; on January 3, 2025, in Kenai; on January 22, 2025, in Anchorage; and on March 3, 2025, in Utqiagvik. These town hall events explained carbon capture, use, and storage, and how Alaska's geology and regulatory framework might allow for carbon storage projects.
On November 25, 2025, AOGCC posted a “Notice of Proposed Changes on Carbon Storage and Underground Injection Control Class VI Wells in the Regulations of the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission.” This notice proposed to adopt changes in Title 20 Chapter 25 of the Alaska Administrative Code, dealing with carbon storage as it relates to Class VI wells and establishing a new Class VI UIC program for Alaska. Additionally, this notice gave the opportunity for written comments to be received by January 13, 2026, as well as the opportunity for a public hearing in Anchorage with the option to participate remotely. On January 13, 2026, AOGCC held a public hearing on the proposed Class VI regulations. AOGCC received one comment during the hearing and six written comments. AOGCC responded to each comment and publicly posted its responses. The State regulatory changes were approved and signed by the Office of the Lieutenant Governor on March 19, 2026, and became effective on April 18, 2026.
Prior to applying for EPA approval of a State UIC program, the State must issue public notice of its intent to do so. In April 2026, AOGCC published notices of its intent to adopt and seek approval of a UIC Class VI program and of a related public hearing. AOGCC published the notice in six Alaska newspapers, through its website, and via email distribution to stakeholders. The notice provided the schedule for the hearing and identified the issues on which AOGCC sought public input. On May 14, 2026, AOGCC hosted an in-person hearing with the option to participate remotely. AOGCC received no comments during the hearing and received two written comments. One comment asserted that AOGCC's final regulations and previous response to comments did not resolve issues raised by the commenter during the comment period for the proposed State regulatory changes. These concerns include that funding is inadequate and uncertain to cover the technical expertise and implementation necessary for a Class VI permitting program; that Alaska's fee-shifting statute and rules discourage citizen oversight lawsuits and undermine key elements of the SDWA; that carbon capture and storage is dangerous, energy-intensive, and ineffective; that Alaska's history of oil and gas safety and environmental oversight and enforcement make adding a new permitting program highly risky; and that AOGCC has the responsibility not to pursue Class VI primacy until it can adequately demonstrate an ability to effectively administer the Class VI UIC program. The other comment supported Alaska's pursuit for Class VI primacy. AOGCC publicly responded to both comments.
Documentation of Alaska's public participation activities, including comments received and responses by the AOGCC, can be found in the EPA's Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2026-4588.
C. Summary of the EPA's Comprehensive Evaluation
The EPA evaluates primacy applications in accordance with SDWA section 1422 to determine whether an applicant has satisfactorily demonstrated that it has adopted after reasonable notice and public hearings, and will implement, a UIC program that meets the requirements of
40 CFR parts 144
,
145
, and
146
.
42 U.S.C. 300h-1(b)(1)(A)(i)
. The EPA conducted a comprehensive technical and legal evaluation of Alaska's primacy application to determine whether the State's proposed UIC Class VI program—including State statutes and regulations, program description, State Attorney General's statement, and MOA—meets the requirements of SDWA section 1422 and EPA regulations. Upon review, the EPA determined that Alaska's primacy application demonstrates that the State has adopted and will implement a UIC Class VI program that meets EPA requirements.
The EPA evaluated Alaska's UIC Class VI program description for consistency with
40 CFR 145.23
, which specifies the information that must be included as part of the program description. The EPA's evaluation of the UIC Class VI program description included reviewing the scope, coverage, processes, and organizational structure of the proposed Class VI program. The EPA evaluated Alaska's permitting, administrative, and judicial review procedures relevant to Class VI permits, as well as the State's permit application, reporting, and manifest forms for Class VI permits. The EPA also reviewed the State's UIC compliance evaluation program and enforcement authorities and the State's demonstration that its UIC Class VI program will have adequate in-house staff or access to contractor support for technical areas including site characterization, modeling, well construction and testing, financial responsibility, and regulatory and risk analysis.
The EPA evaluated Alaska's Attorney General's statement related to Class VI for consistency with
40 CFR 145.24
. In an Attorney General's statement, the
(
printed page 68095)
State's top legal officer affirms that applicable State law (
e.g.,
statutes, regulations, and judicial decisions) provides adequate authority to administer the UIC Class VI program as described in the program description and consistent with the EPA's regulatory requirements for UIC programs.
The EPA determined that the Class VI MOA meets the Federal requirements at
40 CFR 145.25
for primacy MOAs. The MOA is the central agreement that establishes the provisions and arrangements between the State and the EPA concerning the administration, implementation, and enforcement of the State UIC Class VI program. The EPA's evaluation of the Class VI MOA included ensuring that the MOA contained the appropriate provisions pertaining to coordination, permitting, compliance monitoring, enforcement, and EPA oversight. For example, the Class VI MOA specifies that the AOGCC and the EPA agree to maintain a high level of cooperation and coordination to ensure successful and effective administration of the UIC Class VI Program.
Alaska has demonstrated that it meets all UIC permitting requirements found in
40 CFR 145.11
for Class VI permits. Alaska's UIC Class VI permitting provisions and technical criteria and standards meet the Federal requirements in
40 CFR parts 124
and
144
through
146
. The State has incorporated necessary procedures, pursuant to
40 CFR 145.12
, to support a robust UIC Class VI compliance evaluation program. Additionally, Alaska has the necessary civil, administrative, and criminal enforcement authorities pursuant to
40 CFR 145.13
. Alaska's UIC Class VI regulations regarding permitting, inspection, operation, monitoring, reporting, and recordkeeping meet Federal requirements found in
40 CFR parts 145
and
146
.
As a result of this comprehensive review, the EPA is proposing to approve Alaska's UIC Class VI program primacy application because the EPA has determined that the application meets all applicable requirements for Class VI primacy approval under SDWA section 1422 and because the State has demonstrated that it will implement a UIC program in a manner consistent with the SDWA and all applicable UIC regulations.
V. The EPA's Proposed Action
A. Incorporation by Reference
The EPA is proposing to approve the State of Alaska's UIC program primacy application for Class VI injection wells in the State, except for those located within Indian country and those wells located within areas of exclusive Federal jurisdiction. If finalized, this action would amend
40 CFR part 147, subpart C
, and incorporate by reference Alaska's EPA-approved statutes and implementing regulations that contain standards, requirements, and procedures applicable to UIC Class VI well owners or operators within the State. Any provisions incorporated by reference, as well as all permit conditions issued pursuant to such provisions, are enforceable by the EPA pursuant to SDWA section 1423.
40 CFR 147.1(e)
. The EPA would continue to administer the UIC program in Alaska for Class I, III, IV, and V wells and for all well classes within Indian country and within areas of exclusive federal jurisdiction.
The EPA compiled the applicable Alaska statutes and regulations proposed to be incorporated by reference into
40 CFR 147.100
in a document titled “Alaska SDWA § 1422 Underground Injection Control Program Class VI Statutes and Regulations,” dated August 26, 2026. This compilation is publicly available at
https://www.regulations.gov
in the EPA's Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2026-4855 for this proposed rulemaking. The EPA also proposes to codify a table in
40 CFR 147.100
listing the EPA-approved Alaska Statutes and Regulations for Class VI wells that the EPA would incorporate by reference.
B. The EPA's Oversight
Upon approval, the EPA will oversee Alaska's administration of its Class VI UIC program. The EPA will require quarterly reports on instances of permittee non-compliance and annual UIC performance reports pursuant to
40 CFR 144.8
. The MOA between the EPA Region 10 and AOGCC specifies that the EPA will oversee the State's administration of the UIC Class VI program on a continuing basis to ensure that such administration is consistent with the program MOA, the SDWA and implementing regulations, UIC grant agreements, and other applicable requirements.

AGENCY:
Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS) published an interim final rule on August 4, 2026, and republished on August 28, 2026, that amended its arbitration services regulations to clarify when the Office of Arbitration may decline to issue an arbitration panel, make a direct appointment, or provide related services. This document responds to the comments, clarifies the scope of the rule's threshold inquiry, adds procedural provisions governing notice, written disposition, request dates, and fees, and adopts the interim final rule as a final rule.
DATES:
This final rule is effective October 29, 2026. The amendments to
29 CFR 1404.9
,
1404.10
,
1404.11
, and
1404.12
made by the interim final rule have been in effect since August 4, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
The interim final rule, the comments received, and this final rule are available on FMCS's public website at
www.fmcs.gov
.
The comments received are also available for public inspection, by appointment, at the Office of General Counsel, Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, One Independence Square, 250 E St. SW, Washington, DC 20427.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Anna Davis, General Counsel, Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, (202) 606-3737,
adavis@fmcs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
A. FMCS's Arbitration Services and the Interim Final Rule
FMCS maintains a Roster of Arbitrators and, through its Office of Arbitration (OA), furnishes panels of names of Roster arbitrators, makes direct appointments, and provides related services to parties to collective bargaining agreements under
29 CFR part 1404
, which FMCS issues under Title II of the Labor Management Relations Act of 1947,
29 U.S.C. 171-183
.
See
29 CFR 1404.1
. Arbitrators listed on the Roster are not FMCS employees; once an arbitrator is selected or appointed, the arbitrator's relationship is solely with the parties.
29 CFR 1404.4(c)
.
FMCS has no power to compel parties to appear before an arbitrator, to enforce an agreement to arbitrate, to compel parties to arbitrate any issue, to influence or set aside an arbitrator's decision, or to compel, deny, or modify the payment of an arbitrator's compensation.
29 CFR 1404.9(c)
. OA may decline to furnish a panel or make an appointment where a request is overly burdensome or impracticable, and may decline to service a request from a party based on the party's prior non-payment of arbitrator fees or other behavior that constrains the spirit or operation of the arbitration process.
29 CFR 1404.9(d)
. FMCS “retains its authority and responsibility to assure that the needs of the parties using its services are served” and may establish procedures for the preparation of panels and the appointment of arbitrators to that end.
29 CFR 1404.4(d)
.
Before the interim final rule, § 1404.9(b) provided that a request for a panel of seven arbitrators, “whether joint or unilateral, will be honored,” while providing that requests for a panel of other than seven names, for a direct appointment, or for special qualifications or other special service would be honored only if jointly submitted or authorized by both parties, and that OA takes no position on the status of the agreement to arbitrate, the arbitrability of the dispute, or the terms of the parties' contract by issuing a panel or appointing an arbitrator. Section 1404.10 provided that OA will not decide the merits of a claim by either party that a dispute is not subject to arbitration.
On August 4, 2026, FMCS published an interim final rule with request for comments at
91 FR 49273
. The interim final rule restructured § 1404.9(b) into four paragraphs. Paragraph (b)(1) retained the rule that, upon request, OA will refer a randomly selected panel of seven arbitrators to parties to an agreement to arbitrate or to engage in fact-finding, or where labor arbitration or fact-finding may be provided by statute.
Paragraph (b)(2) provides that a request for a panel may be joint or unilateral unless part 1404, applicable law, or the parties' agreement requires joint authorization for the requested service, and retained the requirement of joint authorization for panels of other than seven names, direct appointments, special qualifications, and other special services.
Paragraph (b)(3) provides that OA may conduct a limited threshold inquiry to determine whether issuing a panel, making a direct appointment, or providing related arbitration services would be inconsistent with applicable law, a court order, or FMCS's statutory or regulatory authority; that OA may request from the parties the agreement, statutory provision, regulation, court order, written authorization, or other information necessary to make that determination; and that, following the inquiry, FMCS may issue the panel or appointment, decline to provide the requested service, hold the request in abeyance, or take other administratively appropriate action.
Paragraph (b)(4) provides that OA's issuance of a panel or appointment, refusal to issue one, or decision to hold a request in abeyance does not constitute a decision on the validity of any collective bargaining agreement, the merits of any grievance, the arbitrability of any dispute, or the rights or obligations of the parties under any agreement or law. The interim final rule made conforming amendments to § 1404.10 (arbitrability), § 1404.11(b) and (c) (nominations of arbitrators and additional panels), and § 1404.12(b) and (c) (selection and appointment), and updated the nondiscrimination sentence in § 1404.11(b). 91 FR at 49274-75, 49277-78.
The interim final rule took effect on August 4, 2026, with comments due September 3, 2026. On August 27, 2026, the docket for the rule on
www.regulations.gov
displayed as
(
printed page 68031)
closed to comments before the comment period had ended. To ensure that no interested person was denied the opportunity to comment, FMCS republished the interim final rule in full on August 28, 2026, at
91 FR 55473
, directed that comments be submitted to FMCS's Office of General Counsel by email or mail, and extended the comment period to September 28, 2026. The regulatory text and preamble of the republished rule were identical to those published on August 4. FMCS accepted every comment received on or before September 28, 2026.
FMCS found good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
to issue the rule without prior notice and comment and under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
to make it effective upon publication, because the sentence in former § 1404.9(b) stating that every joint or unilateral request “will be honored” could be read to require OA to furnish panels and make appointments regardless of whether doing so was consistent with applicable law, a court order, or FMCS's authority, and because delay would perpetuate uncertainty about FMCS's obligations when presented with requests raising threshold legal objections. 91 FR at 49276. FMCS invited comment on all aspects of the rule and stated that, after considering timely comments, it would revise, withdraw, or confirm the rule in a subsequent document.
B. The Circumstances That Gave Rise to the Rule
Section 7103(b)(1) of Title 5 authorizes the President to exclude an agency or subdivision from coverage under chapter 71 of Title 5, the Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute, upon determining that the agency or subdivision has as a primary function intelligence, counterintelligence, investigative, or national security work and that chapter 71 cannot be applied to it in a manner consistent with national security requirements and considerations.
Executive Order 14251
,
Exclusions From Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs,
90 FR 14553
(Apr. 3, 2025), and
Executive Order 14343
,
Further Exclusions From the Federal Labor-Management Relations Program,
90 FR 42683
(Sept. 3, 2025), exercised that authority with respect to numerous agencies and subdivisions.
Executive Order 14251
further directed excluded agencies, upon termination of their collective bargaining agreements, to terminate their participation in pending grievance proceedings under
5 U.S.C. 7121
. Determinations under section 7103(b)(1) are committed to the President's judgment, and the courts have declined to review them under the Administrative Procedure Act.
See A.F.G.E.
v.
Reagan,
870 F.2d 723, 727-28 (D.C. Cir. 1989);
Dep't of Defense
v.
F.L.R.A.,
685 F.2d 641, 650 (D.C. Cir. 1982) (holding that section 7103(b)(1) “is for the President alone to invoke”). Legal interpretations and directions issued by the President are controlling on the officers and employees of the Executive Branch. Exec. Order 14215, § 7,
90 FR 10447
,
10449
(Feb. 24, 2025).
When an agency is excluded under section 7103(b)(1), chapter 71 does not apply to it. The agency has no statutory duty to bargain, its employees have no statutory right to a negotiated grievance procedure, and the statutory authorization for binding grievance arbitration in section 7121(b)(1)(C)(iii), which the commenters correctly identify as the source of a union's right to invoke arbitration unilaterally, does not reach it. During 2025 and 2026, many excluded agencies terminated their collective bargaining agreements. The validity of the Executive Orders and of particular terminations has been and remains the subject of litigation in several courts. As of the date of this rule, the Executive Orders remain in effect, and FMCS ensures compliance with applicable court orders related to the Executive Orders through seeking federal agencies' consent as the source of authority for the proceeding itself.
Beginning in the spring of 2026, OA received a growing number of unilateral requests for panels, additional panels, and appointments in matters in which the responding Federal agency asserted that it had been excluded from chapter 71, that the applicable agreement had been terminated, and that it could not lawfully participate in the requested arbitration. Requesting parties, in turn, cited the “will be honored” sentence of former § 1404.9(b) as obligating FMCS to furnish the panel and appoint the arbitrator regardless of the agency's exclusion. On April 22, 2026, FMCS's General Counsel issued a guidance memorandum to the Office of Arbitration,
Aligning FMCS's Arbitration Services with Executive Orders 14251 and 14343,
which FMCS posted on its public website. The memorandum directed that, for agencies identified in the Executive Orders, OA confirm the agency's consent before issuing a panel, hold the request in abeyance if consent was not given, preserve the request's submission date, and charge no fee until the request could be processed. The memorandum stated that FMCS's practice as to agencies not affected by the Executive Orders was unchanged. The regulatory language of former § 1404.9(b) was at the center of a subsequent legal challenge to that memorandum. The interim final rule followed.
II. Comments Received and FMCS's Responses
A. Overview
FMCS received five comments during the comment period, each from one or more labor organizations representing Federal employees. The comments are posted on FMCS's public website, and FMCS refers to them below by number in the order received: Comment 1 (September 10, 2026), submitted jointly by three national labor organizations; Comment 2 (September 20, 2026), submitted by a local of a national labor organization; Comment 3 (September 23, 2026), submitted by an officer of a local union representing employees of a Federal medical facility; Comment 4 (September 28, 2026), submitted jointly by two national labor organizations; and Comment 5 (September 28, 2026), submitted by a coalition of Federal-sector labor organizations joined by twenty-three affiliated organizations.
All five comments oppose the rule. Comments 1, 4, and 5 ask FMCS to withdraw it. Comment 2 asks FMCS to withdraw it or, at minimum, to limit the threshold inquiry to situations involving a clear and controlling legal prohibition or court order. Comment 3 asks FMCS to revise the rule and proposes eight specific changes directed principally at the scope, timing, transparency, and reviewability of the threshold inquiry.
FMCS has considered each comment in full. For the reasons set out below, FMCS concludes that the comments do not identify a basis for withdrawing the rule. They do, however, identify respects in which the scope of the threshold inquiry and the process that accompanies it should be stated more precisely in the regulatory text, and FMCS has made the changes described in section III of this preamble in response. Before addressing the comments individually, FMCS addresses four issues that run through all of them.
B. Issues Common to the Comments
1. The rule does not authorize FMCS to decide arbitrability.
Every commenter contends that the threshold inquiry is, in substance, an arbitrability determination that Congress assigned to arbitrators. Comments 1, 4, and 5 rely on
5 U.S.C. 7121(a)(1)
, which requires every negotiated grievance procedure to provide for the settlement of grievances “including questions of arbitrability,” and on the deference that the Federal Labor Relations Authority (the
(
printed page 68032)
Authority) and the courts accord an arbitrator's construction of the agreement.
See Nat'l Weather Serv. Emps. Org.
v.
F.L.R.A.,
966 F.3d 875, 881-82 (D.C. Cir. 2020).
FMCS does not dispute any of that law. It does not apply to the question the rule addresses. “Arbitrability,” in the sense in which chapter 71, the Authority, and the courts use the term, is whether a particular grievance may be heard by the arbitrator: whether it falls within the scope of the negotiated procedure, whether it was timely filed and processed, whether it is excluded by a statutory exception in section 7121(c), whether the grievant elected another forum, and similar questions of contract and statute that govern the dispute between the parties. The rule leaves every one of those questions to the arbitrator. Section 1404.10 continues to provide that OA will not decide the merits of a claim that a dispute is not subject to arbitration; § 1404.9(b)(4) provides that no action OA takes on a request constitutes a decision on the arbitrability of any dispute; and this final rule adds to § 1404.9(b)(3) an express statement that a party's contention that a grievance lacks merit, is untimely, or is not arbitrable does not, by itself, establish that FMCS may not provide the requested service.
The threshold inquiry concerns a different question: whether FMCS, an agency of the Executive Branch, may lawfully take the administrative action requested of it. That question arises where a court has stayed or enjoined the arbitration or the obligation to arbitrate; where the President has excluded the responding agency from chapter 71 under
5 U.S.C. 7103(b)(1)
, the agreement has been terminated, and the agency has, as the President directed, terminated its participation in the proceeding; or where part 1404 itself requires joint authorization for the service requested. None of those is a question of whether the grievance is arbitrable under the parties' agreement. An arbitrator cannot answer any of them with respect to FMCS, because, as Comment 5 emphasizes at length, FMCS is not a party to the agreement, not a party to the proceeding, and not subject to the arbitrator's jurisdiction. An arbitrator's award that a grievance is arbitrable binds the parties; it does not and cannot determine whether a Federal agency that is not before the arbitrator may lawfully furnish a service.
The commenters' position, taken to its conclusion, is that FMCS must issue a panel and appoint an arbitrator in every case, including where a court has enjoined the arbitration, because the effect of the injunction is a question for the arbitrator. No commenter accepts that conclusion. Comment 2 states that if “an actual court order or clear law prohibits FMCS from providing a panel, FMCS obviously must follow the law.” Comment 3 agrees that “a binding order applicable to a request cannot be ignored,” that FMCS “cannot ignore an applicable legal bar or a court order,” and that “a genuinely applicable prohibition should be honored.” Comments 1, 4, and 5, for their part, nowhere contend that FMCS must furnish a panel in the face of a court order forbidding the arbitration. Once that is conceded, the disagreement is not about whether FMCS may inquire into its own authority before acting but about how narrowly that inquiry is defined and what process accompanies it. Those are the matters FMCS has addressed in this final rule.
2. No commenter identifies any law that requires FMCS to furnish a panel on unilateral request, and the commenters' own statutory analysis confirms that the language characterized as an obligation existed only in FMCS's regulation.
Comment 5 argues, in detail, that neither Title II of the Labor Management Relations Act nor the Administrative Dispute Resolution Act (ADRA) reaches Federal-sector grievance arbitration, and that chapter 71 assigns FMCS a role only in the resolution of bargaining impasses under
5 U.S.C. 7119
. Comment 4 likewise observes that neither chapter 71 nor FMCS's enabling act mentions FMCS in connection with grievance arbitration. Comment 5 states that FMCS “appears in none of” the provisions of chapter 71 governing grievances, arbitrability, review of awards, or unfair labor practices.
FMCS agrees that chapter 71 imposes no obligation on FMCS with respect to grievance arbitration. Section 7121 requires agencies and exclusive representatives to negotiate a grievance procedure ending in binding arbitration; it does not direct them to obtain the arbitrator from FMCS, and many agreements do not. Parties are free to select any arbitrator or arbitration procedure acceptable to them.
29 CFR 1404.8
. FMCS furnishes names from its Roster as a service, for a fee, to parties who choose to use it. The commenters' demonstration that no statute requires FMCS to provide that service is a demonstration that the language characterized as an obligation to honor every unilateral request existed in one place only: the sentence of former § 1404.9(b) that the interim final rule removed. What has been characterized as a regulatory commitment that FMCS made, FMCS may amend, subject to the requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). The commenters do not identify a statute that forbids the amendment, because there is none.
Comment 5's observation that FMCS has, in different documents over the years, cited different provisions of the Labor Management Relations Act as the basis for its Roster does not alter this conclusion. Whether FMCS's furnishing of Roster services to Federal-sector parties rests on the declaration of policy in
29 U.S.C. 171(b)
, which makes governmental facilities available for “voluntary arbitration,” or on
29 U.S.C. 173(f)
, which authorizes FMCS to make its services available to Federal agencies and directs it to consult with the interagency body designated under
5 U.S.C. 573
in maintaining rosters of neutrals and arbitrators, each provision authorizes the service and neither obligates it. The phrase “voluntary arbitration” in section 171(b), and the title of subpart A of part 1404 (“Arbitration Policy”), reflect the premise on which FMCS has always operated: that it facilitates arbitration to which the parties have lawfully agreed. Neither provision contemplates that FMCS will constitute a tribunal for a proceeding that the law does not authorize.
3. Where chapter 71 applies and an agreement is in effect, section 7121 supplies the authorization for binding arbitration; the rule's discussion of consent and sovereign immunity concerns the circumstance in which chapter 71 does not apply.
Comments 4 and 5 devote considerable attention to the interim final rule's citation of
5 U.S.C. 572(a)
and
(c)
and to its discussion of sovereign immunity. Comment 5 argues that ADRA governs an agency's discretionary election of alternative procedures in its own administrative programs and has nothing to do with a grievance procedure that Congress required the parties to negotiate; that consent under chapter 71 is given when the agreement is executed; and that section 7121, which the interim final rule itself cited, is the statutory authorization that the sovereign immunity principle requires. Comment 4 argues that FMCS has not explained how providing a panel would violate the Constitution.
FMCS agrees with the commenters that, where chapter 71 applies and a collective bargaining agreement with a negotiated grievance procedure is in effect, section 7121(b)(1)(C)(iii) is the statutory authorization for binding arbitration, that authorization permits either party to invoke arbitration alone, and the agency's consent is supplied by the agreement it negotiated. 91 FR at
(
printed page 68033)
49274. In that circumstance, FMCS does not require, and under this rule will not seek, any renewed or case-specific consent from the responding agency before issuing a seven-name panel on a unilateral request. Comment 5 reads the interim final rule as applying an ADRA consent requirement to every Federal-sector grievance. It does not. To remove any doubt, FMCS states here that it does not read
5 U.S.C. 572
to require a Federal agency covered by chapter 71 to consent, case by case, to grievance arbitration under an agreement in effect.
The interim final rule's discussion of consent and sovereign immunity addresses the circumstance in which chapter 71 does not apply. Chapter 71's arbitration provisions are, by their terms, components of the chapter. Section 7121 requires grievance procedures ending in binding arbitration in agreements negotiated under the chapter; section 7122 provides for exceptions to, and the finality of, awards rendered in arbitration “under this chapter”; and the chapter defines a “collective bargaining agreement” as one “entered into as a result of collective bargaining pursuant to the provisions of this chapter.”
5 U.S.C. 7103(a)(8)
,
7121
,
7122
.
Those provisions are not freestanding delegations of arbitral power; they are elements of an integrated statutory scheme whose rights and remedies exist only as Congress created them.
United States
v.
Fausto,
484 U.S. 439, 445 (1988);
Karahalios
v.
Nat'l Fed'n of Fed. Emps., Local 1263,
489 U.S. 527, 531-33 (1989). An arbitrator acting under a negotiated grievance procedure exercises a statutory delegation whose content Congress defined,
Cornelius
v.
Nutt,
472 U.S. 648, 660-63 (1985), not an authority arising from the parties' private agreement. Section 7103(b)(1) authorizes the President to exclude an agency “from coverage under this chapter.” When the President does so, sections 7121 and 7122 no longer apply to the agency, and an agreement that survives as a document no longer carries the statutory character the chapter gave it.
With chapter 71 removed, the governing principles are those of sovereign immunity and the limited authority of Federal officers. The United States may be subjected to a binding adjudication only where Congress has consented, and that consent must be “unequivocally expressed in statutory text.”
Lane
v.
Peña,
518 U.S. 187, 192 (1996);
accord United States
v.
Sherwood,
312 U.S. 584, 586 (1941). No officer can supply that consent by contract, conduct, or acquiescence.
United States
v.
Shaw,
309 U.S. 495, 500-01 (1940);
Minnesota
v.
United States,
305 U.S. 382, 388-89 (1939);
United States
v.
Mitchell,
463 U.S. 206, 215-16 (1983). And an award payable from the Treasury requires an appropriation made by law, for which neither an agency's agreement nor its conduct can substitute. U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 7;
Off. of Pers. Mgmt.
v.
Richmond,
496 U.S. 414, 424-32 (1990).
Congress's enactment of
5 U.S.C. 575
, which authorizes agencies to use binding arbitration only where all parties consent in a written agreement that specifies a maximum award, entered by an official with authority to settle the matter, and subject to guidance issued by the agency head in consultation with the Attorney General, and which supplies its own enforcement and review provisions,
5 U.S.C. 575
,
580
,
581
, reflects the settled understanding that an agency may submit to binding arbitration only where a statute authorizes it, and that Congress legislates expressly when it intends arbitral awards to be enforceable against the sovereign.
See Constitutional Limitations on Federal Government Participation in Binding Arbitration,
19 Op. O.L.C. 208 (1995).
Section 7121 is such a statute for agencies covered by chapter 71. When the President excludes an agency under section 7103(b)(1), that authorization no longer reaches the agency, and the agreement through which the agency gave its consent has, in the cases that gave rise to this rule, been terminated.
