This proposal reflects the EPA's reconsideration of additional aspects of the March 2024 Final Rule, including some of the Agency's prior BSER determinations and the legal and policy positions taken in finalizing those determinations. Upon further review, and in light of information considered since promulgation, the EPA no longer believes that some of the “zero-emission” requirements in NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc are predicated on acceptable assessments of emissions reductions, cost effectiveness, and achievability. In some cases, the March 2024 Final Rule moved from requirements that control 95 percent of emissions to standards stated as “zero-emission” requirements. However, achievability limitations and compliance difficulties, including those the EPA anticipated at the time by building in exemptions and those the Agency did not foresee, suggest that the requirements' emission reductions potential are more modest than previously anticipated. At the same time, the Agency very likely underestimated costs because the actual costs of compliance are likely higher than the EPA anticipated in the March 2024 Final Rule. The resulting reconsideration—taking into account more modest emissions reductions and more significant costs—suggests that significant aspects of some BSER determinations and resulting standards in the March 2024 Final Rule are inappropriate. EPA solicits comment on further considerations relative to the March 2024 Final Rule, such as those petitioners have flagged.
In this action, the EPA proposes the following:
Rescinding the Super Emitter Program in NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, OOOOb, and EG OOOOc based on a change in policy direction, concerns with the authority of the program, and a reassessment of the Program's expected effectiveness in light of new information.
Revising several aspects of NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc based on petitions received on the March 2024 Final Rule. Specifically, the EPA proposes changes to the March 2024 Final Rule requirements to address certain petitioner concerns for liquids unloading, process controllers, pumps, fugitive emissions, storage vessels, covers and CVSs, and equipment leaks at gas plants.
Revising the March 2024 Final Rule requirements related to control devices, such as requirements for continuous burning pilot flames, flame monitoring data deviations, control device alerts, visible emissions test conditions for fugitive emissions, control devices used on a temporary or backup basis, temporary process controllers, and control device categories.
Proposing changes related to requirements for controlling emissions from associated gas from wells producing primarily oil. The EPA is proposing that routing to a sales-line is not an appropriate BSER for these emissions. The Agency is proposing that routing associated gas to a control device or a flare that achieves 95%
(
printed page 68238)
reductions in emissions or greater should be BSER instead.
Proposing to add a new subcategory for certain well sites affected and designated facilities based on a variety of operational conditions. This aspect of the proposal also includes revisions to requirements that apply at certain well sites that address concerns related to the appropriateness of the categorization and the burden associated with complying with the March 2024 Final Rule requirements. Specifically, in this action, the EPA is co-proposing two alternative approaches to subcategorizing well sites:
An option based on marginal and non-marginal well sites that would include reduced requirements for marginal wells. The EPA also solicits comment on an alternative approach to a marginal well site subcategory that would further subcategorize marginal wells based on production levels.
An option based on conventional and non-conventional wells that would include reduced requirements for conventional wells.
Allowing for owners and operators to conduct optical gas imaging (OGI) surveys according to Appendix K for NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, and KKK at gas processing facilities.
Making technical corrections and clarifications to NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, OOOOb, and EG OOOOc.
The EPA solicits comments on its proposed regulatory changes. Within this preamble, the EPA is also soliciting broader comment on further issues relevant to the March 2024 Final Rule and resulting NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc, including both the additional issues raised by reconsideration petitioners for which the EPA is not proposing regulatory changes at this time and any additional issues commenters believe are relevant to the lawfulness, reasonableness, or implementability of the 2024 Final Rule. II. General Information
A. Applicability of This Regulatory Action
The source category that is the subject of this proposal is the Crude Oil and Natural Gas Source Category regulated under CAA section 111, NSPS and EG. The 2022 North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) code for the source category is summarized in table 2. The NAICS codes serve as a guide for readers outlining the entities that this proposed action is likely to affect, if finalized. The NSPS codified in
40 CFR part 60, subpart OOOOb
, are directly applicable to affected facilities that begin construction, reconstruction, or modification after December 6, 2022. As shown in table 2, Federal, State, and local government entities would not be affected by the NSPS action.
This table is not intended to be exhaustive but rather provides a guide for readers regarding entities likely to be affected by the NSPS action with respect to new sources. Other types of entities not listed in the table could also be affected by the NSPS action. To determine whether your entity is affected by any of the NSPS action, you should carefully examine the applicability criteria found in the final NSPS rule. If you have questions regarding the applicability of the NSPS rule to a particular entity, consult the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section, your State air pollution control agency with delegated authority for NSPS, or your EPA Regional Office.
The issuance of the CAA section 111(d) EG in March 2024 did not directly impose binding requirements on existing sources, but instead established requirements applicable to states in developing their plans. While the presumptive standard determined by the EPA is the starting point for a state's standards of performance in its state plan, a state may choose to take into account remaining useful life and other factors in applying a standard of performance to a particular source, consistent with the CAA, the EPA's implementing regulations, and the final EG. The EG codified in
40 CFR part 60, subpart OOOOc
, applies to States in the development, submittal, and implementation of State plans to establish performance standards to reduce emissions of GHGs from designated facilities that are existing sources on or before December 6, 2022. Under the Tribal Authority Rule, eligible Tribes may seek approval to implement a plan under CAA section 111(d) in a manner similar to a State.
[
16
]
Tribes may, but are not required to, seek approval for treatment in a manner similar to a State to develop Tribal implementation plans (TIPs) implementing the EG codified in
40 CFR part 60, subpart OOOOc
. The Tribal Authority Rule authorizes Tribes to develop and implement their own air quality programs, or portions thereof, under the CAA. However, it does not require Tribes to develop a CAA program. Tribes may implement programs that are most relevant to their air quality needs. If a Tribe does not seek and obtain the authority from the EPA to establish a TIP, the EPA has the authority to establish a Federal CAA section 111(d) plan for designated facilities that are located in areas of Indian country.
[
17
]
A Federal plan would apply to all designated facilities located in the areas of Indian country covered by the Federal plan unless and until the EPA approves a TIP applicable to those facilities.

C. Purpose of This Regulatory Action
On March 8, 2024, the EPA finalized NSPS for GHG and VOC emissions from new, modified, and reconstructed sources in this source category, codified
(
printed page 68240)
in
40 CFR 60, subpart OOOOb
(NSPS OOOOb) as well as EG for GHG emissions from existing sources in this source category, codified in 401 CFR 60, subpart OOOOc (EG OOOOc).
Prior to the March 2024 Final Rule, NSPS Subparts for this source category underwent multiple rounds of major policy revisions, technical amendments, and congressional actions. For example, NSPS OOOO (2012) applied only to VOC and sulfur dioxide emissions from new, modified, and reconstructed sources mainly in the upstream oil and gas sector. Although methane wasn't directly regulated, many upstream controls that targeted VOCs—like green completions, tank vapor control, and low-bleed pneumatics—also reduced methane as a co-benefit (“co-control”). In 2016, NSPS OOOOa added methane as a regulated pollutant and expanded coverage to include the midstream, adding requirements for transmission and storage, and additional source types (
e.g.,
leak detection and repair (LDAR) at well sites and compressor stations, pneumatic pumps, compressors, hydraulically fractured oil wells). In 2020, EPA issued a rule titled, “Oil and Natural Gas Sector: Emission Standards for New, Reconstructed, and Modified Sources Review,” September 14, 2020 (2020 Policy Rule), which removed the transmission and storage segment from the NSPS OOOO and OOOOa, rescinding VOC and methane emissions standards for that segment, and rescinded methane emissions standards for the production and processing segments. However, a joint congressional resolution disapproved the 2020 Policy Rule.
More recently, in 2024, NSPS OOOOb clarified the scope and coverage for addressing liquids unloading and certain intermittent emissions and added more stringent standards and methods, such as zero-emitting pneumatics, limits on routine flaring of associated gas at new oil wells, stronger LDAR with advanced detection options, tighter compressor requirements, and a super-emitter response program.
After publication of the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA received, and continued to receive, multiple petitions for reconsideration.

D. Statutory Background and Authority
CAA section 111 authorizes the EPA to list and regulate categories of stationary sources that the Administrator, “in his judgment,” finds that the source category “causes, or contributes significantly to, air pollution which may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare.”
[
21
]
The listing of a source category triggers an obligation to promulgate “standards of performance” for new sources and, under limited circumstances, to prescribe regulations under which States submit plans that establish standards of performance for existing sources.
[
22
]
This provision, along with agencies' authority to reconsider prior regulations, provides the EPA's statutory authority for this proposed action.
[
23
]
CAA section 111(b)(1)(A) authorizes the Administrator to publish, and from time-to-time revise, a list of categories of stationary sources that the Administrator, “in his judgment,” finds “causes, or contributes significantly to, air pollution which may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare.” Once the EPA lists a source category under CAA section 111(b)(1)(A), the EPA must, under CAA section 111(b)(1)(B), establish “standards of performance” for “new sources” in the source category. These standards are referred to as NSPS. The NSPS are national requirements that apply directly to new sources within the relevant source category.
Congress intended the NSPS to work together with the geography-based national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS) program in CAA sections 107-110. Similar to national emission standards for hazardous air pollutants (NESHAPs) that limit emissions of hazardous air pollutants (HAPs) listed and regulated under CAA section 112, NSPS under CAA section 111 apply to a new source regardless of whether the area in which the new source is located is subject to NAAQS-related limitations and requirements. Accordingly, CAA section 111(a)(2) defines a “new source” as “any stationary source, the construction or modification of which is commenced after the publication of regulations (or, if earlier, proposed regulations) prescribing a standard of performance under this section, which will be applicable to such source.” CAA section 111(a)(4) further defines “modification” as “any physical change in, or change in the method of operation of, a stationary source which increases the amount of any air pollutant emitted by such source or which results in the emission of any air pollutant not previously emitted.” While this provision treats modified sources as new sources, the EPA's regulations also treat a source that undergoes “reconstruction,” by substantially replacing its components, as a new source.
[
24
]
CAA section 111(a)(1) defines “standard of performance” as “a standard for emissions of air pollutants” that must be promulgated or revised in a specified manner. When the EPA establishes or revises a performance standard, CAA section 111(a)(1) provides that such standard must “reflect[] the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the best system of emission reduction which (taking into account the cost of achieving such
(
printed page 68241)
reduction and any nonair quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements) the Administrator determines has been adequately demonstrated.” Thus, the term “standard of performance” as used in CAA section 111 makes clear that the foundation for the regulatory requirements for the source category is the EPA's determination of the BSER that is “adequately demonstrated” for emissions of the relevant air pollutants.
[
25
]
The EPA has discretion in determining the BSER, and has historically followed a “technology-based approach” that focuses on “measures that improve the pollution performance of individual sources,” such as “add-on controls.”
[
26
]
To determine the BSER, the EPA first identifies the “system[s] of emission reduction” that are “adequately demonstrated” and then determines the “best” of those adequately demonstrated systems, “taking into account” factors including “cost,” “nonair quality health and environmental impact,” and “energy requirements.” After determining the BSER, the EPA derives from that system an “achievable” “degree of emission limitation.” A standard of performance is “achievable” if a technology can reasonably be projected to be available to an individual source at the time it is constructed so as to allow it to meet the standard.
[
27
]
The EPA must then, under CAA section 111(b)(1)(B), promulgate “standard[s] for emissions”—the NSPS—that reflect that level of stringency. The EPA may determine that different sets of sources have different characteristics relevant for determining the BSER for emissions of the relevant air pollutants and may subcategorize sources accordingly.
[
28
]
To qualify as the BSER, the system of emission reduction must be “adequately demonstrated” as “the Administrator determines.”
[
29
]
The plain text of CAA section 111(a)(1), and in particular the terms “adequately” and “the Administrator determines,” confers upon the EPA the discretion to identify the appropriate system, including making scientific and technological determinations and considering a broad range of policy considerations.
[
30
]
The D.C. Circuit has stated that the EPA may weigh the various factors identified in the statute and caselaw to determine the “best” system and has emphasized that the EPA has significant discretion in weighing the factors (cost, health and environmental impact, and energy requirements).
[
31
]
The EPA has broad discretion in determining which adequately demonstrated system of emission reduction is the “best.” The D.C. Circuit has explained that “section 111(a) explicitly instructs the EPA to balance multiple concerns when promulgating a NSPS”
[
32
]
and emphasized that “[t]he text gives the EPA broad discretion to weigh different factors in setting the standard,” including the amount of emission reductions, the cost of the controls, and the nonair quality environmental impacts and energy requirements.
[
33
]
CAA section 111(a)(1) requires the EPA to account for “the cost of achieving [the emission] reduction” in determining the adequately demonstrated BSER. Although the CAA does not describe how the EPA should account for costs to affected sources, the D.C. Circuit has formulated the cost standard in various ways, including by stating on the upper bound that the EPA may not adopt a standard that the cost of which would be “excessive” or “unreasonable.”
[
34
]
The EPA has discretion in considering cost under CAA section 111(a), both in determining the appropriate level of costs and in balancing costs with other BSER factors.
[
35
]
The D.C. Circuit has repeatedly upheld the EPA's consideration of cost in reviewing standards of performance.
[
36
]
Regarding energy impacts, based on the D.C. Circuit's interpretations of CAA section 111, this factor may also include the impact, if any, of the air pollution controls on the energy supply for a particular area or nationwide.
[
37
]
Furthermore, the EPA has considered under this statutory factor whether possible controls would create risks to the reliability of the national electricity system.
[
38
]
The EPA has generally used CAA section 111 to establish NSPS for emissions of specified air pollutants from new sources within a category. In the rare instances in which the new stationary source standards concern air pollutants that are not regulated under the NAAQS program pursuant to CAA sections 108-110, or the NESHAP program pursuant to CAA section 112, the statute provides a separate authority for addressing emissions of such air pollutants from existing sources in the source category.
[
39
]
CAA section 111(a)(6) defines an “existing source” as “any stationary source other than a new source.”
In contrast to the national regime for new sources under CAA section 111(b), CAA section 111(d) establishes a framework of “cooperative federalism for the regulation of existing sources.”
[
40
]
CAA section 111(d)(1) provides that when air pollutants covered by an NSPS for a source category are not already encompassed within the NAAQS program or NESHAP program, the EPA “shall prescribe regulations which shall establish a procedure similar to that provided by” CAA section 110 “under which each State shall submit to the Administrator” a plan for addressing emissions of such air pollutants by existing sources within such source category.
[
41
]
Reference to CAA section 110 incorporates the statute's provision for State submission and EPA review of state implementation plans (SIPs) that provide for the implementation, maintenance, and enforcement of the NAAQS for the areas within such State.
[
42
]
In a comparable manner, State plans required by the regulations authorized in CAA section 111(d) must
(
printed page 68242)
“establis[h] standards of performance for any existing stationary source” for the air pollutant at issue and “provid[e] for the implementation and enforcement of such standards of performance.”
In the relatively few instances in which the EPA applies this provision, the Agency generally promulgates “emission guidelines” that identify the BSER and the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the BSER. (represented in EG OOOOc via presumptive standards in a model rule). The EPA's regulations then require States to establish standards of performance for emissions of the air pollutant at issue by covered sources that reflect that level of stringency. States need not compel regulated sources to adopt the particular components of the BSER itself (or the model rule or presumptive standards); rather, States have discretion in designing the policies and rules used to achieve the degree of emission limitation required by the EPA's emission guidelines. The statute requires the EPA's regulations to permit a State, “in applying a standard of performance to any particular source,” to “take into consideration, among other factors, the remaining useful life of the existing source to which such standard applies.”
[
43
]
Once the EPA approves a State's plan, the provisions in the plan become federally enforceable in the same manner as the provisions of an approved SIP under the CAA.
[
44
]
If a State elects not to submit a plan or submits a plan that the EPA does not find “satisfactory,” the Agency is authorized to promulgate a plan that establishes Federal standards of performance for the state's existing sources.
[
45
]
In establishing Federal standards of performance for existing sources under these circumstances, the EPA must “take into consideration, among other factors, remaining useful lives of the sources in the category of sources to which such standard applies.”
[
46

III. Summary and Rationale of Proposed Amendments to NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc
Sections III.A through III.K of this preamble present the background, the summary of proposed changes, and rationale for proposed amendments to the March 2024 Final Rule.
A. Super Emitter Program
As part of the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA established a novel form of work-practice standard and compliance assurance mechanism known as the Super Emitter Program, which relies on third-party entities certified by the Agency to detect “very large emissions events”
[
71
]
using Agency-approved technologies and submit notifications to EPA personnel. The EPA transmits the third-party notification to relevant owners and operators, thereby triggering an obligation to investigate and to take any necessary corrective actions required under applicable standards. The EPA finalized this program as part of the
40 CFR part 60
NSPS subparts OOOO, OOOOa, and OOOOb and as part of the presumptive requirements applicable to state plans under EG OOOOc, meaning that States are expected to establish super emitter programs analogous to the EPA's. Upon reconsideration, the EPA no longer believes that the Super Emitter Program is well-grounded in policy and law and proposes to rescind the third-party certification, notification, and other related provisions in NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, and OOOOb and EG OOOOc.
In Section III.A.1 of this preamble, the EPA explains its initial conception of the program in the December 2022 Supplemental Proposal, comments received on this initial conception, and changes made to the program by the Agency in the March 2024 Final Rule. In Section III.A.2, the EPA explains the multiple potential bases for the proposed rescission of the Super Emitter Program. First, the EPA proposes to rescind the Super Emitter Program on policy grounds, including because the program has failed to meet the expectations the Agency had when it finalized the program in March 2024 and is unnecessary and ineffective. Second, the EPA also proposes to rescind the Super Emitter Program for legal reasons. While the EPA solicits comment on this proposal within this section, table 34 in section VII also summarizes all solicitations for comment for convenience.
1. Background
In the December 2022 Supplemental Proposal, the EPA sought public comment on a novel program intended “to trigger swift mitigation of super-emitter emissions events when they are identified through credible information provided by regulatory authorities or approved qualified third-party sources.”

72

The EPA proposed two statutory bases for the program: first, that “super-emitters” are “a separate and distinct source of emissions” (and therefore a “designated facility”); and second, that the program “constitutes work practice standards for certain sources and compliance assurance mechanisms for other sources.”

2. Summary of Proposed Rescission and Rationales
The EPA is proposing to rescind the Super Emitter Program on several alternative policy and legal bases. First, the EPA now proposes that this novel program rests on insufficient evidence of the nature and duration of super-emitter events, defined as emissions of 100 kg/hr or greater, and that the same concerns that led the Agency to decline to treat “super emitters” as a distinct “affected source” call into question the
(
printed page 68246)
conceptual basis and need for the program in the first instance. Second, the EPA further proposes that the program is not necessary and provides limited additional value in light of the other requirements applicable to affected sources under NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, OOOOb, and EG OOOOc. Third, the EPA proposes that the Super Emitter Program is not effective and is overly broad as designed. Fourth, the EPA proposes that the statutory authority bases finalized in the March 2024 Final Rule are inadequate to maintain the program. Specifically, as explained below, the EPA has concerns that the program features an inappropriate role for third parties, does not properly function as a work practice standard, and does not properly function as a compliance measure.
If finalized, the proposed rescission would remove provisions related to the Super Emitter Program, including for certification and decertification of third parties, certification and decertification of third-party monitoring technologies, and a source's obligations to respond in the event of a notification received pursuant to the Super Emitter Program, from
40 CFR part 60, subparts OOOO
, OOOOa, OOOOb, and OOOOc.
The EPA proposes that additional information and further study are required to evaluate the underlying premise of the Super Emitter Program, that is, the assertion that “super-emitter events” (defined as emissions of 100 kg/hr or greater) from a select few sources are responsible for the majority of source-category emissions. In the March 2024 Final Rule, and specifically in the December 2022 Supplemental Proposal, the EPA believed that “the top five percent of sources contribute to over 50 percent of the total emissions” from the source category because of super-emitter events.

For this conclusion, the Agency relied on a single study consisting of 2018-2020 aerial surveys of the New Mexico Permian Basin that acknowledged its results departed from those in previous studies and did not endeavor to differentiate among the regulatory status of emission sources or potential causes for the emissions. While informative, the novel analytical approach and results of this study had not been thoroughly vetted at the time of the December 2022 Supplemental Proposal, and the EPA did not revisit the question of the study's quality and utility in the March 2024 Final Rule. Indeed, the Agency acknowledged at the time that results vary by basin and involve a number of different potential causes and explanations depending on the nature and regulatory status of the potential source(s).

While the Agency is aware of some additional information that has become available on this topic since the March 2024 Final Rule, the Agency proposes to conclude that information indicates that the Super Emitter Program is overly broad as designed, as explained below, which is a separate reason for its proposed rescission. B. Liquids Unloading
1. Background
Under the March 2024 Final Rule, both the NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc require each affected and designated gas well facility that unloads liquids to employ techniques (
e.g.
, manual unloading steps taken to unload liquids) or technology(ies) (
e.g.
, plunger lift systems, surface jet pumps, velocity strings) that minimize or eliminate venting of emissions during liquids unloading events. As an alternative, owners or operators may comply with the GHG and VOC standards by routing vented emissions to a control device that reduces methane and VOC emissions (methane only for designated facilities) from each gas well liquids unloading event by 95.0 percent.
For unloading technologies or techniques that could result in venting to the atmosphere, the March 2024 Final Rule requires owners or operators to follow certain work practices. The March 2024 Final Rule requires that owners or operators employ and document best management practices to minimize venting of methane and VOC emissions for each gas well liquids unloading operation. Specifically, owners or operators of affected and designated gas well facilities that undergo liquids unloading events must develop, maintain, and follow a best management practice plan to minimize venting of methane and VOC emissions (methane only for designated facilities) to the maximum extent possible from each gas well liquids unloading operation. This best management practice plan must meet the following minimum criteria: (1) include steps that create a differential pressure to minimize the need to vent a well to unload liquids; (2) include steps to reduce wellbore pressure as much as possible prior to opening the well to the atmosphere; (3) unload liquids through the separator where feasible; and (4) close all wellhead vents to the atmosphere and return the well to production as soon as practicable. The standards are the same for the NSPS and the EG.
Where liquids unloading events are conducted using a technology or technique that eliminates venting to the atmosphere, the March 2024 Final Rule requires owners and operators to report the identification of the well along with the non-venting technology or technique used in their annual report. If more than one non-venting method is used, the March 2024 Final Rule requires that owners and operators maintain records of all the differing non-venting liquids unloading methods used at the well affected/designated facility.
When unplanned venting occurs from these wells during a compliance period, an owner or operator is required to follow their best management practices plan for such events and comply with the associated recordkeeping and reporting requirements for those events. The March 2024 Final Rule requires owners and operators to maintain records for the number of unplanned events where emissions are vented to the atmosphere during a liquids unloading operation. The March 2024 Final Rule requires owners and operators to provide the above recordkeeping information to the EPA in their annual report.

C. Process Controllers
1. Background
Under the March 2024 Final Rule, the NSPS OOOOb final standards and EG OOOOc final presumptive standards contain requirements for each process controller affected or designated facility. These rules define process controller affected and designated facilities as the collection of natural gas-driven process controllers at a well site, centralized production facility, onshore natural gas processing plant, or a compressor station. The definitions of affected and designated facilities exclude natural gas-driven process controllers that function exclusively as emergency shutdown devices as well as process controllers not driven by natural gas, so neither the NSPS nor the EG applies to these types of controllers. The NSPS standards and the EG presumptive standards require process controller affected or designated facilities to have zero methane and VOC emissions to the atmosphere, except for affected or designated process controllers located in Alaska at a site without electrical power. For process controller affected or designated facilities located at Alaska sites that do not have access to electrical power, an owner or operator may either route process controller emissions through a CVS to a control device that reduces emissions by 95.0 percent, or they may use intermittent vent or low-bleed process controllers (
i.e.
, those that have a bleed rate less than or equal to 6 standard cubic feet per hour (scfh)) so long as they perform periodic monitoring of their intermittent controllers to ensure those controllers are not emitting to the atmosphere during idle periods.
To address concerns about new sources' ability to obtain the equipment necessary to demonstrate compliance with the final standard of zero emissions immediately upon the effective date of the final rule, the March 2024 Final Rule NSPS allowed up to 1 year from the effective date of the final rule (
i.e.
, May 7, 2025) to come into full compliance with the final NSPS standard of zero emissions. Until that date of compliance, owners and operators must demonstrate compliance with an interim standard which mirrored the requirements for sites in Alaska that do not have access to electrical power.

The EPA considered the petitioners' concerns and the information provided regarding the costs and emission reductions associated with the process controller requirements at facilities with process controllers that are on high-pressure systems at transmission compressor stations. Based on the information provided by petitioners, it is the EPA's understanding that only the retrofit costs for existing sources to come into compliance with a zero emissions standard are prohibitive. It is the EPA's understanding that when new facilities are being planned and constructed, it is possible for zero emissions process controllers to be incorporated into the facility design at a cost that is similar to the cost of including natural gas-driven process controllers, such that it is cost effective to include zero-emissions process controllers on high pressure systems at natural gas compressor stations. However, if these facilities were built with process controllers that use natural gas and are then required to replace those process controllers with zero emitting equipment, essentially doubling the cost of this already expensive equipment, it could be cost prohibitive and therefore unreasonable considering the relatively small amount of emissions reduction that would be achieved.

b. Modification Criteria for Process Controllers
Background.
Petitioners requested that the EPA clarify that a modification for process controllers occurs only when there is both an increase in emissions and one or more controllers are added to the facility. Petitioners recounted that the EPA changed the definition of affected facility for process controllers from a single process controller to the collection of all the process controllers at a well site in NSPS OOOOb. Petitioners also recounted that in NSPS OOOOb, the EPA changed the modification criteria to state, “[f]or the purposes of § 60.5390b, in addition to the definition in § 60.14, a modification occurs when the number of natural gas-driven process controllers in the affected facility is increased by one or more.” According to the petitioners, the regulatory language seems to indicate that process controllers would be considered modified only if there is an increase in emissions and the number of natural gas-driven process controllers is increased by one or more, but in the March 2024 Final Rule preamble, the EPA focused only on the number of increased controllers, implying that an increase in process controllers automatically increases emissions from the affected facility. According to the petitioners, there are many actions that can take place at the time a new controller is added to offset its emissions, such as when a new controller replaces an existing controller with the same or with higher emissions or when new controller emissions are offset by the removal of other controllers or adjustments in their operations. The petitioner reported that these concepts have long been a part of facility operations management to limit the need for additional permitting.
Summary of Comment Solicitation.
The EPA acknowledges the petitioners' request for clarification and is soliciting comment on whether revisions to the current modification determination language in
40 CFR 60.5365b(d)(1)
for process controllers are warranted. The EPA maintains that increasing the total number of natural gas-driven process controllers at a facility generally increases the emissions of natural gas, methane, and VOC to the atmosphere by the nature of the equipment, which bleeds gas continuously and/or emits gas during actuation events, emits gas during malfunctions of the equipment, or emits gas through leaks in the equipment or from connections to CVSs. Adding one more natural gas-emitting process controller to an existing set of natural gas-emitting process controllers is therefore generally expected to result in increased emissions. The intent and purpose of this provision was to simplify modification determinations by eliminating the need for owners/operators to determine emissions before and after a change in a process controller affected facility and to reduce the burden on permitting authorities reviewing that modification determination. That said, the EPA also recognizes that by statute, an increase in emissions is a necessary condition to a modification determination. The EPA also notes that the number of process controllers in the affected facility does
(
printed page 68255)
not increase when a new natural gas-driven process controller replaces an existing one, or when the addition of a process controller is offset by the removal of one or more existing process controllers. The petitioner suggests that, in some cases, operational adjustments to other controllers could offset the emissions of the new controller. The EPA is soliciting additional information on the relative change in emissions when these process controller replacement events occur and the frequency with which they occur. The EPA also requests comment on whether the existing modification determination language appropriately captures changes resulting in emissions increases, or whether adjustments to the current criteria are needed to reflect industry practices, such as clarifying what constitutes net increases in emissions from the source. D. Pumps
1. Background
Under the March 2024 Final Rule, the NSPS OOOOb final standards and EG OOOOc final presumptive standards contain requirements for each pump affected or designated facility, which is the collection of natural gas-driven pumps at a well site, centralized production facility, onshore natural gas processing plant, or compressor station. Pumps that are in operation less than 90 days per calendar year or that are not natural gas-driven are not included in the definition of affected or designated facility. For pump affected or designated facilities located at a site that has access to electrical power and for those without access to electrical power that have three or more natural gas-driven diaphragm pumps, the pump affected facility must have zero methane and VOC emissions to the atmosphere. For each pump affected or designated facility located at a site that does not have access to electrical power and that also has fewer than three natural gas-driven diaphragm pumps, emissions must be controlled if a control device is otherwise onsite.
Section III.D.2 of this preamble provides additional background, summary of proposed changes, and rationale for proposed changes.
2. Additional Background and Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale
Background.
Petitioners asserted that the EPA failed to justify NSPS OOOOb standards and EG OOOOc presumptive standards of zero emissions for existing natural gas-driven pumps that are already in compliance with NSPS OOOOa, which requires certain natural gas-driven diaphragm pumps to be routed to a control device or process that achieves an emissions reduction of at least 95.0 percent.
[
132
]
Petitioners requested that the EPA's model rule and presumptive standards in EG OOOOc and the standards in OOOOb (for modified and reconstructed facilities) allow these existing pumps that are already reducing emissions by 95 percent to continue to comply with NSPS OOOOa instead of having to convert to the zero emissions standard (100 percent control as opposed to 95 percent control). Petitioners implied that the EPA did not adequately consider the incremental cost effectiveness of requiring existing diaphragm pumps subject to NSPS OOOOa (and already achieving 95 percent control) to achieve zero emissions.
Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale.
The EPA proposes to amend the standards for modified and reconstructed sources under NSPS OOOOb and the presumptive standards in the EG OOOOc model rule for pumps. The proposed amendments include an alternative emissions standard of 95.0 percent control for individual pumps within a pump designated (or affected) facility that were already routing emissions through a CVS to a control device achieving 95.0 percent or greater control of emissions on the effective date of the March 2024 Final Rule (
i.e.
, December 6, 2022). These pumps that are already reducing their emissions by at least 95 percent would not be required to achieve zero emissions (100 percent reduction of emissions), where zero-emitting pumps would be the otherwise applicable standard (
i.e.
, sites with access to electricity or sites without access to electricity that have three or more diaphragm pumps). The modified/reconstructed standards under NSPS OOOOb and the presumptive standards under EG OOOOc for any other pumps in the pump designated facility (meaning those whose emissions were not already reduced by 95.0 percent) would remain those finalized in the March 2024 Final Rule. This proposed alternative standard would apply to any pumps at an affected pump facility or designated facility that were already routing emissions through a CVS to a control device achieving 95.0 percent or greater control of emissions on the effective date of the March 2024 Final Rule, regardless of whether or not those pumps were previously required by NSPS OOOOa to achieve 95.0 percent emissions reductions.
The EPA considered the petitioner's concerns and evaluated the incremental cost effectiveness of moving from 95.0 percent emissions control to zero emissions (
i.e.
, 100 percent emissions control). For sites that have access to power from the electrical grid, the options for achieving zero emissions that were included in this analysis were the use of a compressed air system to power existing pneumatic pumps and the replacement of existing natural gas-powered pneumatic pumps with electrical pumps. For sites that do not have access to power from the electrical
(
printed page 68256)

These options were the most cost effective means of achieving zero emissions that were analyzed for the March 2024 Final Rule. In the analysis, the EPA evaluated the difference in costs and the difference in emissions between the 95.0 percent emissions control scenario and the 100 percent emissions control scenario. As the systems required for 95.0 percent emissions control already exist and operate, and there is no overlap in equipment used between these systems and the systems that would be used for the zero emissions options analyzed, the EPA assumed that the difference in costs equate to the full costs of the zero emissions system. The difference in emissions would be 5 percent of the total emissions (
i.e.

The cost effectiveness values shown in table 3 are based on the estimated total annual costs of each zero-emissions pump option and the emissions reductions associated with going from 95.0 percent to 100 percent emissions control. Further information regarding the analysis conducted for pumps may be found in a technical memorandum, available in the docket for this proposed rule.

]
(
printed page 68257)

As there is no cost
(

Therefore, the EPA proposes to include an alternative standard for modified and reconstructed facilities under NSPS OOOOb and the presumptive standards in EG OOOOc to take into account the updated BSER analysis that properly considers the incremental costs of converting to zero emissions for individual pumps within a designed pump facility that are routed through a CVS to a control device achieving 95.0 percent or greater control of emissions. This alternative standard would require these pumps to achieve 95.0 percent or greater control of emissions as well as meet the compliance requirements for CVSs and control devices in NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc.

Second, based on the EPA's review of the reconsideration petitions, the EPA now acknowledges that the operator of an offsite well may not be the same entity as the operator of the centralized production facility that gathers materials from offsite natural gas and oil production wells. Accordingly, the EPA is proposing to remove the modification criteria currently at

However, recognizing that modifications at offsite well sites can increase production sent to a centralized production facility and increase emissions, the EPA is proposing to add modification criteria for centralized production facilities that are tied to increased throughput from an offsite well. These proposed criteria differ from the current criteria (which require the owner or operator of the centralized production facility to know when a modification occurs at an offsite well), but the EPA believes the proposed criteria will still capture situations in which an emissions increase at the centralized production facility occurs due to increases in production that result from modifications at an offsite well. Specifically, the EPA is proposing that increases in throughput that cumulatively exceed the LPE limit on throughput or the projected maximum average daily throughput established for the centralized tank battery (

The EPA is choosing throughput as a proxy for production because these two measures are closely related. An increase in production at the well site is manifested as throughput increases to a tank battery located at a centralized production facility. Production and throughput can be linked using generally accepted engineering models such as condensate rates derived from gas throughput. Throughput to the tank battery is already tracked, and various methods are available for measuring it. For tank batteries, the LPE limit on throughput is established in operating permits or in other Federal, state, local or Tribal requirements.
In developing these proposed modification criteria, the EPA reviewed how the Agency has previously addressed emissions increases related to production increases (manifested as throughput increases at tank batteries) in midstream operations that receive gas or liquids from other operations not owned or operated by the same entity, such as tank batteries at compressor stations. The EPA believes that examination of this information is relevant for modifications at centralized production facilities for the purposes of fugitive emissions components because the issues are similar: an operation receives liquids from other operations beyond their control. ]
Similarly, in the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA finalized separate modification criteria for existing tank batteries located in the midstream operations at
40 CFR 60.5365b(e)(3)(ii)(D)
which allows the increase in throughput to be compared to the same LPE limit on throughput or the projected maximum average daily throughput used in
40 CFR 60.5365b(e)(2)(iii)
. The EPA stated that such provisions should address the receipt of liquids from upstream production facilities owned by third parties.
[
160
]
The EPA now understands from the petitioners that, similar to compressor stations, centralized production facilities often are “overbuilt” to accommodate future production received from multiple well sites, and that while they can typically accommodate increases in throughput up to forecasted production used in the design, in some instances they are not in control of the offsite actions which increase that throughput. For this reason, the EPA now believes that the same rationale as the EPA used for midstream tank batteries also applies to tank batteries at centralized production facilities, which base their design on planned growth coming online over time to account for future growth, often beyond their control. Thus, for throughput changes brought on by actions (
e.g.
, drilling a new well or fracturing or refracturing a well) at offsite well sites feeding the centralized production facility, while the EPA previously thought that tracking those actions at the offsite wells would be a straightforward method to determine if production to the centralized production facility increased (without tracking throughput), the EPA now proposes that a more appropriate approach is to determine whether a production increase would result in an increase in emissions above the previously estimated emissions based on throughput increases beyond design capacity.
The EPA believes that using increases beyond a centralized production facility's design capacity appropriately captures emissions increases resulting from production-related changes in the method of operation of the stationary source, consistent with the definition of
(
printed page 68264)
“modification” in CAA section 111(a)(4).
[
161
]
This is because a centralized production facility is designed to accommodate the receipt of gases and liquids up to its permitted or design capacity. Under the proposed change, the EPA would not consider production increases that can be accommodated under the permitted or design capacity to constitute a change in the method of operation. Thus, the Agency is proposing that such increases would not trigger a modification, as that term is defined under CAA section 111(a)(4), unless accompanied by a physical change, such as adding a tank, adding additional major production equipment, or otherwise increasing capacity.
[
162
]
In contrast, increases in production above the throughput established in an LPE limit or the design maximum average daily throughput, would be considered changes to the method of operation. Such increases are expected to cause emissions increases from fugitive emission components due to higher pressures, longer duration of flow, or more frequent flow events.
[
163
]
As discussed earlier in this preamble, the EPA has already established a procedure for determining when these increases occur, using the throughput that forms the basis for determining the potential for emissions and that is established in an LPE permit or the projected maximum average daily throughput. In this proposal, the EPA would use a parallel procedure as one method of determining whether a modification has occurred at a centralized production facility.
Third, the March 2024 Final Rule modification criteria at
40 CFR 60.5365b(i)(2)(iii)
also address a production increase that occurs when an offsite well site becomes a wellhead only site and sends its production to an existing centralized production facility. The EPA proposes to delete this action from those modification criteria because, if the EPA finalizes the proposed change related to increases to throughput described above, that approach would already appropriately capture increases in throughput that occur when a well site transitions to a wellhead only site and sends its offsite production to the centralized production facility. As these changes in throughput would be measured against the proposed increase from the design capacity, retaining this standalone modification criterion would be redundant.
Fourth, there also are potential “hardware” changes at the centralized production facility that the EPA proposes to reflect in the modification criteria because they could result in an increase in fugitive emissions. These include the replacement or modification of one or more storage vessels such that the cumulative storage capacity is increased, as these changes could increase throughput beyond design capacity and thus would be considered modifications for the same reasons as discussed above. Other hardware changes that result in additional fugitive emissions include the addition of one or more pieces of “major production and processing equipment” (with attendant additional fugitive emissions components). Because emissions increases are associated with the addition of fugitive emissions components, the Agency is proposing that they would be considered modifications, even if they are not associated with an increase in throughput above design capacity. Further, the EPA recognizes that the addition of a new onsite well (with attendant fugitive emissions components) or the fracturing or refracturing of onsite wells are within the control of the operator of the centralized production facility and may also result in the addition of fugitive emissions components and thus lead to emissions increases. Accordingly, these are included in the proposed modification criteria as well.
The EPA believes that the proposed revisions to the modification provisions would continue to capture all instances in which emissions at a centralized production facility increase. However, these revisions would base that determination on actions occurring at the centralized production facility itself. The EPA believes that the proposed revisions would appropriately focus the modification criteria on actions under the control of, or within the knowledge of, the operator of the centralized production facility rather than on actions occurring at offsite wells for which the operator may not have control or knowledge. The proposed changes are still expected to appropriately identify when there is an increase in VOC and methane emissions a) based on an increase in volumetric throughput above the design capacity to the centralized production facility; or b) when there are additional fugitive emissions components added, but the proposed changes do focus on information known by or actions under control of the centralized production facility.
The EPA solicits comment on this proposal. (Question III.4e)

F. Storage Vessels
1. Background
NSPS OOOOb contains requirements for a storage vessel affected facility, defined as a tank battery that has the potential for VOC emissions equal to or greater than 6 tpy or methane emissions equal to or greater than 20 tpy. The 20 tpy methane threshold for applicability also applies to a tank battery under the EG OOOOc. A tank battery, according to at
40 CFR 60.5430b
and
60.5430c
, is “a group of all storage vessels that are manifolded together for liquid transfer. A tank battery may consist of a single storage vessel if only one storage vessel is present.” Storage vessel affected facilities under NSPS OOOOb and designated facilities under EG OOOOc must determine their applicability (
i.e.,
the potential for VOC or methane emissions) and may include LPE limits in the determination. When determining the potential for VOC or methane emissions, operators of storage vessels not subject to LPE limits may exclude any vapor from that storage vessel which is recovered and routed to a process through a vapor recovery unit (VRU) operated in accordance with the cover and CVS requirements.
Under the March 2024 Final Rule, the applicability thresholds for tank batteries located at well sites and centralized production facilities are determined within 30 days of startup of production, or within 30 days after one of the actions described below relating to modifications. The applicability thresholds for tank batteries not located at a well site or centralized production facility (
e.g.,
tank batteries at onshore natural gas processing plants) are determined prior to startup, or within 30 days of one of the actions described below relating to modifications, using throughput as determined by an LPE limit on throughput or the projected maximum average daily throughput.
[
167
]
The March 2024 Final Rule also established “modification” criteria to determine when an existing tank battery becomes subject to NSPS OOOOb. Under the March 2024 Final Rule, a “modification” of a tank battery occurs when: (1) a storage vessel is added to an existing tank battery; (2) one or more storage vessels are replaced such that the cumulative storage capacity of the existing tank battery increases; or (3) throughput to the tank battery increases, and the potential for VOC or methane emissions meets or exceeds the applicability thresholds of 6 tpy VOC or 20 tpy methane, respectively.
[
168
]
The EPA is proposing changes to this definition of modification at
40 CFR 60.5365b(e)(3)(ii)
based on our evaluation of petitioner concerns related to centralized production facilities. Petitioners claim that a centralized production facility operator may not know when an action is occurring at an offsite well that would trigger modification at the centralized production facility.
[
169
]
Petitioners raised a similar issue regarding modifications for the purposes of fugitive emissions components at centralized production facilities, which are discussed in Section III.E.2.c of this preamble (“Modification Criteria for [Fugitive Emissions at] Centralized Production Facilities”). In that section, the EPA examines the record relating to actions that trigger modifications at centralized production facilities. The discussion and rationale provided in that section, specific to actions which increase throughput, are relevant to tank batteries at centralized production facilities for the purpose of applying the modification criteria to tank batteries and are not repeated here. In parallel to proposing revisions to the modification criteria for tank batteries at a centralized production facility, the EPA also proposes corresponding changes to the determination of the potential to emit for tank batteries at centralized production facilities. The proposed revisions would allow operators to base the potential for emissions on either the throughput as determined by an LPE or the projected maximum average daily throughput as specified in
40 CFR 60.5365b(e)(2)(iii)

40 CFR 60.5365b(e)(2)(ii)

This proposed revision will make the determination of the potential for emissions consistent with the methodology provided for compressor stations and onshore natural gas processing plants, which recognizes that these types of facilities are built for planned growth (with additional receipt of fluids over time) and therefore the first 30 days of production does not accurately reflect the potential for emissions.
The EPA recognizes that other issues raised in reconsideration petitions on the March 2024 Final Rule related to storage vessel affected facilities are of interest to stakeholders. The EPA is still evaluating some of those other issues. One of those issues, for example, relates to the application of LPE limit criteria when determining the potential to emit VOC or methane from storage vessels when determining the applicability of NSPS OOOOb or EG OOOOc standards. Depending on the comments the Agency receives, the EPA may take further action at an appropriate time, and relatedly, solicits further comment on whether the 2024 LPE criteria should be repealed along with supporting reasons for doing so. G. Covers and CVSs
1. Background
Under the March 2024 Final Rule, the NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc final standards include requirements for CVSs. CVSs route emissions from wells (
i.e.,
oil wells when routing associated gas to a control device), process controllers, pumps, centrifugal compressors, reciprocating compressors, and storage vessel affected and designated facilities to a control device or to a process. 2. Additional Background and Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale
Background.
Petitioners asserted that the NIE requirement applicable to covers and CVSs lacks reasoning, pathways to reasonably meet requirements, and technical feasibility over the long-term.
[
193
]
Petitioners contended that fugitive leaks from covers and CVSs occur in the same way as fugitive leaks covered by the equipment leak provisions. Petitioners also stated that the EPA previously rejected the applicability of numeric emissions limitations to fugitive emissions components. Petitioners noted comments made on the December 2022 proposed rule arguing that the requirement to operate with NIE applies as a work practice standard. Petitioners asserted that they also raised concerns with the NIE requirement in the rulemaking process and contended that the EPA declined to address these concerns and did not discuss the consequences of imposing what they allege is a technically infeasible requirement. Petitioners asserted that the EPA's approach effectively creates per se rule violations and that the NIE requirement is contrary to determining the BSER because no single facility has “adequately demonstrated” the BSER.
Petitioners also asserted that an NIE requirement is impossible to meet in practice, because leaks inevitably occur due to normal wear and tear (
e.g.,
a rusty bolt causing a flange leak) and often occur through events that are not reasonably within the control of the operator. Petitioners asserted that as fugitive emissions occur over time, an LDAR program allows operators to address them promptly and responsibly. For this reason, petitioners stated that the rule should differentiate between leaks appropriately attributed to the operator (
e.g.,
forgetting to close a thief hatch) versus leaks that are truly fugitive in nature, and that a violation should not occur from routine fugitive emissions as long as the appropriate action is taken. Petitioners asserted that the EPA should determine that covers and CVSs are subject to a work practice standard, not a zero emissions standard. Petitioners also requested that the EPA determine that pumps and valves required to be operated with “no detectable emissions” (NDE) are subject to a work practice standard, not a zero-emission standard, under the alternative standards for process unit equipment affected facilities.
[
194
]
In addition, petitioners requested that the EPA confirm that “deviations” are not necessarily “violations” and that a leak from a cover or CVS may represent a deviation but not necessarily a violation of the NIE requirement. The
(

title V permitting rules which provide that “[a] deviation is not always a violation.”

Finally, petitioners contended that the NIE requirement could have adverse emission effects because it disincentivizes the use of new detection methodologies and voluntary emissions detection efforts.

The following paragraphs discuss the rationale for the proposed changes relating to NIE for CVSs, covers, and self-contained pneumatic controllers.
The EPA carefully considered the petitioners' concerns regarding emissions and defects from CVSs, covers, and process controllers and re-evaluated those requirements in the March 2024 Final Rule. The provisions for the CVS and cover intend for the control device (or process) to capture and route emissions generated at the emissions source, such as a storage vessel or compressor, thereby ensuring achievement of the underlying standard of performance for the emissions source. The EPA has seen, through implementation of the NSPS, that inadequate sizing of the CVS and cover (notably on storage vessels subject to the March 2024 Final rule) can result in the inability to accommodate all emissions, leading to over-pressurization events. An example includes liquid flowing from a separator to the storage vessel.
[
198
]
These over-pressurization events can result in actuations of pressure-relief devices which route emissions directly to the atmosphere. In this way, the pressure-relief device routes only some emissions to the control device, so the facility fails to meet the underlying emissions standard. Therefore, the EPA continues to believe that CVS and covers must meet robust design requirements, ensured by adequate ongoing monitoring.
As discussed previously, after reviewing the comments and examples provided by the petitioners, the EPA believes that even under the best scenarios, components on the CVS and cover may have wear and tear from the environment and emissions may often be beyond the control of the operator, making them similar to other fugitive emissions sources which allow for routine monitoring and repair without
(
printed page 68272)
subjecting a source to an immediate deviation when emissions are detected. Similarly, even with properly designed gasket materials, which include weighted mechanisms and withstand weather conditions and exposure to the composition of the fluid in the storage vessel, dirt and debris can affect the seating and seal of covers such that emissions may occur. The EPA also supports new detection methodologies and voluntary emissions detection efforts and recognizes that a NIE requirement which subjects a source to immediate violations from the detection of emissions may be counter to the Agency's goals of incentivizing the use of advanced technology. For these reasons, the EPA believes that making changes to the March 2024 Final Rule's requirements would still enable owners, operators, and the Agency to identify design flaws in covers and CVSs while allowing for flexibility in repairing emissions and defects related to normal wear and tear without subjecting the source to immediate non-compliance.
To accommodate these changes, the EPA re-evaluated the current criteria in the March 2024 Final Rule, which requires that the source “design and operate” the CVS or cover with NIE (as determined by OGI, AVO, or EPA Method 21).
[

The current provisions at
40 CFR 60.5411b
and
60.5411c

As discussed previously, the EPA proposes no changes to these design criteria. However, in enabling a leak detection and repair paradigm for emissions and defects related to normal wear and tear, the current criteria at
40 CFR 60.5411b(a)(3)
and
(b)(4)

all

Accordingly, the EPA proposes to delete the requirement that the CVS and cover be “designed” to operate with NIE. In doing so, the EPA proposes a clear design requirement and a clear operational requirement. However, these requirements are not entirely independent of one another because—like with all monitoring—leak detection inspections provide evidence of the underlying performance of a system. Similarly, in this case, the design of the CVS or cover impacts its proper operation. Therefore, the design and operational requirements are linked for compliance and enforcement purposes. To address this interplay, the EPA proposes changes to the “no identifiable emissions test methods and procedures” in
40 CFR 60.5416b
and
60.5416c

Specifically, the EPA proposes that covers and CVSs on well, centrifugal compressor, reciprocating compressor, process controller, pump, storage vessel, and process unit equipment affected facilities used to comply with the requirements to route to a process or to control, as applicable, should be monitored for emissions and defects and those emissions and defects related normal wear and tear be repaired upon identification or within a short timeline. The EPA recognizes that a short timeline of 24 hours, while sufficient for some companies to make routine maintenance fixes such as tightening, cleaning, or lubricating equipment, might pose challenges for other companies. Therefore, the EPA requests comment on all aspects of this proposed timeline, including suggested alternative timelines and supporting rationales. (Question III.6a) Further, the EPA believes that fixes which take longer than 24 hours could be indicative of a larger problem, such as a design flaw, and potentially signal a deviation of the design requirements. Deviations suggest potential violations with the design requirement, but they are not automatically considered a violation. Consistent with the current requirements, owners and operators must record and report a description of the emissions or defect, each attempt to repair the emissions or defect, each corrective action taken to repair the defect, and the date of repair completion. The EPA will use this information, and/or other credible evidence or inspections, to determine whether a violation of the design requirement has occurred.

The second proposed change to the current provisions recognizes that in addition to requirements to design the CVS and cover to capture and route all emissions to the control device, there is an ongoing operational requirement to operate with NIE. Compliance with the operational requirement includes a proposed leak detection and repair program. While the 24-hour repair timeline also applies, sources may also demonstrate compliance with the operational requirement by making repairs on a longer timeframe. For the reasons discussed above, the EPA believes that defects which require longer than 24 hours to repair indicate a design flaw. However, the EPA still believes there should still be a pathway towards compliance for the operational requirements. Therefore, a source which cannot repair within 24 hours may still make repairs under the current timeline of “as soon as practicable,” but no later than 5 days for the first attempt at repair and 30 days for the final repair (counted from the detection of the emissions or defect). Sources which comply with these operational requirement timelines may also place equipment on delay of repair (DOR) for valid reasons, as currently provided in the rule. Therefore, the EPA is not proposing to change the current DOR provisions for the 5/30 day repair timelines. i.e.

In addition to deviations of the design requirement for repairs which cannot be made in 24 hours, the EPA proposes an investigative analysis for chronic leakers to further synchronize the design and operational requirements. The EPA believes that continued detection of emissions or defects from the same CVS or cover indicates failures of the system due to design, operation, maintenance, failure to adequately repair, or other causes. For this reason, the EPA proposes that after the same CVS or cover experiences emissions or defects three or more times in a rolling calendar year, the facility must perform an investigative analysis. The EPA proposes this threshold because it represents a reasonable indicator that an underlying design, operational, or maintenance issue exists. A first leak occurrence can often be reasonably attributed to normal wear and tear. A second emission occurrence may signal
(
printed page 68273)
a developing issue but could still reasonably be attributed to normal wear and tear. However, a third emission occurrence involving the same cover or CVS would strongly signal a larger issue that warrants a formal resolution and potentially enforcement, because the design and operational ability of the CVS to route all emissions to the control device impacts the 95 percent control BSER for the underlying emission source. The EPA proposes that the facility conduct an investigative analysis within 10 days after detecting the emissions or defect for the third time in a rolling calendar year, and the owner or operator must determine the cause of the defect. The EPA proposes that if the design caused the emissions or defect, this constitutes a deviation of the design requirement; if a failure to adequately repair the source of the emissions or defect during prior attempts caused the emissions or defect, this constitutes a deviation of the repair requirements; and if due to operation, maintenance, or other cause(s), this constitutes a deviation of the operational requirements of the rule. Following the analysis, the owner or operator must determine what corrective actions are necessary to ensure the design, operational, repair, or other requirements are met and must implement the corrective actions. For design flaws, the EPA proposes that the corrective actions must be made no later than 90 days after completion of the investigative analysis and for other flaws, the Agency proposes that the facility must complete corrective actions no later than 30 days after completion of the investigative analysis. This repair timeline is consistent with already established repair timeline requirements for fugitive emissions and covers and CVSs.
