H. Control Devices
1. Background
In the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA finalized various requirements regarding control devices. Since the publication of this rulemaking, reconsideration petitioners have raised several issues on the March 2024 Final Rule requirements for control devices.
[
213
]
In this action, the EPA proposes changes to the March 2024 Final Rule related to flame monitoring data deviations, control device alerts, visible emissions test conditions for fugitive emissions, control devices used on a temporary basis, temporary process controllers used on temporary control devices, and control device categories. In addition, the EPA is not proposing changes but is instead soliciting comment on continuous burning pilot flames, backup control devices, and standalone temporary process controllers.
a. Continuous Burning Pilot Flame
Background.
Petitioners requested that the EPA revise the continuous burning pilot or combustion flame requirement from “at all times of operation” to “at all times when emissions from affected facilities are routed to the control device.”
[
214
]
Petitioners also requested that the continuous pilot requirements exclude times when a site is not operating (
e.g.,
an emergency shutdown) and the pilot or combustion flame is also shut down.
Petitioners explained that pilot flames go out for a variety of reasons and that the suggested revised language of “at all times when emissions from affected facilities are routed to the control device” allows operators to maintain compliance by temporarily isolating the affected facility from the control device while addressing a known pilot outage situation. In addition, the petitioners claimed that this flexibility reduces the need for a site shutdown to address a pilot outage, which may result in greater emissions than a pilot flame outage.
Petitioners further asserted that maintaining a continuous pilot flame creates an environmental disbenefit by burning more fuel and generating unnecessary emissions when no vent streams are routed to the control device. As an alternative, the petitioners suggested the use of an automatic ignition system which can light a pilot or combustion flame only when needed to control emissions from affected sources. Petitioners recommended that the EPA revise the continuous pilot requirements to clearly exclude times when a site is not operating (
e.g.,
an emergency shutdown). Petitioners explained that, during these instances, the combustion control device also has to shut down. Therefore, the combustion control device may not have a pilot or combustion flame due to safety considerations or have a lack of fuel gas where field gas is used as the pilot.
Summary of Comment Solicitation.
The March 2024 Final Rule, past iterations of the NSPS (OOOO and OOOOa), and the Part 60 General Provisions (
40 CFR 60.18(c)
) necessitate that flares and ECDs have a combustion (
i.e.,
pilot) flame present at “all times of operation.” Currently, the EPA understands that owners and operators primarily use natural gas from their production streams to fuel the continuously lit pilot flames. At sites without sufficient natural gas, or sites with a lot of sour gas in their streams, owners and operators instead rely on propane not from their production streams to fuel pilot flames. Some reconsideration petitioners contend that the usage of propane in these scenarios contributes to unnecessary emissions, particularly when nothing is routed to the control device.
[
215
]
However, the EPA has not received information on the incidence of sites that are unable to route on-site gas to fuel the continuous pilot flame and whether the additional emissions from this process are substantial. Therefore, the EPA has not been able to quantify the additional emissions emitted from the usage of propane in these scenarios.
While petitioners want the EPA to change the provision from at “all times of operation” to at “all times when emissions are routed to the control device,” at this time the EPA is maintaining the provision as stated in the March 2024 Final Rule. The EPA is not proposing any changes to these requirements in this action. The EPA has opined in previous rulemakings on the reliability and performance of automatic igniter pilots.
[
216
]
In short, the EPA has not received sufficient information that suggests that automatic igniters perform comparably to continuously lit pilots. Put another way, the EPA's assessment of automatic igniter pilots is that they often fail and continue to have reliability issues, which results in uncontrolled venting when emissions are routed to the control device. Reasons for this insufficiency, compared to continuously lit pilot flames, include the rapid degradation of automatic igniters over time, the instability in the flame caused by the intermittent nature of the device, the high frequency of reignition failures, and the delays between ignition and the point at which streams are routed to the control devices. A comprehensive study of combustion-based control devices at oil and gas facilities corroborates these findings.
[
217
]
More specifically, a review of those results indicates that the incidence of unlit flares exceeded expected values, even for flares equipped with automatic flame re-igniter technology. Thus, relying on automatic igniter pilot flames in lieu of more reliable technology, such as
(
printed page 68276)
continuously lit pilot flames, could increase the rate of unlit flares and lead to dramatically higher emissions of methane and VOC from uncontrolled venting. Some States do allow for the usage of automatic igniters in their provisions, but the provisions are typically narrow in scope. For example, New Mexico allows for ECDs to use automatic igniters during start-up procedures, or when reigniting the continuous pilot flame after it went out.
[
218
]
Similarly, in the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA allowed automatic igniter pilots only to reignite the continuous pilot flame, not to replace it outright.
[
219
]
Since the EPA has not received any recent information indicating that the technology or reliability of these automatic igniter pilot has changed and improved, in this proposed rule the EPA solicits comment on the reliability, efficacy, and overall performance of automatic igniter pilot technology to ascertain if the devices perform comparably to continuously lit pilot flames. Moreover, the EPA solicits comment on the number of sites that have to use additional fuel (
i.e.,
not from their production streams) to sustain a continuous pilot flame. EPA also solicits comment on the emissions and costs associated with maintaining a continuous pilot light when no emissions from the unit are being sent to the flare (whether the fuel used for the pilot light is an additional fuel (such as propane) or from the sites production stream (
e.g.,
natural gas)). (Question III.7a)
b. Flame Monitoring Data Deviations
Background.
The March 2024 Final Rule requires owners and operators to continuously monitor that a combustion flame is lit at all times of operation in their combustion-based control device(s). The presence of a combustion flame is measured parametrically by a thermocouple that records the temperature of the device. The thermocouple system, in turn, must record a value at least once every 5 minutes of operation. Currently, any lack of (
i.e.,
failure to collect) monitoring data not directly related to a malfunction of the combustion-based control device(s) results in a deviation.
[
220
]
Petitioners requested the EPA revise these provisions so that a lack of control device monitoring data does not automatically constitute a deviation.
[
221
]
Petitioners have noted that their data acquisition and storage systems sometimes malfunction independently of the control device. As such, petitioners contend that a lack of monitoring data (
e.g.,
a gap in the data when the monitoring equipment was not working properly due to a telecommunications loss rather than a process failure) should not be considered a deviation, provided that other available information (
i.e.,
other data which was recorded) indicates the presence of a pilot flame. For instance, if a combustion-based control device with no automatic igniter pilot installed had high temperature readings that indicate a lit flame before and after the lapse in data recording, and the lapse in data recording was relatively short, that would provide a reasonable assurance that the control device itself properly operated during the lapse in data recording.
Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale.
Under the March 2024 Final Rule, any lack of monitoring data not directly related to a malfunction of the combustion-based control device results in a deviation. Here, the EPA proposes to revise the March 2024 Rule to clarify that time-limited gaps in pilot or combustion flame monitoring data do not automatically constitute a deviation, if other available documented information indicates a pilot flame's presence during the data gap, coupled with a confirmation that the data gap was due to data collection equipment problems. Consistent with the current monitor availability requirements specified throughout NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc, a deviation occurs when the monitoring data are not available for at least 75 percent of the operating hours in a day. Under this proposed rule, the 75 percent monitor availability requirement would apply to the combination of both the primary monitoring data and other available documented information, for those periods where there is a gap in the primary monitoring data. Specifically, the EPA proposes to make changes to NSPS OOOOb (
40 CFR 60.5417b(g)(6)(iii)
and
60.5417b(i)(6)(v)
) and EG OOOOc (
40 CFR 60.5417c(g)(6)(iii)
and
60.5417c(i)(6)(v)
).
The EPA recognizes the petitioner's concerns that gaps in (or the absence of) flame monitoring data may result from interruptions in recordings by data acquisition and storage systems rather than from an actual loss of flame or improper operation. As a result, the EPA proposes to consider additional available documented information, such as combustion-based control device data from before and after the lapse that indicates a pilot flame's presence during the data gap, before determining whether a deviation occurred. By considering this additional information, the EPA provides flexibility for industry to meet the monitoring requirements while still maintaining accountability for ensuring continuous pilot flames. If other available documented information indicates a pilot flame's presence during the data gap, the EPA clarifies that a deviation has not occurred. With this proposed change, the EPA believes that allowing operators to demonstrate, through supplemental documentation, that the data gap did not stem from an unlit flame would be responsive to petitioners' concerns.
c. Control Device Alerts
Background.
The March 2024 Final Rule requires owners and operators to report any instances in which a pilot or combustion flame becomes unlit to the “nearest” control room.
[
222
]
In a recent letter the EPA received from some industry stakeholders, petitioners suggest removing or revising this requirement.
[
223

Petitioners argued that the installation and maintenance of reliable data acquisition and storage systems are particularly difficult at remote sites, largely due to the cost associated with installing new telecommunications to automate alarm systems. Furthermore, petitioners claimed that implementing these telecommunications upgrades often requires extensive permits and approvals from various federal agencies.
[
224
]
For sites that have access to telecommunications, petitioners argued that the provisions as written are untenable. Specifically, petitioners contended that the requirement to notify the nearest control room unnecessarily restricts facilities as the nearest control room (or closest facility) might not be best suited to address the unlit control device. Petitioners claimed that operators often rely on centralized dispatch control facilities stationed
(
printed page 68277)
sometimes miles away (or in another state) from the location to respond to such issues.
Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale.
In the current rule, an unlit pilot or combustion flame requires that an alert be sent to the nearest control room. The EPA proposes to revise the requirement to allow owners or operators to send these alerts to either the nearest control room or to a centralized control room during instances of an unlit pilot or combustion flame. Specifically, the EPA proposes to make changes to NSPS OOOOb (
40 CFR 60.5412b(a)(1)(viii)
,
40 CFR 60.5412b(a)(3)(viii)
,
40 CFR 60.5413b(e)(2)
,
40 CFR 60.5415b(f)(1)(vii)(A)
(
1
), and
40 CFR 60.5417b(d)(8)(i)
) and EG OOOOc (
40 CFR 60.5412c(a)(1)(viii)
,
40 CFR 60.5412c(a)(3)(vii)
,
40 CFR 60.5413c(e)(2)
,
40 CFR 60.5415c(e)(1)(vii)(A)
(
1
), and
40 CFR 60.5417c(d)(8)(i)
).
The EPA considers that a centralized control room (or control center) equipped with reliable telecommunications to collect and store data works as an acceptable alternative to the March 2024 Final Rule requirements to report lapses in pilot or combustion flame lighting to the nearest control room, even if that control room is located further away from the combustion device because that centralized control room may be better equipped and situated to respond to the unlit flame in an efficient and timely manner. Take, for example, a hypothetical situation where the nearest control room is 3 miles from the site (as measured on a map in a direct line “as the crow flies”) and a centralized control room is 50 miles from the site. The EPA finds no reason to limit the alert to the control room at 3 miles and prohibit the alert from instead going to the control room at 50 miles.
The EPA originally included the requirement for sending alerts when the pilot or combustion flame becomes unlit to the nearest control center because of its proximity to the site. When equipped with proper telecommunications equipment, the nearest control room (or control center) remains an effective option, and the EPA will continue to allow it as one of the locations to fulfill this requirement. However, the EPA acknowledges that sites lacking the ability to address the unlit flame from their nearest control room currently rely on resources from a centralized control room, regardless of where the owner or operator first sends the alert. Since the response time should remain unchanged under these circumstances, allowing owners and operators to directly send alerts to a centralized control room should not negatively impact the time taken to address the issue. In addition, the EPA agrees with petitioners that adding certain telecommunications equipment to sites in remote locations could have additional installation costs and may require a burdensome permitting process. Allowing operators the option to send the alert to an established centralized control room would provide flexibility and reduce burden on industry, while maintaining the effectiveness of the alert systems at the same level as prescribed in the March 2024 Final Rule.
d. EPA Method 22 “As Found” Conditions
Background.
The March 2024 Final Rule requires operators to conduct 15-minute EPA Method 22 visible emissions observations (
i.e.,
a determination of whether fugitive visual emissions occur) at least once each calendar month for various operating scenarios while each affected combustion control device operates.
[
225
]
Petitioners requested greater flexibility for operators to conduct EPA Method 22 (
40 CFR part 60, Appendix A
-7) observations.
[
226
]
Petitioners explained that due to substantial investment and ongoing efforts to maximize gas recovery for sales prior to liquids entering storage vessels, routing to a combustion control device occurs only intermittently. As a result, they argued that any EPA Method 22 observation conducted in the “as-found” condition of the combustion control device should count towards satisfying the monthly requirement. Otherwise, the petitioners cautioned that requiring operators to conduct EPA Method 22 observations only when combustion control devices actively receive emissions from affected and designated facilities would make compliance infeasible or force operators to intentionally flare.
Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale.
The EPA proposes to add a 24-operating hour “grace period” beyond each calendar month test period to allow operators to complete the monthly EPA Method 22 observation under normal operating conditions for each affected source. Specifically, the EPA proposes changes to NSPS OOOOb (
40 CFR 60.5412b(a)(1)(ix)
,
40 CFR 60.5413b(e)(3)
,
40 CFR 60.5415b(f)(1)(vii)(A)
(
2
), and
40 CFR 60.5417b(d)(8)(v)
), and EG OOOOc (
40 CFR 60.5412c(a)(1)(ix)
,
40 CFR 60.5413c(e)(3)
,
40 CFR 60.5415c(e)(1)(vii)(A)
(
2
), and
40 CFR 60.5417c(d)(8)(v)
).
The EPA recognizes that, due to various circumstances, operators may be unable to perform the required monthly EPA Method 22 observation. However, the EPA finds that performing a monthly EPA Method 22 test under “as found” conditions would not always comprehensively represent the applicable source's operation. For example, if the source is not operating at the time a facility performs an “as found” EPA Method 22 test, the EPA Method 22 results would indicate no presence of fugitive visual emissions. However, any such observation in that situation would stem from the source not being in operation, as opposed to confirming that the source operated without emitting fugitive visible emissions. Put another way, in order to determine if the combustion device is leaking gas one needs to observe the device with gas flowing through it. Observing no leaks when no gas is flowing in the device does not necessarily mean that the device is operating properly. By way of analogy, a plumber needs to observe a drainpipe with water flowing through it in order to determine if the drainpipe is leaking. If a plumber looks at a drainpipe while no water is flowing through it and sees no leaks, that does not necessarily mean the pipe is sound because it could leak as soon as you run water through the pipe due to a problem that was not otherwise easily observable without water running through the pipe.
With the proposed 24-operating-hours (as opposed to clock-hours) grace period being allowed after the conclusion of each calendar month in order to perform the monthly Method 22 observation, the EPA believes that these changes provide a reasonable accommodation to account for intermittent process flow, unpredictable operational schedules, and the time needed for staff to reach the site to perform the test.
[
227
]
The EPA further notes that if a facility utilizes the proposed 24 operating hours grace period, the facility cannot use that particular EPA Method 22 observation for the calendar month in which the “grace period test” occurred. That is, the “grace period test” would apply to the month with the missed “original” EPA Method 22 test, and a standard EPA Method 22 test would still need to occur in the month that the “grace period test” occurred (with the two observations separated by at least 15 days as currently prescribed by the
(
printed page 68278)
rule). The EPA solicits comment on whether a 24-operating-hours grace period suffices to accommodate the potential situations raised by petitioners, particularly considering the frequency of intermittent venting or accessibility of some sites. (Question III.7b)
e. Temporary Control Devices and Backup Control Devices
Background.
Under the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA regulates temporary and backup equipment in the same manner as permanently installed equipment that operates on a regular basis. Petitioners requested that the EPA exempt temporary control devices (TCDs) from the monitoring and performance testing requirements of the March 2024 Final Rule, because, given the short duration of their use, compliance is impracticable, if not impossible.
[
228
]
One petitioner provided liquids unloading as an example, noting that the ongoing compliance assurance requirements related to both a CVS and control device do not appropriately apply to liquids unloading operations. Petitioners state that because liquids unloading events occur intermittently, many of the required monitoring would take place while no liquids unloading activities occur.
[
229
]
Therefore, the petitioner asserted that the EPA should authorize the use of a temporary flare or portable control device to handle the emissions from liquids unloading events without stringent monitoring and recording requirements. Due to the temporary nature of these activities, the petitioner requested that the EPA mimic the requirements of control devices utilized for well completion affected facilities for any intermittent activities (
e.g.,
emergencies, routine maintenance, liquids unloading events, and blowdowns). In addition, petitioners expressed concerns regarding testing requirements for TCDs when the devices do not stay on-site long enough to meet the minimum testing durations. Petitioners used the 14-day NHV alternate sampling requirement as an example of an instance where the TCD may not remain on site long enough to meet the minimum testing duration.
Petitioners further asked the EPA to exempt backup control devices (BCDs) from monitoring and recordkeeping provisions. Petitioners defined BCDs as auxiliary and stationary control devices that are mostly used when a control device malfunctions or is out of service for maintenance. Because of their infrequent use, petitioners claimed difficulty in meeting prescribed testing and other compliance requirements. Petitioners asked the EPA to allow for exemptions up to 90 days per year per site for BCDs.
Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale.
Under the March 2024 Final Rule, temporary equipment is regulated in the same manner as permanently installed equipment that operates on a regular basis. The EPA agrees with the petitioner's assertion that TCDs should be exempted from some monitoring and performance testing requirements during intermittent activities, mainly due to the relatively short and unpredictable time the TCD could be on-site (which renders a permanently installed monitoring device such as a gas chromatograph or a 14-day sampling window infeasible for both sampling and scheduling purposes), coupled with the fact that these devices are typically rented from vendors not subject to the same air permit requirements as the facility itself. The EPA agrees that the rule's equal treatment of temporary and permanent devices creates practical burdens, because temporary devices (1) currently must maintain the same documentation, monitoring, and reporting as permanent devices, (2) are routinely moved, rented, or deployed quickly for short-term operational scenarios not conducive to stable monitoring, (3) often lack the integrated infrastructure and continuous monitoring systems of permanent units, and (4) must demonstrate destruction efficiency and proper operation under highly variable conditions and compressed timelines. These issues together explain why temporary control devices face disproportionate difficulty demonstrating compliance, even though the regulatory requirements themselves do not change with regards to temporary versus permanent control device use. Hence, the EPA agrees with the petitioner's assertions on the need for additional flexibility to be able to use mobile or quickly installable equipment when necessary.
Currently, some States have already set a precedent and offer exemptions for TCDs, with the duration of the exemptions centering around 30 days per year per site. For instance, the State of Texas allows for 480 hours (20 days) of exemptions per year from monitoring and record keeping for temporary control devices.
[
230
]
Industry stakeholders noted that most intermittent activities get resolved within 30 days. Hence, when an owner or operator uses a TCD, it usually is not on site for more than 30 days. As described above, this short timeframe makes it difficult for the owners or operators who use the TCD to comply with the monitoring and performance testing requirements of the March 2024 Final Rule. Moreover, based on industry feedback, some emergencies or other unanticipated scenarios can necessitate the use of TCDs beyond 30 days.
[
231
]
Therefore, the EPA proposes to exempt temporary control devices that are used for 30 operational days or less per site per year (on a 12-month rolling basis) from the NHV monitoring and performance testing requirements in the March 2024 final Rule. However, temporary control devices used for 30 operational days or less per site per year, on a 12-month rolling basis, must maintain certain records, including (1) performance certification documentation from the device manufacturer or rental vendor verifying that the flare can meet the required destruction efficiency of 95.0 percent for methane and VOC emissions, (2) make, model, and type of rental or temporary equipment (
e.g.,
trailer-mounted, skid-mounted, etc.), (3) location, date, and duration of operation of the device in hours, including start and stop time for each day of operation, (4) the volume of gas flared or vented, (5) documentation that the pilot flame is active at all times of operation of the device, (6) the specific reasons for the use of the temporary control device in lieu of capture or combustion, (7) the equipment rental agreement, and (8) documentation of whether or not a temporary process controller was used as part of the temporary control device configuration.
The EPA is also proposing that thereafter owners and operators can have an additional extension of the exemptions up to 60 additional operational days per site per year (on a 12-month rolling basis). For this additional extension period, the EPA proposes to require additional recordkeeping.
[
232
]
More specifically, for temporary control devices used for 90 operational days or less and greater than 30 operational days per site per year, on a 12-month rolling basis, the same
(
printed page 68279)
recordkeeping requirements previously summarized would still apply, along with gas composition data (including the net heating value) from a single grab sample for every 30 days of operation and documentation of equipment inspections and maintenance activities, including those prescribed by the manufacturer of the temporary control device. After 90 operational days of use, the TCD would then be subject to the same requirements as a permanently installed device at the facility would be. These proposed changes would impact NSPS OOOOb (
40 CFR 60.5413b(a)
,
40 CFR 60.5415b(f)
,
40 CFR 60.5417b(b)
, and
40 CFR 60.5420b(c)
) and EG OOOOc (
40 CFR 60.5413c(a)
,
40 CFR 60.5415c(e)
,
40 CFR 60.5417c(b)
, and
40 CFR 60.5420c(c)
).
In this proposed rule, the EPA proposes to define temporary control devices as control devices that are either mobile (whether on wheels, trucks, railcars, barges, ships,
etc.
) or skid mounted. This definition is modeled after the definition set by the State of Texas for TCDs.
[
233
]
Based on information provided by reconsideration petitioners, the EPA concluded, for the purposes of this proposal, that TCDs and stationary control devices had no other functional differences other than the aforementioned criterion.
[
234
]
Therefore, the EPA finds the performance of TCDs at controlling emissions as comparable to the performance of stationary control devices. Put another way, TCDs must still comply with the requirement in the March 2024 final Rule to reduce emissions that are routed to the TCD by 95.0 percent. The EPA's proposed changes for TCDs only relate to certain monitoring provisions.
Summary of Comment Solicitation.
The EPA acknowledges the petitioner's request to also exempt BCDs from the monitoring and performance testing provisions. While the EPA understands the need to exempt TCDs to address emergencies and other intermittent activities, the Agency has not received sufficient information to propose exempting BCDs. Specifically, the EPA lacks clarity on how BCDs differ from stationary control devices in a way that would warrant such a change. Moreover, the EPA understands that an air permit includes a BCD and lists BCDs as permitted equipment, along with the other permanent, stationary equipment and emission sources located at the facility. Unlike BCDs, the EPA understands that operators use TCDs on a temporary and situational ad hoc basis. Additionally, the EPA has not received sufficient information on the incidence of use or the number of BCDs across the industry.
Therefore, the EPA solicits comment on the use of BCDs, specifically on how BCDs differ from the permanently installed control devices operating at a given facility. The EPA additionally requests information on the incidence of use and the number of BCDs across the industry. The EPA also solicits comment on how to define BCDs, so as to not inadvertently incentivize their use over permanently installed control devices. (Question III.7c)
f. Temporary Process Controllers
Background.
Reconsideration petitioners highlighted that while permanent equipment runs routine production after flowback, oil and gas sites routinely rely on short-term equipment such as temporary process controllers (TPCs) to fulfill specific purposes during intermittent operations. Petitioners provided several examples (
e.g.,
temporary fuel conditioning skids, small compressor injection, and liquids unloading events) that require the usage of TPCs. For these scenarios, petitioners requested that the EPA exempt TPCs from the zero-emissions standards prescribed by the March 2024 Final Rule. Petitioners cited several reasons to provide relief for these devices, including the economic burden of retrofitting a handful of TPCs for minimal incremental emissions benefit, the risk of triggering a modification when bringing TPCs on site, and operational challenges with zero-emitting controllers when the necessary infrastructure is not yet in place.
Petitioners classified the intermittent usage of TPCs into two main scenarios: (1) embedded into TCD/BCDs and (2) used during the construction phase at a given facility (
e.g.,
drilling or well completions). For the scenario of embedment into TCD/BCDs, petitioners claimed that third parties often lease or own TPCs, thereby limiting the inventory of devices able to “plug in” to the site's permanent design. Moreover, petitioners stated that the March 2024 Final Rule is prohibitive in these scenarios since natural-gas-driven TPCs that permanently attach to TCD/BCDs could trigger modification without significant capital spending or planning if brought on site. Furthermore, petitioners claimed difficulty in retrofitting natural-gas-driven TPCs to comply with the zero-emission standards in a relatively short amount of time, without significant financial investment, for equipment that owners and operators might not directly own.
[
235
]
For the scenario of usage during the construction phase at a given facility, petitioners claimed that facilities readily use TPCs during this scenario. Even if a site intends on using low emitting process controllers during normal operations, the site may not have electricity or compressed air available to power the actuation of these devices. As such, sites may use TPCs in the interim to continue the construction of the site. Petitioners asked the EPA to exempt process controllers used during the construction phase of a site to provide relief.
Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale.
After further review and consideration of the petitions regarding TPCs embedded into TCDs, the EPA acknowledges that, while TPCs are not always needed as part of a TCD configuration, TPCs are nevertheless frequently attached to TCDs for certain phases of operation. The EPA also finds the petitioners' concerns legitimate in that temporary equipment cannot plug into permanent site utilities (
e.g.,
instrument air or electrical systems), which are designed only for permanent equipment. Retrofitting rented equipment that the facility does not own is also likely not allowed by the rental company per the rental agreement, along with being considered impractical and uneconomical. Moreover, certain site construction and flowback phases lack the necessary infrastructure to support zero emission controllers (where zero-emission infrastructure is often not present during construction, drilling, or flowback), temporary equipment is on-site only briefly, and the compliance requirements in the March 2024 Final Rule were designed under a framework for permanent, and not transient, devices.
As such, the EPA proposes to revise the requirements in NSPS OOOOb, and the presumptive standards in EG OOOOc, for process controllers that are embedded to TCDs for intermittent activities. These proposed changes entail treating process controllers that are permanently embedded into TCDs differently. The proposed changes will still allow these process controllers to comply with the zero-emission standard but will also provide an alternate “low bleed” standard for up to 30 operational days per site per year (on a 12-month
(
printed page 68280)
rolling basis), with associated recordkeeping. This “low bleed” standard takes after provisions introduced in the March 2024 final rule for process controllers in Alaska with natural gas-driven continuous bleed that lack access to power because of the site's limited infrastructure and remoteness. In these provisions, the low-bleed process controllers allow for no greater than 6 scfh in bleed rate.
[
236
]
The EPA proposes that following 30 operational days, a site may continue to comply with the alternate “low bleed” standard for these process controllers up to 60 additional operational days per site per year (on a 12-month rolling basis), with additional recordkeeping as described in section III.H.1.e. of this preamble. These proposed changes impact NSPS OOOOb (
40 CFR 60.5390b(b)
) and EG OOOOc (
40 CFR 60.5394c(b)
).
The March 2024 Final Rule also includes a yet to be fully “phased in” zero-emitting standard for process controllers that did not take into account process controllers used at a particular site for a limited amount of time, before removal from the site. Operators can comply by using multiple options, including using electricity- or compressed air-powered devices, instead of natural gas. Because TPCs are usually rented, owners and operators find it difficult to locate controllers that are compatible with the large variety of site designs. While some sites may have electricity from the power grid or air compressors already on site, remote locations or other certain locations often do not. To address this issue, TPC rental companies need to have varied TPC types at the ready to “plug-in” to sites with potentially different emission control requirements. Logistically, it may be difficult to maintain an inventory of multiple TPC types, particularly when multiple owners and operators in a region require the same type of TPC at the same time.
Moreover, there may also be emergency situations where owners and operators will need to use TCD/BCDs that are permanently attached to natural-gas-driven process controllers. In these cases, the facility would need to retrofit and potentially modify equipment they do not own to meet the zero-emitting provisions or risk being out of compliance. Given the urgency in response, these modifications could increase the site's response time or lead to unnecessary venting. Therefore, the EPA proposes to provide alternate compliance standards from the zero-emitting provisions for TPCs embedded to TCDs.
Summary of Comment Solicitation.
The EPA agrees with petitioners that standalone TPCs used during the construction phase of an oil and gas site fundamentally differ from TPCs embedded into TCDs. While both devices function similarly, standalone TPCs used during the construction phase can connect to transient machinery that normal well operation does not require. Thus, the number of standalone TPCs on site during the construction phase may vary substantially during this time. The EPA has not received sufficient information on the number of standalone TPCs used for the construction phase of a well, or the average number of days of having these devices on site. Thus, the EPA proposes no changes for standalone TPCs that are not embedded into TCDs. The EPA invites comment on the incidence of standalone TPCs present during the construction phase of a well and what the alternate standard from the zero-emitting provisions in the March 2024 Final Rule for these devices should be, along with providing any supporting information that the EPA can consider regarding TPCs that are not utilized as part of a TCD configuration. (Question III.7d)

I. Equipment Leaks at Gas Plants
1. Background
Under the March 2024 Final Rule, the NSPS OOOOb standards and the OOOOc EG (presumptive standards) apply to the “process unit equipment” affected and designated facilities and require that, for each piece of equipment that has the potential to emit methane or VOC (methane only for designated facilities), owners and operators conduct bimonthly (
i.e.,
once every other month) OGI monitoring in accordance with
40 CFR part 60, Appendix K
to detect equipment leaks from pumps in light liquid service, pressure relief devices in gas/vapor service, valves in gas/vapor or light liquid service, connectors in gas/vapor or light liquid service, and CVSs. As an alternative to the bimonthly OGI monitoring, facilities may use EPA Method 21 to detect leaks from the same equipment at frequencies specific to the process unit equipment type (
e.g.,
monthly for pumps, quarterly for valves). Facilities must use AVO to monitor open-ended valves and lines, pumps, valves and connectors in heavy liquid service, and pressure relief devices in light liquid or heavy liquid service. The March 2024 Final Rule, including the presumptive standards, requires that a facility must repair a leak after its detection. Facilities must repair valves by replacing the leaking valve with a low emission (low-E) valve, where technically feasible. The March 2024 Final Rule also requires that facilities must tag the leaking equipment for identification, commence a first attempt at repair for all identified leaks within 5 days after detection, and complete final repair within 15 days after detection (unless the delay-of-repair provisions apply). The EPA allows delay of repair where it is technically infeasible to complete repairs within 15 days without a process unit shutdown. In addition to the monitoring and repair requirements, the March 2024 Final Rule includes other equipment and monitoring requirements for specific types of equipment (
e.g.,
an open-ended valve or line must be equipped with a closure device).
Under the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA requires semiannual reporting for process unit equipment affected facilities. Inspection records required in the March 2024 Final Rule consist of:
Equipment identification
Date of inspection
Start and end times of inspection
Inspector name
Leak determination method
Monitoring instrument identification
Type of equipment monitored
Process unit identification
Appendix K records (where applicable)
EPA Method 21 instrument readings and calibration results (where applicable)
For visual inspections, the date, name of inspector, and result of inspection

Petitioners contended that without this first attempt at repair allowance, additional emissions could result from process unit shutdowns and/or piping blowdowns that a low-E repair may require.
[
244

The second issue raised by petitioners involves a request that the EPA reconsider the elimination of the applicability threshold of 10 percent VOC by weight and that the EPA add a threshold of 1 percent methane by weight in order to limit the number of additional components with low or no concentrations of the regulated pollutant from tagging and monitoring.
Sections III.I.2.a and b of this preamble provide the petitioners' concerns and supporting information, summary of proposed changes, and basis for proposed changes for both of these issues.
a. Low-E Valve Repair Requirements
Background.
Petitioners raised concerns with the March 2024 Final
(
printed page 68282)
Rule requirement that leaking valves at natural gas processing plants be repaired with low-E packing or replaced with low-E valves unless demonstrated to be technically infeasible.
[
245
]
[
246

Petitioners requested that the low-E valve repair requirements be revised to allow for a first repair attempt using other, less costly actions such as those found in NSPS KKK, OOOO, and OOOOa, which include:
Tightening of bonnet bolts;
Replacement of bonnet bolts;
Tightening of packing gland nuts; and
Injection of lubricant into lubricated packing.
Petitioners explained that most leaks can be repaired using these first repair attempt actions and expressed concern that eliminating these first repair attempt actions and requiring a low-E repair would create environmental disbenefits. Specifically, they noted that additional emissions could result from process unit shutdowns and/or piping blowdowns that may be required for a low-E repair. Petitioners recommended that the EPA revise the March 2024 Final Rule to allow these first repair attempt actions instead of a low-E valve repair or at a minimum before requiring a low-E valve repair.
Petitioners asserted that the March 2024 Final Rule inaccurately characterized low-E valves and packing as having no additional costs compared to traditional valves and packing. In their experience, low-E valves and packing are more expensive. They stated that they were not able to provide cost information or comments on this issue prior to the March 2024 Final Rule because the low-E valve repair requirements were not included in the November 2021 Proposal or December 2022 Supplemental Proposal. Consequently, they requested administrative reconsideration of the low-E valve repair requirements.
Summary of Proposed Changes and Rationale.
Petitioners
[
247
]
are correct that the low-E valve repair requirements that the EPA finalized in 2024 were not included in the November 2021 Proposal or December 2022 Supplemental Proposal. In the November 2021 Proposal, the EPA proposed repair requirements for leaking equipment. In the November 2021 Proposal, the EPA proposed that the definition of “repaired” (for equipment) included that the equipment be adjusted, replaced, or otherwise altered, in order to eliminate equipment leaks and that the equipment be re-monitored to verify that emissions from the equipment are below the leak definition.
[
248
]
The EPA explained at that time that valve repairs can include replacement with low-E valves, valve packing, or drill-and-tap with a low-E injectable (“low-E equipment”) but the Agency did not require replacement with low-E equipment. The EPA explained that low-E equipment meets the specifications of the American Petroleum Institute (API) 622 or API 624 and typically includes a manufacturer written warranty or a performance guarantee that it will not emit fugitive emissions at a concentration greater than 100 ppmv during the first 5 years.
[
249
]
In the December 2022 Supplemental Proposal, the EPA proposed a definition of “repaired” (for equipment) consistent with that discussed in the November 2021 Proposal. The EPA did not propose to require the replacement of leaking valves with low-E equipment, noting that the technology is not appropriate for all repairs, but reiterated the position from the November 2021 Proposal that due to the performance expectations, low-E equipment can be a viable option for valve repair.
[
250
]
The EPA received comments on the December 2022 Supplemental Proposal that urged the Agency to require replacement of leaking equipment with low-E valves. One commenter cited a recent rulemaking, where Colorado found these options to be similar in cost to non-low-E valves and packing and directed operators to consider them.
[
251 252
]
The commenter also noted that some manufacturers claimed that their low-E packing can reduce emissions of harmful gases by up to 95.0 percent versus valves with traditional packing, with minimal cost impacts.
The EPA responded to these comments on the December 2022 Supplemental Proposal by stating that the commenter's understanding of the cost for low-E equipment aligns with that of the EPA in that they are similar in cost to non-low-E equipment. Therefore, the EPA concluded that replacing leaking valves with low-E equipment would result in lower emissions with no additional cost burden (compared to using non-low-E equipment). As such, the final standard in NSPS OOOOb, and the presumptive standard in EG OOOOc, requires replacing leaking valves with low-E valves or repacking existing valves with low-E packing, except where it is not technically feasible. If delay of repair is required to repack or replace the valve, the final rule allows the use of the delay of repair requirements provisionally, but an owner or operator would not be able to delay valve repair or replacement beyond the next process unit shutdown. e.g.,
cost savings from less product loss, less compliance and penalty risks). However, some estimates indicate that the upfront costs of a low-E valve can be 25 percent more than the upfront costs for a non-low-E valve, and the EPA acknowledges that there may be even greater upfront cost differences for some low-E valves (depending on the level of automation and valve functionality and temperature and pressure conditions).

A valve may qualify as a low-E valve if it is as an extension of another valve that has qualified as a low-E valve.

Petitioners on the March 2024 Final Rule raised as they had previously in their comments on the proposed rule, concerns that some streams at gas processing plants contain methane or VOC in such low concentrations that facilities almost always receive monitoring results of no detected emissions, rendering monitoring obsolete. However, petitioners provided information that such streams also include, but are not limited to pure ethane, acid gas streams (
i.e.,
H
2

The EPA also acknowledges that equipment leak component monitoring on process units subject to NSPS KKK, NSPS OOOO, or NSPS OOOOa (which include a VOC content of 10 percent by weight applicability threshold) have resulted in many components not being subject to LDAR requirements and have never previously been tagged or subject to the equipment leak monitoring requirements of NSPS KKK, NSPS OOOO, or NSPS OOOOa. Under the March 2024 Final Rule provisions, the EPA recognizes that having to tag each equipment emissions component located at a natural gas processing plant for monitoring would be a significant undertaking considering the number of equipment emissions components located at a natural gas processing plant.
EPA Method 18 is designed for ppm level sources (EPA Method 18, section 1.2.1). As such, very small traces of methane or VOC in a gas stream may be detectable using EPA Method 18. This supports the petitioners' statements that the current requirements related to potential to emit methane or VOC could effectively require monitoring of all process unit equipment components. The EPA Method 21 leak definition is 500 ppmv. As such, it is possible to have gas streams that have a detectable concentration of methane and/or VOC that do not result in a process unit equipment component with a detectable leak. In general, the Agency expects that the vast majority of process unit equipment components at a natural gas processing plant will be in methane or VOC service when implementing a 1 percent by weight and 10 percent by weight thresholds for methane and VOC, respectively.
The average methane compositions for components in VOC and non-VOC service when modeling the impacts of different LDAR programs were well over 50 percent by weight.

J. Associated Gas From Wells Producing Primarily Oil
1. Background
Under the March 2024 Final Rule, NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc establish standards and presumptive standards, respectively, for associated gas from wells operated primarily for oil production at well affected and designated facilities. Subject to certain caveats for existing sources, the rule generally requires each well producing associated gas to reduce emissions to the atmosphere through work practices, with some limited allowances for routine or emergency flaring as discussed in more detail below. The work practice standards require operators to recover the associated gas from the separator and either route it to a gas gathering flow line or a collection system leading to a sales line, use it as an onsite fuel source, use it for another beneficial purpose that would otherwise rely on a purchased fuel, chemical feedstock, or raw material, or reinject it into the same well or into another well.

The NSPS OOOOb provisions under the March 2024 Final Rule separated new wells that produce associated gas into groups based on when construction is/was commenced. New wells in the first group (
i.e.,

The final standards do not allow these wells to routinely flare emissions because the EPA determined, when it finalized the March 2024 rule, that, with advance planning, at least one of the options to avoid routine flaring would be feasible at these wells (including routing the gas to a sales line, using the gas as an onsite fuel source, using the gas for another beneficial purpose that a purchased fuel, chemical feedstock, or raw material would serve, or reinjecting it into the well or into another well).
Wells in the second group (

3. EPA Considerations and Proposed Action
a. Revisions to BSER
The EPA is proposing to revise BSER to routing associated gas through a CVS to a control device or flare that achieves 95 percent reduction in emissions or greater. This section discusses the Agency's proposal that the previous BSER determination of routing associated gas to a sales line is not BSER, followed by a discussion of the proposed BSER determination for associated gas.
i. Routing Associated Gas to a Sales Line Is Not BSER
The EPA is proposing that routing associated gas to a sales line may no longer be included as a viable control option in the BSER analysis. The BSER analysis conducted for this control option in the March 2024 Final Rule included several key assumptions, predictions, and foundational underpinnings that recent information has shown are not accurate. New facts significantly call into question the
(
printed page 68290)
achievability of this control option. Further, the control option too heavily relies on actions of third parties that owners and operators (those subject to the EPA's regulations) have no control over.
In the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA anticipated that “owners planning on drilling new wells in the future have the ability to plan ahead to ensure that the associated gas is routed to a sales line.”
[
299
]
But this statement was based on predictions about the industry that have not come to fruition and thus inaccurate. In that rulemaking, the EPA cited to some States that have essentially banned routine flaring of associated gas, and to a voluntary commitment from some companies to end routine flaring by 2030.
[
300
]
However, these States and companies do not represent the entire industry that the EPA is charged with regulating. Further, neither these state regulations nor the voluntary commitments are governed by (required by) the CAA, so their existence does not necessarily mean that similar requirements are permissible under the CAA. As discussed in sections III.J.2.a through III.J.2.d of this preamble, some companies in certain parts of the country cannot route their associated gas to a sales line, even with advanced planning.
While the EPA was aware of these potential issues, in the 2024 Final Rule, the Agency made assumptions about the industry that presumed there would be timely and sufficient sales line infrastructure development. However, new information (see sections III.J.2.c and d of this preamble) since promulgation of the March 2024 Final rule shows that the EPA's assumptions have not been borne out by real-world industry development.
In the EPA's TSD for the March 2024 Final Rule, the Agency identified several “challenges” with the control option of routing to a sales line.

301

302

Second, the EPA acknowledged that “[b]uilding a gathering pipeline system and associated compressors is a large capital expense and requires permits and negotiations with landowners.”
[
303

Third, the EPA recognized that “oil wells are drilled by exploration and production companies; to tie into a gathering pipeline system would require coordination with midstream gas companies and would depend on multiple variables of the associated gas produced from the oil well.”

304

Despite all of these identified obstacles, the Agency still finalized routing to sales as the BSER based on the general idea that owners and operators would find a way to comply; that “opportunities exist for advance planning” and that “owners and operators of newly drilled wells have the flexibility to plan and coordinate the construction of gas gathering systems even over extended distances.”

The frequent and widespread flaring of associated gas in the context of a requirement that purports to prohibit flaring demonstrates that the EPA's previous BSER analysis was flawed. The fact that oil wells must so often rely on these flaring exemptions calls into question whether routing to a sales line can be considered the BSER, and it calls into question the EPA's previous claims that the BSER resulted in 100% emission reduction.
The EPA previously assumed that all associated gas would be routed into a sales line at all times, but in reality, sources often flare under the current rule's exceptions. As such, it is very likely that the EPA overestimated the true emission reduction from routing to a sales line and thus made a decision based on an inaccurate BSER analysis that does not reflect how these sources actually operate in the real world. In other words, the difference between the “100 percent capture” via routing to a sales line is actually lower than that and closer to 95 percent which is the efficiency from flaring. In reality, many sources are still flaring because they cannot route all of their associated gas to a sales line all of the time.
Lastly, with regard to costs, the EPA's BSER analysis did not account for the added costs of buying, installing, and operating a flare to comply with the temporary flaring exceptions, nor did the EPA assume that flares already onsite for other purposes could accept the increase gas flow during these periods. Since temporary flaring is needed for the route to sales standard, many (if not all) owners and operators routing to a sales line need to purchase, install, and maintain a flare. The EPA did not consider this cost. As such, the 2024 BSER analysis underestimated the true costs of the current standard and overestimated emission reductions; in reality, routing to a sales line has proven less effective and more costly than the EPA previously anticipated.
Next, the March 2024 Final Rule reflected an overbroad reading of CAA section 111 that did not recognize or account for the scale of the infrastructure required for compliance, including the difference between systems that sources can apply to meet the standards that apply to them and systems that require significant investment and performance by third parties. Owners and operators of oil wells subject to the “route to sales line” requirements are dependent on third parties to develop and operate virtually all the components of the sales line. Many owners and operators of upstream facilities do not own or operate the midstream pipelines that are required to implement the standard for associated gas. Companies cannot compel midstream operators to expand their infrastructure so that they can accept additional natural gas. This system differs from the types of equipment the Agency has historically selected as BSER. All relevant third parties would need to timely complete their components of the infrastructure across large geographic areas for the owners and operators to be able to comply with the standard by the time the well begins producing, and thereafter, owners and operators must rely on the continued cooperation and operation of these third parties. Upon further consideration, the EPA concludes that the scale of the necessary infrastructure, including the necessary involvement of third parties nationwide, is different in kind from control measures historically considered under CAA section 111 and thus not an allowable form of BSER.
Put another way, the EPA has, upon further review, determined that the novelty of a BSER predicated on widespread infrastructure developed and operated by third parties warns strongly against its selection. Much of the necessary gathering and sales line infrastructure requires the involvement, both for initial development and ongoing performance, of external third parties over whom the owners and operators of regulated facilities have limited, if any, control. For example, the EPA correctly explained in the TSD for the March 2024 Final Rule that routing gas to a sales line entails third parties and depends on “multiple variables”, including permitting and “negotiating with landowners.”

It is possible that in some instances a landowner might simply refuse to allow any gas pipeline to cross their land. Further, a midstream company (not the regulated owner/operator) would very likely be the entity planning, contracting, and maintaining the necessary sales line and be the third party that controls which owner/operators may route gas into their sales line. This situation is not within the oil well owner's or operator's control. Moreover, natural resources such as oil reservoirs only occur in certain geographic areas of the country. Owners and operators do not get to pick and choose where the oil is located; they must develop their regulated source where the oil exists and in some cases the oil exists in locations where these variables prove unworkable. In some
(
printed page 68292)

In other cases, the oil wells may be located in proximity to an existing sales line but the downstream infrastructure is not capable of handling new volumes of natural gas. The owner/operator of the sales line may not be able to accept new gas for a variety of reasons. For instance, the pressure in the existing sales line pipeline may be too great for the new oil wells to be able to inject their gas into the pipeline much of the time, or the natural gas processing plant may not have the capacity to accept the additional gas. Even after an oil well site is connected to a sales line, there may be multiple reasons why the pipeline is unable to accept the gas. This could be due to the quality of the natural gas at the oil well site; or similarly, it could be due to the quality of natural gas at neighboring well sites owned by other companies, resulting in a situation where the midstream operator is unwilling to accept any natural gas in the area until the source of the poor-quality natural gas is identified. There can also be bottlenecks at some point in the pipeline network that prevent the midstream operators from accepting all of the natural gas from a well site.
A BSER based on routing associated gas to a sales line thus requires involvement, at multiple steps, of a complex web of different entities across a wide range of disciplines, some of whom may not be part of the regulated source category, or even the broader industry of which it is part,
i.e.,
the oil and gas industry. As just one example, the BSER could entail several different government permitting offices at the local (town, city, and/or county), State and/or federal (other than the EPA) level, multiple individual landowners, and a midstream gas gathering and sales company. The implication is that these third parties are not subject to the same regulatory impetus as the owner or operator of an oil well that would be subject to requirements under the March 2024 Final Rule. The scale of the ancillary infrastructure required to support implementation of the standard and the multitude of parties outside of an owner or operator's control at multiple steps of the process that are necessary to successfully design, permit, construct, test, operate, and maintain a system to route associated gas to a sales line makes it unreasonable to base federally enforceable requirements on the presumption of a best-case scenario for implementation when tardy- or non-performance by a single party has the potential to cause or exacerbate delays that ripple through the deployment of the entire system upon which the standard relies. All this compounds the likelihood of not having the necessary infrastructure in place when oil production begins, which further supports the unreasonableness of the current standard.
The tenuousness of timely compliance given the scope of the requisite infrastructure for routing associated gas to a sales line, coupled with the novelty of the standard and the need for a large number of third parties, is especially apparent when it is contrasted with an air pollution control technology that has been in widespread use in the oil and gas sector for decades: combustion devices (flares), a control technology that does not rely on extensive pipeline infrastructure. It simply requires the owner/operator to purchase, install, and operate the device on-site. While that process does in some ways involve third parties (for example, to build and, perhaps, install the device), the industry has a long history of using these deceives such that completing the request steps is not overly complex or unreasonably dependent upon novel third party interactions.
The EPA acknowledges that some owners/operators of oil wells also own and operate their own midstream sales line infrastructure such that these characterizations of heavy reliance on third-party involvement may not be accurate for all sources (although there may be requirements that the midstream company cannot give preference to an upstream company owned by the same parent company). However, the EPA understands this is not often the situation and that in most cases the oil well site owner/operator has little to no control over the sales line infrastructure. The EPA is soliciting comment and information on the proportion of owners and operators that also own or operate their own midstream sales line infrastructure. (Question III.9a)
To be sure, many oil wells can and do route at least some of their associated gas to a sales line. However, in those instances, routing to sales has not been required by federal regulation under enforceable timelines or at a similar nationwide scale, meaning that any non-performance by third parties has not resulted in noncompliance with federally enforceable obligations.
In reaching these conclusions, the EPA notes that CAA section 111 anticipates analyses and regulatory requirements that turn on actions by the regulated source. Pursuant to CAA section 111(a)(1), the Agency must promulgate standards that “reflec[t] the degree of emission limitation achievable through the
application
of the [BSER],” and the resulting emission standards apply, in turn, to the regulated source. Consistent with the EPA's historical understanding, this language is most naturally read as tying the BSER to results that are achievable through the source's application of the selected control technology. While sources commonly rely on third parties in the normal operation of their business, the extensive infrastructure requirements for routing to a sales line, coupled with the high level of dependence on third parties, undermines the ability of sources to achieve the emission standards. If any third-party provider responsible for any of the many links in the sales line infrastructure chain fails to develop the necessary infrastructure in a particular area, is delayed in such development for any reason, or ceases operation for any reason, the source would no longer be able to comply. These circumstances are different in kind from other BSERs that entail substantially less reliance on third-party infrastructure.
The EPA is thus finding that the March 2024 Final Rule erred by not considering the extent of the ancillary infrastructure and reliance on third parties needed for routing associated gas to a sales line to be deployable at scale.

Each of these options are discussed below.
Use as an Onsite Fuel Source
The use of associated gas from an oil well as an onsite fuel source is only technically feasible under certain operating conditions. This control option is generally most feasible where gas volumes and pressures are sufficiently stable to support operation of generators or heaters, and where gas composition is compatible with such use, either directly or with limited conditioning. Onsite use may be particularly advantageous when there is a consistent demand for power or heat, enabling offset of diesel or grid electricity consumption. However, the EPA recognizes that not every oil well is suitable for recovering and using associated gas onsite because technical limitations often make it impractical. In many instances, site-specific conditions preclude its implementation. For example, associated gas production may be intermittent, variable, or of insufficient quantity to support stable operation of generators, heaters, or processing equipment. In addition, associated gas may contain contaminants such as hydrogen sulfide (H
2
S), carbon dioxide (CO
2
), water vapor, or heavy hydrocarbons, which may necessitate extensive conditioning to avoid corrosion, engine damage, or unsafe combustion. Additionally, the intermittent nature of production, especially in unconventional reservoirs, can lead to unreliable or inconsistent gas supply, which hinders the functioning of fuel systems that require steady input. Further, some existing well sites may lack the physical space or infrastructure needed to safely handle, treat, and distribute gas to onsite equipment. Lastly, some sites where onsite use is technically feasible may only be able to use a portion of the associated gas that the oil well produces due to the demand that exists on that site for such fuels. Sites that do not have sufficient onsite demand for all of their associated gas would then have remaining gas that they could not use onsite. While the use of associated gas as an onsite fuel source may constitute a feasible emissions control strategy at some facilities, it is not widely practicable across the affected source category.
Accordingly, while using associated gas as an onsite fuel source is adequately demonstrated, it is not achievable across the country.
Reinject the Recovered Gas Into the Well or Inject the Recovered Gas Into Another Well
Reinjecting recovered associated gas into the producing well or injecting it into another nearby well may be an attractive option because it can allow operators to avoid flaring or venting while also enhancing reservoir performance. By returning the gas underground, producers may be able to maintain reservoir pressure, which can improve oil recovery and extend the productive life of the field. This approach may also reduce emissions, eliminate the need for immediate gas processing or transportation infrastructure, and offer flexibility by storing the gas for future use when market conditions or infrastructure availability are more favorable. However, reinjection is not technologically feasible for every oil well because it requires reservoirs with the right geological and pressure characteristics to safely accept additional gas. Some geological formations cannot accommodate more gas via reinjection without risking loss of reservoir integrity, unwanted fluid migration, or disruption of natural flow patterns. In certain wells, gas reinjection may interfere with oil displacement mechanisms or alter fluid composition in ways that reduce recovery efficiency. Additionally, not all fields have nearby wells or formations suitable for injection, and some reservoirs may lack the pressure, permeability, or structural stability needed to retain injected gas without risking leakage or contamination of other subsurface zones.
Considering the same adequately demonstrated and achievable criteria for BSER discussed above, the EPA concludes that reinjecting the recovered gas into the well or inject the recovered gas into another well is not achievable across the country.
Recover Associated Gas and Use It for Another Purpose Displacing Purchased Fuel or Raw Material Consumption
Using the recovered gas for another useful purpose that a purchased fuel or raw material serves as a generic “catch-all” provision that does not provide sufficient specificity for establishing BSER. In the December 2022 Supplemental Proposal, the EPA discussed examples of potential “other useful purpose” options to utilize associated gas and avoid venting or flaring, namely methane pyrolysis and condensing the gas and transporting it to other sites for use.

ii. Routing to a Flare or Control Device
The EPA considered two types of flaring options (which includes other control devices): flares or devices that control 95 percent reduction and those that achieve 98 percent reduction. These options are described below.
Flares and Devices That Achieve 95 Percent Reduction
Associated gas can be routed to a flare or another control device capable of achieving 95 percent reduction in emissions. Achieving this level of performance depends on having a consistently lit pilot flame, sufficient combustion temperature, appropriate gas flow rates, and effective mixing of air and hydrocarbons so that the gas fully burns rather than escapes un-combusted. Routing to a flare is an adequately demonstrated technology that is applicable across the country.
In the 2022 Supplemental Proposal Technical Support Document (TSD),

The EPA also presented flare costs estimates of $100,579 in capital costs and $36,000 in annual costs (including capital recovery and operation and maintenance). After updating these costs to a 2024 base year, the estimated total annual cost of a flare is $47,411. On that basis, the cost effectiveness is estimated at $145 per ton of methane reduced and $523 per ton of VOC reduced for the representative well. These values are in the range that the Agency has considered reasonable in the past.
Flare and Devices That Achieve 98 Percent Reduction
Flares can also achieve 98 percent destruction efficiency when they are properly designed, operated, and maintained. As with a flare designed to achieve 95 percent reduction, performance at a 98 percent reduction also depends on having a consistently lit pilot flame, adequate combustion temperature, favorable gas flow rates, and effective mixing of air and hydrocarbons. However, achieving this higher efficiency requires even more stable conditions—such as steady pressure, wind protection, and appropriate flare tip design—that help ensure complete combustion and enable flares to reach or exceed 98 percent emission reduction under ideal operating environments.
In the November 2021 Proposed Rule, the EPA indicated that combustion devices that are designed to meet a 98 percent control efficiency may not continuously meet this efficiency in practice in the oil and gas industry due to factors such as variability of field conditions. The EPA specifically requested comment on the potential to require more rigorous monitoring requirements for the oil and natural gas industry to ensure 98 percent reduction, such as those contained in NESHAP for the Petroleum Refinery Sector,

iii. Proposed BSER Determination
Based on this evaluation of all technically viable options for managing associated gas from oil wells, the EPA concludes that neither onsite use, reinjection, nor other beneficial-use technologies satisfy the statutory criteria of being both adequately demonstrated and achievable. Emerging technologies likewise cannot serve as BSER because they are not yet sufficiently proven or commercially practical. In contrast, routing associated gas to a flare or other control device capable of achieving a 95-percent reduction in methane and VOC emissions is an adequately demonstrated, widely applicable, and cost-effective system, with performance and cost-effectiveness values that fall within ranges the Agency has historically considered reasonable. Additional analysis shows that a 98 percent reduction is potentially not achievable in field conditions and would impose incremental costs exceeding levels the Agency has found reasonable. Therefore, the record supports a conclusion that a 95-percent reduction in methane and VOC emissions represents BSER for associated gas.
iv. Proposed Standards and Presumptive Standards for Associated Gas
Therefore, for associated gas, the EPA is proposing that the associated gas must be routed through a closed vent system to a control device that achieves 95 percent reduction in emissions or greater, or route through a closed vent system to a flare that meets the applicable flare requirements. The EPA is proposing that owners and operators would be free to utilize compliance methods that achieve even greater reductions, including capturing and routing to a sales line 100 percent of their associated gas or using 100 percent of their associated gas for another beneficial purpose. The EPA is also proposing that if a portion of the associated gas is routed to sales or used for another purpose, the remaining portion must comply with the 95 percent standard. For example, if a company could route 40 percent of their associated gas to a sales line or for another potential purpose, the company would need to route the other 60 percent to a control device with a 95 percent reduction or to a flare.

1. Option 1. Subcategorization of Marginal Wells
There is considerable diversity throughout the many different oil and natural gas wells, and well sites, across the country. One significant aspect of this diversity is related to the level of oil and/or gas production from each well, which can vary over the life of the well. An important subset of the industry are wells that have lower production levels. Low production wells (
i.e.,
wells with less than 15 barrels of oil equivalent per day) are the most numerous types of existing wells, comprising more than 78 to 80 percent of existing oil and natural gas wells in the United States. These wells accounted for approximately 7 percent of total U.S. oil and natural gas produced in 2024.
[
334
]
These “low production wells” are frequently existing wells (existing sources subject to EG OOOOc) that are nearing the end of their productive life but continue to produce at low levels for a decade or more. Within the oil and natural gas industry, there are several commonly used terms to describe wells that produce less oil and/or gas that are used for a variety of reasons. Different industry groups and government entities can use slightly different terms, sometimes to describe the same or similar wells, and sometimes to describe slightly different wells. Further, these terms can sometimes be used in conjunction with different defining criteria such as production-based thresholds and/or defined at the site level (which can consist of multiple individual wells) instead of the individual well level. The inconsistent use of terminology, and the associated defining criteria, can lead to confusion. For example, several state tax codes have different tax requirements for low production wells and often peg the applicability of those different requirements to a specific volume of production of oil and/or gas. Although the definition and requirements can vary, they tend to center around a threshold of a maximum daily average oil production of 15 barrels of oil or a maximum daily average gas production of 90 thousand cubic feet of gas per day (Mcfd) over a set time period.
[
335
]
For example, Colorado Title 39. Section 39-29-105(1)(b) exempts gross income from the sale of oil and gas produced from “any wells that produce fifteen barrels per day or less of oil and gas produced from wells that produce ninety thousand cubic feet or less of gas per day for the average of all producing days” for the taxable year. Similarly, the definition from the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (codified at
42 U.S.C. 15903
) for a “marginal property” refers to an onshore unit, communitization agreement, or individual lease that produces, on average over the prior three production months, less than 15 barrels of oil per well per day or 90 million BTU of gas per well per day, considering only wells that produced on more than half of those days. However, many wells produce both oil and natural gas, which makes applying these criteria for low producing wells challenging. Barrel of Oil Equivalent (boe) is a common metric that is used to provide a standardized way to express energy content across different fuel types, allowing a comparison of oil and natural gas wells on an equal footing, as well as accounting for wells that produce both. Because oil is measured in barrels and natural gas in cubic feet, boe serves as a common metric that converts both oil and natural gas into a single, comparable unit. The conversion is straightforward: one thousand cubic feet of natural gas contains approximately one-sixth of the energy of a barrel of oil; therefore, 6,000 cubic feet of natural gas (6 Mcf) has the energy
(
printed page 68298)
equivalent of one barrel of oil. Accordingly, the criteria used to define a marginal well can alternatively be defined as a well with a maximum daily average oil and/or gas production level of 15 boe per day. By way of another example of how various terms for low production wells have been defined, the federal Internal Revenue Code defines a “stripper well
336

Although “marginal well” is a commonly used term, defining what classifies a well as economically marginal is challenging, as the profitability depends on a number of factors, including the cost of production and the price of oil and natural gas. However, the EPA notes that most stripper/low production wells are likely to be marginally profitable wells, (
i.e.,

CAA section 111(b)(2) authorizes the EPA to distinguish among classes, types, and sizes within categories of new sources for the purpose of establishing standards of performance.
