The basic approach for the evaluation in this proposal is summarized as follows: first, the EPA created representative well sites to characterize the production levels, equipment, and baseline emissions at typical marginal well sites; next, the Agency identified potential control options for each emission source at the representative marginal well site, and estimated the capital and annual costs, as well as the cost effectiveness values for each potential control at each emissions source; third, the EPA compared the anticipated costs of compliance for each potential control option to the estimated well site profits to assess cost reasonableness of the individual control option; fourth, the EPA developed regulatory alternatives that included different combinations of potential control options, considering cost effectiveness and cost reasonableness of the individual control options; finally, the EPA compared the total compliance costs of the emissions control options for all of the emissions sources for each regulatory alternative considered at the representative sites to the total facility emissions reductions and the estimated facility profits at the representative site to assess the cost reasonableness of the combination of potential control requirements in each regulatory option considered. The common measure used for this evaluation is “cost effectiveness,” which is expressed as a cost per ton of emission reduction achieved.
While cost effectiveness on an individual emission source basis has historically been the primary factor in determining BSER for this industry, the EPA also has evaluated costs at a sector level by assessing the projected new capital expenditures required under each rule (compared to overall new capital expenditures by the sector) and the projected compliance costs (compared to overall annual revenue for the sector) if the rule were to require such controls.

Previously, the EPA had not directly considered whether the costs of the standards are excessive or greater than each segment of the industry could bear. The Agency's prior analyses were based on the whole onshore oil and natural gas production sector, even though there is a wide difference in the amount of production and associated revenue between different types of wells. Newly drilled sites may produce over 1,000 boe per day, while many older wells have production levels of less than 15 boe per day. While the revenue generated from selling oil and natural gas differs greatly between these lower and higher production sites, the costs of emissions controls are often largely the same. For instance, the cost to install the infrastructure to route associated gas to a sales line is substantially the same regardless of the amount of oil and associated gas that is produced from a site. Due to these circumstances, the emissions control costs for sites producing less oil and natural gas represent a much larger share of the revenue generated for a marginal well site than for a site with high production volumes. Put another way, the oil and natural gas industry, as a whole, includes a very wide range of operations such that certain costs may be reasonable for some regulated entities and simultaneously unreasonable for others. The EPA's historic approach to considering industry-wide costs did not account for these real-world differences that are unique to this industry considering the very large number of sources in the industry. In reality, this particular industry has sub-industries, or select portions of the larger industry, that operate very differently from the larger industry. To account for the divergent revenues of these different oil and gas site types, in this proposal, the EPA is both evaluating cost effectiveness on a cost per ton of emissions reduction basis for each control option at the source level and cost reasonableness based on the capital and ongoing compliance costs compared to overall revenue less operating costs (
i.e.,
profits) for this subcategory of the industry (
i.e.,
marginal wells). In this action, the Agency is proposing that for a control option to be considered BSER, the associated costs would have to be reasonable under both cost metrics.
Additionally, the EPA has historically assessed the cost effectiveness of potential standards for oil and natural gas sources (for all past NSPS and EG for oil and gas) on a particular type of equipment or process in isolation,
i.e.,
without consideration of the compliance costs of co-located equipment integral to
(
printed page 68304)
production. This approach for this industry resulted in cases wherein some control options appeared cost reasonable in isolation. However, owner/operators that are subject to the NSPS and EG do not just own and operate one isolated piece of equipment or process. An owner/operator in this industry likely has to bear the compliance costs of multiple standards simultaneously. For example, at an individual oil well site an owner/operator might be subject to five different standards: (1) fugitives monitoring, (2) associated gas, (3) pneumatic pumps, (4) process controllers, and (5) storage vessels. As such, under this scenario, the particular owner/operator would have to pay to implement all five standards. The EPA has previously determined for this industry that each standard was cost reasonable in isolation with little regard to the total, cumulative, compliance costs that the NSPS or EG imposed on the owner/operator.
[
380
]
As explained more below, the approach that the EPA is proposing here seeks to correct this oversight for marginal wells, where this issue matters most because profit margins can be very small, by considering the total cumulative costs that the oil and gas regulations are imposing on those owners and operators. The EPA proposes that this is a better way to assess costs in the BSER analysis for the marginal well subcategory of the industry.
Because the marginal well subsector of the onshore oil and natural gas production sector operates under distinct economic conditions, such that the traditional cost effectiveness approach may not fully represent the potential impact on this subsector, the EPA is proposing that it is appropriate to consider the cost reasonableness of the potential standards at the site-level, instead of piecemeal. As previously noted in section III.K.1.b, the EPA estimates that between 100,000 and 200,000 marginal wells could cease operations due to the costs of complying with the NSPS OOOOb or EG OOOOc. In light of these concerns, the Agency is including consideration of the total compliance costs in relation to profitability on a site basis in the BSER analysis for marginal well sites. The EPA proposes that this approach to cost reasonableness for purposes of the BSER analysis is more appropriate for this NSPS and EG for marginal wells because it allows the Agency to fully account for all compliance costs imposed on the owner/operator of these particular emissions sources and to compare those costs to the distinct economics of marginal well sites. Further, by incorporating profitability into the cost consideration for marginal wells, the EPA can more accurately assess the reasonableness of the total cost of compliance for this segment of sources relative to the guidelines that courts have outlined in CAA section 111 caselaw. Put another way, incorporating profitability into the cost prong of the BSER analysis here allows the Agency to more accurately characterize whether a particular cost is exorbitant, excessive, or greater than this subcategory of the industry (marginal wells), could bear and survive. By way of a simplified example, a total NSPS compliance costs of $100 per year would objectively not be more than an industry could survive if the average source in that industry generated $10,000,000 in profit each year. However, if the average source generated only $90 in profit each year, then, depending on the circumstances and any relevant related facts, the EPA might conclude that same $100 in compliance costs was more than the industry could bear and survive.
A key aspect of this marginal well BSER analysis is the consideration of the profitability of a representative well site to assess cost reasonableness. To assess cost reasonableness, the EPA calculated the expected revenue for different levels of production and estimated the associated operating costs and profit levels. Specifically, the Agency estimated low-, high-, and mid-range profit levels for different production levels of marginal wells for both oil wells and gas wells. The different profit levels were based on different pricing scenarios for oil and natural gas. The EPA recognizes there are numerous uncertainties associated with these pricing scenario estimates and is requesting comment on this aspect of the analysis. (
See
section III.IV.J.1.l.).
For the BSER analysis, the EPA created representative well sites to characterize the production levels, equipment, and baseline emissions at marginal well sites. Next, the EPA identified potential control options for each emission source at the representative marginal well site, and estimated the capital and annual costs, as well as the cost effectiveness values for each control option at each emissions source. Third, the EPA then compared the annual costs of individual control options to the profit levels of marginal wells. In instances where the annual costs for just one control for one source type were relatively high relative to the expected profits, the EPA removed the control option from further consideration as the BSER because the Agency is proposing to determine that the costs are unreasonable under this metric. For example, for oil well sites with average production levels less than 15 boe/day, the estimated cost of routing associated gas to a sales line represented over 200 percent of the estimated profits for the mid-range pricing option, and over 150 percent of the estimated profits for the highest pricing option (see table 8 in this preamble for a comparison of costs in the March 2024 Final Rule and see the Marginal Well TSD for further details on the analysis of costs). The EPA therefore ruled out this control option for associated gas from the BSER analysis because the costs for this control option are unreasonable (the costs are more than the sub-industry of marginal wells can bear) even before considering the costs of controls for other sources at the site.
Owners and operators recognize revenue and profits at the site level, and make the decision whether to shut-in, or continue to operate, the well(s) at a site. Accordingly, the EPA next combined the control options for all emission sources at a well site previously covered by the NSPS and EG into site-wide regulatory alternatives. The Agency calculated the total site-wide capital and annual compliance costs of the control options considered, as well as the total site-wide emissions reductions and cost effectiveness. The EPA then compared the total annual compliance costs for the regulatory options considered for both a representative marginal well site and a representative marginal well site with major production and processing equipment (a “large well-site”) to the profit levels for marginal wells. The Agency proposes to determine the BSER based on the combination of emissions reductions and cost effectiveness, at both the individual control level and the site-level, and how total site-wide annual compliance costs compare to estimated annual profits for the representative site.
The EPA recognizes that there is substantial variation in the equipment and operations at oil and natural gas well sites, even for sites with similar production levels. This representative site evaluation considers these differences by using weighted averages of the number and types of emission sources present and other factors.

d. Proposed Subcategory for Marginal Wells
CAA section 111(b)(2) authorizes the EPA to distinguish among classes, types, and sizes within categories of new sources for the purpose of establishing standards of performance. In this action, to distinguish sources within the crude oil and natural gas source category that have lower oil and gas production rates, the Agency proposes to create a new subcategory within the crude oil and natural gas category for marginal well sites under NSPS OOOOb. The EPA also proposes to create a corresponding subcategory for existing marginal wells sites under the EG of OOOOc. In order to evaluate and establish separate standards for this subcategory of marginal well sites, the EPA must establish definitions for “marginal wells” and “marginal well sites.” The Internal Revenue Code, in
26 U.S.C. 613A(c)(6)(E)
, defines a “stripper well property,” with respect to any calendar year, as any property with respect to which the average daily production of domestic crude oil and domestic natural gas from producing wells on such property for such calendar year divided by the number of producing wells is less than 15 boe. The production level used in this stripper well definition of 15 boe/day is a long-recognized criterion in the oil and natural gas industry. Using a production-based definition, like that in the “stripper well” definition above, provides a clear, measurable, and quantifiable metric. Thus, it is well understood in the industry.”
[
383
]
Therefore, the EPA is proposing to base the definition of “marginal well” on these established concepts. However, the Agency proposes a slightly different approach to the definition of a marginal well site than the definition of stripper well property used in the Internal Revenue Code. In this action, the EPA is proposing to define a marginal well site as a well site that has a production below the threshold of 15 boe/day total for all wells at the well site. The Agency considers that establishing a definition at the site level is necessary to establish emission controls for equipment located at a marginal well site, such as process controllers and pumps, which service more than one well at the site. A site level definition is also consistent with the EPA's approach to evaluating BSER for this oil and natural gas production source subcategory, where the Agency is considering site-level compliance costs and profits. In addition, the EPA also used the same threshold in a previous action on NSPS OOOOa. Accordingly, the Agency is proposing definitions for both a “marginal well” and a “marginal well site”, where a marginal well is a well that produced less than or equal to 15 barrels of oil equivalent per day over the prior 12-month period, and marginal well sites are well sites with only marginal wells and where the total oil and natural gas produced from all the wells at the site is less than or equal to 15 boe per day over the prior 12-month period.
The EPA proposes a marginal well site subcategory that is defined as well sites producing 15 boe/day or less of oil and/or gas, but the Agency recognizes that there may be meaningful differences between marginal well sites producing at or near 15 boe/day and those producing substantially less. Certainly, profits decrease as production decreases, as well as the emissions for the sources that are more closely correlated with production levels (
e.g.,
associated gas, storage vessels). In addition, smaller, lower production wells often have fewer process units and less equipment, which results in less emissions from sources such as fugitive components and controllers when compared to larger production sites that have more controllers and more equipment to monitor for fugitives. While the EPA is proposing a single marginal well subcategory that is based on production level, the Agency is also requesting comment on an alternative approach that would create two separate subcategories: one for marginal well sites with oil and/or gas production levels between 6 and 15 boe/day, and another for marginal well sites with oil and/or gas production levels of less than 6 boe/day. This is discussed in detail in section III.J.1.l of this preamble.

i. Population and Economic Profile
Marginal wells account for a large share of the nation's well count but only a small share of total production. According to the Energy Information Administration, out of a total of 918,000 active U.S. wells in 2024, approximately 717,000 were marginal wells.

This means that marginal wells account for approximately 78 to percent of all wells nationwide. These wells accounted for approximately 7 percent of total U.S. oil and natural gas produced in 2024.

Based on our analysis of Enverus data, the EPA estimates that oil and gas wells in 2023 were owned and operated by more than 11,000 unique operators.

Most marginal wells are owned by firms that also operate many other wells. For example, 51.3 percent of all marginal wells in the U.S are owned by only 127 firms that operate 1,000 or more wells each. At the same time, most firms are small operators. Over 65 percent of firms (7,320 firms) own ten or fewer oil and gas wells. These firms own 3.2 percent of all marginal wells in the U.S. and account for 1.9 percent of all marginal well production.

ii. Process Controllers
Process controllers are automated instruments used for maintaining a process condition, such as liquid level, pressure, pressure difference, or temperature. In the oil and natural gas industry, many process controllers are powered by pressurized natural gas and emit methane and VOC-containing natural gas to the atmosphere. Process controllers may also be powered by electricity or compressed air, and these types of controllers do not use or emit natural gas.
Natural gas-driven process controllers can be categorized based on the emissions pattern of the controller. Some controllers are designed to have the supply-gas provide the required pressure to power the end-device, and the excess amount of gas is emitted. The emissions of this excess gas are referred to as “bleed,” and this bleed occurs continuously. Controllers that operate in this manner are referred to as “continuous bleed” process controllers. These controllers can be further categorized based on the amount of bleed they are designed to have. Those that have a bleed rate of less than or equal to 6 scfh are referred to as “low bleed,” and those with a bleed rate of greater than 6 scfh are referred to as “high bleed.” Another type of controller is designed to release gas only when the process parameter needs to be adjusted by opening or closing the valve, and there is no venting or bleeding of gas to the atmosphere when the valve is stationary. These types of controllers are referred to as “intermittent vent” process controllers. A third type of process controller, a self-contained process controller, is a controller that routes the exhaust gas into the downstream piping instead of the atmosphere. Emissions from natural gas-driven process controllers are primarily dependent on the number of controllers at a site, the designed bleed rate (for continuous bleed controllers), and the condition of the controller and frequency of malfunction. Emissions from controllers are not directly tied to production levels.
The EPA does not expect that there are natural gas-driven controllers at every marginal well site. For sites that do have such controllers, the Agency assumed there would be two intermittent vent controllers based on available data regarding the number and predominant type of process controllers at well sites.

iii. Pumps
In the oil and natural gas industry, operators frequently use pumps to inject precise amounts of chemicals into a process stream or to circulate glycol. These pumps may use natural gas, compressed air, or electricity as a power source. Of these pumps, those that are pneumatic units driven by natural gas emit methane and VOC to the atmosphere as part of normal operation. In many situations across all segments of the oil and gas industry, operators often rely on natural gas-driven pneumatic pumps where electricity is not readily available. Emissions from natural gas-driven pumps are primarily dependent on the number of pumps at a site and not directly tied to production levels. Based on available data regarding the number of pumps at well sites, the EPA does not expect that there are natural gas-driven pumps at every marginal well site.

For those sites that do, the Agency assumed there would only be one such pump, based on the available data.

iv. Oil Well Associated Gas
Associated gas is natural gas that originates at wells operated primarily for oil production that is released from the liquid hydrocarbon during the initial stage of separation after the wellhead. Associated gas is one of the emission sources where emissions are primarily dependent on production levels. More specifically, the volume of associated gas is related to the amount of gas extracted along with the oil or condensate. Put another way, generally speaking and subject to some caveats, the more oil that a well produces, the higher the potential for associated gas emissions there will be from that well because the crude oil is mixed with some natural gas that contains VOCs and methane. If a well site is producing a small amount of oil, usually the uncontrolled VOC and methane emissions from the natural gas associated with that oil will likewise be small. If, however, the well site is producing a very large amount of oil, then usually there will also be higher amounts of associated natural gas, and the uncontrolled emissions from that gas would usually be higher. Operators typically route the mixture of oil and natural gas to a separator, which sends the liquid to a storage vessel. If the gas exiting the separator is of sufficient quality and quantity, operators generally route it to a gas line, provided there is
(
printed page 68309)
a sales line nearby that has the capacity to accept the gas and that the gas meets quality specifications. In the absence of a sales line, operators may use the gas for another purpose, such as for onsite fuel (provided the quality is adequate) or recover the gas and reinject it into the same well or another well. If none of these options are feasible, operators typically flare or vent the associated gas.
The EPA estimates that the annual associated gas methane emissions from the average marginal well are 10.9 tpy of methane and 3.0 tpy VOC. As previously noted, the amount of associated gas is directly correlated to production levels. The Agency estimates the methane emissions from associated gas could range from around 2 tpy from a well site with 1 boe per day to over 100 tpy from a well site with 15 boe per day and that VOC emissions could range from 0.6 tpy from a well site with 1 boe per day to around 29 tpy for a well site with 15 boe per day. The Marginal Well TSD provides detailed explanations of these estimates.

v. Storage Vessels
Storage vessels at oil and natural gas well sites contain crude oil, condensate, intermediate hydrocarbon liquids, or produced water. They are almost exclusively fixed roof tanks. Typically, the most significant cause of emissions from storage vessels at oil and natural gas sites is the “flashing” that occurs when the pressure of a hydrocarbon liquid (oil, condensate, or water) drops, causing volatile components in the liquid to vaporize and be emitted. Flash emissions are somewhat dependent on throughput, as well as a number of other factors (
e.g.,
volatility, composition, density, temperature, pressure drop). Working loss emissions are directly dependent on the throughput of liquid through the vessel.
In order to estimate methane emissions from storage vessels at marginal wells, the EPA developed emissions factors based on the barrels of oil or condensate per day of the well. The EPA created separate methane and VOC emissions factors for storage vessels containing condensate and those containing heavy oil, then averaged the two factors to estimate the storage vessel emissions. The representative marginal well site storage vessel emissions are 0.63 tpy methane and 2.9 tpy VOC. The origin of the emissions factors and estimated emission levels are provided in the Marginal Well TSD, available in the docket for this proposed rule.

vi. Gas Well Liquids Unloading
In new gas wells, there is generally sufficient reservoir pressure/gas velocity to facilitate the flow of water and hydrocarbon liquids from the wellbore through the well head and to the surface along with produced gas. In mature gas wells, the accumulation of liquids in the wellbore can occur when the bottom well pressure/gas velocity approaches the average reservoir pressure, and there is not enough pressure to force the liquids to the surface. This accumulation of liquids can impede and sometimes halt gas production. When the accumulation of liquid results in the slowing or cessation of gas production, the operator must remove the fluids to maintain production. Mature gas wells therefore often need to remove or “unload” the accumulated liquids (
i.e.,
liquids unloading) so that gas production is not inhibited.
The choice of what liquids unloading technique to employ is based on a well-by-well and reservoir-by-reservoir analysis. To address the complex science and engineering considerations to cover well unloading requirements, many technologies, techniques, and practices have been developed to address an individual well's characteristics. At the onset of liquids loading, operators typically use techniques that rely on the reservoir pressure. Eventually a well's reservoir pressure is not sufficient to remove the liquids from the well and it is necessary to add energy to the well to continue production. Owners and operators can choose from several techniques to remove the liquids, including manual unloading, velocity tubing or velocity strings, beam or rod pumps, electric submergence pumps, intermittent unloading, gas lift (
e.g.,
use of a plunger lift), foam agents, and wellhead compression. Each of these methods/procedures removes accumulated liquids and thereby maintains or restores gas production. Although the unloading method employed by an owner or operator can itself be a method that mitigates/eliminates venting of emissions from a liquids unloading event, choosing a particular method to meet a particular well's unloading needs is a production engineering decision.
The EPA estimates that the representative emissions from uncontrolled liquids unloading are 2.5 tpy methane and 0.7 tpy VOC per marginal gas well. The Marginal Well TSD, available in the docket for this proposed rule, provides additional detail on the baseline emission level.

g. NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc Requirements and Estimated Impacts for Marginal Well Site Representative Emission Sources
Following are brief summaries of the NSPS OOOOb standards and EG OOOOc presumptive standards for the six emission source types that may be present at marginal well sites.
i. Fugitive Emissions Components
Table 7 provides an overview of the monitoring requirements in NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc for each type of well site. If any source of fugitive emissions is identified via the monitoring survey using audible, visual, and olfactory (AVO) methods, the owner or operator must make a first attempt at repair within 15 days of detection and must complete the repair 15 days after the first attempt. If a leak or malfunction is identified via OGI or Method 21, the owner or operator must make a first attempt at repair within 30 days of detection and must complete the repair 30 days after the first attempt.
[
411
]
ii. Process Controllers
The standards in NSPS OOOOb and presumptive standards in EG OOOOc require zero methane and zero VOC emissions for all controllers at well sites. The exception is for controllers at Alaska sites without access to electrical grid power, where the requirement is to use low-bleed controllers and perform OGI monitoring of intermittent controllers to ensure proper operation.
iii. Pumps
The standards in NSPS OOOOb and presumptive standards in EG OOOOc establish requirements that vary depending on the number of natural gas-driven diaphragm pumps at the well site and whether the site has access to electrical grid power. For any site with access to electrical grid power and for sites without access to electrical grid power that have three or more natural gas-driven diaphragm pumps, the standard for all pumps in the affected facility is zero emissions of VOC and methane. For sites without access to electrical grid power that have fewer than three diaphragm pumps (two or one), the standards require owners and operators to route methane and VOC emissions from all natural gas-driven pumps at the affected facility to a process if a VRU is onsite. If a VRU is not onsite, owners and operators must reduce emissions by 95 percent if a control device with at least this emissions reduction capability is already available onsite. If a control device is onsite but is not capable of reducing 95 percent, owners and operators must reduce emission to the maximum extent achievable by the control device.
iv. Oil Well Associated Gas
NSPS OOOOb requires owners and operators to route all associated gas to a sales line, use it for another purpose, or reinject it back into the reservoir or another well, unless they demonstrate that it is technically infeasible. In limited circumstances related to when construction of the well commenced, owners and operators may flare associated gas provided they demonstrate that it is technically infeasible to route the gas to a sales line, capture and use it for another purpose, or reinject it back into the reservoir or another well. In the model rule for EG OOOOc, owners and operators of wells with associated gas methane content of 40 tpy or less may route to a flare. For wells with associated gas contents greater than 40 tpy, owners and operators must route the gas to a sales line, capture it and use it for another
(
printed page 68311)
purpose, or reinject it back into the reservoir or another well, unless they demonstrate that these options are technically infeasible.
v. Storage Vessels
In both NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc, the storage vessel affected/designated facility is the tank battery, which is defined as “a group of all storage vessels that are manifolded together for liquid transfer. A tank battery may consist of a single storage vessel if only one storage vessel is present.”
[
412
]
Under NSPS OOOOb, if the potential emissions are greater than 6 tpy VOC or 20 tpy methane, owners and operators must route emissions via a closed vent system to a control device that achieves 95 percent reduction or to a flare. Under EG OOOOc, the applicability threshold is 20 tpy methane.
vi. Gas Well Liquids Unloading
Both NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc require that owners and operators perform best management practices to minimize or eliminate methane and/or VOC emissions to the maximum extent possible during liquids unloading events that vent emissions to the atmosphere. For unloading technologies or techniques that eliminate venting of emissions during liquids unloading events, NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc require only minimal recordkeeping and reporting. For unloading technologies or techniques that could result in venting to the atmosphere, NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc require owners and operators to follow work practices. Specifically, owners and/or operators must employ and document best management practices to minimize or eliminate venting of methane and VOC emissions for each gas well liquids unloading operation.

annual compliance costs in the March 2024 Final Rule for fugitive component emissions at well sites or centralized production facilities that contain major production and processing equipment represent 13 percent of the mid-range profits for marginal oil wells and 48 percent of the mid-range profits for marginal gas wells. The cumulative cost impact on an individual marginal well site would be based on adding up all of the costs for all of the specific emission sources at the site. As such, the cumulative annual compliance costs could represent a significant percentage of the profits for a marginal well, even to the extent of exceeding the profits. For example, at a marginal gas well site that contains major production and processing equipment with fugitive components and process controllers, the estimated cumulative annual compliance costs represent over 120 percent of the mid-range profit level. This finding supports the idea that the true cost of compliance with the March 2024 Final Rule for marginal wells is unreasonable. The true cumulative cost of compliance appears to be more than the marginal well subcategory of the industry can bear and survive. Accordingly, the EPA proposes to determine that the collective suite of standards from the March 2024 Final Rule, as applied to marginal wells, do not together represent the BSER because their collective costs are excessive and unreasonable, as shown in table 9.
h. Control Options for Marginal Well Sites
This section introduces the control options the EPA identified and evaluated for emission sources at marginal oil and natural gas well sites. For each control option for each emissions source, the Agency assessed the cost and emissions reductions and calculated the costs in relation to the associated emissions reduction (
i.e.,
the cost effectiveness). When the cost effectiveness was higher than the Agency has historically considered reasonable for a control option, the EPA is proposing to determine that that option is not viable and the Agency removed it from consideration in the marginal well regulatory options.
Next, the EPA compared the annual costs of the control option to the estimated profit levels for the mid-range price scenario for marginal wells (see table 8). Where the Agency is proposing to determine that the annual cost of a control option, in isolation, was unreasonably high given the mid-scenario profit level (
i.e.,
that the compliance costs of that specific control option represented a sizable portion of the estimated profit), the Agency is proposing that that control option is not cost reasonable and removed it from consideration in the marginal well regulatory options. Note that, later in the regulatory alternatives section (see section III.J.1.i), the EPA further discusses comparisons between the cumulative annual compliance costs of the full well site suite of control requirements in each regulatory alternative and the mid-range profits used to assess the cost reasonableness of the overall compliance package for a marginal well site. In this first step, the EPA is assessing the cost reasonableness of an individual control option for an emission source type to determine whether it should be included as part of the set of alternatives to be further evaluated.
Finally, a factor that the EPA considered in assessing the viability of control options for marginal well sites is the relationship to the requirements in NSPS OOOO and NSPS OOOOa. Emission sources at oil and natural gas well sites constructed, reconstructed, or modified between August 23, 2011, and September 18, 2015, are subject to NSPS OOOO. Emission sources at oil and natural gas well sites constructed, reconstructed, or modified between September 18, 2015, and December 6, 2022, are subject to NSPS OOOOa. Under the EG OOOOc model rule, emission sources constructed, modified, or reconstructed before December 6, 2022, will be designated facilities. Therefore, all NSPS OOOO and NSPS OOOOa affected facilities will also be designated facilities subject to state or federal rules in accordance with EG OOOOc.
This situation is not unique to marginal wells. The EPA discussed this overlap in detail in section VII.C of the preamble for the March 2024 Final Rule.

At a marginal well site, the flow rate of associated gas to a flare or other control device would likely be significantly larger than that of another emission source. k. Proposed Marginal Well Requirements
i. Affected/Designated Facility Definition
The affected/designated facility is defined as a marginal well site. The EPA is proposing definitions for both a marginal well and a marginal well site that are based on oil and natural gas production levels.
Specifically, the EPA proposes the following definitions:
Marginal well
means a well that produced less than or equal to 15 barrels of oil equivalent per day over the prior 12-month period.
Marginal well site
means a well site with only marginal wells and the total oil and natural gas produced from all the wells at the site is less than or equal to 15 barrels of oil equivalent per day over the prior 12-month period.
The EPA is also proposing definitions for “non-marginal well” and “non-marginal well site.” Specifically, the EPA proposes the following definitions:
Non-marginal well
means a well that produced an annual average of greater than 15 barrels of oil equivalent produced per day over the prior 12-month period.
Non-marginal well site
means a well site where the total cumulative oil and natural gas produced from all the wells at the site is greater than 15 barrels of oil equivalent per day over the prior 12-month period.
One aspect of these definitions is what constitutes a new marginal well site affected facility subject to NSPS OOOOb and an existing marginal well site designated facility subject to a state or federal plan via EG OOOOc. The EPA is proposing that if any emission source at an existing marginal well site is modified or reconstructed, the entire well site becomes an NSPS OOOOb affected facility (or facilities, if the marginal status no longer applies post-modification). The specific instances that constitute a modification to an existing marginal well site include the following.
If a new well is drilled at an existing marginal well site.
If an existing well at a marginal well site is hydraulically fractured or hydraulically refractured.
A well at the well site is stimulated in any manner beyond that of normal well maintenance (
e.g.,
acid simulation, recompletion to a new zone) for the purpose of increasing production, including well workover.
A well at the well site is shut-in for the purpose of increasing production from another well at the site.
If the number of natural gas-driven process controllers is increased by one or more.
If a storage vessel is added to a tank battery at an existing marginal well site, if one or more storage vessels at an existing marginal well site are replaced such that the cumulative storage capacity of the existing tank battery increases, or if a tank battery at an existing marginal well sites receives additional crude oil, condensate, intermediate hydrocarbons, or produced water throughput from actions, including but not limited to, the addition of operations, the addition of a production well, or changes to operations of a production well (including hydraulic fracturing or refracturing of the well).
If the number of natural gas-driven pumps is increased by one or more.
Another aspect of the marginal well affected/designated facility definition is how owners and operators must demonstrate that production levels are below 15 boe per day. Owners and operators must base this determination on the daily combined oil and natural gas production at the well site for each day during the previous 12 months divided by the number of operating days in the 12-month period. A facility may make this initial determination at any time. After the facility makes the initial determination that the site has production levels below 15 boe per day, any modification, reconstruction, or action taken that will increase production from one or more wells at the site triggers a requirement to make a new determination. Owners and operators must complete this new determination within 45 days of completion of the activity using information based on the daily average production level from the first 30 days of operation following completion of the activity.
The proposed requirements in NSPS OOOOb and the model rule in EG OOOOc allow facilities to comply with the requirements that apply to marginal well sites after submission of a notification of marginal well site determination. For facilities subject to NSPS OOOOb, if this determination shows that production from the site is above 15 boe per day, the proposed requirements of NSPS OOOOb are that the facility would no longer be a marginal well site affected facility and must comply with the applicable requirements of NSPS OOOOb for affected facilities that are not marginal well site affected facilities by the dates described in
40 CFR 60.5370b
. For facilities subject to a state or Federal plan implementing EG OOOOc that completed a modification or reconstruction, the proposed requirements are that the facility would become subject to NSPS OOOOb and must comply with the applicable requirements of NSPS OOOOb for sites that are not marginal well sites by the dates described in
40 CFR 60.5370b
. For facilities subject to a state or Federal plan implementing EG OOOOc that did not complete a modification or reconstruction, the proposed model rule in EG OOOOc requires that the facility follow the applicable requirements of EG OOOOc for designated facilities that are not marginal well site designated facilities by the dates described in
40 CFR 60.5370b
.
ii. Proposed Standards
The EPA is proposing the same standards for marginal wells in both the NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc. The following paragraphs discuss these proposed standards.
For fugitive component emissions, the EPA is proposing to require that owners and operators conduct quarterly AVO inspections to detect any leaking or malfunctioning components. Specifically, the Agency is proposing that AVO inspections must include all fugitive emissions components at the marginal well site, except buried yard piping and associated components (

connectors). 2. Option 2. Subcategorization of Conventional Wells
Another method of characterizing wells is by the resource type; U.S. onshore oil and gas production consists of both conventional and unconventional resources, which typically require different extraction approaches. Conventional wells are relatively shallow and are drilled vertically (or slightly deviated) to access structural reservoirs with permeability typically sufficient for hydrocarbon flow without intensive stimulation. Unconventional wells extract hydrocarbons from low permeability shale and other tight formations or formations containing viscous oils that resist flow. Unconventional wells can be much deeper and are typically horizontally drilled and hydraulically fractured to create flow. Conventional well production sites usually service single well sites while unconventional well sites trend toward integrated operations that can support up to 10 or more wells. Conventional wells generally operate at lower wellhead pressures and production rates. Unconventional wells exhibit much higher wellhead pressures coupled with high initial hydrocarbon and produced water production rates. Conventional wells typically experience increasing produced water loads over time that must be managed to maintain production.
[
422 423 424
]
These differences in conventional and unconventional wells are expected to result in differences in the types and amount of equipment at the site and the number of potential emission points. With up to an order of magnitude higher initial well head pressures and high initial flow rates, unconventional well sites can require multistage heated gas, liquid, and water separation, with additional associated components and controls, to properly manage production.
[
425 426
]
In general, the EPA expects that unconventional well sites would have more fugitive components and major production and processing equipment at the site than conventional well sites. Unconventional muti-well production sites with common header produced water and condensate tank batteries may also have a higher propensity for process upset and malfunction-related emissions compared to conventional sites.
[
427
]
As an alternative to defining a marginal well subcategory based on production levels, the EPA is co-proposing an option to define a conventional well site subcategory based on the type of formation in which the well is drilled. The EPA considered alternative definitions to establish a conventional well site subcategory. One stakeholder noted that conventional wells typically have depths less than 8,000 feet.
[
428
]
Supporting information provided by the stakeholder also included a letter asserting that there are fundamental differences between high-GOR shale wells and low-GOR conventional wells and suggested that the EPA classify oil and gas producers into distinct categories using GOR, production rate, and cumulative production as primary indicators.
[
429
]
(
printed page 68333)
Although GOR and vertical depth could be reasonable indicators of the type of well, the EPA is proposing a definition of unconventional wells that is based on widely accepted resource type and required extraction need descriptions, drawn, in comparison to conventional resources.
[
430
]
The EPA believes it is appropriate to base definitions on underlying resource type because the complexity of extraction and surface processing, coupled with production intensity, can differ between resource types, which could lead to differences in emission potential. The Agency is proposing the following definitions associated with this option.
Unconventional formation
means a low-permeability geological formation typically composed of shale or other similar fine-grained, organic-rich sedimentary rocks—where oil and natural gas generally remain in the source rock unless natural or artificial fractures occur. Unconventional formations can also include somewhat more porous and permeable formations that contain higher viscosity oils that resist flow. These formations cannot be produced at economic flow rates or in economic volumes except by vertical or horizontal well bores stimulated by intensive multistage hydraulic fracture treatments or by using multilateral well bores or other techniques to expose more of the formation to the well bore or to generate flow.
Unconventional well
means a bore hole drilled or being drilled for the purpose of or to be used for the production of oil and natural gas from an unconventional formation.
Conventional well
means any well drilled for the purpose of producing oil or natural gas that is not an unconventional well.
Conventional well site
means a well site with only conventional wells.
The EPA is also proposing to add to the definition of “well site” the phrase “this term encompasses both unconventional and conventional well sites.” The EPA requests comment on these definitions. (Question III.10l).
A key difference in conventional and unconventional wells is that unconventional wells typically decline quickly and have total productive lives of only 10 to 15 years, in contrast to conventional wells that can remain productive for several decades, often 40 to 50 years or longer.
[
431
]
Due to this decline curve, and the long history of conventional vertical well drilling compared to unconventional (primarily horizontal) wells, the vast majority of the lower production wells in operation in the U.S. (>90 percent) are conventional vertically drilled wells.
[
432

As a result, the EPA proposes to conclude that the subset of total oil and gas wells that are conventional is largely the same subset of wells that have production levels of 15 boe per day or less (
i.e.,
marginal wells). The EPA is requesting comment on the conclusion that the subset of wells that are marginal largely overlaps with the subset that are conventional wells. (Question III.10m).
Due to this substantial overlap, all the concerns raised by petitioners and industry representatives that are summarized in section III.K.1.b for marginal wells are relevant for conventional wells. Since most conventional wells are lower production wells, these sites will largely have the same concerns about cost and affordability. As noted in this section, the EPA also expects that all conventional well sites will have fewer components and pieces of major production and processing equipment than unconventional well sites. The EPA also expects that the marginal well site representative emission sources are also generally representative for all conventional well sites, as the type of site is expected to correlate with the numbers of components and pieces of major production and processing equipment. Section III.k.1.f describes the well site representative emission sources for marginal wells, which also generally represent sources at conventional well sites. Thus, the Agency would expect conventional well sites to have similar emissions profiles to marginal well sites. Further, all other aspects of the marginal well site BSER analysis discussed in section III.K.1 for marginal well sites are also applicable to conventional well sites.

V. Appendix K
A. Summary of Provisions Promulgated in March 2024 Final Rule
In the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA finalized
40 CFR part 60, Appendix K
as the monitoring survey requirement to monitor for leaks using OGI at onshore natural gas processing plants subject to NSPS OOOOb. The EPA also included Appendix K in the model rule (presumptive standards) in EG OOOOc for the same purpose. Appendix K, which is the protocol used to determine whether a source has a VOC and/or GHG leak using OGI, was also finalized as part of the March 2024 Final Rule. Put another way, in the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA promulgated a new appendix to part 60 (Appendix K), which the Agency then allowed to be used in a new NSPS that the Agency promulgated at the same time (NSPS OOOOb). However, the appendix is broader than just NSPS OOOOb and could be used for other subparts in 40 CFR part 60, as appropriate. The Appendix K protocol covers surveys of process equipment using OGI cameras in sectors where the majority of constituents (>75 percent by volume) in the emissions streams have a response factor (as defined in Appendix K, section 3.0) of at least 0.25, when
(
printed page 68347)
compared to the response factor of propane, and can be imaged by the equipment specified in section 6.0 of Appendix K.
[
443
]
B. Petitioners' Concerns and Supporting Information, Summary of Proposed Changes, and Basis for Proposed Changes
Petitioners' Concerns and Supporting Information.
Reconsideration petitioners requested that the EPA allow existing gas processing plants (
i.e.,
gas plants that are currently subject to either NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, or KKK) to utilize OGI with Appendix K in lieu of EPA Method 21 monitoring.
[
444
]
Currently, NSPS OOOO and OOOOa sources must follow the EPA Method 21 procedures specified by NSPS VVa in
40 CFR 60.485a
, and NSPS KKK sources must follow the EPA Method 21 procedures specified by NSPS VV in
40 CFR 60.485
. The reconsideration petitioners claim that the March 2024 Final Rule allows for States to incorporate this compliance option into their State plans under EG OOOOc. However, they asserted that operators should be allowed to use this compliance option now, prior to full implementation of EG OOOOc via either a State or federal plan. Moreover, in their view, the EPA has demonstrated that OGI with Appendix K is an acceptable alternative to traditional EPA Method 21 monitoring and there should not be a time delay on when operators can start implementing such programs.
[
445
]
Petitioners also claimed that because the applicability of NSPS is on a process unit basis, gas processing plants often have some units subject to NSPS KKK, OOOO, or OOOOa and other units subject to OOOOb, which allows the use of Appendix K, OGI, or EPA Method 21, creating inconsistent compliance options and confusion within a given oil and natural gas facility.
Petitioners argued that OGI with Appendix K is a viable option for certain operators, reducing personnel time spent on complying with LDAR inspection requirements and removing the obligation to tag and maintain an inventory of all components at a facility. Petitioners asserted that, due to the demonstrated equivalency of the two methods (
i.e.,
OGI and EPA Method 21), there should be no delay in allowing OGI with Appendix K to be implemented at existing facilities subject to NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, and KKK.
Summary of Proposed Changes.
In the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA limited the Appendix K “advanced technology” option as a novel approach to the rules they were actively promulgating (
i.e.,
NSPS OOOOb and EG OOOOc), and did not reopen NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, or KKK in that action.
[
446
]
In this reconsideration proposal, the EPA proposes regulatory revisions to provide the option for owners and operators to perform OGI surveys conducted according to Appendix K for NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, and KKK gas processing facilities. Under this proposal, consistent with the provisions in NSPS OOOOb and the model rule in EG OOOOc for gas processing facilities, if the “Appendix K option” is chosen, facilities would need to monitor for equipment leaks using OGI in accordance with Appendix K, at a bimonthly survey frequency, with any emissions observed using OGI defined as a leak. These proposed changes would be made to NSPS OOOO (
40 CFR 60.5401
and
60.5421
), NSPS OOOOa (
40 CFR 60.5401a
and
60.5421a
), and NSPS KKK (
40 CFR 60.632
and
60.635
), consistent with the provisions already included in NSPS OOOOb (
40 CFR 60.5400b
and
60.5421b
) and EG OOOOc (
40 CFR 60.5400c
and
60.5421c
).
Basis for Proposed Changes.
These proposed revisions provide additional flexibility for the regulated community by expanding the option to use OGI surveys conducted according to Appendix K for all eligible facilities. The EPA further notes that operators could currently seek approval to use Appendix K on an operator-by-operator basis through the CAA section 111(h)(3) Alternative Means of Emission Limitation (AMEL) process, but if multiple requests for the same technology occur, using the AMEL process would be less efficient and more burdensome as opposed to adding the Appendix K option NSPS OOOO, NSPS OOOOa, and NSPS KKK, as described earlier, for both the regulated community and the EPA.
Moreover, the EPA found in the March 2024 Final Rule that bimonthly OGI conducted according to the procedures in Appendix K provides equivalent or greater emissions reduction in comparison to EPA Method 21 conducted according to NSPS VV and VVa (which is required under NSPS OOOO, OOOOa, and KKK) for gas processing plants.
[
447
]
Based on this information included in the March 2024 Final Rule record, the EPA proposes to find that allowing owners and operators the option to use Appendix K instead of EPA Method 21 will result in equivalent or better emissions reductions. As such, the EPA proposes that Appendix K is an appropriate alternative to allow in these scenarios.
As stated in the preamble to the March 2024 Final Rule, the EPA also intends for the Appendix K protocol to have broad applicability, where Appendix K would have applicability to facilities when specified in a referencing subpart of
40 CFR part 60
to help determine the presence and location of leaks (but is not applicable for use in direct emission rate measurements from sources). That is, the Appendix K protocol does not on its own apply to any sources; it applies only where a specific rule subpart adopts it by reference and specifies the sources to which it applies. In this case, the EPA proposes to expand the use of the Appendix K protocol implementing the standards for process units at existing natural gas processing plants subject to NSPS KKK, OOOO, and OOOOa.
If the EPA finalizes this proposal, once incorporated into subparts KKK, OOOO, and OOOOa, the limitations and requirements that currently apply to Appendix K would also apply to its use for purposes of these subparts. For example, as described in the March 2024 Final Rule, the protocol would only be applicable for surveys of process equipment using OGI cameras where the majority of compounds (>75 percent by volume) in the emissions streams have a response factor of at least 0.25 when compared to the response factor of propane. Additionally, the OGI camera used for surveying must also be capable of detecting (or producing a detectable image of) methane emissions of 19 grams per hour (g/hr) and either butane emissions of 29 g/hr or propane emissions of 22 g/hr at a viewing distance of 2.0 meters and a delta-T of 5.0 °C in an environment of calm wind conditions around 1.0 meter per second or less. Verification that the OGI camera meets these criteria may be performed by the owner or operator, the camera manufacturer, or a third party.
[
448
]
Additional requirements would also apply, as described in the March 2024
(
printed page 68348)
Final Rule.
[
449
]
However, the EPA notes that no changes to the Appendix K procedures are being proposed in this action.

The Federal Communications Commission will hold an Open Meeting on the subjects listed below on Thursday, October 29, 2026 which is scheduled to commence at 10:30 a.m. in the Commission Meeting Room of the Federal Communications Commission, 45 L Street NE, Washington, DC.
While attendance at the Open Meeting is available to the public, the FCC headquarters building is not open access, and all guests must check in with and be screened by FCC security at the main entrance on L Street. Attendees at the Open Meeting will not be required to have an appointment but must otherwise comply with protocols outlined at:
www.fcc.gov/​visit
.
Open Meetings are streamed live at:
www.fcc.gov/​live
and on the FCC's YouTube channel.
Item no.
Bureau
Subject
1
Wireless TeleCommunications
Title:
Auctioning the 1675-1695 MHz and 2020-2025 MHz Bands (WT Docket No. 26-284); Unleashing Licensed Spectrum for Direct-to-Device (GN Docket No. 26-281); Allocation and Service Rules for the 1675-1680 MHz Band (WT Docket No. 19-116).
Summary:
The Commission will consider a Further Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (FNPRM) that would unlock 25 megahertz of prime mid-band spectrum for advanced commercial communications services, including terrestrial, direct-to-device (D2D), or a hybrid of both. The rules proposed in this item, if adopted, would enable the auctioning, licensing, and rapid development of the 1675-1695 MHz and 2020-2025 MHz bands. In particular, the FNPRM would propose and seek comment on policies, service and technical rules, and coordination requirements for the 1675-1695 MHz and 2020-2025 MHz bands.
(
printed page 68147)
2
Wireless Telecommunications
Title:
Unleashing Licensed Spectrum for Direct-to-Device (GN Docket No. 26-281); Single Network Future: Supplemental Coverage from Space (GN Docket No. 23-65).
Summary:
The Commission will consider a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that would modernize the Commission's rules for Direct-to-Device (D2D) services in licensed spectrum. The rules proposed in this item, if adopted, would make an additional 482 megahertz of spectrum available for Supplemental Coverage from Space (SCS), eliminate burdensome SCS requirements, and consider measures to modernize and harmonize the SCS and the Mobile Satellite Service (MSS) rules.
3
Wireless Telecommunications
Title:
Unleashing American Drone Dominance (GN Docket No. 26-74); Spectrum Rules and Policies for the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (WT Docket No. 22-323); Facilitating Opportunities for Advanced Air Mobility (WT Docket No. 24-629).
Summary:
The Commission will consider a Report and Order (R&O) that would eliminate an outdated restriction that prevents drone operations in the 800 MHz Cellular band. The R&O would unlock 50 megahertz of licensed, nationwide, low-band spectrum for drone use and promote parity with other similar flexible-use bands.
4
Office of Engineering and Technology
Title:
Prohibiting Test Labs and Certification Bodies in Non-Reciprocal Countries (ET Docket No. 24-136).
Summary:
The Commission will consider a Third Report and Order and Third Further Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (FNPRM) aimed to strengthen the integrity, security, and resiliency of the FCC's equipment authorization program by prohibiting the recognition of Test Labs, Telecommunications Certification Bodies, and laboratory accreditation bodies located in non-Reciprocal Economies, which are territories lacking a Mutual Recognition Agreement or other comparable reciprocal trade agreement with the United States. It would also require all substantive FCC testing, certification, and accreditation activities on which equipment authorization depends, to occur in the U.S. or Reciprocal Economies. The item would adopt a uniform transition period ending December 1, 2028, that would enable Test Labs to expand capacity and manufacturers in the U.S. and Reciprocal Economies two years to find alternative Test Labs and expand capacity. The accompanying FNRPM would seek comment on a range of additional equipment authorization integrity measures.
5
Office of International Affairs
Title:
Review of International Section 214 Authorizations to Assess Evolving National Security, Law Enforcement, Foreign Policy, and Trade Policy Risks (IB Docket No. 23-119); Amendment of the Schedule of Application Fees Set Forth in Sections 1.1102 through 1.1109 of the Commission's Rules (MD Docket No. 23-134).
Summary:
The Commission will consider a Report and Order and Further Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that would modernize the Commission's international section 214 framework to strengthen protections for U.S. telecommunications services and infrastructure, while reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens.
6
Wireline Competition
Title:
Connect America Fund: A National Broadband Plan for our Future High-Cost Universal Support (WC Docket No. 10-90); Reforming the High-Cost Program for an All-IP Future (WC Docket No. 26-96); Safeguarding Universal Service Funding Through Effective Applicant Vetting (WC Docket No. 26-288).
Summary:
The Commission will consider a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that, if adopted, would seek comment on proposals for implementing the Rural Broadband Protection Act (RBPA). The RBPA, enacted on May 11, 2026, directs the Commission to initiate a rulemaking proceeding within 180 days to establish a vetting process for applicants for, and other recipients of, a new covered funding award, which the Notice interprets as an award of high-cost support based on an application for funding to support the deployment of a broadband-capable network and the provision of supported services over the network.
7
Consumer and Governmental Affairs
Title:
Implementation of Sections 716 and 717 of the Communications Act of 1934, as Enacted by the Twenty-First Century Communications and Video Accessibility Act of 2010 (CG Docket No. 10-213); Telecommunication Relay Services and Speech-to-Speech Services for Individuals with Hearing and Speech Disabilities (CG Docket No. 03-123); Consumer and Governmental Affairs, Media, and Wireless Telecommunications Bureaus Seek Update on Commission's Fulfillment of the Twenty-First Century Communications and Video Accessibility Act (GN Docket No. 21-140).
Summary:
The Commission will consider a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to modernize its accessibility rules to keep pace with the rapidly changing communications landscape, promote innovation, better match consumer expectations, and remove barriers to accessibility.

[Docket Number USCG-2026-1075]

AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a safety zone for certain navigable waters of the Sanders Ferry, near Hendersonville, TN. This safety zone is necessary to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards during a fireworks show at various times from October 29, 2026, through October 31, 2026. This rulemaking prohibits entry of vessels or persons into this safety zone during enforcement periods unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Ohio Valley or their designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective from 7:15 a.m. local time on October 29, 2026, through 5:30 p.m. local time on October 31, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
To view available documents, go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and search for USCG-2026-1075.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have questions about this rule, contact MST3 Zachary T. Epps, Sector Ohio Valley Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone (206) 815-7006, or email
STL-SMB-MSDNASHVILLE@USCG.MIL
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations
CFR Code of Federal Regulations
COTP Captain of the Port
DHS Department of Homeland Security
FR Federal Register
NPRM Notice of proposed rulemaking
§ Section
U.S.C. United States Code
II. Background and Authority
On July 17, 2026, an organization notified the Coast Guard that it will sponsor two fireworks displays launched from a barge on the Cumberland River near Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tennessee. The first fireworks display (including a 15-minute safety buffer before and afterwards) is scheduled to occur on October 29, 2026, from approximately 7:15 a.m. until 8:15 a.m., Central Time. The second fireworks display is scheduled to occur on October 31, 2026, from approximately 4:45 p.m. until 5:30 p.m., Central Time. On October 16, 2026, the Coast Guard published a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) titled Safety Zone; Cumberland River, Hendersonville, TN (
91 FR 65698
). In that NPRM, we stated why we issued the NPRM and invited comments on our proposed regulatory action related to this fireworks display.
Under the authority in
46 U.S.C. 70034
, the COTP has determined that this rule is necessary to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with the fireworks. No vessel or person will be permitted to enter the safety zone without obtaining permission from COTP or their designated representative.
Because of the hazards associated with this event, the Coast Guard finds that under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
, good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
because it is impracticable and contrary to the public interest. We must establish this safety zone by October 29, 2026, to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment.
III. Discussion of Comments and the Rule
During the comment period that ended on October 23, 2026, we received two comments. Two commenters identified inconsistencies in the NPRM concerning the dates and times of the planned fireworks displays and associated safety-zone enforcement periods. Specifically, the commenters noted that the NPRM contained conflicting references to October 30 and October 31 for the second enforcement period, as well as inconsistent morning enforcement periods for October 29. One commenter also requested clarification regarding the difference between the overall effective period and the periods when the safety zone would be actively enforced; the basis for pre- and post-display safety buffers; the applicable local time zone; notice to mariners; and procedures for requesting entry into the safety zone.
In response to these comments, the Coast Guard has revised the
(
printed page 68044)
enforcement periods to accurately reflect the scheduled fireworks displays. The safety zone will be enforced from 7:15 a.m. until 8:15 a.m., on October 29, 2026, and from 4:45 p.m. until 5:30 p.m., on October 31, 2026. It is always standard that in Coast Guard safety zone rulemaking documents refer to the local time at the location of the safety zone, in this case that is Central Daylight Time (CDT). These enforcement periods include a 15-minute safety buffer before and after each fireworks display to allow for final safety preparations, fireworks-launch operations, monitoring for falling debris, post-display safety assessment, and cleanup.
The Coast Guard has also corrected the conflicting references to an October 30 enforcement period and clarified that the safety zone will not be continuously enforced between the two specified enforcement periods. In other words, this safety zone will be enforced for one hour on October 29, 2026, from 7:15 a.m. until 8:15 a.m., and 45 minutes on October 31, 2026, from 4:45 p.m. until 5:30 p.m. The Coast Guard will provide notice of enforcement through a Broadcast Notice to Mariners on VHF-FM channel 16. The Broadcast Notice to Mariners will include information regarding the enforcement periods and may include sponsor contact information for event-related coordination, as appropriate. Only the Captain of the Port (COTP), Ohio Valley or the COTP's designated representative may authorize entry into the safety zone.
This rule establishes a safety zone on all navigable waters of the Cumberland River from mile marker 221.7 to mile marker 222 near Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tennessee. During the stated enforcement periods, no vessel or person may enter the safety zone without obtaining permission from COTP or the COTP's designated representative.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analysis based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (RFA),
5 U.S.C. 601-612
, as amended, requires Federal agencies to consider the potential impact of regulations on small entities during rulemaking. The term “small entities” comprises small businesses, not-for-profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000. Section 605 of the RFA allows an agency to certify a rule, in lieu of preparing an analysis, if the rulemaking is not expected to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
The Coast Guard certifies that, although some small entities may intend to transit the safety zone above, this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. This safety zone will only impact a small, designated area for one hour on October 29, 2026, and for 45 minutes on October 31, 2026. It will be enforced during times when vessel traffic is normally low. In addition, the Coast Guard will issue a Broadcast Notice to Marines via VHF FM marine channel 16, which will allow small entities to adjust their transit plans, and the rule allows vessels to request permission to enter the zone from the COTP.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (
Pub. L. 104-121
), if this rule will affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions, contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section.
Small businesses may send comments to the Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and the Regional Small Business Regulatory Fairness Boards by calling 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247).
B. Collection of Information
This rule will not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this rule under
Executive Order 13132
, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.
Also, this rule does not have tribal implications under
Executive Order 13175
, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because it does not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
As required by The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
), the Coast Guard certifies that this rule will not result in an annual expenditure of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted for inflation) by a State, local, or tribal government, in the aggregate, or by the private sector.
E. Environment
We have analyzed this rule under Department of Homeland Security Directive 023-01, Rev. 1, associated implementing instructions, and Environmental Planning COMDTINST 5090.1 (series), which guide the Coast Guard in complying with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (
42 U.S.C. 4321

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title:
Requirements for Derivatives Clearing Organizations, OMB Control No. 3038-0076. This is a request for an extension of a currently approved information collection.
Abstract:
Commission Regulations 39.10, 39.11, 39.12, 39.13, 39.14, 39.15, 39.16, 39.17, 39.18, 39.19, 39.21, 39.24 and 39.27 establish reporting requirements for registered derivatives clearing organizations (DCOs). Regulation 39.3 requires any person seeking to register as a DCO to submit a completed Form DCO as provided in Appendix A to part 39, accompanied by all applicable exhibits. Subpart C of part 39 includes additional requirements for systemically important DCOs and DCOs that elect to be subject to subpart C. Subpart D of part 39 includes requirements for DCOs subject to alternative compliance. The rules establish reporting and recordkeeping requirements that implement Section 5b of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA), and are necessary for the Commission to assess compliance of DCOs and DCO applicants with requirements prescribed in the CEA and Commission regulations.
On August 6, 2026, the Commission published in the
Federal Register
notice of the proposed extension of this information collection and provided 60 days for public comment on the proposed extension.
91 FR 50816
(60-Day Notice). The Commission received two relevant comments on the 60-Day Notice. The first comment stated that the 60-Day FRN's aggregate estimate of the average burden hours for all respondents to the collection obscures that applicants for DCO registration face a proportionally higher burden in preparing applications compared to registered entity's comparatively lower ongoing compliance burdens.
[
1
]
The Commission, however, provides granular burden estimates in the Supporting Statement submitted to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, which includes estimates for applicants under Subpart A of Part 39, as well as Subparts B, C, and D, which apply to registered DCOs.
The second comment did not address the Commission's burden estimates, but recommended new substantive recordkeeping and risk-analysis requirements relating to tokenized collateral.
[
2
]
The commenter's recommendations were based primarily on CFTC Staff Letter No. 25-39, Tokenized Collateral Guidance (Dec. 8, 2025). That guidance, however, reflects only the views of the Commission staff divisions that issued the letter and does not create additional rights or requirements. Accordingly, the guidance does not provide a basis for modifying this information collection or adopting new forms to require additional recordkeeping, as recommended by the commenter.
Burden Statement:
The Commission is revising its estimate of the burden for this existing collection of information. The Commission is increasing its estimate of the total number of registered DCOs from 13 to 24. Similarly, the Commission is increasing its estimate of the total number of applicants for full DCO registration from one to 10. The estimates are based on the number of DCOs registered with the Commission, as well as pending applications for full DCO registration as of July 2026.
The respondent burden for this collection is estimated to be as follows:

109.
Estimated annual reports per respondent:
240.
Estimated total annual responses:
26,119.
Estimated average burden hours per respondent:
907.
Estimated total annual burden hours:
98,886.
Frequency of collection:
Daily, monthly, quarterly, annually, and on occasion.
The capital and start-up or operations and maintenance costs associated with this collection are estimated at $821,470.

SUMMARY:
Pursuant to the provisions of the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended, notice is hereby given that the Farm Credit Administration (FCA or Agency) is amending an existing system of records, FCA-5—Assignments and Communication Tracking System—FCA. The Assignments and Communication Tracking System—FCA system is used to track draft correspondence and other memoranda, employee assignments, and notes from oral and written correspondence and communications between FCA and FCSIC staff and external parties.
