TDEC's modeling analysis was developed in accordance with the EPA's Guideline on Air Quality Models (Modeling Guideline)
[
92
]
and the Modeling Guidance provided in appendix A of the EPA's SO
2
Nonattainment Area Guidance. The modeling was performed using the EPA's preferred air dispersion modeling system—the American Meteorological Society/Environmental Protection Agency Regulatory Model (AERMOD)—consisting of the AERMOD (version 22112) air dispersion model
[
93
]
and multiple data input preprocessors as described below.
TDEC used regulatory default options in the AERMOD modeling. Based upon an evaluation of the land use within three kilometers of Eastman, more than 50 percent of the land use is classified under urban land use categories rather than rural land use categories. Therefore, urban dispersion coefficients were used in the modeling. Due to the larger amount of heat released from Eastman, although the facility is located in a city with a population of about 50,000, a surrogate population value of 200,000 was calculated by Eastman for use with the urban option in AERMOD as the “effective population.” Additional details about the procedures used for the urban option are provided in the EPA's Sullivan County SO
2
Modeling TSD.
AERMET and AERMINUTE are data pre-processors for the EPA's AERMOD air quality dispersion model, generating meteorological observations and wind data information, respectively. AERMET (version 22112) and AERMINUTE (version 15272) were used to process one year (April 2012-March 2013) of site-specific meteorological data
[
94
]
(wind speed and direction, temperature, and turbulence parameters), collected at a 100-meter tower equipped with a Sound Detection and Ranging (SODAR) wind profiler system specifically installed near Eastman for this modeling analysis. Additional meteorology inputs needed for AERMOD that were not collected at the site-specific meteorology station (
e.g.,
cloud cover data) were obtained from the Bristol/Johnson/Kingsport, Tri-Cities Regional Airport (KTRI) National Weather Service (NWS) automated surface observing system (ASOS) station (WBAN No. 13877), in combination with twice daily upper-air meteorological soundings from the Nashville, Tennessee NWS station (WBAN No. 13897). The Tri-Cities Regional Airport is located approximately 8.5 miles east/southeast of Eastman, and the Nashville Airport is located approximately 200 miles west of Kingsport, but it has mean mixing heights comparable to the Kingsport area. The pre-processor AERSURFACE (version 20060) was used to process 2011 National Land Cover Database (NLCD) data to derive the albedo, Bowen ratio, and surface roughness surface characteristics needed for AERMET.
The pre-processor AERMAP (version 18081) was used to generate terrain inputs for the receptors, based on a digital elevation mapping database from the National Elevation Dataset developed by the U.S. Geological Survey. Model receptors were placed at 50-meter intervals along the fence-line, public access roads, and riverbanks as well as in a 100-meter grid throughout the remainder of the three-km non-attainment area (excluding the area inside the Eastman fence-line because access is controlled by fences, gates, and other restrictions to limit public access and is therefore not considered to be ambient air).
TDEC's modeling analysis is based upon permitted allowable emissions limits for the primary SO
2
emissions sources at Eastman
[
95
]
and the other nearby sources that are included in the modeling.
[
96
]
Smaller SO
2
emissions sources at Eastman, which will not have emissions limits incorporated into the SIP, were modeled at maximum uncontrolled hourly emissions rates. One batch chemical manufacturing source at Eastman was excluded from the modeling analysis based upon the intermittent nature of its operation. Additional details about this intermittent source are provided in Tennessee's May 20, 2026, supplement to the redesignation request SIP submittal and the EPA's Sullivan County SO
2
Modeling TSD. The allowable emissions limits for the B-83 and B-325 coal-fired boilers, B-248 liquid and solid hazardous waste incinerator, and B-351 Coal Gasification
(
printed page 68084)
Flares are 30-day average SO
2
emissions limits. The modeling analysis must be based upon the maximum allowable 1-hour SO
2
emissions. Therefore, TDEC used the procedures contained in EPA's SO
2
Nonattainment Area Guidance to determine the short-term 1-hour critical emission value (CEV) for each of these sources based on modeling and then established comparably stringent LTA permit limits. As described in the SO
2
Nonattainment Area Guidance, the CEV is the maximum modeled emission rate that results in attainment and can be used as a reference point for setting the longer term emission rates. Modeling multiple sources of emissions together to determine the worst-case attainment scenario will result in a CEV associated with each source.
As discussed in the LTA TSD, TDEC derived longer term emission limits from modeled CEVs for three sets of emission sources. For the coal-fired boilers (B-83 and B-325), Tennessee established a new single, combined emission limit of 1,248 lb/hr of SO
2
emissions on a 30-day rolling average. TDEC derived this limit from the CEV of 1,600 lb/hr and an adjustment factor of 0.78. An adjustment factor is the ratio that accounts for the variability of the hourly emissions for a source. For the hazardous waste incinerators (B-248-1 and B-248-2), Tennessee established separate CEVs for each of the incinerators at 20 lb/hr and 10 lb/hr, respectively. After determining the CEVs for each incinerator, Tennessee followed the SO
2
Nonattainment Area Guidance to establish comparably stringent 30-day rolling average emission limits for each incinerator at 15.2 lb/hr (adjustment factor of 0.76) and 2.0 lb/hr (adjustment factor of 0.2), respectively. For the Coal Gasification Flares (B-351-5), Tennessee established a longer term emission limit of 14.6 lb/hr on a 30-day rolling average. This emission limit was derived from the CEV of 16.28 lb/hr of SO
2
emissions. Additional details about the process for determining the CEVs and 30-day average permit limits are contained in the EPA's Sullivan County SO
2
Modeling TSD and LTA TSD.
The Building Profile Input Program for Plume Rise Model Enhancements (BPIPPRM) (version 04274) preprocessor was used to generate direction-specific building downwash parameters for input into AERMOD. The stack heights used in the modeling meet the Good Engineering Practice stack height criteria specified in
40 CFR 51.118
. Twenty-four buildings/structures were processed for the four primary boiler stacks at Eastman (B-83 Boilers B-18-22, B-83 Boilers B-23-24, B-325, and B-253). TDEC's modeling also evaluated the potential building downwash effects from these same twenty-four buildings/structures for smaller emissions sources at Eastman, and the Primster, Domtar and Cardinal Glass facilities. The BPIPPRM results indicated that these buildings influenced modeled concentrations for a total of 31 modeled Eastman sources and the Primester source. Building downwash was not found to influence concentrations from the other nearby sources included in the modeling analysis (Domtar and Cardinal Glass) because of their distance from the nonattainment area (1 km and 23 km, respectively).
TDEC evaluated other large sources of SO
2

2

2

a. General SIP Requirements
General SIP elements and requirements are delineated in section 110(a)(2) of title I, part A of the CAA. These requirements include, but are not limited to, the following: submission of a SIP that has been adopted by the State after reasonable public notice and hearing; provisions for establishment and operation of appropriate procedures needed to monitor ambient air quality; implementation of a source permit program; provisions for the implementation of part C requirements (PSD); provisions for the implementation of part D requirements (NNSR); provisions for air pollution modeling; and provisions for public and local agency participation in planning and emission control rule development.
CAA section 110(a)(2)(D) requires that SIPs contain certain measures to prevent sources in a State from significantly contributing to air quality problems in another State. To implement this provision, the EPA has required certain States to establish programs to address the interstate transport of air pollutants. CAA section 110(a)(2)(D) requirements for a State are not linked with a particular nonattainment area's designation and classification in that State. The transport SIP submission requirements, where applicable, continue to apply to a State regardless of the designation of any one area in the State. As a result, the EPA maintains that the CAA's interstate transport requirements should be construed to be applicable for purposes of redesignation.
In addition, the other CAA section 110(a)(2) elements that are neither connected with nonattainment plan submissions nor linked with an area's attainment status are not applicable requirements for purpose of redesignation. The area will still be subject to these requirements after the area is redesignated. CAA section 110 and part D requirements which are linked with a particular area's designation and classification are the relevant measures to evaluate in reviewing a redesignation request. This approach is consistent with the EPA's existing policy on applicability (

CAA section 175A requires that a maintenance plan includes such contingency measures as the EPA deems necessary to assure that the State will promptly correct a violation of the NAAQS that occurs after redesignation. The maintenance plan identifies the contingency measures to be adopted, a schedule and a procedure for adoption and implementation, and a time limit for action by a State. In cases where attainment revolves around compliance of a single source or a small set of sources with emissions limits shown to provide for attainment, the EPA interprets “contingency measures” to mean that the State agency has a comprehensive program to identify sources of violations of the SO
2
NAAQS and to undertake aggressive follow-up for compliance and enforcement, including expedited procedures for establishing enforceable consent agreement pending the adoption of revised SIPs.

The maintenance plan must include a requirement that a State will implement all measures with respect to control of the pollutant that were contained in the SIP before redesignation of the area to attainment in accordance with CAA section 175A(d). The contingency plan included in the maintenance plan contains triggers to determine when contingency measures are needed and what kind of measures should be used.
Tennessee's maintenance plan provides a primary trigger and contingency measures upon activation of that trigger. This language provides that upon notification by the Tennessee Technical Secretary to the permittee that a reference monitor in the Area has registered four validated ambient SO

The permittee must submit a written system audit report within 30 days of the notification. The system audit report must detail the operating parameters of all emissions units, including smaller modeled emission units, for four 10-day periods up to and including the date upon which the reference monitor registered each exceedance, together with recommended provisional SO
2
emission control strategies for each affected unit and evidence that these control strategies have been deployed, as appropriate.
Upon consultation with the Technical Secretary, the permittee shall develop and implement operational changes as necessary to prevent future monitored violations of the standard. These changes may include fuel switching, physical or operational reduction of production capacity, or other changes as appropriate. If a permit modification is deemed necessary, any changes to existing permit conditions shall follow the applicable procedures of TAPCR 1200-03-09. If an emission source is found to be noncompliant with a SIP emission limit, the Technical Secretary will, in addition to conducting enforcement proceedings to bring the source into compliance with its SIP limit, determine whether additional limits must be added to the SIP in accordance with CAA section 175A.

Six months to identify appropriate contingency measures, including identification of emission sources and appropriate control technologies;

Between nine and twelve months to implement the contingency measures. This step would include the time required to draft rules or SIP amendments, complete the rulemaking process, and submit the final plans to the EPA.

Further, under CAA section 110(l), the EPA may not approve a SIP if it would interfere with any applicable requirement concerning NAAQS attainment, reasonable further progress toward attainment, or any other applicable requirement of the CAA. This requirement is often referred to the “anti-backsliding” provision of the CAA. As demonstrated in sections V.A.-C., Tennessee's February 9, 2023, and

Under the CAA, the Administrator is required to approve a SIP submission that complies with the provisions of the Act and applicable Federal regulations.

Thus, in reviewing SIP submissions, the EPA's role is to approve State choices, provided that they meet the criteria of the CAA. Furthermore, redesignation of an area to attainment and the accompanying approval of a maintenance plan under section 107(d)(3)(E) are actions that affect the status of a geographical area and do not impose any additional regulatory requirements on sources beyond those imposed by State law. Abstract:
This ICR is a renewal of the previously approved UST Finder ICR (No. 2696.01; OMB No. 2080-0086) to update the UST Finder application on a semiannual basis. To successfully maintain and improve the data quality and usability of UST Finder, the Agency seeks to continue gathering, on a voluntary basis, location and other relevant data about USTs and LUSTs that are currently collected and managed by states and territories. The application may be used for many purposes, such as helping regulators, owners, and operators in decision-making; prioritizing site cleanups or inspections; triaging risk; and identifying sites that may be more likely to have a release based on UST age and substance stored. The application may also be used by emergency response personnel to protect UST facilities from extreme weather events. After disasters, the UST Finder can be used to rapidly identify LUST site cleanups impacted by natural disasters and assist in restarting cleanups after these events.
Form Numbers:
None.
Respondents/affected entities:
The respondents for the information collection activity are state and territorial delegated agencies. The United States Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code for the
(
printed page 68143)
respondents is SIC 9511, which corresponds to the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) 924110 for Administration of Air and Water Resource and Solid Waste Management Programs. Source compliance data assembled by delegated agencies covers numerous NAICS categories.
Respondent's obligation to respond:
Voluntary.
Estimated number of respondents:
56 (total).
Frequency of response:
Semiannual.
Total estimated burden:
989 hours (per year). Burden is defined at
5 CFR 1320.03(b)
.
Total estimated cost:
$72,475 (per year), which includes $1,067 annualized capital or operation & maintenance costs.
Changes in the Estimates:
There is a decrease of 2481 hours in the total estimated respondent burden compared with the ICR currently approved by OMB. This decrease is due to the following factors.
Most respondents have previously submitted data and will not require any time to set up their data delivery option. Thus, they will only incur a burden to submit the semi-annual data updates unless they choose to set up a new option.
The last information collection was conducted prior to the first round of data collection for UST Finder, so the burden calculated in the previous ICR were based on estimates for respondents who had not yet submitted data. This uncertainty led to overestimated burden.
EPA estimates the burden calculations in this ICR based on hours estimates provided by state agencies in the consultations conducted by EPA. Some of the responses indicated that the data set-up and semiannual update burden estimates were lower than previous estimates due to respondents' increased familiarity with the requirements of the data collection.
The previous ICR considered subcontractor labor hours as part of the annual burden; however, this ICR considers subcontractor labor as a one-time capital cost to set up data delivery options.

Deputy Director, Data and Enterprise Programs Division.

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Notice of charter renewal and request for nominations for the Great Lakes Advisory Board.
SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has determined that, in accordance with the provisions of the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA), the EPA Great Lakes Advisory Board (GLAB) is a necessary committee which is in the public's interest. Accordingly, the Advisory Board will be renewed for an additional two-year period. In addition, EPA is seeking member nominations for the GLAB from qualified candidates to serve a two-year term. The purpose of the GLAB is to provide advice and recommendations to the EPA Administrator through the Great Lakes National Program Manager on matters related to the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative and on domestic matters related to the implementation of the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. The Advisory Board's major objectives are to provide advice and recommendations on: Great Lakes protection and restoration activities; long term goals, objectives and priorities for Great Lakes protection and restoration; and other issues identified by the Great Lakes Interagency Task Force/Regional Working Group.
DATES:
Nominations for the GLAB must be submitted by January 15, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Alana Davicino, Designated Federal Officer, Great Lakes National Program Office, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 77 West Jackson Boulevard, (G-9J), Chicago, Illinois; telephone number: 312-886-2307, email address:
davicino.alana@epa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background:
The GLAB was established in accordance with the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA) of 1972 (
5 U.S.C. 10
) and
41 CFR 102-3.50(d)
. The board will provide advice and recommendations on matters related to the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative. The board will also advise on domestic matters related to implementation of the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement between the U.S. and Canada.
The major objectives will be to provide advice and recommendations on:
a. Great Lakes protection and restoration activities;
b. Long term goals, objectives, and priorities for Great Lakes protection and restoration; and
c. Other issues identified by the Great Lakes Interagency Task Force/Regional Working Group.
The GLAB is expected to meet in person or by electronic means (
e.g.,
telephone, videoconference, webcast, etc.) approximately two (2) times per year, or as otherwise needed and approved by the Designated Federal Officer. In-person meetings will be held in the Great Lakes region.
Nominations:
The GLAB will be composed of approximately fifteen (15) members who will serve as representative members of non-Federal interests. In selecting members, EPA will consider candidates representing a broad range of Great Lakes stakeholders, including, but not limited to: Environmental groups; agricultural groups; industry and/or business groups; citizen groups; foundations; academia; and State, local and Tribal governments. In selecting members, EPA will consider the differing perspectives and breadth of collective experience needed to address the GLAB's charter. Other criteria used to evaluate nominees will include:
Experience with Great Lakes issues;
Leadership and consensus-building experience in Great Lakes organizations, businesses, and workgroups;
Membership in professional societies involved with Great Lakes issues;
Academic leadership and expertise;
Community leadership; and
Representation of multiple constituencies within the Great Lakes basin.
How To Submit Nominations
Any interested person or organization may nominate qualified persons to be considered for appointment to the GLAB. Individuals may self-nominate. For appointment consideration, interested nominees should submit the application materials electronically via email to
davicino.alana@epa.gov
with the subject line “GLAB Nominations 2027”.
To be considered, nominations should include:
Current contact information for the nominee, including the nominee's name, organization (and position within that organization), current business address, email address and daytime phone number;
(
printed page 68138)
A brief statement describing the nominee's interest in serving on the GLAB;
A resume and a short biography (no more than two paragraphs) describing the professional and educational qualifications of the nominee, including a list of relevant activities and any current or previous service on Federal advisory committees; and
A description of the nominee's EPA grant funding history including current EPA grant activities if applicable. If this does not apply to the nominee, please provide a brief statement indicating so.
Optional:
Letter(s) of recommendation from a third party supporting the nomination. Letter(s) should describe how the nominee's experience and knowledge will bring value to the work of the GLAB.
To help the Agency evaluate the effectiveness of its outreach efforts, nominees are requested to use their submission packages to identify how they became aware of this request for nominations.
Public Interest Determination
Pursuant to
41 CFR 102-3.65
, this notice, announcing that the GLAB is being renewed, must include the written public interest determination (PID) approved by the head of the agency described in
41 CFR 102-3.60(a)
and any assessment provided by the General Services Administration's Committee Management Secretariat (the Secretariat). The PID included in this Unit has been provided to the Secretariat. The Secretariat has approved this PID without comment or assessment.
Pursuant to
41 U.S.C. 102
-3.60(a), to establish, renew, reestablish, or merge a discretionary (agency discretion) advisory committee, an agency must first consult with the Secretariat and, as part of the consultation, provide a written public interest determination approved by the head of the agency to the Secretariat with a copy to the Office of Management and Budget. In addition, pursuant to
41 U.S.C. 102
-3.35, an agency shall follow the same consultation process and document in writing the same determination of need before creating a subcommittee under a discretionary committee that is not made up entirely of members of a parent advisory committee. Information on the following factors for the committee was provided to the Secretariat to demonstrate that reestablishing the committee is in public interest:
1.
Annual budget:
The estimated Annual Budget for the GLAB is $129,389. The estimated annual federal personnel on a full-time equivalent (FTE) basis is 0.5 FTE. The estimate for other Federal internal costs is $32,139. The GLAB will be composed of approximately 15 representative members who will not be paid.
2.
If applicable, the total dollar value of grants expected to be recommended during the fiscal year is:
N/A.
3.
Criteria for selecting members to ensure the committee has the necessary expertise and fairly balanced membership:
In selecting members, EPA will consider candidates from a broad range of interests relating to the Great Lakes, including but not limited to, state, Tribal, and local governments, environmental groups, industry, business groups, agricultural groups, foundations, and academia.
4.
List of all other Federal advisory committees of the agency:
Science Advisory Committee on Chemicals
National Environmental Education Advisory Council
National Drinking Water Advisory Council
Local Government Advisory Committee
Human Studies Review Board
Hazardous Waste Electronic Manifest System Advisory Board
Good Neighbor Environmental Board
Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act Scientific Advisory Panel
Farm, Ranch, and Rural Communities Advisory Committee
EPA Science Advisory Board
Environmental Financial Advisory Board
Clean Air Scientific Advisory Committee
Children's Health Protection Advisory Committee
Pesticide Program Dialogue Committee
5.
Justification that the information or advice provided by the Federal advisory committee or subcommittee is not available from another Federal advisory committee, another Federal Government source, or any other more cost-effective and less burdensome source:
The GLAB provides EPA with the collective recommendations of state and local governments, Tribes and other Great Lakes interests to more effectively carry out Great Lakes restoration. There are no other existing EPA advisory committees that have a mission to advise on protecting and restoring the Great Lakes. Likewise, existing committees do not have the breadth of experience that is needed to inform the Agency on Great Lakes environmental issues from various viewpoints. Bringing together a cross-section of individuals with the needed range of experience and perspectives facilitates a more effective discussion of the technical issues and policy options that will support adequate evaluation of, and input into, EPA positions and actions.
6.
If the consultation is a committee renewal, a summary of the previous accomplishments of the committee and the reasons it needs to continue:
The GLAB did not convene in the previous Fiscal Year, but will be refocused and updated for FY27 and upcoming FYs. Accomplishments from previous GLABs include reports with specific, actionable near-term and long-term recommendations for EPA regarding pressing Great Lakes issues.
7.
Explanation of why the committee/subcommittee is essential to the conduct of agency business:
The Great Lakes Advisory Board (GLAB) supports the EPA in achieving the restoration and protection goals of the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative (GLRI) as outlined in Section 118 of the Clean Water Act. The Great Lakes is a vast, shared resource and protecting and restoring them requires the collective ideas and experience of the Great Lakes community. The GLAB provides a forum where EPA can have the full benefit of the ideas and experience of both government and non-governmental partners.
In conclusion, this public interest determination documents that renewing the committee is in the public interest, essential to the conduct of agency business, and that the information to be obtained is not already available through another advisory committee or source within the Federal Government.

Abstract:
This information collection request (ICR) addresses the paperwork requirements contained in the current Chemical Data Reporting (CDR) rule (
40 CFR part 711
)
under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA). Under TSCA section 8(a) (
15 U.S.C. 2607
), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is authorized to collect certain information on chemical substances manufactured (including imported) or processed in the United States. The CDR was formerly known as the Inventory Update Rule (IUR).
The CDR collection provides chemical manufacture, processing, and use information that helps EPA identify chemicals to which the public may be exposed as consumers or as workers in commercial and industrial settings. The data also helps EPA assess routes of potential exposure to those chemicals. The CDR data collection is on a four-year reporting cycle and contains detailed manufacturing, processing, and use information drawn from the principal reporting year; as well as basic information on production volume, by
(
printed page 68132)
year, for the three years prior to the principal reporting year. The next CDR collection will occur in 2028; there are no changes to the reporting requirements.
The ICR, which is available in the docket along with other related materials, provides a detailed explanation of the collection activities and the burden estimate that is only briefly summarized here:
Form Number:
9600-010.

Entities potentially affected by this ICR include companies manufacturing (including importing) certain chemical substances listed on the TSCA Inventory and regulated under TSCA section 8(a) CDR regulation. North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) codes are identified in question 12 of the ICR.

Mandatory.
15 U.S.C. 2607
;
40 CFR part 711
.

Once every four years.

5 CFR 1320.03(b)
.

Changes in the estimates:
This ICR includes an increase of 161,568 hours in the total estimated burden compared with that currently approved by OMB. The increase reflects the use of 2020 CDR data (rather than 2016 CDR used for the previous ICR update) for estimating the reporting universe. Although in 2020 fewer sites reported to CDR than in 2016 (
i.e.,
fewer Form Us submitted), on average the sites reported a greater number of chemicals. This change resulted in a substantial increase in the number of chemical reports submitted. In addition, fewer chemical reports were for partially exempted chemicals (see
40 CFR 711.6
for a list of chemicals that are partially exempted from reporting under CDR). In 2016 CDR, approximately 21% of reports were partial reports, whereas in 2020 CDR the share of partial reports was about 7%. The average burden for each chemical report is higher because a greater percentage of the chemical reports are full reports. This change is an adjustment.

I. Executive Summary
A. What proposed action is the EPA taking?
The EPA is proposing to approve the RFP demonstration and associated emissions inventory and budgets for the Coachella Valley 2008 ozone NAAQS Extreme nonattainment area.
B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements?
Under CAA section 109, the EPA promulgates NAAQS for criteria air pollutants, such as ozone. In 2008, the EPA revised the ozone NAAQS by setting the acceptable level of ozone in the ambient air at 0.075 parts per million (ppm) averaged over an 8-hour period.
Requirements for an emissions inventory for nonattainment areas are specified in CAA section 172(c)(3). CAA section 172(c)(3) requires that each nonattainment plan SIP submission include a “comprehensive, accurate, current inventory of actual emissions from all sources of the relevant pollutant or pollutants in [the] area.”
Requirements for RFP for ozone nonattainment areas are specified in CAA sections 172(c)(2), 182(b)(1), and 182(c)(2)(B). CAA section 172(c)(2) requires that plans for nonattainment areas provide for RFP, which is defined as such annual incremental reductions in emissions of the relevant air pollutant as are required under part D (“Plan Requirements for Nonattainment Areas”) or that may reasonably be required by the EPA for the purpose of ensuring attainment of the applicable NAAQS by the applicable attainment date. CAA section 182(b)(1) specifically requires that ozone nonattainment areas that are classified as “Moderate” or above demonstrate a 15 percent reduction in volatile organic compounds (VOC) over an initial six-year period.
Requirements for conformity are specified in CAA section 176(c). CAA section 176(c) requires Federal actions in nonattainment and maintenance areas to conform to the SIP's goals of eliminating or reducing the severity and number of violations of the NAAQS and achieving timely attainment of the standards.
II. Background
A. Ozone Standards, Area Designations, and SIPs
Ground-level ozone pollution is formed from the reaction of VOC and oxides of nitrogen (NO) in the presence of sunlight.
[
1
]
These two pollutants, referred to as ozone precursors, are emitted by many types of sources, including on-and off-road motor vehicles and engines, power plants and industrial facilities, and smaller area sources such as lawn and garden equipment and paints.
Under CAA section 109, the EPA promulgates NAAQS for criteria air pollutants, such as ozone. The Agency promulgated NAAQS for ozone in 1979 and 1997.
[
2
]
In 2008, the EPA revised the ozone NAAQS by setting the acceptable level of ozone in the ambient air at 0.075 ppm averaged over an 8-hour period.
[
3
]
Although the Agency further revised the 8-hour ozone NAAQS to 0.070 ppm in 2015,
[
4
]
this action relates to the requirements for the 2008 ozone NAAQS.
Following promulgation of a new or revised NAAQS, the EPA is required under CAA section 107(d) to designate areas of the country as attaining or not attaining the NAAQS. Ozone nonattainment areas are further classified under CAA section 181 according to the severity of the ozone pollution problem, with classifications ranging from “Marginal” to “Extreme.” State planning and emissions control requirements for ozone are determined, in part, by the nonattainment area's classification. In 2012, the EPA designated the Coachella Valley as nonattainment for the 2008 ozone NAAQS and the area was classified as “Severe-15.”
[
5
]
In 2020, the EPA approved portions of two SIP revisions, the “Final 2016 Air Quality Management Plan” and the “2018 Updates to the California State Implementation Plan,” for the Coachella Valley area.
[
6
]
Collectively, we referred to the relevant portions of the two SIP revisions as the “2016 Coachella Valley Ozone SIP.” The 2016 Coachella Valley Ozone SIP addressed ozone nonattainment area requirements, including the requirements for an emissions inventory, emissions statement rule, attainment demonstration, RFP, reasonably available control measures, contingency measures, and budgets. The Agency approved the 2016 Coachella Valley Ozone SIP as meeting all the applicable Severe-15 ozone nonattainment area requirements except for the contingency measure requirements, for which the EPA deferred action.
On March 8, 2023, the EPA granted a request from California to reclassify the
(
printed page 68061)
Coachella Valley as Extreme for the 2008 ozone NAAQS.
[
7
]
The SIP revisions that are the subject of today's proposed action address specific Extreme nonattainment area requirements that apply to the Coachella Valley for the 2008 ozone NAAQS.
B. The Coachella Valley Nonattainment Area
The Coachella Valley is located within Riverside County, and its boundaries generally align with the Riverside County portion of the Salton Sea Air Basin.
[
8
]
The Coachella Valley is downwind from the South Coast Air Basin and is subject to significant transport of ozone from that area; both ozone nonattainment areas are regulated by the South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD or “District”).
C. CAA and Regulatory Requirements for 2008 8-Hour Ozone Nonattainment Area SIPs
States must implement the 2008 ozone standards under Title 1, part D of the CAA, which includes CAA sections 171 through 179B of subpart 1 (“Nonattainment Areas in General”) and CAA sections 181 through 185 of subpart 2 (“Additional Provisions for Ozone Nonattainment Areas”). To assist States in developing effective plans to address ozone nonattainment problems, the EPA has issued a SIP Requirements Rule for the 2008 ozone standards (“2008 Ozone SRR”) that addresses implementation of the 2008 standards, including attainment dates, requirements for emissions inventories, and RFP demonstrations, as well as the transition from the 1997 ozone standards to the 2008 ozone standards and associated anti-backsliding requirements.
[
9
]
The 2008 Ozone SRR is codified at
40 CFR part 51, subpart AA
. We discuss the CAA and regulatory requirements for the elements of 2008 ozone plans relevant to this proposal in more detail in section IV of this document.
The EPA's 2008 Ozone SRR was challenged, and on February 16, 2018, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit (“D.C. Circuit”) published its decision in
South Coast Air Quality Management District
v.
EPA
[
10
]
(“
South Coast II”
)
[
11
]
vacating portions of the 2008 Ozone SRR. The only aspect of the
South Coast II
decision that affects this proposed action is the vacatur of the alternative baseline year for RFP plans. More specifically, the 2008 Ozone SRR required States to develop the baseline emissions inventory for RFP plans using emissions data for the most recent calendar year for which States submit a triennial inventory to the Agency under subpart A (“Air Emissions Reporting Requirements”) of
40 CFR part 51
, which for the 2008 ozone NAAQS was 2011. However, the 2008 Ozone SRR allowed States to use an alternative year, between 2008 and 2012, for the baseline emissions inventory provided that the State demonstrated why the alternative baseline year was appropriate. In the
South Coast II
decision, the D.C. Circuit vacated the provisions of the 2008 Ozone SRR that allowed States to use an alternative baseline year for demonstrating RFP.

IV. Evaluation of the 2022 Coachella Valley RFP Plan
A. Emissions Inventories
1. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements
CAA section 172(c)(3) requires that each nonattainment plan SIP submission include a “comprehensive, accurate, current inventory of actual emissions from all sources of the relevant pollutant or pollutants in [the] area.” The accounting required by this section provides a “base year” inventory that serves as the starting point for attainment demonstration air quality modeling, for assessing RFP, and for determining the need for additional SIP control measures. EPA regulations require that the base year be consistent
(
printed page 68062)
with the baseline year for the RFP demonstration, which is the most recent calendar year for which a complete triennial inventory is required to be submitted to the Agency under the Air Emissions Reporting Requirements (AERR).
[
15
]
The EPA has issued guidance on the development of base year and future year emissions inventories for ozone and other pollutants.
[
16
]
Emissions inventories for ozone must include emissions of VOC and NO
X
and represent emissions for a typical ozone season weekday.
[
17
]
States should include documentation explaining how they calculated emissions data. In estimating mobile source emissions, States should use the latest emissions models and planning assumptions available at the time they develop the SIP submission.
[
18
]
2. Summary of the State's Submission
The 2022 Coachella Valley RFP Plan includes a 2011 base year emissions inventory based on actual emissions to meet the requirements of CAA sections 172(c)(3) and 182(a)(1). The Plan also includes projected inventories for the years 2017, 2020, 2023, 2026, 2029, and the Coachella Valley's 2031 Extreme attainment year to meet the requirements of CAA section 182(c)(2)(B).
This inventory includes VOC and NO
X
emissions because these pollutants are the precursors to ozone formation and includes emissions across all source categories during an ozone season day as defined in
40 CFR 51.1100(cc)
.
40 CFR 51.1115(c)
requires emissions values included in the base year inventory to be actual ozone season day emissions as defined by
40 CFR 51.1100(q)
. While the Coachella Valley has a year-round ozone season, the 2022 Coachella Valley RFP Plan identifies summer, defined as May through October, as the time when the highest concentrations of ozone occur.
A description of the base year and projected year emissions inventories can be found in Chapter 5 of the Plan. The complete emissions inventory and documentation are found in Appendix I (“Summer Planning Emissions Inventory by Major Source Category”), and Appendix II (“Emissions Inventory Methodology for the 2008 8-Hour Ozone Extreme Area Plan Using CEPAM 2022 v1.01”) of the Plan.
VOC and NO
X
emissions can be grouped into two general source categories: emissions from stationary sources and emissions from mobile sources. Stationary sources can be further divided into “point” and “area” sources. Point sources typically refer to permitted facilities that have one or more identified and fixed pieces of equipment and emissions point. Per the AERR, permitted facilities were required to report their actual emissions to the District by the facility operators through the calendar year 2011. Stationary area sources are many smaller point sources and include sources that have internal combustion engines and gasoline dispensing facilities (gas stations). These sources are not inventoried individually; their emissions are estimated as a group and reported as a single source category. Area sources consist of widespread and numerous smaller emission sources, such as small permitted facilities and households.
The mobile source category can be divided into two major subcategories: “on-road” and “off-road” mobile sources. On-road mobile sources include light-duty automobiles; light-duty, medium-duty, and heavy-duty trucks; and motorcycles. Off-road mobile sources include aircraft, locomotives, construction equipment, mobile equipment, and recreational vehicles.
CARB and the District worked together to develop the emissions inventories for the 2022 Coachella Valley RFP Plan. Data were provided by CARB, the California Department of Transportation, the Department of Motor Vehicles, the Department of Pesticide Regulation, the California Energy Commission, and regional transportation agencies to develop estimates of mobile and area source emissions. The emission estimates for point sources reflect reported emissions, whereas estimates for mobile and area sources are based on projections obtained through use of emissions models and methodologies along with actual activity data for 2011 (
e.g.,
vehicle miles traveled). The District applied different methodologies to estimate over sixty different types of individual stationary sources. CARB and the District also reviewed the growth profiles for point and area source categories and updated them as necessary to ensure that the emission projections were based on data that reflect historical trends, current conditions, and recent economic and demographic forecasts.
CARB provided emission estimates for stationary sources, including nonagricultural diesel engines, agricultural irrigation pumps, laundering (dry cleaning), degreasing (solvents), oil and gas production, and gasoline dispensing facilities. CARB and the District estimated emissions for area sources, including consumer products, pesticides/fertilizers, fireplaces, farming operations, and other sources using models and associated methodologies.
CARB developed the emissions inventories for mobile sources. CARB estimated on-road mobile sources emissions, which include passenger vehicles, buses, and trucks, using their EMFAC2017 model.
[
19
]
They calculated on-road emissions by applying EMFAC2017 emission factors to the transportation activity data provided by the Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG) from their adopted 2020 Regional Transportation Plan. CARB estimated off-road mobile source emissions using either newer category-specific models or, where a new model was not available, the OFFROAD2007 model.

B. Reasonable Further Progress Demonstration
1. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements
Requirements for RFP for ozone nonattainment areas are specified in CAA sections 172(c)(2), 182(b)(1), and 182(c)(2)(B). CAA section 172(c)(2) requires that plans for nonattainment areas provide for RFP, which is defined as such annual incremental reductions in emissions of the relevant air pollutant as are required under part D (“Plan Requirements for Nonattainment Areas”) or that may reasonably be required by the EPA for the purpose of ensuring attainment of the applicable NAAQS by the applicable attainment date. CAA section 182(b)(1) specifically requires that ozone nonattainment areas that are classified as Moderate or above demonstrate a 15 percent reduction in VOC between the years of 1990 and 1996. The Agency has typically referred to CAA section 182(b)(1) as the rate of progress (ROP) requirement. For ozone nonattainment areas classified as Serious or higher, CAA section 182(c)(2)(B) requires reductions averaged over each consecutive 3-year period, beginning 6 years after the baseline year until the attainment date, of at least 3 percent of baseline emissions per year. The provisions in CAA section 182(c)(2)(B)(ii) allow an amount less than 3 percent of such baseline emissions each year if the State demonstrates to the EPA that the plan includes all measures that can feasibly be implemented in the area in light of technological achievability.
In the 2008 Ozone SRR, the EPA provided that areas classified as Moderate or higher will have met the ROP requirements of CAA section 182(b)(1) if the area has a fully approved 15 percent ROP plan for the 1-hour or 1997 8-hour ozone NAAQS.
[
21
]
For such areas, the Agency interprets the RFP requirements of CAA section 172(c)(2) to require areas classified as Moderate to provide a 15 percent emissions reduction of ozone precursors within 6 years of the baseline year. Areas classified as Serious or higher must meet the RFP requirements of CAA section 182(c)(2)(B) by providing for an 18 percent reduction of ozone precursors in the first 6-year period, and an average ozone precursor emissions reduction of 3 percent per year for all remaining 3-year periods thereafter.
[
22
]
The 2008 Ozone SRR allows substitution of NO
X
reductions for VOC reductions to meet the CAA section 172(c)(2) and 182(c)(2)(B) RFP requirements.
[
23
]
Except as specifically provided in CAA sections 182(b)(1)(C) and (D), emissions reductions from all SIP-approved, federally promulgated, or otherwise SIP creditable measures that occur after the baseline year are creditable for purposes of demonstrating that the RFP targets are met.
[
24
]
Because the EPA has determined that the passage of time has caused the effect of certain exclusions to be
de minimis,
the RFP demonstration is no longer required to calculate and specifically exclude reductions from measures related to motor vehicle exhaust or evaporative emissions promulgated by January 1, 1990; regulations concerning Reid vapor pressure promulgated by November 15, 1990; measures to correct previous RACT requirements; and measures required to correct previous inspection and maintenance programs.
[
25

The 2008 Ozone SRR requires the RFP baseline year to be the most recent calendar year for which a complete triennial inventory was required to be submitted to the EPA. For the purposes of developing RFP demonstrations for the 2008 ozone NAAQS, the applicable triennial inventory year is 2011. As discussed previously, the 2008 Ozone SRR provides States with the option to use an alternative baseline year for RFP, but that provision of the 2008 Ozone SRR was vacated by the D.C. Circuit in the
South Coast II

C. Motor Vehicle Emissions Budgets for Transportation Conformity
1. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements
CAA section 176(c) requires Federal actions in nonattainment and maintenance areas to conform to the SIP's goals of eliminating or reducing the severity and number of violations of the NAAQS and achieving timely attainment of the standards. Conformity to the SIP's goals means that such actions will not: (1) cause or contribute to violations of a NAAQS; (2) worsen the severity of an existing violation; or (3) delay timely attainment of any NAAQS or any interim milestone.
[
28
]
Actions involving Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) or Federal Transit Administration (FTA) funding or approval are subject to the EPA's transportation conformity rule, codified at
40 CFR part 93, subpart A
. Under this rule, MPOs in nonattainment and maintenance areas coordinate with State and local air quality and transportation agencies, the EPA, the FHWA, and the FTA to demonstrate that an area's regional transportation plans and transportation improvement programs conform to the applicable SIP. This demonstration is typically done by showing that estimated emissions from existing and planned highway and transit systems are less than or equal to the motor vehicle emissions budgets (“budgets”) contained in all control strategy SIPs. Budgets are generally established for specific years and specific pollutants or precursors. Ozone plans should identify budgets for on-road emissions of ozone precursors (
i.e.,
NO
X
and VOC) in the area for each RFP milestone year (and the attainment year, if the plan demonstrates attainment).
[
29
]
For budgets to be approvable, they must meet, at a minimum, the EPA's adequacy criteria at
40 CFR 93.118(e)(4)
. To meet these requirements, the budgets must be consistent with the attainment and RFP requirements and reflect all of the motor vehicle control measures contained in the attainment and RFP demonstrations.
[
30
]
The Agencies' process for determining adequacy of a budget consists of three basic steps: (1) providing public notification of a SIP submission; (2) providing the public the opportunity to comment on the budget during a public comment period; and (3) making a finding of adequacy.
[
31
]

Background
The mission of the Institute of Education Sciences (IES) is to: “Provide national leadership in expanding fundamental knowledge and understanding of education from early childhood through postsecondary study, in order to provide parents, educators, students, researchers, policymakers, and the general public with reliable information about, including the condition and progress of education in the United States, including early childhood education and special education; educational practices that support learning and improve academic achievement and access to educational opportunities for all students; and the effectiveness of Federal and other education programs.” (See: 20 U.S.C. § 9511).
IES carries out that mission through four centers, including the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES). NCES is specifically responsible for collecting and analyzing education-related statistical data. ESRA requires NCES to “collect, report, analyze, and disseminate statistical data related to education in the United States and in other nations, including—(1) collecting, acquiring, compiling (where appropriate, on a State-by-State basis), and disseminating full and complete statistics (disaggregated by the population characteristics described [below]) on the condition and progress of education, at the preschool, elementary, secondary, postsecondary, and adult levels in the United States . . .” (See:
20 U.S.C. 9543
).
Like its fellow Centers, NCES is seeking to align its priorities more closely with state and local education needs, accelerate the speed at which high-quality data and evidence are produced, and increase the use of those data and evidence by educators and policymakers so that student outcomes can be dramatically improved. This RFI seeks public comment on how it might do each.
The Challenge
The task of comprehensively describing the condition of education is daunting. The statutory remit that Congress has established for NCES, which spans multiple levels of education and topics in both the domestic and international context, is already an ambitious one. Further complicating its work is the breadth of stakeholders that NCES seeks to serve. The Center considers state and federal policymakers, students and families, educators, researchers, business leaders, and the media to be key constituents for its products—and is cognizant that each has its own information needs. As evidenced by the multiple observers who have commented as such, the need for NCES to prioritize what it collects, for whom, and for what purpose is a well-understood concern.
Perhaps less well understood is the role of time in NCES's work. When time
is
considered as a factor in NCES work, it is most often operationalized as “the speed with which data are collected and released.” This is neither unsurprising nor wrong: the production of statistics in a timely manner is a core function of a statistical agency because the timeliness of data directly impacts its utility. But time and its passage is more than just a metric by which NCES's operational efficiency can be judged (though it should be that, too).
As time passes, the conditions that surround education change—sometimes profoundly—and stakeholders' information needs can change in turn. NCES has not, to date, adopted a process of strategic foresight designed to systematically envision potential futures and the information needs they demand. Over time, this has the potential to minimize the value of the data NCES produces because, due to changing conditions, data products may not be maximally responsive to the issue of the day. Honing this skill and leveraging its outcomes as NCES considers its portfolio of work is a critical element in any strategic redesign effort.
Purpose of This RFI
NCES seeks to develop a framework that can guide the strategic redevelopment of its portfolio of work. To do so, NCES is soliciting insights
(
printed page 68120)
from experts and innovators in state and local education policy and practice, federal statistics, data collection methods, and other interested stakeholders to address questions such as:
1. What data do states and districts, educators, and families currently most need to inform their efforts to improve outcomes for all learners?
2. How can we prepare data collections for future data needs reflecting the potential for changed educational conditions and challenges?
3. What data collection methods are best suited to meet current and evolving information needs?
4. How might data collection and dissemination be optimized for future Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) applications and uses?
5. What dissemination methods are best suited to meet the information needs of NCES's diverse audiences?
6. Which data collection and dissemination methods are most efficient, optimizing the value of the outputs generated by those activities and the resources needed to execute them?
7. What federal, state, local, and industry partnerships are needed to enable those methods and make the most of the data NCES collects?
Additional Areas of Interest
We also welcome comments on the two issues below.
1. NCES is particularly interested in minimizing burden on respondents, particularly in the context of declining survey response rates. However, NCES is committed to the utility of the data it provides to the public. How might NCES prioritize and streamline its data collections to balance respondent burden and benefit?
2. Historically, NCES has sought to maximize the potential value of its data by developing data assets and products for non-technical audiences. This has included extensive derivation of analytic variables drawing across multiple study data sources, imputation designed to maximize data's analytic utility, and the development of extensive user documentation. These activities necessarily compete with NCES's timeliness goals. How might NCES resolve this tension in a way consistent with its responsibilities as statistical agency serving the public?

Acting Commissioner, National Center for Education Statistics.

Department of Commerce
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
[RTID 0648-XF849]
AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Notice; issuance of an incidental harassment authorization.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the regulations implementing the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), as amended, notification is hereby given that NMFS has issued an incidental harassment authorization (IHA) to PetroMarine Services (PM) to incidentally harass marine mammals incidental to Juneau International Airport (JNU) Rock Dump Fuel Terminal Reconstruction Project in Juneau, Alaska (AK).
DATES:
This IHA is effective from October 26, 2026, through October 25, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
Electronic copies of the application and supporting documents, as well as a list of the references cited in this document, may be obtained online at:
https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/​permit/​incidental-take-authorizations-under-marine-mammal-protection-act
.
In case of problems accessing these documents, please call the contact listed below.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Carter Esch, Office of Protected Resources, NMFS, (301) 427-8401.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
MMPA Background and Determinations
The MMPA prohibits the “take” of marine mammals, with certain exceptions. Sections 101(a)(5)(A) and (D) of the MMPA (
16 U.S.C. 1361
et seq.
) direct the Secretary of Commerce (as delegated to NMFS) to allow, upon request, the incidental, but not intentional, taking of small numbers of marine mammals by U.S. citizens who engage in a specified activity (other than commercial fishing) within a specified geographical region if certain findings are made and the public has an opportunity to comment on the proposed IHA.
Specifically, NMFS shall issue an IHA if it finds that the taking will have a negligible impact on the species or stock(s) and will not have an unmitigable adverse impact on the availability of the species or stock(s) for taking for subsistence uses (where relevant). Further, NMFS must prescribe the permissible methods of taking and other “means of effecting the least [practicable] adverse impact” on the affected species or stocks and their habitat, paying particular attention to rookeries, mating grounds, and areas of similar significance, and on the availability of such species or stocks for taking for certain subsistence uses (referred to here as “mitigation”). NMFS must also prescribe requirements pertaining to the monitoring and reporting of such takings. The definitions of key terms, such as “take,” “harassment,” and “negligible impact,” are found in the MMPA and NMFS' implementing regulations (see
16 U.S.C. 1362
;
50 CFR 216.103
).
On September 10, 2026, NMFS' proposal to issue an IHA to PM for take of marine mammals incidental to the JNU Rock Dump Fuel Terminal Reconstruction Project in Juneau, AK, was published in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 57550
). In that notice, NMFS provided estimates of the numbers, types, and methods of incidental take proposed for each species or stock, as well as the mitigation, monitoring, and reporting measures that would be required should the IHA be issued. The
Federal Register
notice also included an analysis to support NMFS' preliminary conclusions and determinations that the IHA, if issued, would satisfy the requirements of section 101(a)(5)(D) of the MMPA for issuance of the IHA. The
Federal Register
notice included web links to a draft IHA for review, as well as other supporting documents.
No substantive comments were received during the public comment period. There are no changes to the specified activity, the species taken, the proposed numbers, type, or methods of take, or the mitigation, monitoring, or reporting measures in the proposed IHA notice. No new information that would change any of the preliminary analyses, conclusions, or determinations in the proposed IHA notice has become available since that notice was published, and therefore, the preliminary analyses, conclusions, and determinations included in the proposed IHA are considered final.
National Environmental Policy Act
To comply with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA;
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
) and NOAA Administrative Order (NAO) 216-6A, NMFS must review our proposed action (
i.e.,
the issuance of an IHA) with respect to potential impacts on the human environment.
This action is consistent with categories of activities identified in Categorical Exclusion B4 (IHAs with no anticipated serious injury or mortality) of the Companion Manual for NAO 216-6A, which do not individually or cumulatively have the potential for significant impacts on the quality of the human environment and for which we have not identified any extraordinary circumstances that would preclude this categorical exclusion. Accordingly, NMFS has determined that the issuance of this IHA qualifies to be categorically excluded from further NEPA review.
Endangered Species Act
Section 7(a)(2) of the ESA of 1973 (
16 U.S.C. 1531
et seq.
) requires that each Federal agency ensures that any action it authorizes, funds, or carries out is not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of any endangered or threatened species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of designated critical habitat. To ensure ESA compliance for the issuance of incidental take authorizations, NMFS
(
printed page 68114)
consults internally whenever we propose to authorize take for ESA-listed species, in this case with the NMFS Alaska Regional Office (AKRO).
There is one marine mammal species, the Western DPS Steller sea lion, with confirmed occurrence in the project area that is listed under the ESA. The NMFS AKRO issued a Biological Opinion on October 22, 2026, under section 7 of the ESA, on the issuance of an IHA modification to PM under section 101(a)(5)(D) of the MMPA by the NMFS Permits and Conservation Division. The Biological Opinion concluded that the proposed action is not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of the Western DPS stock of Steller sea lion.
Authorization
Accordingly, consistent with the requirements of section 101(a)(5)(D) of the MMPA, NMFS has issued an IHA to PM for authorization to take marine mammals incidental to the JNU Rock Dump Fuel Terminal Reconstruction Project in Juneau, AK.
Dated: October 27, 2026.
Kimberly Damon-Randall,
Director, Office of Protected Resources, National Marine Fisheries Service.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice of public meeting.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Transportation announces a public meeting of the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy (USMMA) Board of Visitors (Board).
DATES:
November 12, 2026, from 2:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. EST. Requests to virtually attend this public meeting must be received by October 29, 2026. Written statements to be considered during the meeting must be received via email to
ExternalAffairs@usmma.edu
no later than November 5, 2026. Requests for accommodations for a disability must be received via email to
ExternalAffairs@usmma.edu
no later than November 5, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
The meeting is open to the public and will be held in person with remote participation by certain Board members and presenters. Public attendees may only attend the meeting virtually. The meeting will be held at the U.S. Department of Transportation Headquarters, Dr. Gladys West Room, Ninth Floor, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590. Members of the public who request virtual attendance by October 29, 2026 will be welcomed via a link posted on the USMMA Board of Visitors web page prior to the event. The USMMA Board of Visitors web page and information about the Board is found at
https://www.usmma.edu/​about/​leadership/​board-visitors
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
The Board's Designated Federal Officer and Point of Contact, Michael O'Hagan, 516-726-6048 or
ExternalAffairs@usmma.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The Board is a Federal Advisory Committee originally established as a Congressional Board by
46 U.S.C. 51312
“to provide independent advice and recommendations on matters relating to the United States Merchant Marine Academy.” The Board was originally chartered under the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA) on October 24, 2017.
Agenda
The meeting agenda will cover, but is not limited to, the following proposed topics:
1. Welcome remarks and Board maintenance items.
2. Academy modernization and budget requirements.
3. Statutory and legislative matters affecting Academy operations.
4. Honor Code and Code of Conduct.
5. Regimental Commander brief.
6. Board questions and discussion.
Public Participation
The meeting is open to the public and will be held in person with remote participation by certain Board members and presenters. In person attendance is not available to the public. However, the public may request to attend the meeting virtually. The U.S. Department of Transportation is committed to providing equal access to this meeting for all participants. If you need alternative formats or services because of a disability, such as sign language, interpretation, or other ancillary aids, please contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section.
Members of the public wishing to attend virtually must register by emailing
ExternalAffairs@usmma.edu
no later than October 29, 2026.
Any member of the public is permitted to file a written statement with the Board. Written statements intended for consideration during the November 12, 2026, meeting must be sent to the Designated Federal Officer listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section no later than November 5, 2026.
No member of the public will be allowed to present questions or speak during the meeting unless requested to do so by a member of the Board.

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (

), this notice announces the intention of the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) to request approval for a revision of a currently approved information collection request for the Agricultural Foreign Investment Disclosure Act of 1978 (AFIDA).

ADDRESSES:
USDA invites interested persons to submit comments on this notice. Comments may be submitted, identified by OMB Control Number 0509-0001, by one of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
This website provides the ability to type short comments directly into the comment field on this web page or attach a file for lengthier comments. Go to

.
Follow the on-line instructions at that site for submitting comments.
