[Release No. 34-106731; File No. SR-FINRA-2026-022]
October 26, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 22, 2026, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Inc. (“FINRA”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by FINRA. FINRA has designated the proposed rule change as constituting a “non-controversial” rule change under paragraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 under the Act,
[
3
]
which renders the proposal effective upon receipt of this filing by the Commission. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
FINRA is proposing to amend FINRA Rules 2220, 2351, 2357, 2360, and 4210 to address binary options, options whose payout is based on specified metrics, and options cleared by a registered clearing agency other than The Options Clearing Corporation.
The text of the proposed rule change is available on FINRA's website at
http://www.finra.org
and at the principal office of FINRA.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, FINRA included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. FINRA has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
(
printed page 68191)
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
Background
Multiple national securities exchanges have filed proposals with the Commission to list and trade new types of binary options whose exercise settlement amount is established at the creation of the option and whose payout is based on the value of an issuer's reported financial or operating metrics (“binary metric options”), some of which may be cleared by a registered clearing agency other than The Options Clearing Corporation (“OCC”), and the Commission has approved at least one such proposal.
[
4
]
While the specific proposals vary in some respects, these proposals collectively reflect a new category of exchange-listed options product: cash-settled, European-style binary options whose payouts are determined solely by whether an issuer's reported financial or operating metric (or other specified condition), such as quarterly revenue, earnings per share, or another metric disclosed in the issuer's SEC filings, meets or exceeds a defined threshold at expiration. These products generally have an exercise settlement amount of $1, meaning that at expiration each contract pays either $1 or $0 depending on whether the underlying metric has met or exceeded the specified threshold.
Binary metric options differ from most historically listed options products by referencing an underlying metric rather than a security or an index of securities, and in some cases by clearing through a registered clearing agency other than OCC.
[
5
]
The applicable trading mechanics of each binary metric option are governed by the rules of the exchange on which the contracts are listed.
FINRA Rule 2360 (Options) sets forth a number of requirements for FINRA members specific to options activity, including, among other things, requirements relating to position limits, large options position reporting (“LOPR”), delivery of disclosure documents, confirmations, transactions with issuers, account statements, account opening, recordkeeping, suitability, and supervision. Additionally, FINRA Rule 2220 (Options Communications) sets forth options-specific communications requirements and FINRA Rule 4210 (Margin Requirements) includes margin requirements specific to options. FINRA intends that the rules apply to all listed options products, including binary options, options on metrics, and options cleared through any registered clearing agency.
[
6
]
FINRA is therefore proposing amendments to Rules 2220, 2360, and 4210 to clarify the application of existing options requirements to binary options, options on metrics, and options cleared through a registered clearing agency other than OCC, which would include the new binary metric options products discussed above. As described in further detail below, the proposed rule change would accomplish this goal by updating the definitional framework under Rule 2360 to, among other clarifying changes, add new terms for binary options, registered clearing agencies, and underlying metrics; clarify the application of position limit and LOPR requirements in Rule 2360 to binary options and options on metrics; amend the disclosure document delivery requirement in Rule 2360 to include options issued by a registered clearing agency other than OCC; update provisions throughout Rules 2220, 2357, 2360, and 4210 to refer to registered clearing agencies generally rather than specifically to OCC, as appropriate; update provisions throughout Rules 2220 and 2360 to incorporate references to “metric;” and update Rules 2351 and 2360 to make other needed changes, including updating cross-references, making stylistic changes, and minor corrections to existing provisions.
The proposed changes are collectively designed to clarify the application of existing options requirements to binary options, options on metrics, and options cleared by any registered clearing agency, such that the rules apply to such options—including binary metric options—in a manner that is substantially comparable to other listed options products.
Proposed Amendments to Rule 2360
Rule 2360 establishes a comprehensive regulatory framework governing members' options trading activity. Rule 2360(a) sets forth a number of definitions for terms used in Rule 2360, including to distinguish between standardized options (
i.e.,
listed options) and conventional options, (
i.e.,
over-the-counter or “OTC” options). Rule 2360(b) clarifies the applicability of Rule 2360 and sets forth provisions regarding positions and exercise limits, LOPR requirements, delivery of disclosure documents, confirmations, transactions with issuers, account statements, account openings, recordkeeping, suitability, and supervision. Rule 2360(c) sets forth requirements for the portfolio margining disclosure statement and acknowledgement, and Supplementary Material .01 through .03 to Rule 2360 provide illustrative examples of position limit requirements, further explanation regarding the delta hedging exemption control relationship, and clarification regarding position limits for exchange-traded funds. The proposed changes to Rule 2360 are described in greater detail below.
Definitions
FINRA is proposing changes to Rule 2360(a) to include three new defined terms. First, FINRA proposes to add a new defined term, “Registered Clearing Agency,” meaning a clearing agency registered with the Commission pursuant to Section 17A of the Exchange Act.
[
7
]
This proposed definition is necessary to enable FINRA's options rules to apply to listed options regardless of which SEC-registered clearing agency issues or guarantees the contracts. FINRA is making several changes throughout Rule 2360 to replace references to OCC with Registered Clearing Agency.
Second, FINRA proposes to add a new defined term, “binary option,” meaning a cash-settled option contract having an exercise settlement amount that is established at the creation of the option and where the option holder is entitled to the exercise settlement amount only if the settlement value of the binary option overlying a security, index, or
(
printed page 68192)
metric, at expiration, (1) equals or is greater than the exercise price for a call binary option, or (2) is less than the exercise price for a put binary option. The proposed definition would further provide that the applicable trading mechanics for such contracts are governed by the rules of the exchange on which they are listed. This proposed definition is intended to broadly encompass a variety of binary options structures.
[
8
]
Third, FINRA proposes to add a new defined term, “underlying metric,” meaning a metric underlying an option, including any financial or operating metric or condition on which an option's payout is based. This proposed definition would complement the existing definitions of “underlying security” and “underlying index.”
In addition to these newly defined terms, FINRA proposes to consolidate and replace the existing definitions of “standardized equity option” and “standardized index option,” with a single, unified definition of “standardized option” that encompasses any options contract issued, or subject to issuance, by a Registered Clearing Agency that is not a FLEX Option and not an OCC Cleared OTC Option. The consolidated definition identifies standardized equity options, standardized index options, and standardized metric options as examples of standardized options. This proposed consolidation preserves the existing treatment of standardized equity options and standardized index options while ensuring standardized binary options listed on national securities exchanges and issued or guaranteed by a Registered Clearing Agency are subject to the same treatment. Conforming changes would be made throughout Rule 2360 to reflect this new consolidated term.
FINRA also proposes conforming and clarifying amendments to various other definitions set forth in Rule 2360(a). First, FINRA proposes to amend the definitions of “call,” “put,” “class of options,” and “series of options” to add “metric” alongside “security” and “index,” so that these terms explicitly include options overlying a metric. Corresponding conforming amendments are proposed to the definitions of “exercise price,” “expiration date,” “FLEX Equity Option” (to be renamed as “FLEX Option” as described below), “clearing member,” “conventional option,” “conventional index option,” “covered,” “OCC Cleared OTC Option,” “options trading,” and “underlying security.”
[
9
]
Second, FINRA proposes conforming and clarifying amendments to the definitions of “clearing member,” “conventional index option,” “conventional option,” “covered,” “expiration date,” “FLEX Equity Option” (to be renamed as “FLEX Option” as described below), “options trading,” and “underlying security” to replace references to OCC with references to a Registered Clearing Agency. The definitions of “call” and “put” would also be amended to remove unnecessary and duplicative language specifically referencing OCC.
Third, FINRA proposes conforming and clarifying amendments to the definition of “exercise price” to explicitly reference cash-settled options, including binary options and options on metrics. For cash-settled options, the proposed rule change would define “exercise price” as the price or value (measured in the applicable units (
e.g.,
amount of currency, percentage, or number)) to which the settlement value of the underlying index, security, or metric is compared to determine whether the holder is entitled to receive a dollar amount, which may be a fixed exercise settlement amount in the case of a binary option.
Finally, FINRA proposes to make other simplifying and clarifying changes to the definitions in Rule 2360(a), including to revise the defined term “FLEX Equity Option” to refer to “FLEX Option,” redesignate paragraph numbers to reflect new and consolidated definitions, and update cross-references.
Applicability
Rule 2360(b)(1) clarifies the applicability of Rule 2360. Rule 2360(b)(1) provides, among other things, that paragraphs (b)(3) through (12) of Rule 2360 apply only to standardized and conventional options on common stock. FINRA proposes to amend that provision to clarify that such limitation applies except as otherwise provided in those subparagraphs. The proposed rule change is intended to ensure that provisions within paragraphs (b)(3) through (12) that are expressly tailored to index options or binary options, such as the proposed binary options position limit and LOPR provisions discussed further below, are not limited by the general applicability language in Rule 2360(b)(1).
Position Limits
Rule 2360(b)(3) establishes position limits for options. FINRA is not proposing substantive changes to the existing provisions governing position limits for standardized equity options, standardized index options, conventional options, and FLEX Options. FINRA proposes to add a new paragraph (b)(3)(D) to Rule 2360 specifically addressing binary options position limits. Under this proposed provision, except in highly unusual circumstances and with FINRA's prior written approval pursuant to the Rule 9600 Series for good cause shown, no member shall effect for any account in which such member has an interest, or for the account of any partner, officer, director or employee thereof, or for the account of any customer, an opening transaction in any class of binary option if the member has reason to believe that, as a result of such transaction, the member, partner, officer, director, employee, or customer, would, acting alone or in concert with others, directly or indirectly, hold or control or be obligated in respect of an aggregate position in excess of the position limits established by the exchange on which the binary option trades. This proposed provision parallels the existing position limits provision applicable to standardized equity options. Thus, the proposed rule change is intended to apply substantially comparable position limit requirements to positions in binary options, consistent with FINRA's approach to position limits for other listed options products.
FINRA also proposes conforming changes to Rule 2360(b)(6) (Liquidation of Positions and Restrictions on Access) to add references to options overlying a metric. The proposed rule change would clarify that FINRA's existing authority relating to positions that exceed applicable position limits applies to options overlying a metric in the same manner as it applies to options overlying a security or index.
Reporting of Options Positions
Rule 2360(b)(5) sets forth requirements for reporting options positions, generally referred to as the “LOPR requirements.” Existing provisions refer to an underlying “security or index” and require a member that conducts a business in standardized options (but that is not a member of the listing exchange) to file position reports with FINRA when a reportable position threshold is reached,
i.e.
, an aggregate position of 200 or more
(
printed page 68193)
options contracts on the same side of the market.
[
10
]
FINRA proposes to add an explicit reference to “metric” so that the reporting obligation clearly extends to options on metrics.
Additionally, exchanges have proposed reporting and aggregation conventions for the treatment of binary metric options contracts for purposes of options position reporting requirements that may differ from the conventions for other listed options.
[
11
]
FINRA therefore proposes to amend its rules to require a member to determine its aggregate position for standardized options in accordance with the contract equivalency conventions established by the exchange on which such standardized options are listed. FINRA believes the proposed rule change would promote consistency for market participants.
Delivery of Disclosure Documents
Rule 2360(b)(11)(A)(i) requires each member to deliver OCC's current Options Disclosure Document (“ODD”) to each customer at or prior to the time such customer's account is approved for trading options issued by OCC, other than an OCC Cleared OTC Option. Thereafter, a copy of each amendment to the ODD must be distributed to each customer to whom the member previously delivered the ODD not later than the time a confirmation of a transaction in the category of options to which the amendment pertains is delivered to such customer. FINRA proposes to amend Rule 2360(b)(11)(A)(i), which currently requires delivery of OCC's disclosure document to customers approved for trading OCC-issued options. Under the proposed rule change, members would instead be required to deliver the current disclosure document of the applicable Registered Clearing Agency to customers approved for trading options issued by that Registered Clearing Agency, other than OCC Cleared OTC Options. The proposed rule change would also require delivery of amendments to such disclosure documents in a manner substantially consistent with the existing requirements applicable to OCC disclosure documents.
FINRA also proposes conforming changes to Rule 2360(b)(16)(D) (Account Agreement) to reflect the delivery of disclosure documents issued by any Registered Clearing Agency and to require customers engaging in transactions in options issued by such Registered Clearing Agency to acknowledge receipt of the applicable disclosure document and agreement to be bound by the rules of the applicable Registered Clearing Agency.
The proposed rule change is intended to preserve the existing customer disclosure framework regardless of which Registered Clearing Agency issues or guarantees the contracts. These changes would ensure that members remain subject to substantially comparable disclosure obligations and customers receive substantially comparable disclosures regarding the characteristics and risks of standardized options.
Confirmations
FINRA Rule 2360(b)(12) requires members to provide customers with written confirmations containing specified information regarding options transactions, including the underlying security or index. FINRA proposes to amend Rule 2360(b)(12) to add a reference to an underlying “metric.” The proposed rule change clarifies the application of the existing confirmation requirements to options on metrics by requiring confirmations to identify the underlying metric, as applicable, thus ensuring that customers receive comparable information for options on metrics as they receive for other listed options products.
Transactions With Issuers
Rule 2360(b)(13) provides that no member shall enter a transaction for the sale (writing) of a call option contract for the account of any corporation which is the issuer of the underlying security thereof. FINRA proposes to amend Rule 2360(b)(13) to also encompass a corporation that is the subject of the underlying metric, thereby clarifying the rule's application to options on metrics. FINRA believes the proposed change is appropriate to clarify that options on metrics are covered by the prohibition on selling call options for the account of an issuer given the substantially similar potential conflicts of interest that may be present for such transactions.
Other Amendments to Rule 2360
FINRA proposes conforming amendments throughout Rule 2360(b) to replace OCC-specific references with references to a Registered Clearing Agency in provisions governing rights and obligations of holders and writers (paragraph (b)(9)), confirmations (paragraph (b)(12)), account agreements (paragraph (b)(16)(D)), violation of rules (paragraph (b)(21)), and stock transfer tax (paragraph (b)(22)).
Finally, FINRA proposes conforming and stylistic amendments to various provisions of Rule 2360 and its Supplementary Material to renumber paragraphs to reflect amended provisions, update cross-references, appropriately refer to newly defined or amended defined terms, and make various stylistic changes.
Proposed Amendments to Rule 2220
Rule 2220 governs members' communications with the public concerning options, including provisions specific to standardized options. The existing definition of “standardized option” in Rule 2220(a)(2) refers to issuance by OCC and to the terms of the option including the amount of the underlying security. The proposed rule change would amend the definition to replace the reference to OCC with a reference to a Registered Clearing Agency, as defined in Rule 2360(a), and to add “index or metric” to the list of standardized terms alongside “underlying security.” This proposed change would clarify that the options communications requirements applicable to standardized options apply to options on metrics.
Proposed Amendments to Rules 2351 and 2357
The FINRA Rule 2350 Series establishes specific requirements for trading in index warrants, currency index warrants and currency warrants, including, among other things, account approval, suitability, communications with the public, and recordkeeping requirements. Rule 2351 provides for the general applicability of the Rule 2350 Series to these warrant products and defines specified terms used in the Rule 2350 Series, while Rule 2357 extends the Rule 2220 options communications requirements to such products. Although the Rule 2350 Series would not apply to binary metric options, FINRA is proposing two conforming changes to these rules in connection with the proposed changes to Rule 2360 described above. First, the proposed rule change would amend the cross-reference in Rule 2351 to the “control” definition in Rule 2360(a)(6) to reflect the renumbering of the paragraphs setting forth the definitions in Rule 2360(a). Second, the proposed rule change would update Rule 2357 to replace the reference to OCC with a reference to a Registered Clearing Agency.
(
printed page 68194)
Proposed Amendments to Rule 4210
Rule 4210(f)(2) sets forth strategy-based margin requirements for options. Various definitions in Rule 4210(f)(2)(A) contain references to OCC. FINRA proposes to replace those references with references to “the Registered Clearing Agency that guarantees the option contract” in the definitions of “aggregate discount amount,” “American-style option,” “call,” “put,” “current cash market price,” “European-style option,” “exercise settlement amount,” and “expiration date.” These changes would ensure that these definitions continue to operate appropriately where an option contract is guaranteed by a registered clearing agency other than OCC.
FINRA has filed the proposed rule change for immediate effectiveness and has requested that the SEC waive the requirement that the proposed rule change not become operative for 30 days after the date of the filing, so FINRA can implement the proposed rule change immediately.
2. Statutory Basis
FINRA believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with the provisions of Section 15A(b)(6) of the Exchange Act,
[
12
]
which requires, among other things, that FINRA rules be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. FINRA believes that the proposed rule change will ensure that the investor protection and market integrity requirements under FINRA's existing rules governing options clearly and appropriately apply to all categories of exchange-listed options products. The proposed rule change is designed primarily to clarify the application of existing FINRA requirements to binary options, options on metrics, and options cleared through a registered clearing agency other than OCC—including binary metric options—and thus to preserve substantially comparable regulatory treatment for all listed options products and promote consistent application of FINRA's options framework. Further, FINRA's options rules apply to the options activities of all FINRA members. Clarifying the application of FINRA's options requirements to all listed options products therefore promotes the clear and consistent application of FINRA's options framework across all FINRA members. FINRA believes this application of its options framework promotes just and equitable principles of trade and protects investors and the public interest.
FINRA believes the proposed amendments relating to binary options are consistent with Section 15A(b)(6) of the Act because they clarify the application of FINRA's existing options framework to listed options with a binary payout structure. In particular, the proposed amendments are designed to ensure that FINRA members are subject to substantially comparable requirements with respect to binary options as to other types of listed options, promoting just and equitable principles of trade and protecting investors and the public interest.
FINRA believes the proposed amendments relating to standardized options cleared by a registered clearing agency other than OCC are consistent with Section 15A(b)(6) of the Act. FINRA's existing options rules contain numerous references to OCC, reflecting the historical clearing structure for listed options. The proposed amendments are designed to ensure that FINRA's options framework continues to operate appropriately where an option is issued or guaranteed by another registered clearing agency. By providing for substantially comparable regulatory treatment without regard to the registered clearing agency associated with a listed option, including with respect to customer disclosures and other investor protections, the proposed amendments promote consistent application of FINRA's options requirements and protect investors and the public interest.
FINRA believes the proposed amendments relating to options overlying metrics are consistent with Section 15A(b)(6) of the Act because they clarify that FINRA's existing options requirements apply where the underlying interest is a metric rather than an individual security's price or index's value. The proposed amendments are designed to ensure the application of FINRA's existing regulatory protections, including requirements relating to position reporting, confirmations, and transactions with issuers, to options overlying metrics. FINRA believes that providing consistent regulatory treatment of options activity regardless of whether an option overlies a security, index, or metric promotes just and equitable principles of trade and protects investors and the public interest.
Finally, FINRA believes the proposed clarifying and conforming amendments are consistent with Section 15A(b)(6) of the Act. These amendments are designed to improve the clarity, consistency, and operation of FINRA's options rules in light of the foregoing changes, including by consolidating related definitions, updating cross-references and terminology, and making other conforming changes. FINRA believes these amendments will facilitate the clear and consistent application of FINRA's options rules by members and thereby promote just and equitable principles of trade and protect investors and the public interest.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
FINRA does not believe that the proposed rule change will result in any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
Economic Impact Assessment
FINRA has undertaken an economic impact assessment to analyze the potential economic impacts of the proposed rule change, including anticipated costs, benefits, distributional and competitive effects, relative to the applicable baseline, and the alternatives considered in assessing how best to meet FINRA's regulatory objectives.
Regulatory Need
As discussed above, multiple national securities exchanges have filed proposed rule changes to list and trade binary metric options, which may be cleared by a Registered Clearing Agency other than OCC, and the Commission has approved at least one such filing. Current FINRA rules governing listed options activity were developed principally around listed options that settle based on the price of an individual security or index and that clear through OCC. While FINRA intends for its options framework to apply broadly to listed options products, current rule text does not expressly address certain listed options structures, including options overlying metrics, binary options, and options cleared by a Registered Clearing Agency other than OCC. As a result, uncertainty and associated costs may arise regarding the application of existing FINRA requirements to such products. The proposed rule change would clarify that the existing rules for listed options apply broadly to all listed options products, including binary options, options on metrics, and options cleared by a Registered Clearing Agency other than OCC.
(
printed page 68195)
Economic Baseline
The economic baseline for this analysis is the application of FINRA's current rules in a market where exchanges have received, or may receive, Commission approval of proposed rule changes to list and trade binary metric options. Under the baseline, FINRA members considering participation in these products would need to determine how existing FINRA requirements apply to various listed options structures not expressly addressed under current rule text, including options based on metrics, binary options, and options cleared by a Registered Clearing Agency other than OCC. This uncertainty could result in additional legal, compliance, and operational costs and may delay or deter participation by some firms, potentially imposing limitations and costs on customers who seek to trade these option contracts.
Economic Benefits and Costs
The proposed rule change would affect FINRA members that currently participate, or may participate in the future, in listed options activity involving any of the options products addressed by the proposed amendments. By clarifying the application of FINRA rules to these products, the proposed rule change may reduce legal, compliance, and operational uncertainty and promote more consistent regulatory treatment across products. To the extent that exchanges introduce additional products with similar characteristics in the future, the proposed rule change may also reduce the need for subsequent conforming changes to FINRA's rules, avoiding delay and uncertainty to market participants in such circumstances.
The magnitude of these benefits depends on the extent of member participation, on their own behalf or on behalf of customers, in binary metric options products, or other products addressed by the proposed rule change, and the degree to which uncertainty under the current rules would otherwise delay or deter such activity. By clarifying the application of FINRA rules to binary options, options on metrics, and options cleared by a Registered Clearing Agency other than OCC, the proposed amendments may facilitate participation by FINRA members and may expand the range of firms through which customers can access these products to the extent that uncertainty under the current rules would otherwise have delayed or deterred such activity. Any such effect would be incremental to the effects of an exchange's introduction of the product or changes to clearance of a product and the Commission's approval of the applicable exchange and any clearing agency proposals.
Participating firms may incur costs to update systems, supervisory procedures, training materials, account-opening processes, disclosure practices, reporting processes, and other operational controls necessary to accommodate binary metric options or other products addressed by the proposed rule change. The magnitude of these costs would vary depending on a firm's business model, existing options infrastructure, and expected level of participation in these products. Members are likely to incur the compliance and operational costs associated with the proposed amendments only where the anticipated business opportunities are deemed sufficient to justify participation in binary metric options or other options products.
Competitive and distributional effects may differ across firms based on the extent of their activities in binary metric options or other options products addressed by the proposed rule change. Members already participating in existing options markets may face lower incremental costs than firms requiring new systems or commercial arrangements to participate in options markets, and costs may vary depending on a member's role as an introducing, carrying, or clearing firm.
The economic impact and competitive and distributional effects of the proposed rule change may vary based, in part, on the extent to which the requirements applicable to FINRA members under the proposed rule change differ from the requirements applicable to members of exchanges listing options products addressed by the proposed rule change.
Alternatives
No alternatives were considered.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
Written comments were neither solicited nor received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
13
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
14
]
A proposed rule change filed under Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
15
]
normally does not become operative prior to 30 days after the date of the filing. However, pursuant to Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii),
[
16
]
the Commission may designate a shorter time if such action is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. FINRA has asked the Commission to waive the 30-day operative delay so that the proposed rule change may become operative upon filing. Waiver of the operative delay would allow FINRA to update its rules immediately consistent with developments in exchange-listed options related to binary options, including binary metric options, and options cleared by a registered clearing agency other than the OCC. This should help to ensure consistent regulatory treatment of all market participants trading binary options, including binary metric options. For these reasons, the Commission finds that waiver of the operative delay is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. Accordingly, the Commission waives the 30-day operative delay and designates the proposed rule change to be operative upon filing.
[
17
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
18
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
(
printed page 68196)
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
. Please include File Number SR-FINRA-2026-022 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to File Number SR-FINRA-2026-022. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of FINRA. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to File Number SR-FINRA-2026-022 and should be submitted on or before November 19, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
19
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; ICE Clear Credit LLC; Order Approving Proposed Rule Change Relating to the ICE Clear Credit Recovery Plan and ICE Clear Credit Wind-Down Plan
full_text:

                    the following:

                      the document amends, proposes to amend, or is directly
                      related to

the RIN which identifies each regulatory action listed in
                      the Unified Agenda of Federal Regulatory and Deregulatory
                      Actions
See the

for more details.
Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106738; File No. SR-ICC-2026-009]
October 26, 2026.
I. Introduction
On August 27, 2026, ICE Clear Credit LLC (“ICC” or “ICE Clear Credit”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”), pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act” or the “Act”)
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
a proposed rule change (the “Proposed Rule Change”) to revise the ICC Recovery Plan (the “Recovery Plan”) and the ICC Wind-Down Plan (the “Wind-Down Plan”) (collectively, the “Plans”) to reflect changes that impacted ICC in the past year and to accommodate ICC's U.S. Treasury clearing service (the “Treasury Clearing Service”). The proposed rule change was published for comment in the
Federal Register
on September 14, 2026.
[
3
]
The Commission did not receive comments regarding the proposed rule change. For the reasons discussed below, the Commission is approving the proposed rule change.
II. Description of the Proposed Rule Change
A. Background
ICC is registered with the Commission as a clearing agency for the purpose of clearing covered default swap (“CDS”) contracts and for transactions involving U.S. Treasury securities.
[
4
]
ICC is a central counterparty (“CCP”), which means that it interposes itself as the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer for transactions in CDS contracts and U.S. Treasury securities.
[
5
]
Because it acts as a CCP, ICC is a “covered clearing agency” as defined in Rule 17ad-22(a).
[
6
]
As such, ICC is regulatorily obligated to have plans for (i) recovery, which must address any uncovered loss, liquidity shortfall, or capital inadequacy, whether arising from participant default or other causes, as necessary to maintain its viability as a going concern and to continue its provision of core services and (ii) wind-down, which encompasses actions to effect the permanent cessation, sale, or transfer of one or more of its core services.
[
7
]
ICC proposes to make changes to the Plans, which include the policies and procedures that ICC uses to govern its recovery and wind-down.
[
8
]
ICC has stated that the Proposed Rule Change amends the Plans to reflect changes that impacted ICC in the past year, including its expansion of clearance and settlement services to cover U.S. Treasury securities as part of its new Treasury clearing service.
[
9
]
ICC further stated that the Proposed Rule Change would update and revise the Plans for clarity and streamlining purposes, and to ensure that the information provided is current.
[
10
]
B. Proposed Changes Common to Both Plans
In general, ICC proposes to incorporate references to the Treasury clearing service throughout the Plans and distinguish between the Treasury and CDS clearing services, where applicable. As proposed, both Plans would clarify that the information provided in the amended documents is current as of March 6, 2026, unless otherwise stated. ICC also proposes to add a footnote stating that the Treasury clearing service has not yet launched, while incorporating Treasury clearing service-specific information throughout the Plans that is based on the anticipated launch of the service.
ICC proposes to update the terminology referencing its members. Under the proposal, ICC Clearing Participants (“Clearing Participants” or “CPs”) would refer to members in the CDS clearing service and ICC Treasury Participants (“Treasury Participants” or “TPs”) would refer to members in the Treasury clearing service. These changes in terminology, as well as references to the CDS Rules versus the Treasury Rules, would be extended throughout the Plans.
ICC proposes to update language in the Plans about its role and scope of critical operation; its financial resources in case of a member default; and its stress scenarios. ICC proposes to insert a description of its role as a CCP for the Treasury clearing service, as well as additional language about its original founding as a CCP for the CDS market. ICC states that these brief descriptions would distinguish its existing CDS clearing services and approvals from its recently approved Treasury clearing services and planned Treasury clearing activities.
[
11
]
The current Plans describe ICC's CDS clearing services as its sole critical operation. However, to accommodate the inclusion of the recent Treasury clearing service, ICC proposes revisions to clarify that “clearing services,” broadly, are its sole critical operation. Additionally, ICC proposes to use the terms “General Guaranty Fund” for the CDS clearing service and “Treasury Guaranty Fund” for the Treasury clearing service. Although stress scenarios are and would continue to be listed in both Plans, ICC proposes to incorporate references to the Treasury clearing service and distinguishing between the Treasury and CDS clearing services, where applicable. ICC further proposes to specify in both Plans that it ensures that it is in compliance with all
(
printed page 68208)
regulatory capital requirements at the entity level.
Across the Plans, ICC proposes to remove references to withdrawn regulatory guidance.
[
12
]
ICC states that, despite this regulatory withdrawal, it would continue to consider the principles underlying such guidance in its recovery planning.
[
13
]
As such, ICC proposes to replace references to such guidance with references to “industry best practices.”
Regarding governance structure, ICC proposes to amend the Plans to reflect that ICC has a board-level Board Risk Committee
[
14
]
by revising the existing governance chart to include the Board Risk Committee and to include a new subsection describing the role and responsibilities of the Board Risk Committee. This governance chart likewise would incorporate Treasury clearing service-specific committees and groups,
[
15
]
and new language would describe their roles and responsibilities. ICC proposes additional language describing required prior consultation with the Treasury Risk Committee as to certain Specified Actions,
[
16
]
including certain matters relating to the acceptance for clearing of Treasury transactions, modifications to the Treasury Rules relating to margin and the Treasury Guaranty Fund, as well as certain recovery-related matters such as commencing reduced gain distribution or implementing full clearing service termination. For consistency with CDS and Treasury Rules, ICC also proposes a clarifying edit to provide that a majority of each Risk Committee constitutes a quorum for doing business. ICC further proposes to update terminology throughout the Plans to distinguish between the CDS and Treasury clearing services, including references to the CDS Risk Committee versus the Treasury Risk Committee.
With regard to the annual review process for the Recovery Plan and Wind-Down Plan, the current language specifies that the annual review and material amendments are presented to the Risk Committee,
[
17
]
which then makes a recommendation to the Board regarding their approval. However, under the Proposed Rule Change, this review and any material amendments instead would be presented to the Board Risk Committee, who would then make a recommendation to the Board regarding their approval. As proposed, the CDS and Treasury Risk Committees would continue to review material matters impacting the Recovery Plan and the Wind-Down Plan but would no longer be required to conduct a separate review solely in connection with each Plan.
[
18
]
ICC proposes to specify that the results of testing of the Recovery Plan and the Wind-Down Plan will be provided to the Treasury Risk Committee and Board Risk Committee, in addition to the CDS Risk Committee and Board.
ICC proposes to update the relevant agreement governing certain services in the list of critical services provided to ICC by affiliates shown in each Plan. Similar to the existing identification of core services for the CDS clearing service, ICC proposes to include in the Plans the core services for the Treasury clearing service, including the acceptance of new trades, management of positions, production of risk and banking reports, and movement of funds. Regarding staffing considerations and specifically as to the roles necessary to support the core services on a daily basis and in the event of recovery or wind-down, ICC proposes to state that, in general, all staff in a functional area provide support for all cleared products and markets at ICC and personnel are not split between the CDS and Treasury clearing services. ICC also proposes to clarify that ICC separately holds the dedicated funds used to meet financial resources requirements for the CDS clearing service from the Treasury clearing service.
The remaining changes proposed to the Recovery Plan and the Wind-Down Plan would renumber subsections, correct typographical errors, and update relevant information to ensure that it is current and accurate. For example, such changes would include a list of Clearing Participants;
[
19
]
updated financials;
[
20
]
identification of ICC's counterparties and contractual agreements;
[
21
]
changes in contact information for relevant regulatory staff;
[
22
]
projected estimated recovery and wind-down costs and financial resources to support wind-down;
[
23
]
and updated stress scenario analyses.
[
24
]
C. Proposed Changes Specific to the Recovery Plan
ICC proposes to amend its Recovery Plan, the purpose of which is to describe the actions and steps that would be taken to restore ICC to a stable and sustainable condition in the event that it came under severe stress; and to maintain effective arrangements for ensuring losses that threaten ICC's viability as a going concern are allocated.
In addition to the above common changes to both Plans, ICC proposes to make conforming changes in Section IV., which provides an overview of key recovery elements. ICC proposes to align language about membership qualifications with that found in the CDS Rules and Treasury Rules. ICC proposes to replace “must” with “may” in the Recovery Plan for consistency with CDS Rule 201(c), which states that “the following categories of persons
may
be approved by ICE Clear Credit as Participants” before listing the categories.
[
25
]
As amended, the language in the Recovery Plan would state that an entity “may be one of the following” to qualify as a Clearing Participant. Similarly, ICC proposes to amend language in the Recovery Plan and add a corresponding footnote to align with recently revised Treasury Rule 201(c),
[
26
]
which states that to qualify as a Treasury Participant for the Treasury clearing service, an entity may be one of the following: registered broker-dealer,
(
printed page 68209)
registered investment company, bank, insurance company, futures commission merchant, registered clearing agency, or an entity which may not fall within the above categories, as designated appropriate by the SEC. ICC further proposes to incorporate information into the Recovery plan about participation in the Treasury clearing service in accordance with its Treasury Rules.
ICC further proposes to amend Section IV. regarding operational capacity, financial responsibility and capital requirements, funding requirements, and collateral management. Under the Proposed Rule Change, the Recovery Plan would state that the CDS and Treasury clearing services operate separately in terms of financial resources. Specifically, the Recovery Plan would state that the CDS clearing service maintains a separate General Guaranty Fund and calls for and holds margin payments from Clearing Participants independently of margin payments called for in connection with the Treasury clearing service. Similarly, regarding collateral management, ICC proposes to specify that the Treasury clearing service determines its liquidity needs separately from the CDS clearing service and maintains separate liquidity resources. ICC proposes to state the eligible forms of collateral for Initial Margin and Treasury Guaranty Fund contributions for the Treasury clearing service as of March 6, 2026, in accordance with Treasury Rule 401 and Schedule 401 to the Treasury Rules.
Additionally in Section IV., ICC proposes to remove references to “direct liquidation” as a hedging and liquidation mechanism in the context of managing a defaulting CP's portfolio. This removal would reflect previously approved changes to ICC's Clearing Participant Default Management Procedures and CDS Rules.
[
27
]
ICC further proposes to update titles and committee memberships to reflect current committee composition.
In Section VII., which addresses stress scenarios, ICC proposes to state that whether a member is in default in each clearing service will be determined independently under the rules of each clearing service, except when, specifically, should a common member default in a single clearing service, such event will not automatically lead to a default declaration of such common member in the other ICC clearing service. However, as ICC further proposes, the fact the common member has defaulted in a single clearing service could lead to the determination that such common member is, in the judgement of ICC, likely to fail to meet any of its obligations to the other clearing service, which could be a basis for declaring such common member in default in the other clearing service. Other proposed minor changes and clarifying edits to Section VII. include the addition of Treasury Participants to ICC's existing monitoring mechanisms, and the removal of modifiers from and an addition of a parenthetical to the list of monitored metrics to apply to both clearing services.
[
28
]
Regarding Section VIII., which describes available recovery tools, ICC proposes to state that the use of these recovery tools is done separately under the rules of each clearing service.
[
29
]
ICC proposes to clarify that as each of the CDS and Treasury clearing services are designed to be independent with their own separate rulebooks, memberships and default resources, ICC does not expect that a recovery caused by a participant default in one clearing service will cross over to cause a recovery scenario in the other service. Under the Proposed Rule Change, Section VIII. would state that the CDS General Guaranty Fund and CDS margin assets will not be used to cover losses from a default in the Treasury clearing service, or vice versa, consistent with the separate rulebooks for the two clearing services. As proposed, new language would state that this design minimizes the financial risks posed by the Treasury clearing service to the CDS clearing service and vice versa.
With respect to the tools available to address credit losses in a participant default scenario, ICC proposes to amend Section VIII. by specifying that, for the Treasury clearing service, these tools generally include a declaration of a Treasury Participant default, communicating the default, and conducting default management actions to eliminate, settle, reduce, or replace the risk of the defaulter's open Treasury positions. Other revisions to Section VIII. would add a subsection describing ICC's ability to run one or more default auctions to address credit losses in a participant default scenario in the Treasury clearing service,
[
30
]
and include ICC's financial resources hierarchy for the Treasury clearing service, in the order of consumption. ICC proposes to add a description of ICC's Treasury Guaranty Fund,
[
31
]
specifying which recovery tools are applicable to each clearing service in accordance with their respective rulebooks, and making clean-up changes to the overview of initial default auctions for the CDS clearing service.
[
32
]
With respect to tools used to address liquidity shortfalls in participant and non-participant default scenarios, ICC proposes to incorporate references to the Treasury clearing service, while differentiating from the CDS clearing service, where applicable. Under the Proposed Rule Change, Section VIII. would incorporate references to the Treasury Clearing Service Liquidity Risk Management Framework (“LRMF”) and describe the LRMF's objectives and ICC's liquidity waterfall, as well as include a subsection listing additional liquidity tools for the Treasury clearing service. ICC proposes to state that it is likely that a recovery scenario in one clearing service would not trigger a significant reduction in ICC's employee headcount because the other clearing service would continue business-as-usual operations. Also in Section VIII., ICC proposes to remove a duplicate entry in the insurance coverage table.
As proposed, Section IX. would be amended by removing stale statements about direct customer participation in governance, since the CDS and Treasury Risk Committees provide for customer participation. ICC proposes to update terminology from “full tear-up” to “full termination” for consistency with the rulebooks, which use “termination” rather than “tear-up” when discussing the termination of clearing.
[
33
]
D. Proposed Changes Specific to the Wind-Down Plan
ICC proposes to amend its Wind-Down Plan, which establishes how ICC could be wound-down in an orderly manner in the event the recovery actions described in the ICC Recovery Plan failed to preserve ICC's viability as a going concern, but before resolution has been triggered.
[
34
]
(
printed page 68210)
In addition to the above common changes to both Plans, ICC proposes to amend Section VI., which covers wind-down options that will be used in the event that the recovery actions described in the Recovery Plan failed to preserve ICC's viability as a going concern and resolution has not been triggered. In particular, ICC proposes amendments to its approach, timeline, resources, considerations and/or potential impediments of each wind-down option to include the Treasury clearing service. The wind-down options of transfer, sale and termination currently apply to the CDS clearing service and would continue to do so, while extending to the Treasury clearing service under the Proposed Rule Change. As in the Recovery Plan, references to “tear-up” would be replaced with “termination.”
[
35
]
Regarding all three options of transfer, sale, and termination described in Section VI., ICC proposes to update the description of these options to contemplate the transfer or sale of either the CDS clearing service or the Treasury clearing service, as well as the transfer or sale of both services. Regarding the transfer and termination options, ICC proposes to state that if only one clearing service will be transferred or terminated, ICC will need to continue to maintain risk, treasury, compliance, and operations teams on a business-as-usual basis for the remaining clearing service. In the case of either a transfer or sale, ICC proposes to include language that already exists for the CDS clearing service and apply it to the Treasury clearing service, allowing the transfer or sale of Treasury clearing activities from ICC to an alternative clearing house or another entity, respectively.
[
36
]
For both the transfer and sale options, ICC proposes to state that both CDS and Treasury clearing services will be transferred or sold, ICC anticipates pursuing the relevant processes in parallel, such that the anticipated timeline will not be delayed. With respect to the transfer option, ICC proposes adding a description as to potential impediments or considerations, specifying that there may be a limited number of potential recipient clearing houses because such clearing houses would be required to have all appropriate registrations. With respect to the sale option, ICC proposes to state that if only one clearing service will be sold, a service provider may prefer to provide transitional services to the recipient clearing house for a specified time period. With respect to the termination option, ICC proposes to define the termination option to include the termination of open Treasury positions ideally through orderly close out, and if orderly close out is not achieved, through the termination of open positions.
In Section VIII., ICC proposes to incorporate references to the Treasury clearing service in the description of contractual arrangements in the context of continuation of services during wind-down, while distinguishing it from the CDS clearing service and identifying which arrangements are applicable to each clearing service. Specifically, ICC proposes to make conforming changes to the description of the relevant contractual provisions and to analysis of the potential impact that such provisions would have on wind-down implementation.
[
37
]
Lastly, ICC proposes updating Section XI. regarding certain clearing process charts in Section XI.B and C. ICC proposes to specify that these charts reflect the CDS clearing service, as the Treasury clearing service has not yet launched. Accordingly, Treasury clearing process charts would not be included at this time, and this section will need to be updated in a future filing.
III. Discussion and Commission Findings
Section 19(b)(2)(C) of the Act requires the Commission to approve a proposed rule change of a self-regulatory organization if it finds that the proposed rule change is consistent with the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the organization.
[
38
]
Under the Commission's Rules of Practice, the “burden to demonstrate that a proposed rule change is consistent with the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations issued thereunder . . . is on the self-regulatory organization [`SRO'] that proposed the rule change.”
[
39
]
The description of a proposed rule change, its purpose and operation, its effect, and a legal analysis of its consistency with applicable requirements must all be sufficiently detailed and specific to support an affirmative Commission finding,
[
40
]
and any failure of an SRO to provide this information may result in the Commission not having a sufficient basis to make an affirmative finding that a proposed rule change is consistent with the Exchange Act and the applicable rules and regulations.
[
41
]
Moreover, “unquestioning reliance” on an SRO's representations in a proposed rule change is not sufficient to justify Commission approval of a proposed rule change.
[
42
]
After carefully considering the proposed rule change, the Commission finds that the proposed rule change is consistent with the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to ICC. More specifically, for the reasons given below, the Commission finds that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act,
[
43
]
and Rules 17ad-22(e)(3), 17ad-26(a)(1), 17ad-26(a)(8), and 17ad-26(a)(9) under the Act.
[
44
]
A. Consistency With Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act
Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act requires, among other things, that the rules of ICC be designed to promote the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and, to the extent applicable, derivative agreements, contracts, and transactions.
[
45
]
A recovery, wind-down, or business disruption could lead to the failure of ICC's business operations in the CDS and Treasury clearing spaces, which could, in turn, inhibit the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of transactions at ICC. Because the Recovery Plan and the Wind-Down Plan would facilitate the continuity and orderly functioning of ICC's clearing services in the case of a business disruption severe enough to necessitate recovery or wind-down, the Plans help ensure that ICC can continue to operate in those situations, and thus continue clearing and settling securities transactions in CDS and U.S. Treasury markets.
As noted above, the Proposed Rule Change primarily would update the Plans with current information by incorporating references to the recently established Treasury clearing service throughout the Plans and distinguishing between the Treasury and CDS clearing services, where applicable. The
(
printed page 68211)
Proposed Rule Change also would incorporate into the Plans current information about, among other things, internal governance groups and committees, finances, references to industry best practices rather than withdrawn regulatory guidance, the annual review process and testing of the Plans, contractual arrangements, and recovery tools and wind-down options. By providing the most current information about the incorporation of the Treasury clearing services and other key topics, the Proposed Rule Change will support ICC's ability to monitor its finances, assess its Plans annually under the appropriate governance, and evaluate its regulatory capital. This in turn will help ensure ICC has the financial resources to promptly and accurately clear and settle transactions during recovery and, if necessary, conduct an orderly wind-down.
Additionally, these proposed changes help ensure visibility into and transparency of the Plans and into the processes ICC has developed to ensure continuity, or an effective wind-down, should certain circumstances threaten its viability. The updated information ensures that the Plans remain current and relevant, and thereby effectively serve their intended purpose. Since both the transparency and relevancy of the Plans are factors that support the Plans' ability to help facilitate the continuity and orderly functioning of ICC in the case of a recovery or winddown, those factors help ensure ICC can meet its business obligations in such situations, and thus continue clearing and settling securities transactions.
Accordingly, the Proposed Rule Change promotes the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of transactions at ICC, consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act.
[
46
]
B. Consistency With Rule 17ad-22(e)(3) Under the Act
Rule 17ad-22(e)(3)(ii) requires that ICC establish, implement, maintain and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to, among other things, maintain a sound risk management framework for comprehensively managing legal, credit, liquidity, operational, general business, investment, custody, and other risks that arise in or are borne by the covered clearing agency, which includes plans for the recovery and orderly wind-down of the covered clearing agency necessitated by credit losses, liquidity shortfalls, losses from general business risk, or any other losses.
[
47
]
As described above, ICC proposes to update its Recovery Plan and Wind-Down Plan to include provisions pertaining to the newly established Treasury clearing service and distinguish recovery and wind-down operations from those applicable to the CDS service, where applicable. As proposed, the Plans would align many provisions regarding governance, financials, contractual arrangements, review processes of Plans, and terminology. Under the Proposed Rule Change, the Recovery Plan would clarify key recovery elements, such as by stating that the CDS and Treasury clearing services operate separately in terms of financial resources. The proposed changes to the Recovery Plan also would address stress scenarios, including by clarifying that, generally, the determination as to whether a member is in default in each clearing service will be determined independently. The Recovery Plan also would be updated to include current descriptions of available recovery tools, other tools available to address credit losses in a participant default scenario, and tools used to address liquidity shortfalls in participant and non-participant default scenarios. Likewise, under the Proposed Rule Change, the Wind-Down Plan would update ICC's approach, timeline, resources, considerations and/or potential impediments of each wind-down option to include the Treasury clearing service, while retaining the wind-down options of transfer, sale and termination that currently apply to the CDS clearing service. The Wind-Down Plan, as proposed, also would incorporate references to the Treasury clearing service in the description of contractual arrangements in the context of continuation of services during wind-down, while distinguishing it from the CDS clearing service and identifying which arrangements are applicable to each clearing service. Overall, the Plans, as proposed, would align not only to each other, but also with applicable CDS Rules and Treasury Rules.
These proposed changes reduce the risk that the Plans may not contain current information and provide a more accurate and useful playbook for ICC in case of recovery and/or orderly wind-down. Thus, these proposed changes should improve ICC's ability to conduct a recovery and/or orderly wind-down using the Plans.
Accordingly, the Proposed Rule Change is consistent with the requirements of Rule 17ad-22(e)(3)(ii) under the Act.
[
48
]
C. Consistency With Rule 17ad-26(a)(1) Under the Act
Rule 17ad-26(a)(1)(i)-(ii) requires ICC's plans for recovery and orderly-wind down to identify and describe ICC's core payment, clearing, and settlement services and address how ICC would continue to provide such core services in the event of a recovery and during an orderly wind-down, including by identifying the staffing roles necessary to support such core services; and analyzing how such staffing roles necessary to support such core services would continue in the event of a recovery and during an orderly winddown.
[
49
]
As described above, ICC's proposed changes identify staffing roles necessary to support core services of the CDS clearing service and the Treasury Clearing service. Regarding staffing considerations and specifically as to the roles necessary to support the core services on a daily basis and in the event of recovery or wind-down, ICC proposes to state in both Plans that, in general, all staff in a functional area provide support for all cleared products and markets at ICC and personnel are not split between the CDS and Treasury clearing services. Additionally, these staffing roles do not refer to specific personnel or employees, but instead to positions, roles, and personnel functions that are necessary for the continuation of core services. By confirming that all staff in a functional area are not split between the CDS and Treasury clearing services, and thus existing staff in the CDS service support the core services of the Treasury clearing service, these changes would identify the staffing roles necessary to support core services for the Treasury clearing and how those would continue in the event of a recovery and during an orderly winddown.
Therefore, the Proposed Rule Change is consistent with the requirements of Rule17ad-26(a)(1)(i)-(ii) under the Act.
[
50
]
D. Consistency With Rule 17ad-26(a)(8) Under the Act
Rule 17ad-26(a)(8)(iii) requires ICC's plans for recovery and orderly wind-down to include procedures for testing ICC's ability to implement the recovery and orderly wind-down plans at least every 12 months, including by, among other things, providing for reporting the results of such testing to ICC's board of directors and senior management.
[
51
]
(
printed page 68212)
As described above, under the Proposed Rule Change, the results of testing of the Plans will be provided to the Treasury Risk Committee and Board Risk Committee, in addition to the CDS Risk Committee and Board. This would accommodate the splitting off of the separate CDS Risk Committee and the Treasury Risk Committees for consistency with the CDS Rules and Treasury Rules. The CDS and Treasury Risk Committees would continue to review material matters impacting the Recovery Plan and the Wind-Down Plan but would no longer be required to conduct a separate review solely in connection with each Plan. ICC further proposes to specify that the results of testing of the Plans will be provided to the Treasury Risk Committee and Board Risk Committee, in addition to the CDS Risk Committee and Board, thus providing for reporting the results of such testing to ICC's board of directors and senior management.
Therefore, the Proposed Rule Change is consistent with the requirements of Rule 17ad-26(a)(8)(iii) under the Act.
[
52
]
D. Consistency With Rule 17ad-26(a)(9) Under the Act
Rule 17ad-26(a)(9) requires ICC's plans for recovery and orderly wind-down to include procedures requiring review and approval of the Plans by the ICC's Board at least every 12 months or following material changes to ICC's operations that would significantly affect the viability or execution of the plans, with such review informed, as appropriate, by ICC's testing of the plans.
[
53
]
As proposed, the annual review process of the Plans would be extended to incorporate references to Treasury clearing service and Treasury Rules, and distinguish between the Treasury and CDS clearing services and respective rulebooks. Additionally, the Proposed Rule Change would update the governance process to include that the annual review of the Plans and any material amendments to them would be presented to the Board Risk Committee, who would then make a recommendation to the Board regarding their approval. As such, the Plans would continue to include procedures requiring review and approval of the Plans by ICC's Board at least every 12 months or following material changes to ICC's operations that would significantly affect the viability or execution of the Plans, but would encompass as part of those operations ICC's newly established Treasury clearing service and changes to risk committees.
Therefore, the Proposed Rule Change is consistent with the requirements of Rule 17ad-26(a)(9) under the Act.
[
54
]
IV. Conclusion
On the basis of the foregoing, the Commission finds that the proposed rule change is consistent with the requirements of the Act, and in particular, with the requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act,
[
55
]
and Rules 17ad-22(e)(3), 17ad-26(a)(1), 17ad-26(a)(8), and 17ad-26(a)(9)
[
56
]
thereunder.
It is therefore ordered
pursuant to Section 19(b)(2) of the Act
[
57
]
that the proposed rule change (SR-ICC-2026-009) be, and hereby is, approved.
[
58
]
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
59
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.
